**13.26.45**  Touching the waters of the Mahāhrada with a purified mind, fasting for one month, a man attains the realm reached by Jamadagni.

**13.26.46**  Mortifying himself on the Vindhya, true to his word and harmless, standing on one spot for six months, he is purified in but a single month thereafter.

**13.26.47**  Touching the waters of the Narmadā and likewise the waters of Śūrpāraka, fasting for a fortnight, a man is ordained to be born a king's son.

**13.26.48**  At Jambūmārga, restrained and well-composed for three months, a man wins perfection in but a single day and night.

**13.26.49**  Plunging into the waters at Kokāmukha and going to the hermitage of Caṇḍālikā, living on herbs and clad in bark, a man obtains ten maidens.

**13.26.50**  He whose dwelling is at the Kanyā-pool never goes to the abode of Vaivasvata; rather, he attains the world of the gods.

**13.26.51**  At Prabhāsa, in a single night on the new moon, the composed man attains perfection here, O mighty-armed one—the man who is born again.

**13.26.52**  Touching the waters at Ujjānaka, at the hermitage of Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, and bathing at the hermitage of Piṅgā, a man is released from all sins.

**13.26.53**  Touching the waters at Kulyā and reciting the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn, fasting three nights and pure, a man obtains the merit of the Horse Sacrifice.

**13.26.54**  Touching the waters at Piṇḍāraka and fasting for one night, a man, pure when the night brightens into dawn, obtains the merit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.

**13.26.55**  So too, having gone to the Brahmā-lake, adorned by the Dharma forest, a man, pure when the night brightens into dawn, obtains the merit of the Puṇḍarīka sacrifice.

**13.26.56**  Bathing on Mount Maināka and worshipping at the twilight hours, and conquering desire for a month, a man wins the fruit of the Sarvamedha sacrifice.

**13.26.57**  Renowned and holy is the Himavat, the mountain that is Śaṃkara's father-in-law, the mine of all gems, frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas.

**13.26.58**  There the twice-born man who has reached the end of the Veda, knowing life to be impermanent, may lay down his body according to the rite, fasting unto death.

**13.26.59**  Having there worshipped the deities and bowed to the sages, he then, made perfect, goes to heaven, to the eternal world of Brahman.

**13.26.60**  He who, having conquered desire, anger, and greed, dwells at a sacred ford—there is nothing he has not gained by his pilgrimage to that ford.

**13.26.61**  Those sacred fords that are unreachable, hard of access, and perilous may be reached in the mind, by gathering together all the fords within oneself.

**13.26.62**  This is holy, this brings prosperity, this leads to heaven, this gives happiness; this is the secret of the gods, and the purifier of those who bathe.

**13.26.63**  This one should impart to the twice-born, to the virtuous, or to one's own son; and one may whisper it in the ear of friends, or of a devoted disciple.

**13.26.64**  This Aṅgiras of great austerity gave to Gautama, with the sanction of his teachers and of the wise Kāśyapa.

**13.26.65**  This is the supreme prayer of the great purifying sages; reciting it, ever risen from sleep, a man becomes spotless and attains heaven.

**13.26.66**  And whoever hears this secret, the teaching of Aṅgiras, wins birth in an exalted family and remembers his former lives.

**13.27.1**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: His equal to Bṛhaspati in wisdom, like Brahmā in forbearance, equal to Śakra in valour, and matching the Sun in splendour—

**13.27.2**  upon the son of Gaṅgā of abundant lustre, struck down by Arjuna in battle, Yudhiṣṭhira waited in attendance, together with his brothers and others.

**13.27.3**  To that best of the Bhāratas, the unshaken one lying upon his hero's bed and awaiting his appointed hour, the great sages came, desiring to behold him.

**13.27.4**  Atri, Vasiṣṭha, and Bhṛgu, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Aṅgiras, Gautama, Agastya, Sumati, Svāyu the self-possessed,

**13.27.5**  Viśvāmitra, Sthūlaśiras, Saṃvarta, Pramati, Dama, Uśanas, Bṛhaspati, Vyāsa, Cyavana, Kāśyapa, Dhruva,

**13.27.6**  Durvāsas and Jamadagni, Mārkaṇḍeya and Gālava, Bharadvāja and Raibhya, Yavakrīta and likewise Trita,

**13.27.7**  Sthūlākṣa and Śakalākṣa, Kaṇva, Medhātithi, Kṛśa, Nārada and Parvata, Sudhanvan, and then Ekata and Dvita,

**13.27.8**  Nitaṃbhū, Bhuvana, Dhaumya, Śatānanda, Akṛtavraṇa, and Rāma the son of Jamadagni, and Kāmya, and others such as these—great-souled sages all, gathered to behold Bhīṣma.

**13.27.9**  To those great-souled ones who had come, Yudhiṣṭhira, together with his brothers, paid homage in due form, one after another.

**13.27.10**  Thus honoured and seated at ease, the great sages held discourse—discourse centred upon Bhīṣma, most sweet, and delighting every sense.

**13.27.11**  Bhīṣma, hearing the discourse of those sages of disciplined soul, deemed himself already dwelling in heaven, filled with the highest contentment.

**13.27.12**  Then those great sages, taking leave of Bhīṣma and the Pāṇḍavas, all vanished from sight while everyone looked on.

**13.27.13**  Those most blessed sages, though they had vanished, the Pāṇḍavas all praised, and bowed to them again and again.

**13.27.14**  With serene minds, those best of the Kurus, skilled in sacred verses, attended upon the son of Gaṅgā as upon the rising Sun.

**13.27.15**  Beholding, through the power of their austerities, those sages illumining all the quarters of the sky, the Pāṇḍavas were filled with the utmost wonder.

**13.27.16**  Reflecting upon the supreme greatness of those sages, the Pāṇḍavas, together with Bhīṣma, made them the subject of their discourse.

**13.27.17**  At the close of the talk, the son of Dharma, touching Bhīṣma's feet with his head, put to him a question concerning dharma—Yudhiṣṭhira, the Pāṇḍava.

**13.27.18**  Which lands, which realms, which hermitages, and which mountains are most excellent in holiness; and which rivers should be known as such, O grandsire?

**13.27.19**  Bhīṣma said: On this point, too, they tell an ancient tale, the dialogue between one who lived by gleaning ears of grain and a Siddha, O Yudhiṣṭhira.

**13.27.20**  A certain man, best among bipeds, having wandered again and again over this earth adorned with mountains, came to the house of an excellent householder—

**13.27.21**  he reached the home of the gleaner, who, having fulfilled his duty, honoured him in due form and then attended upon that Siddha as his guest.

**13.27.22**  Those two great souls, meeting and seated at ease, held auspicious discourse bound up with the Veda and marked by what completes its purport.

**13.27.23**  At the close of the talk, the gleaner, an intelligent man, earnestly addressed the Siddha and asked him the very question that you now ask of me:

**13.27.24**  The gleaner said: Which lands, which realms, which hermitages, and which mountains are most excellent in holiness; and which rivers should be known as such—let that be told.

**13.27.25**  The Siddha said: Those lands, those realms, those hermitages, and those mountains are most excellent through whose midst the Bhāgīrathī Gaṅgā, best of rivers, flows.

**13.27.26**  That goal which a creature attains by resorting to the Gaṅgā, he could not win even by austerity, by chastity, by sacrifices, or again by renunciation.

**13.27.27**  Those embodied beings whose limbs have been touched and laid to rest by the waters of the Gaṅgā—for them no expulsion from heaven is ever ordained.

**13.27.28**  Those men all of whose rites have been performed with the waters of the Gaṅgā, O brāhmaṇa, having left the earth, abide unshaken in heaven.

**13.27.29**  Those men who, having done evil deeds in their earlier years, afterward resort to the Gaṅgā—they too attain the highest goal.

**13.27.30**  The fruit that comes to men of disciplined soul who have bathed in the pure waters of the Gaṅgā—that comes not even from a hundred sacrifices.

**13.27.31**  For as many thousands of years as a man's bone rests in the waters of the Gaṅgā, so long does he, having attained heaven, abide there in honour.

**13.27.32**  As the sun, scattering the dense darkness at its rising, shines forth, so, scattering his sin, shines the man sprinkled with the waters of the Gaṅgā.

**13.27.33**  As nights are without the moon, as trees are without blossom, so are the lands and the regions that are bereft of the holy waters of the Gaṅgā.

**13.27.34**  As all the castes and stages of life would be, were they stripped of the knowledge of their own duty, and as sacrifices would be without the Soma—so is the world without the Gaṅgā.

**13.27.35**  As the sky would be without the sun, the earth without mountains, and space without wind, so are the lands and regions that lack the Gaṅgā—of this there is no doubt.

**13.27.36**  Whatever living beings there are in the three worlds, all of them, when refreshed with the holy waters of the Gaṅgā, attain the highest satisfaction.

**13.27.37**  He who drinks the water of the Gaṅgā warmed by the sun gains more than from barley-gruel freed of the cattle's dung-fuel.

**13.27.38**  Whether a man perform for a thousand lunar fasts the cleansing of the body, or whether he drink the water of the Gaṅgā—whether these two be equal or not equal, who can say?

**13.27.39**  Whether a man stand for a thousand ages upon a single foot, or whether he dwell but one month by the Gaṅgā—whether these two be equal or not equal, who can say?

**13.27.40**  Though a man hang head-downward for ten thousand ages, yet he who dwells at the Gaṅgā as he pleases surpasses him.

**13.27.41**  As cotton cast into the fire is burnt utterly away, O best of the twice-born, so all the sin of one who plunges into the Gaṅgā is burnt away.

**13.27.42**  For all beings here whose minds are stricken with sorrow and who seek a refuge, there is no refuge like the Gaṅgā.

**13.27.43**  As serpents are rendered venomless at the sight of Tārkṣya, so by the sight of the Gaṅgā a man is released from all his sins.

**13.27.44**  To whatever beings are without support, and to whatever beings take refuge in unrighteousness, the Gaṅgā here is their support, their refuge, their comfort, and their armour.

**13.27.45**  Men of the lowest sort, seized by manifold and grievous evils and falling into hell — if they have taken refuge in the Gaṅgā, she will carry them across once they have passed beyond death.

**13.27.46**  Those who continually resort to the Gaṅgā — to whom the gods themselves resort — surely share fellowship with the sages and with the gods, Vāsava at their head.

**13.27.47**  Even those basest of men, devoid of discipline and right conduct and inauspicious in nature — O brāhmaṇa, they become auspicious if they take refuge in the Gaṅgā.

**13.27.48**  As nectar is to the gods, as the funerary oblation is to the ancestors, as ambrosia is to the serpents, so is the water of the Gaṅgā to mortals.

**13.27.49**  As children tormented by hunger attend upon their mother, so do embodied beings here, longing for what is highest, attend upon the Gaṅgā.

**13.27.50**  As the abode of the Self-born is declared the highest of all stations, so the Gaṅgā is here declared, for those who bathe, the foremost of rivers.

**13.27.51**  As the cow is held the sustainer of those who live by her, and the earth of the gods and the rest, so is the Gaṅgā the sustainer here of all that draws breath and lives by her.

**13.27.52**  As the gods live upon the nectars that abide in soma and the sun, won through the satra and other sacrifices, so do men live upon the water of the Gaṅgā.

**13.27.53**  Sprinkled with the sands that rise from the banks of the Jāhnavī, a man deems himself made radiant, as though dwelling in heaven.

**13.27.54**  He who bears upon his head the clay born of the Jāhnavī's bank bears a form pure and stainless as the sun's, for it destroys all darkness.

**13.27.55**  And when the wind, anointed by the waves of the Gaṅgā, touches a man, it wipes away his sin that very instant.

**13.27.56**  For a man scorched by calamities and on the verge of ruin, the joy born of beholding the Gaṅgā draws those calamities away.

**13.27.57**  With the cries of swans, the calls of the cakravāka, and the songs of other birds the Gaṅgā vies with the gandharvas, and with her sandbanks she rivals the mountains.

**13.27.58**  Beholding the Gaṅgā thronged with swans and a great many varied birds, and crowded with herds of cattle, one forgets even heaven.

**13.27.59**  Not even for one dwelling in heaven and enjoying every desire is there such joy as the supreme joy of men upon the bank of the Gaṅgā.

**13.27.60**  Even a man here seized by sins born of word, mind, and deed becomes purified by beholding the Gaṅgā — of this I have no doubt.

**13.27.61**  By beholding, touching, and plunging into the Gaṅgā, a man delivers seven generations of ancestors below, seven above, and those still beyond them.

**13.27.62**  Heard of, longed for, seen, touched, drunk, and bathed in, the Gaṅgā carries across both lineages of men in full measure.

**13.27.63**  By the sight of her, the touch of her, the drinking of her, and the mere uttering of the name 'Gaṅgā,' she purifies men of no merit by hundreds and by thousands.

**13.27.64**  He who would have his birth, his life, and his learning bear fruit should go to the Gaṅgā and there satisfy the ancestors and the gods.

**13.27.65**  Not by sons, nor by wealth, nor by ritual works could a man ever win that utmost fruit which he attains on reaching the Gaṅgā.

**13.27.66**  Those who, though able, do not look upon the Gaṅgā with her holy and auspicious waters are here the equals of the blind from birth, of the dead, and of cripples.

**13.27.67**  What man would not wait upon the Gaṅgā, attended as she is by the great sages who know past, present, and future, and by the gods with Indra at their head?

**13.27.68**  What man would fail to take refuge in the Gaṅgā, to whom forest hermits, householders, ascetics, celibate students, and the learned have resorted?

**13.27.69**  He who, self-controlled and honored by the wise, with his life-breaths departing fixes his mind in thought upon the Gaṅgā, attains the supreme goal.

**13.27.70**  The man here who waits upon the Gaṅgā until his body falls away has no fear of any terrors, nor of sins, nor of the king.

**13.27.71**  That most holy goddess whom Maheśvara, as she fell from the sky, upheld upon his head — her very self he honors in heaven.

**13.27.72**  The three worlds are adorned by her three pure courses; and the man who resorts to her water becomes one whose every purpose is fulfilled.

**13.27.73**  As the sun is the light in heaven, and the moon the light of the ancestors, and the lord of the gods supreme among men, so is the Gaṅgā here among rivers.

**13.27.74**  The grief of one parted from mother, father, sons, wife, or wealth is not so great as the grief born of separation from the Gaṅgā.

**13.27.75**  Not from forests, nor from beloved objects of sense, nor from sons, nor from the gaining of wealth comes such serenity to men as comes from beholding the Gaṅgā.

**13.27.76**  As the sight of men grows serene at beholding the full moon, so does their sight grow serene at beholding the Gaṅgā, who flows along three paths.

**13.27.77**  He whose being is in her, whose mind is set upon her, who is established in her and devoted to her, and who follows the Gaṅgā with devotion, comes to be dear to her.

**13.27.78**  By beings high and low — those that dwell on earth, those in the air, and those in heaven — the Gaṅgā is ever to be entered; this is the foremost duty of the good.

**13.27.79**  Throughout the three worlds the fame of the Gaṅgā is renowned for her holiness, in that she led the sons of Sagara, reduced to ashes, up to heaven.

**13.27.80**  Kindled by the gleaming waves of the Gaṅgā — driven by the wind, swift, mightily resounding, and reared up exceedingly high — he shines like the thousand-rayed sun.

**13.27.81**  Those steadfast ones who, having gone to the Gaṅgā — rich in waters, rich in butter, exceedingly bountiful, abounding, swift, and hard to ford — have given up their bodies there, have attained equality with the gods.

**13.27.82**  The glorious, mighty, all-formed Gaṅgā, served by the gods with Indra, by sages, and by men, joins the blind, the dull, and the destitute to every desire fulfilled.

**13.27.83**  Those who have taken refuge in the Gaṅgā — full of vigor, full of sweetness, most holy, flowing along three courses, the guardian of the three worlds — have gone to heaven.

**13.27.84**  To the mortal who shall dwell beside her or even behold her, the gods grant joys; and to him whose heart is fixed upon her touch and sight, the gods appoint the goal he desires.

**13.27.85**  Those who have gone to the Gaṅgā — skillful, broad, mighty, far-extending, auspicious, true, sweet-watered, most serene, radiant, and the foundation of all beings — have gone to the third heaven.

**13.27.86**  She whose renown of old stood firm forever throughout the sky, heaven, and earth, and through the quarters and the intermediate quarters — by resorting to the water of that best of rivers, all mortals attain their every purpose.

**13.27.87**  'This is the Gaṅgā' — she is the steadfast support, the bearer in her womb of Guha and of the golden one; at dawn she runs along three paths, carrying butter, free of all sin, descended from the firmament, her waters poured forth on every side.

**13.27.88**  The consort of Hara, who bears the mountains, befitting the girdle alike of heaven and of earth, gracious, the destiny of the earth — she shines, O king: the Gaṅgā, bestower of merit upon the three worlds.

**13.27.89**  Her stream is sweet as honey, adorned by great waves uplifted with the hue of butter and by brāhmaṇas as well; fallen from heaven and borne upon Bhava's head, the Gaṅgā, upholder of the earth, is the garland of the third heaven.

**13.27.90**  The most excellent womb, stainless, far-spreading, mighty, the nourishing draught, the bearer of waters, the giver of fame, all-containing, very form itself, the sacrifice, kindled — the Gaṅgā is the path of the world for those whom she has sprinkled.

**13.27.91**  In forbearance the equal of the earth, in protecting and upholding, and in radiance the equal of fire and of the sun, the Gaṅgā is ever honored by the brāhmaṇas and by Guha's devotion to the brahman.

**13.27.92**  Those who in this world have taken refuge with their whole being — even in mind — in the Jāhnavī, praised by sages, sprung from Viṣṇu's foot, ancient, of most holy waters, have gone forth to the abode of Brahmā.

**13.27.93**  She who leads these worlds onward as a mother leads her sons, endowed in her whole being with every excellence — the Gaṅgā is ever to be honored by the self-controlled who here seek their own desired and holy station, the abode of Brahmā.

**13.27.94**  The self-controlled man who longs for perfection should take refuge in the Gaṅgā — radiant, beloved, ever-watchful, watered on every side, the nourishing draught, armed with the thunderbolt, abounding, the refuge of the mountains, the refuge of the wise, immortal, beloved of Brahmā.

**13.27.95**  Bhagīratha, having propitiated all the gods together with their lords, by fierce austerity brought the Gaṅgā down to earth; and the man who resorts to her unceasingly knows no fear, neither here nor hereafter.

**13.27.96**  Of her virtues I have, having pondered with my understanding, set forth before you but a single portion in every way; I have no power here to tell, or likewise to measure out, all her virtues.

**13.27.97**  The whole hoard of jewels of Meru and the ocean, the number of the pebbles, or even of the drops of water, might be told — but here the recital of the virtues of the Gaṅgā's waters can neither be told nor measured out.

**13.27.98**  Therefore let a man, joined with supreme devotion and possessed of the highest faith, honor by speech, by mind, and by deed all these virtues of the Jāhnavī, which I have spoken with supreme faith.

**13.27.99**  Spreading your fame across these three worlds, and winning that great and hard-won perfection, you shall ere long roam at will through the desired worlds that the Gaṅgā bestows.

**13.27.100**  May the mind of you and of me, exalted in spirit, ever delight in the virtues that belong to our own dharma; for the Gaṅgā, tender toward those who come to her, cherishes the devout one and joins him to every joy.

**13.27.101**  Bhīṣma said: Having thus in manifold ways instructed Śilaratin in the many true virtues that pertain to the discourse on the threefold-pathed river, that radiant siddha of supreme wisdom entered the vault of heaven.

**13.27.102**  And Śilavṛtti, then enlightened by the words of the siddha, having honored the Gaṅgā according to the rule, attained that perfection most hard to win.

**13.27.103**  Therefore you too, son of Kuntī, joined with supreme devotion, resort unceasingly to the Gaṅgā, and you shall attain the highest perfection.

**13.27.104**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard this tale told by Bhīṣma, joined with the praise of the Gaṅgā, Yudhiṣṭhira together with his brothers attained the highest joy.

**13.27.105**  Whoever should hear or recite this holy tale, joined with the praise of the Gaṅgā, would be released from all his sins.

**13.28.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: Since you, O best of the upholders of dharma, are endowed with wisdom and learning, with conduct and character, with all the virtues, and with the fullness of years, therefore I ask you concerning dharma.

**13.28.2**  By what means, O best of kings, might a kṣatriya, or a vaiśya, or a śūdra attain brāhmaṇahood? This you ought to explain to me.

**13.28.3**  If one should desire brāhmaṇahood, whether by very great austerity, or by ritual works, or by sacred learning — tell me this, grandsire.

**13.28.4**  Bhīṣma said: Brāhmaṇahood, dear son, is hard for the three orders headed by the kṣatriyas to attain; for this, Yudhiṣṭhira, is the highest station of all beings.

**13.28.5**  Passing through many wombs, being born again and again, only in some turn of the cycle, dear son, is one born as a brāhmaṇa.

**13.28.6**  On this point too they tell this ancient tale, Yudhiṣṭhira: the dialogue of Mataṅga and the she-ass.

**13.28.7**  There was, dear son, a mighty son of a certain twice-born man, of like color to his father, Mataṅga by name, endowed with every virtue.

**13.28.8**  That performer of sacrifice, O son of Kuntī, scorcher of foes, sent forth by his father, set out upon a swift-going chariot yoked with asses.

**13.28.9**  He, O king, with his goad pierced again and again upon the nose a young ass that was drawing the chariot beside its mother.

**13.28.10**  But the she-ass, yearning for her offspring, seeing him grievously wounded, said: 'Grieve not, my child; it is a caṇḍāla who sits over you.'

**13.28.11**  'In a brāhmaṇa there is no cruelty; a brāhmaṇa is called the friend of all. He is the teacher and chastiser of all beings — why would he strike?'

**13.28.12**  'But this one, of evil nature, shows no mercy to a young creature; he does but honor his own origin — a nature passes on to its like.'

**13.28.13**  Hearing this harsh speech of the she-ass, Mataṅga quickly stepped down from the chariot and answered her.

**13.28.14**  'Tell me, gracious she-ass, by whom was my mother defiled? How do you know me to be a caṇḍāla? Quickly, she-ass, declare it to me.'

**13.28.15**  'By whom was I born a caṇḍāla, so that my brāhmaṇahood is lost to me? Tell me this truly, O most wise one, all of it without reserve.'

**13.28.16**  The she-ass said: 'You were begotten by a śūdra, a barber, upon a brāhmaṇa woman maddened with drink; therefore you are a caṇḍāla, and therefore your brāhmaṇahood is lost.'

**13.28.17**  Thus addressed, Mataṅga turned back homeward; and seeing him return, his father then spoke these words.

**13.28.18**  'By me you were appointed to the weighty task of the completion of the sacrifice; why have you turned back? Is it that all is not well with you?'

**13.28.19**  Mataṅga said: 'He may be well whose birth is from no womb, or from the highest womb; but whence can there be well-being for him whose mother is such as this, O father?'

**13.28.20**  Father, this she-donkey, no mere beast but more than human, declares me born of a brāhmaṇa woman by a man of the lowest sort; therefore I shall practice a mighty austerity.

**13.28.21**  Having spoken thus to his father, his resolve fixed, he set out; and going to the great forest, he practiced a mighty austerity.

**13.28.22**  Then Mataṅga, endowed with austerity, scorched the gods with the heat of his penance, seeking to win a blissful station beyond even that gained by right conduct.

**13.28.23**  To him, thus engaged in austerity, the bearer of the bay steeds said: "Mataṅga, why do you mortify yourself, casting aside the pleasures of men?"

**13.28.24**  "Come, I grant you a boon; choose whatever you desire. And whatever else may be obtained, declare it all to me without delay."

**13.28.25**  Mataṅga said: "Longing for brāhmaṇahood, I have undertaken this austerity. May I attain it and reach that state here; this is the boon I have chosen."

**13.28.26**  Hearing these words, Puraṃdara said to him: "You crave brāhmaṇahood, which is unattainable by those whose selves are unperfected."

**13.28.27**  "Craving that supreme thing, the foremost among all beings, which no austerity can surpass, you will soon perish."

**13.28.28**  "That which is held the highest purity among gods, asuras, and mortals can in no way be attained by one born in the womb of a caṇḍāla."

**13.29.1**  Bhīṣma said: Thus addressed, Mataṅga, his soul resolute and his vows controlled, stood upon one foot for a hundred years, O unfaltering one.

**13.29.2**  Then the greatly renowned Śakra spoke to him once again: "Mataṅga, you seek that highest station, which is most hard to win."

**13.29.3**  "Do not act so rashly, my son; this is not the path of dharma for you. Craving what cannot be attained, you will soon perish."

**13.29.4**  "Mataṅga, though restrained by me once, you still strive by austerity for the highest station; by no means will you attain it."

**13.29.5**  "If any creature fallen into the womb of beasts comes at last to human birth, it is born now and then as a pulkasa or a caṇḍāla."

**13.29.6**  "Whoever here is marked as a son of a wanton woman or of a sinful womb, Mataṅga, revolves in that very condition for a very long time."

**13.29.7**  "Then, after a tenfold span of time, he attains even the state of a śūdra; and in the śūdra womb thereafter he revolves many times."

**13.29.8**  "Then, after a thirtyfold span of time, he attains even the state of a vaiśya; and in that vaiśya condition he revolves for a long time."

**13.29.9**  "Then, after a sixtyfold span of time, he is born one called a rājanya; and in that kṣatriya estate he revolves for a long time."

**13.29.10**  "Then, after a sixtyfold span of time, he attains kinship with brāhmaṇas; and as such a brahma-kinsman he revolves for a long time."

**13.29.11**  "Then, after twice a hundred such spans, he attains the state of a kāṇḍapṛṣṭha; and as a kāṇḍapṛṣṭha he revolves for a long time."

**13.29.12**  "Then, after thrice a hundred such spans, he attains even the state of a twice-born; and having reached it, he revolves there for a long time."

**13.29.13**  "Then, after four hundred such spans, he is born one called a śrotriya, learned in the Veda; and in that śrotriya estate he revolves for a long time."

**13.29.14**  "And even then anger and elation, desire and hatred, excessive pride and harsh speech, my son, enter that lowest of the twice-born."

**13.29.15**  "If he conquers those enemies, he then attains the good path; but if they conquer him, he is cast down as from the top of a palm tree."

**13.29.16**  "Mataṅga, having weighed this, on account of which I have urged you, choose some other desire; for brāhmaṇahood is very hard to win."

**13.30.1**  Bhīṣma said: Thus addressed, Mataṅga, sunk deep in grief, went to Gayā and stood there poised upon his great toe for a hundred years.

**13.30.2**  Sustaining a most difficult discipline, grown gaunt with his veins standing forth, reduced to skin and bone, that righteous soul fell down at last—so we have heard.

**13.30.3**  As he fell, Vāsava rushed forward and caught him—the lord and bestower of boons, devoted to the welfare of all beings.

**13.30.4**  Śakra said: "Mataṅga, your attaining of brāhmaṇahood is hedged about by obstacles. He who honors the brāhmaṇa wins happiness; he who fails to honor him wins sorrow."

**13.30.5**  "In the brāhmaṇa the welfare and security of all beings rests secure; through brāhmaṇas the ancestors and the gods alike are satisfied."

**13.30.6**  "The brāhmaṇa, Mataṅga, is declared the highest of all beings; for the brāhmaṇa accomplishes whatever and however he wishes."

**13.30.7**  "Passing through many wombs, being born again and again, only at some turn in the round, my son, does one here come upon brāhmaṇahood."

**13.30.8**  Mataṅga said: "Why do you torment me, stricken with grief, and slay me who am already dead? But I grieve for that man who, having gained brāhmaṇahood, cares not to be a brāhmaṇa."

**13.30.9**  "If brāhmaṇahood is hard to win for the three other varṇas, O lord of a hundred sacrifices, yet having gained that thing so hard to win, men do not live up to it."

**13.30.10**  "He is the most sinful of the sinful, the basest among them, who slights his brāhmaṇahood as a man might slight a hard-won treasure he has gained."

**13.30.11**  "Hard indeed to attain is the brāhmaṇa's estate, and once attained, hard to maintain; yet having won this thing so hard to win, men do not live up to it."

**13.30.12**  "I delight in solitude, O Śakra, free from the pairs of opposites, owning nothing, established in non-violence, self-restraint, and giving—how am I not worthy of the brāhmaṇa's estate?"

**13.30.13**  "Grant then that I may roam at will, a bird that takes what form it wishes; that I may receive honor without offense to brāhmaṇa or kṣatriya; and that my fame, O Puraṃdara, may become imperishable."

**13.30.14**  Indra said: "Renowned as Chandodeva, you shall become an object of worship among women."

**13.30.15**  Bhīṣma said: Having granted him this boon, Vāsava vanished; and Mataṅga too, giving up his life-breaths, attained that highest station.

**13.30.16**  So this highest station, called brāhmaṇahood, O Bhārata, is hard to win in this world, even as the words of great Indra declared.

**13.31.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: I have heard this great tale, O upholder of the Kuru line; you declare brāhmaṇahood most hard to win, O best of speakers.

**13.31.2**  Yet it is heard that long ago Viśvāmitra attained brāhmaṇahood; and still you say it is hard to win, O most virtuous one.

**13.31.3**  And I have heard that the royal sage Vītahavya passed into the brāhmaṇa's estate; that very story, son of Gaṅgā, I wish to hear, O mighty one.

**13.31.4**  By what deed did he attain brāhmaṇahood, O best of kings—by a boon, or by austerity? That you should be pleased to explain to me.

**13.31.5**  Bhīṣma said: Hear, O king, how the greatly renowned king Vītahavya, though a kṣatriya, came to attain the brāhmaṇahood that the world reveres.

**13.31.6**  Of the great-souled Manu, who ruled by the dharma of a guardian of his people, there was a righteous son, renowned by the name of Śaryāti.

**13.31.7**  In his line, O king, there arose two kings, Hehaya and Tālajaṅgha, among the Vatsas, O best of the victorious.

**13.31.8**  Of Hehaya's sons by ten wives, O Bhārata, there came to be a famed hundred, heroes who never turned back in battle.

**13.31.9**  Equal in form and power, learned and skilled in war, they had labored diligently in every branch of the science of archery and of the Veda.

**13.31.10**  Among the Kāśis too, O king, there was a ruler, the grandfather of Divodāsa, renowned as Haryaśva, best of the victorious.

**13.31.11**  The heirs of Vītahavya came against him, O bull among men, and in the land between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā he was struck down in battle.

**13.31.12**  Having slain that finest of men, those Hehaya great chariot-warriors returned, free from all fear, to the lovely city of the Vatsas.

**13.31.13**  Then Haryaśva's heir Sudeva, godlike in his splendor, like Dharma himself made manifest, was consecrated king of Kāśi.

**13.31.14**  As the righteous joy of the Kāśis was ruling the earth, those sons of Vītahavya came once more and in battle utterly defeated him.

**13.31.15**  Having defeated him too in the fray, they returned as they had come; and then Sudeva's son Divodāsa was consecrated lord of Kāśi.

**13.31.16**  But Divodāsa, knowing well the prowess of those great-souled foes, in his great splendor built the city of Vārāṇasī at Śakra's command.

**13.31.17**  It was thronged with brāhmaṇas and kṣatriyas, teeming with vaiśyas and śūdras, heaped with goods of every kind, rich in its markets and its stalls.

**13.31.18**  On the northern bank of the Gaṅgā, by the edge of the rampart, O best of kings, and on the southern side of the Gomatī—like Śakra's own Amarāvatī.

**13.31.19**  There, as that tiger among kings, the lord of the earth, was dwelling, the Hehayas came once again and assailed him on every side, O Bhārata.

**13.31.20**  That mighty king of great radiance, Divodāsa, sallied forth and gave them battle, dreadful as the clash of gods and asuras.

**13.31.21**  In that battle, O great king, for a thousand days, with the most of his mounts slain, he was at last brought to wretchedness.

**13.31.22**  His warriors slain and his treasury drained, O king, the lord of the earth Divodāsa abandoned his city and gave himself over to flight.

**13.31.23**  Coming to the hermitage of the wise Bharadvāja, the king sought refuge with folded hands, O subduer of foes.

**13.31.24**  The king said: "Holy one, the sons of Vītahavya have destroyed my line in battle; I alone, utterly afflicted, have come to you for refuge."

**13.31.25**  "By your affection for a pupil, holy one, you ought to protect me; for my line has been left without remnant by those doers of evil deeds."

**13.31.26**  To him the blessed and mighty Bharadvāja said: "Fear not, fear not, son of Sudeva; let your dread depart."

**13.31.27**  "This very day I shall perform a sacrifice for a son for you, O lord of the people, that you may overcome the thousands of Vītahavya's kin."

**13.31.28**  Then the sage performed for him that sacrifice for the gaining of a son; and there was born to him a boy renowned as Pratardana.

**13.31.29**  No sooner was he born than he grew, on the instant, to a youth of thirteen years, and mastered the whole Veda and the science of archery, O Bhārata.

**13.31.30**  Pervaded by the yoga of the wise Bharadvāja, he gathered into himself the splendor of the world and entered into that prince.

**13.31.31**  Then, mailed, bow in hand and arrows ready, blazing like fire, he marched forth, brandishing his bow like a rain-cloud about to pour.

**13.31.32**  Beholding him, Sudeva's son was filled with the highest joy, and that king reckoned in his mind that the sons of Vītahavya were already consumed.

**13.31.33**  Then, having installed Pratardana in the office of heir-apparent, the king rejoiced, accounting himself to have accomplished his purpose.

**13.31.34**  Then for the slaying of the sons of Vītahavya that lord of the earth sent forth his son, Pratardana, the subduer of foes.

**13.31.35**  Swiftly that valiant one, conqueror of hostile cities, crossed the Gaṅgā with his chariot and marched upon the city of the sons of Vītahavya.

**13.31.36**  But the sons of Vītahavya, hearing the swelling thunder of his chariot, sallied forth on chariots vast as fortresses, crushers of the chariots of their foes.

**13.31.37**  Sallying forth, those tigers among men, mailed and skilled in varied fighting, weapons raised, struck at Pratardana with showers of arrows.

**13.31.38**  With missiles of every kind and floods of chariots, O Yudhiṣṭhira, they rained upon the king as rain-clouds upon the Himālaya.

**13.31.39**  Warding off their missiles with his own, king Pratardana of great splendor slew them with arrows that were like the thunderbolt and like fire.

**13.31.40**  Their heads severed by his broad-headed arrows, O king, they fell in their hundreds and thousands, their limbs drenched in blood, like kiṃśuka trees cut down.

**13.31.41**  When all those sons were slain, Vītahavya fled, abandoning his city, and made his way even to the hermitage of Bhṛgu.

**13.31.42**  The king Vītahavya went to Bhṛgu for refuge, and Bhṛgu, O king, granted that king his protection; then, becoming Bhṛgu's disciple, he was offered a seat as well.

**13.31.43**  Then, hard upon his heels, Pratardana swiftly arrived there; and reaching the precincts of the hermitage, the son of Divodāsa spoke.

**13.31.44**  "Ho there! Who are present in this hermitage as disciples of the great-souled Bhṛgu? I wish to see the sage; announce me to him."

**13.31.45**  When Bhṛgu learned of him, he came forth from the hermitage and honored him then with the highest ceremony.

**13.31.46**  And he said to that prince, O lord of kings, "What is your purpose?" And the king told him the reason for his coming.

**13.31.47**  "This king Vītahavya, O brahman, let him be given up from here; for by his sons, O brahman, my whole lineage was destroyed, and the realm of the Kāśis with its store of treasures was laid waste."

**13.31.48**  "The hundred sons of this man, drunk with his might, were slain by me; now by his death, O brahman, I shall become free of my debt to my father."

**13.31.49**  To him Bhṛgu, foremost of the upholders of dharma, filled with compassion, said: "There is no kṣatriya here at all; for all these are brahmans."

**13.31.50**  Hearing this truthful word of Bhṛgu, Pratardana gently touched his feet and, smiling, spoke these words:

**13.31.51**  "Even so, O blessed one, I have accomplished my purpose, without doubt, since by my prowess this king has been made to forsake his own caste."

**13.31.52**  "Give me leave, O brahman, and think of me with kindly intent; for by me this king has been made to lose his caste, O scion of Bhṛgu."

**13.31.53**  Then, granted leave by him, King Pratardana departed as he had come, O great king, like a serpent that has discharged its venom.

**13.31.54**  And by the mere word of Bhṛgu, Vītahavya attained, O great king, the state of a brahman seer and the mastery of brahman-lore.

**13.31.55**  His son was Gṛtsamada, in beauty like a second Indra, who was once seized by the Daityas with the cry, "You are Śakra!"

**13.31.56**  And there is a foremost sacred text in this regard in the Ṛgveda, O lord of peoples, wherein that Gṛtsamada, O brahman, is exalted by the brahmans.

**13.31.57**  That Gṛtsamada became a celibate brahman seer, illustrious; and Gṛtsamada's son too was a brahman named Sucetas.

**13.31.58**  Varcas was the son of the mighty-splendored one, and Vihavya was his offspring; Vihavya's son was Vitatya, and his offspring in turn.

**13.31.59**  Vitatya's son was Satya, and Santa was Satya's offspring; his son was the seer Śravas, and from Śravas came Tamas.

**13.31.60**  And from Tamas was born a son, Prakāśa, best of the twice-born; and from Prakāśa came Vāgindra, foremost of the victorious.

**13.31.61**  His son was Pramati, master of the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas; and to him by Ghṛtācī was born a son named Ruru.

**13.31.62**  And to Ruru by Pramadvarā was born a son, a brahman seer named Śunaka, whose son in turn was Śaunaka.

**13.31.63**  Thus did the king Vītahavya attain to brahman-hood, by the grace of Bhṛgu, O lord of kings, though a kṣatriya, O bull among kṣatriyas.

**13.31.64**  So too has the lineage of Gṛtsamada been recounted by me to you in full, O great king. What else do you ask?

**13.32.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: Who are to be honored, who are to be reverenced by men, O bull of the Bhāratas? Tell me this in full, for I am not sated; let it be told.

**13.32.2**  Bhīṣma said: On this too they recount this ancient tale, the dialogue of the two, Nārada and Vāsudeva.

**13.32.3**  Seeing Nārada with joined palms doing honor to the bulls among the twice-born, Keśava asked him: "Blessed one, whom do you reverence?"

**13.32.4**  "Toward whom is your highest regard, those whom you reverence? If it may be heard, I wish to know; tell me this, O best of the knowers of dharma."

**13.32.5**  Nārada said: Hear, O Govinda, those whom I honor, O crusher of foes; for what man in the world other than you is worthy to hear this here?

**13.32.6**  Varuṇa, Vāyu, the Sun, Parjanya, the fire-born Jātavedas, Sthāṇu, Skanda, and Lakṣmī, Viṣṇu and Brahmā too—

**13.32.7**  Vācaspati, the Moon, the Waters, the Earth, and Sarasvatī—those who reverence these unceasingly, them do I reverence, O mighty one.

**13.32.8**  Those rich in austerity, knowers of the Veda, ever devoted to the Veda, most worthy—O tiger of the Vṛṣṇis, them I always honor.

**13.32.9**  Those who, before eating, perform the rites of the gods, free of boastfulness, content and endowed with forbearance—them I reverence, O mighty one.

**13.32.10**  Those who give rightly to the worthy—patient, self-controlled, masters of their senses—grain, wealth, land, and cattle, them I reverence, O Yādava.

**13.32.11**  Those who dwell in austerity in the forest, feeding on roots and fruits, hoarding nothing, performing their rites—them I reverence, O Yādava.

**13.32.12**  Those intent upon supporting their dependents, ever fond of guests, who eat what remains after offering to the gods—them I reverence, O Yādava.

**13.32.13**  Those who, having mastered the Veda, are unassailable, eloquent, expounders of the brahman, ever engaged in performing sacrifices and in teaching—them I honor.

**13.32.14**  And those of serene heart toward all beings always, devoted to their study even to the point of bodily exhaustion—them I honor.

**13.32.15**  Those who strive for the favor of their teacher and for their study, steadfast in their vows, eager to serve and free of envy—them I reverence, O Yādava.

**13.32.16**  Those sages of good vows, devoted to the brahman, true to their pledges, bearers of offerings to gods and ancestors—them I reverence, O Yādava.

**13.32.17**  Those devoted to the practice of begging, lean, sheltering in the teacher's house, without comfort and without wealth—them I reverence, O Yādava.

**13.32.18**  Free of possessiveness, free of rivalry, free of false shame, free of selfish ends, devoted to non-injury, and those men vowed to truth, self-controlled and intent on tranquillity—them I reverence, O Keśava.

**13.32.19**  Householders devoted to the worship of gods and guests, who live always like the dove, gleaning only what suffices—them I reverence, O Yādava.

**13.32.20**  Those in whose deeds the three aims of life abide and are not diminished, who follow the conduct of the cultivated—them I reverence always.

**13.32.21**  Those brahmans in the three worlds who pursue the three aims of life, free of greed, of holy character—them I reverence, O Keśava.

**13.32.22**  Those who feed always on water, on air, or on nectar, and who are bound by various vows—them I reverence, O Mādhava.

**13.32.23**  Those of no womb, those born of fire, those born of the brahman, and those born of the self that is the source of all beings—those twice-born I reverence.

**13.32.24**  These I reverence always, O Kṛṣṇa—the seers who make the worlds, eldest of the worlds, fixed in knowledge, destroyers of darkness, lights of the world.

**13.32.25**  Therefore you too, O scion of the Vṛṣṇis, honor the twice-born always; for when honored, those worthy of honor will grant you happiness, O sinless one.

**13.32.26**  For in this world and in the next these are ever givers of happiness; honored as they deserve, they will indeed bestow happiness upon you.

**13.32.27**  Those who are ever hospitable to all, devoted always to cattle and to brahmans and to truth—they pass beyond all hardships.

**13.32.28**  Those ever intent on tranquillity, and those free of envy, and those ever devoted to their study—they pass beyond all hardships.

**13.32.29**  Those who reverence all the gods while relying upon a single god, full of faith and self-controlled—they pass beyond all hardships.

**13.32.30**  And likewise those who, having reverenced the foremost brahmans of disciplined vows, become devoted to giving—they pass beyond all hardships.

**13.32.31**  Those who, having established the sacred fires according to rule, maintain them with care and have attained the soma-offering—they pass beyond all hardships.

**13.32.32**  Those who always conduct themselves rightly toward mother and father and teachers, just as you do, O tiger of the Vṛṣṇis—so saying, he fell silent.

**13.32.33**  Therefore you too, O son of Kuntī, rightly honor ancestors, gods, the twice-born, and guests, by which you shall attain the goal you desire.

**13.33.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: Of all a king's duties, which is the weightiest, O grandsire? By doing what deed does a king win both worlds?

**13.33.2**  Bhīṣma said: This is the foremost duty of a consecrated king, O Bhārata: the serving of brahmans. One who desires the highest happiness should ever honor the learned, the brahmans, and the aged.

**13.33.3**  And the brahmans of city and countryside, deeply learned, he should honor with conciliating words, with gifts of enjoyments, and with marks of reverence.

**13.33.4**  He should mark this as ever the foremost duty of a king; he should cherish them as he would himself, as he would his own sons.

**13.33.5**  And those among them who are most worthy of honor he should honor steadfastly; when they are at peace, the whole realm shines forth.

**13.33.6**  They are to be honored, they to be reverenced, they to be guarded like one's own fathers; upon them rests the world's course, as upon Vāsava that of beings.

**13.33.7**  By sorceries and by stratagems, even by their own fiery power, they could consume; when angered, the fierce ones, whose valor is truth, could leave nothing remaining.

**13.33.8**  I see no limit to their power, nor any quarter left uncovered; when angered they blaze up like flames of fire in a forest conflagration.

**13.33.9**  There are found in them daring qualities in the extreme; some are like wells covered over with grass, while others are pure as the sky.

**13.33.10**  Some among them act by force, others are soft as cotton; some of them are exceedingly crafty, while still others are exceeding ascetics.

**13.33.11**  Some practice farming and the tending of cattle, others live by begging; some are thieves, others liars, and yet others actors and dancers.

**13.33.12**  They are seen in all occupations, the peaceful and the other kind, and endowed with manifold ways of life are the brahmans, O bull of the Bhāratas.

**13.33.13**  Engaged though they are in diverse occupations and living by many trades, they are knowers of dharma and good men; their praise one should ever proclaim.

**13.33.14**  Of ancestors and of gods, of men, serpents, and rākṣasas, the brahmans, O lord of men, are the highly blessed household priests.

**13.33.15**  These twice-born cannot be conquered by gods, nor by ancestors, nor by gandharvas, nor by rākṣasas, nor by asuras, nor by piśācas.

**13.33.16**  They could make a non-god into a god, and a god into a non-god; whomever they wish, he becomes king, and whomever they hate, he comes to ruin.

**13.33.17**  And those senseless ones who utter reproach against the brahmans—the twice-born, skilled in blame and praise, who dispense fame and infamy, high and low, grow ever wrathful, O king, toward those who hate them.

**13.33.18**  The man whom the brahmans praise, that man prospers; but he who is reviled by the brahmans comes to ruin in an instant.

**13.33.19**  The Śakas, Yavanas, and Kāmbojas, and those various kṣatriya races, have fallen into the condition of degraded men through the absence of brahmans.

**13.33.20**  The Dramiḷas and Kaliṅgas, the Pulindas and Uśīnaras, the Kaulas, Sarpas, and Māhiṣakas—those various kṣatriya races—

**13.33.21**  have fallen into the condition of degraded men through the absence of brahmans. Better is defeat at their hands than victory, O best of the victorious.

**13.33.22**  Even one who should slay all this world—there is nothing equal to slaying a brahman; the killing of a brahman is a grievous sin, so say the supreme seers.

**13.33.23**  Reviling of the twice-born must never be listened to under any circumstance. Either let a man sit silent with face bowed down, or let him rise and walk away.

**13.33.24**  There is none born, nor to be born, upon this earth, who by setting himself against the brāhmaṇas could dare to live in ease.

**13.33.25**  Hard to seize with the fist is the wind, hard to touch with the hand is the moon, hard to bear upon the head is the earth—and hard to conquer upon this world are the brāhmaṇas.

**13.34.1**  Bhīṣma said: The brāhmaṇas, ever and always, one should honor with the utmost zeal, for they have Soma for their king and are the masters of joy and sorrow.

**13.34.2**  With enjoyments, with adornments, and with whatever else they may desire, they are ever to be honored, saluted, and protected by kings as one's own fathers; for from this comes the peace of the realm, as the peace of all beings comes from Vāsava.

**13.34.3**  Let there be born in the realm a pure brāhmaṇa radiant with sacred lore; and a mighty-chariot warrior of the royal line, a scorcher of foes, is to be wished for.

**13.34.4**  A brāhmaṇa endowed with noble birth, knowing dharma, of well-honed vows—him, O king, let one settle in one's house; truly there is nothing higher than that.

**13.34.5**  The oblation given to brāhmaṇas the gods receive, and the fathers of all beings; than these there is known nothing higher.

**13.34.6**  The sun, the moon, the wind, the earth, the waters, the sky, the quarters—all of these, entering into the brāhmaṇa, partake of the good food offered.

**13.34.7**  The fathers do not eat of the man whose brāhmaṇas do not eat; nor do the gods partake of that sinner who hates the brāhmaṇas.

**13.34.8**  But when the brāhmaṇas are content, the fathers too are ever pleased, and likewise the gods, O king; in this no doubt need be entertained.

**13.34.9**  Likewise are those pleased to whom that oblation comes; and they do not perish after death, but attain the supreme goal.

**13.34.10**  By whatever oblation a man satisfies the brāhmaṇas, by that very same the fathers are pleased, and the gods as well.

**13.34.11**  From the brāhmaṇa alone arises that being whence creatures spring, whence this world comes forth, and whither it goes after death.

**13.34.12**  He knows the path of heaven and likewise of hell, both what has come and what has not yet come—the brāhmaṇa, best of two-footed beings. The brāhmaṇa, O finest of the Bhāratas, knows his own dharma by his wisdom.

**13.34.13**  And those who follow him go not to ruin; they do not perish after death, nor do they come to downfall.

**13.34.14**  Those who accept the word received from the brāhmaṇa's mouth—the perfected of soul, the great-spirited—they go not to downfall.

**13.34.15**  Of the kṣatriyas who blaze forth with energy and with might, their splendors and their powers find their quenching in the brāhmaṇas alone.

**13.34.16**  The Bhṛgus conquered the Tālajaṅghas, the Aṅgirases conquered the Nīpas, and Bharadvāja conquered the Vaitahavyas and the Ailas, O bull of the Bhāratas.

**13.34.17**  These, with the black antelope-skin for their banner, conquered even the Citrāyudhas; and having cast away the water-jars, one should set out upon him who would carry men across.

**13.34.18**  Whatever is told in the world, whatever is heard or seen, all of that abides in the brāhmaṇas, as fire lies hidden in wood.

**13.34.19**  On this point, too, they recite this ancient tale, the dialogue between Vāsudeva and the Earth, O bull of the Bhāratas.

**13.34.20**  Vāsudeva said: O auspicious one, mother of all beings, I ask you my doubt: by what deed does a householder put away his sin?

**13.34.21**  The Earth said: Let him serve the brāhmaṇas, for this is the highest purifier; for one who serves the brāhmaṇas, all his impurity is destroyed.

**13.34.22**  From this comes prosperity, from this glory, from this is wisdom born—for those below, for those above, and for those still beyond the highest.

**13.34.23**  The man whom the brāhmaṇas praise, he flourishes; but he who is reviled by the brāhmaṇas comes to ruin before long.

**13.34.24**  As a lump of unbaked clay cast into the great ocean dissolves away, so an ill-doing deed conduces to one's downfall.

**13.34.25**  Behold the mark set upon the moon, the salt water in the ocean, and great Indra branded with the thousand marks.

**13.34.26**  By their very power he became the thousand-eyed one, the lord of a hundred sacrifices—behold, O Mādhava, of what kind that was.

**13.34.27**  Desiring prosperity and glory and the higher worlds, O slayer of Madhu, let a man abide pure and self-possessed by the consent of the brāhmaṇas.

**13.34.28**  Having heard this word of the Earth, the slayer of Madhu, saying "Well said, well said, so be it," did reverence to the Earth in return.

**13.34.29**  Having heard this parable, O Pārtha, with diligence honor the bulls among brāhmaṇas continually; thereby you shall attain to good.

**13.35.1**  Bhīṣma said: By his very birth the one called brāhmaṇa is born greatly blessed, to be saluted by all beings, a guest who eats the first portion set forth.

**13.35.2**  All the brāhmaṇas are our well-wishers, my son, kindly of face; when honored, they wish us well with words laden with blessing.

**13.35.3**  But all the brāhmaṇas become our foes, my son, their wrath aroused, and when slighted they would strike with words laden with menace.

**13.35.4**  On this point those who know the past recite verses sung by Brahmā; for the Ordainer, having created the twice-born, addressed them as of old.

**13.35.5**  Nothing else here, nothing beyond, need be done by you according to rule: guarded yourselves, guard the sacred lore—therein lies your fair and excellent good.

**13.35.6**  As you perform your own proper work, the splendor of Brahman shall be yours; you shall become the measure of all beings, and shall attain to mastery over them.

**13.35.7**  No śūdra's work should be done by a learned brāhmaṇa, for when one performs a śūdra's work, his dharma is obstructed.

**13.35.8**  Splendor and wisdom and energy and majestic dominion—and through self-study alone you shall attain a stainless greatness of soul.

**13.35.9**  Having offered into the fire set in the āhavanīya hearth, established in high blessedness, you are the first to be fed among created beings, fashioned with the splendor of Brahman.

**13.35.10**  Endowed with supreme faith, gained without malice, devoted to self-restraint and self-study, you shall attain all your desires.

**13.35.11**  Whatever there is in the world of men, and whatever among the gods, all of that is attainable by austerity, by knowledge, and by discipline.

**13.35.12**  Thus have these verses sung by Brahmā been recounted to you by me, O sinless one; for this was uttered by that wise one out of compassion for the brāhmaṇas.

**13.35.13**  Greater still I deem the power of those ascetics than even that of a king: unapproachable, fierce, impetuous, swift to act.

**13.35.14**  Among them are some of lion-nature and others of tiger-nature, some of boar-and-deer nature and others of elephant-nature.

**13.35.15**  Some are soft as cotton, while others strike like the makara; some slay by mere speech, and others slay with a glance.

**13.35.16**  There are those like venomous serpents, and there are others mild; manifold are the ways of the brāhmaṇas here, O Yudhiṣṭhira.

**13.35.17**  The Mekalas, the Dramiḍas, the Kāśas, the Pauṇḍras, and the Kollagiras, the Śauṇḍikas, the Daradas, the Darvas, the Cauras, the Śabaras and Barbaras—

**13.35.18**  the Kirātas and the Yavanas too—those various kṣatriya races sank into the state of low-born men through failing to behold the brāhmaṇas.

**13.35.19**  Through their contempt for the brāhmaṇas, the asuras lie sunk in the waters; and through the grace of the brāhmaṇas, the gods are dwellers in heaven.

**13.35.20**  The sky cannot be touched, the Himavān mountain cannot be moved, the Gaṅgā cannot be dammed by any dike—and the brāhmaṇas cannot be conquered upon this earth.

**13.35.21**  By setting oneself against the brāhmaṇas, the earth cannot be ruled; for the brāhmaṇas, the great-souled, are deities even of the gods.

**13.35.22**  Honor them continually with gifts and with service, if you wish to enjoy this earth that is girdled by the sea.

**13.35.23**  By the receiving of gifts the energy of the brāhmaṇas is quieted, O sinless one; and those who would not wish to receive gifts—they too are to be protected by you, O sinless one.

**13.36.1**  Bhīṣma said: On this point, too, they recite this ancient tale, the dialogue between Śakra and Śambara; mark it well, O Yudhiṣṭhira.

**13.36.2**  Śakra, in a form unrecognized, having become a matted-haired ascetic ruddy with dust, and taking on an ugly shape, put a question to Śambara.

**13.36.3**  By what conduct, O Śambara, do you stand above those of your own race? For what reason do they hold you to be the best? Tell me that, who ask you.

**13.36.4**  Śambara said: I never spurn the brāhmaṇas, nor Brahmā the grandfather; the brāhmaṇas, as they expound the sacred texts, I honor to their full content.

**13.36.5**  And having heard them, I do not despise them, nor do I ever offend; the worshipful I question with deference, and I clasp the feet of the wise.

**13.36.6**  Trustful, they speak freely and ever restrain me from error; among the heedless I am heedful, and among the sleeping I keep ever awake.

**13.36.7**  Those teachers pour upon me—set on the path of the scriptures, devoted to the brāhmaṇas, free of envy—their instruction, as bees pour out their honey.

**13.36.8**  And whatever they, well-pleased, declare, that I receive with my understanding, ever keeping the composure of my soul attuned and undisturbed in thought.

**13.36.9**  Thus I, the licker of the savors poured forth from the tip of their speech, stand above those of my own race, as the moon above the constellations.

**13.36.10**  This is the nectar upon the earth, this the unsurpassed eye—the teaching which, heard here from the brāhmaṇa's mouth, sets one upon his way.

**13.36.11**  Having learned this cause, and having beheld of old the war between the gods and the asuras, my father, glad of heart and amazed, came to acknowledge it.

**13.36.12**  And having beheld the greatness of the great-souled brāhmaṇas, he asked the moon, the night-maker, "How is it that these have attained perfection?"

**13.36.13**  Soma said: The brāhmaṇas all attain perfection through austerity, their strength ever in their speech; for kings have their valor in their arms, but the twice-born have speech for their weapon.

**13.36.14**  Even while abroad let him study, dwelling through many hard sojournings; free of wrath and free of pride, an ascetic let him be, looking on all alike.

**13.36.15**  Even if one of noble birth should study all the Vedas in his father's house, yet study as if boasting of it, him they call a vulgar man.

**13.36.16**  The earth swallows up these two, as a serpent swallows creatures that lie in their holes: the king who will not fight, and the brāhmaṇa who will not go abroad.

**13.36.17**  Excessive pride destroys the fortune of a man of little understanding; a maiden is spoiled by an untimely conceiving, and a brāhmaṇa by mere staying at home.

**13.36.18**  Having heard this from Soma of wondrous aspect, my father honored the brāhmaṇas of great vows—and even so do I.

**13.36.19**  Bhīṣma said: Having heard this word fallen from the mouth of the lord of the dānavas, Śakra honored the twice-born, and attained the sovereignty of great Indra.

**13.37.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: A worthy recipient may be one newly come, or one who has dwelt long with us, or one arrived from afar; who, O grandfather, is a fit recipient?

**13.37.2**  Bhīṣma said: For some, the rite is this—a vow kept in silence is the highest: "Whoever begs whatever it may be, all of it let us give."

**13.37.3**  Yet without oppressing one's dependants—thus have we heard it taught; for he who oppresses his dependants drags himself down.

**13.37.4**  Whether the recipient be newly come, or one who has dwelt long, or one arrived from afar—the wise know him too to be a fit recipient.

**13.37.5**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: Without oppressing our dependants, and without harm to dharma, let us know in truth that recipient to whom a gift, once given, brings no regret.

**13.37.6**  Bhīṣma said: The officiating priest, the family priest, the teacher, disciples, kinsmen, and relations—all are to be honored and revered, provided they are endowed with sacred learning and good conduct.

**13.37.7**  Those who conduct themselves otherwise than this are none of them worthy of honor; therefore one should ever examine men, observing them closely with care.

**13.37.8**  Freedom from anger, truthful speech, non-injury, self-restraint, uprightness, freedom from malice, absence of pride, modesty, forbearance, austerity, tranquillity—

**13.37.9**  the man in whom these are seen, firmly settled by their very nature, O Bhārata, and who does no forbidden deeds—that one is a worthy vessel, deserving of honor.

**13.37.10**  So too one long abiding here, or one but newly arrived, whether a stranger never seen before or an old acquaintance—such a vessel deserves honor.

**13.37.11**  To deny the authority of the Vedas, to overstep the sacred treatises, and to lack steadfastness in all things—this is the ruin of one's own self.

**13.37.12**  The brāhmaṇa who fancies himself learned, who reviles the Vedas, who is devoted to the science of logic and to fruitless disputation,

**13.37.13**  who utters arguments of mere reasoning amid the good, a refuter who confounds those who do not so reason, and who is forever a reviler and abuser of brāhmaṇas—

**13.37.14**  suspicious of all, deluded, childish, and harsh of tongue—such a one, my son, is to be recognized for what he is, for they call him a dog among men.

**13.37.15**  As a dog is let loose to bark and to bite, so are such men loosed for wrangling and for the slaughter of all the scriptures; men of little learning, given to crooked logic—such false scholars are seen and met with everywhere.

**13.37.16**  One should seek out the learned—those versed in śruti, smṛti, the chronicles, the purāṇas, and the forest-treatises, men of wide knowledge who grasp the essence of things.

**13.37.17**  The course of worldly life must be observed, and dharma, and what is for one's own good; the man who so conducts himself flourishes through everlasting years.

**13.37.18**  Having discharged his debt to the gods, and likewise to the seers, to the ancestors, to the brāhmaṇas, and as the fifth, to guests,

**13.37.19**  in due order, with pure and well-cleansed action—thus the householder, performing his works, falls not away from his sacred duties.

**13.38.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: I wish to hear of the nature of women, O best of the Bhāratas; for women are the root of faults, and light of mind, O grandsire.

**13.38.2**  Bhīṣma said: On this they relate an ancient tale of old—the dialogue between Nārada and the wanton apsaras Pañcacūḍā.

**13.38.3**  Of old, as the wise divine seer Nārada wandered through the worlds, he beheld the blameless apsaras Pañcacūḍā, born of Brahmā.

**13.38.4**  Seeing her, lovely in every limb, the sage questioned the apsaras: 'A certain doubt stirs within my heart; tell me of it, O slender-waisted one.'

**13.38.5**  Thus addressed, she answered the brāhmaṇa Nārada: 'If it lie within my province I shall speak of it, and if you deem me equal to the task.'

**13.38.6**  Nārada said: I shall in no way set you, gentle lady, to a matter beyond your province; I wish to hear from you, O fair-faced one, the nature of women.

**13.38.7**  Bhīṣma said: Hearing this word of the divine seer, the foremost of apsarases replied: 'I shall not be able, being myself a woman, to censure women.'

**13.38.8**  'Women are known to you, both who they are and of what nature they are; you ought not, O divine seer, to set me to a question such as this.'

**13.38.9**  To her the divine seer said: 'Speak the truth, O slender-waisted one; in false speech there is fault, but in truth no fault is found.'

**13.38.10**  Thus addressed, the sweetly smiling one made up her mind, and set herself to declare the everlasting and true faults of women.

**13.38.11**  Pañcacūḍā said: Women of good family, beautiful, and possessed of protectors do not abide within the bounds of propriety; that, Nārada, is the fault in women.

**13.38.12**  There is indeed nothing else more given to wickedness than women, for women are the root of faults; this too you yourself well know.

**13.38.13**  Though their husbands be renowned, prosperous, comely, and wholly devoted, women, finding an opening, are unable to remain faithful.

**13.38.14**  This is the wicked way of us women, O lord—that, casting off shame, we consort with men more base than our own.

**13.38.15**  For whoever woos a woman, draws near to her, and renders her but a little service—him the women desire.

**13.38.16**  Only because men do not solicit them, and out of fear of their kinsfolk, do women—unrestrained though they are—abide within bounds and stay with their husbands.

**13.38.17**  For them no man is forbidden, nor have they any fixed regard for age; be he ugly or handsome, they enjoy him simply because he is a man.

**13.38.18**  Not from fear, nor from compassion, nor for the sake of wealth in any way, nor from the bond of kindred and family do women remain with their husbands.

**13.38.19**  Women of good families yearn after those women who, being in the flush of youth, adorned with bright ornaments and raiment, live as they please.

**13.38.20**  Even those women who are forever highly esteemed, cherished, and guarded—even they cleave to hunchbacks, the blind, the dull-witted, and dwarfs.

**13.38.21**  Even to the lame, O divine seer, and to other men despised—in this world, O great sage, there is no man forbidden to women.

**13.38.22**  If, O holy one, access to men in no way befalls them, they will resort even to one another, for they cannot abide content with their husbands.

**13.38.23**  For want of men, from fear of their household, and from dread of slaying and bondage, they keep themselves guarded of their own accord.

**13.38.24**  Fickle by nature, hard to serve, and by their disposition hard to grasp—women are even as the speech of a wise man here below.

**13.38.25**  As fire is never sated with fuel, nor the great ocean with rivers, nor Death with all beings, so are the fair-eyed ones never sated with men.

**13.38.26**  And here is another secret of all womankind, O divine seer: at the mere sight of a pleasing man, a woman's loins grow moist with desire.

**13.38.27**  Even a husband who grants their every desire, who shows them honor and tender words, who is their guardian—even such a peerless husband women do not patiently endure.

**13.38.28**  They do not prize abundant enjoyments, nor heaps of ornaments and wealth, so highly as they prize the favor of the act of love.

**13.38.29**  The Ender, the Subduer, Death, the netherworld, the submarine fire, the razor's edge, poison, the serpent, and flame on the one side—and women on the other.

**13.38.30**  From whatever source the five great elements arose, and the worlds were ordained by the Creator, from that same source men and women were fashioned—and from that very moment, O Nārada, the faults were set in women.

**13.39.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: These men in the world cleave again and again to women, possessed utterly by a delusion ordained by fate, O king; and women too, plainly and with the world for witness, cleave to men.

**13.39.2**  Herein a keen doubt revolves within my heart: how do men form attachment to these women, O delight of the Kurus, and how do women take pleasure in them, or again grow weary of them?

**13.39.3**  Such being so, O tiger among men, how are women able to be guarded by a man in this world? That you ought to explain to me.

**13.39.4**  For these women beguile men here with the wiles of Maya, and no man once come into their hands escapes them; like cattle to fresh grass, they seize on ever-new men.

**13.39.5**  All the sorcery that was Śambara's, and the sorcery of Namuci, of Bali, and of Kumbhīnasī—all of it women know.

**13.39.6**  At one who laughs they laugh, and at one who weeps they weep; and one who is unwelcome to them they take captive with sweet words, as the moment requires.

**13.39.7**  The science that Uśanas knows, and that which Bṛhaspati knows, are not superior to the cunning of women—how then are they to be guarded by men?

**13.39.8**  They call falsehood truth, and likewise truth they call falsehood; how, O hero, are such women to be guarded by men in this world?

**13.39.9**  By drawing forth the very cunning of women, O slayer of foes, the treatises on statecraft, I think, were composed by the good—by Bṛhaspati and the rest.

**13.39.10**  When honored by men, women turn their minds away from those men; and when cast off as well, O king, women turn their minds away likewise.

**13.39.11**  Who could be able to guard them?—this is my great doubt. Tell me of it, O mighty-armed one, increaser of the line of the Kurus.

**13.39.12**  If their guarding can in any way be accomplished, O best of the Kurus, or has ever been accomplished of old, that you ought to explain to me.

**13.40.1**  Bhīṣma said: So it is, O mighty-armed one; in this there is nothing false, even as you say concerning woman, O Kaurava, O lord of men.

**13.40.2**  On this I shall relate to you an ancient tale—how of old a guarding was accomplished by the great-souled Vipula.

**13.40.3**  And how women were created by Brahmā, O bull of the Bhāratas, and to what end—that too I shall declare to you, my son, O lord of the earth.

**13.40.4**  For there is nothing, my son, more given to wickedness than women; a woman is blazing fire, and the wiles born of Maya, O lord; the razor's edge, poison, the serpent, and Death on the one side—and women on the other.

**13.40.5**  These creatures, O mighty-armed one—being righteous, so we have heard—were attaining godhood of their own accord; and thereupon fear came upon the gods.

**13.40.6**  Then those gods came to the Grandsire, O subduer of foes; and having laid bare what was in their minds, they stood silent, their faces downcast.

**13.40.7**  Knowing what lay hidden within those gods, the Grandsire, the lord, for the deluding of men, created women as instruments of bewitchment.

**13.40.8**  In the first creation, O son of Kuntī, women here were virtuous; but the unvirtuous, the instruments of bewitchment, arose from the later creation of Prajāpati.

**13.40.9**  To them the Grandsire granted desires according to their wish; and those women, greedy for pleasure, then set to tormenting men.

**13.40.10**  The lord of gods created Anger as the helper of Desire; and all creatures, fallen under the sway of desire and anger, grew enthralled.

**13.40.11**  And no sacred rite belongs to women—so the law is established; women are without sacred rites and without mantras, untruth itself—so says the śruti.

**13.40.12**  Couch and seat, adornment, food and drink, ignobleness, foul-tongued speech, and the pleasure of love—these Prajāpati gave to women.

**13.40.13**  Their guarding cannot in any way be accomplished by a man—not even by the Maker of All, my son; how much less by mortal men here?

**13.40.14**  Neither by word, nor by slaying and bonds, nor by manifold torments can women be guarded; for they are ever unrestrained.

**13.40.15**  But this, O tiger among men, I have heard in former times: how of old a guarding was wrought by Vipula over his preceptor's wife.

**13.40.16**  There was a seer of great fortune, renowned by the name of Devaśarman; his wife was named Ruci, unmatched in beauty upon the earth.

**13.40.17**  By her beauty were maddened the gods, gandharvas, and dānavas, and most of all, O king of kings, the slayer of Vṛtra, the chastiser of Pāka.

**13.40.18**  Now Devaśarman, the great sage, knew well the ways of women, and he guarded that wife of his to the utmost of his power and resolve.

**13.40.19**  And he knew Puraṃdara to be one who lusted after other men's wives; therefore he kept watch over his wife with diligent care.

**13.40.20**  Once, my son, that seer, minded to perform a sacrifice, fell to pondering how the guarding of his wife might be accomplished.

**13.40.21**  Having devised in his mind the manner of her guarding, that great ascetic summoned his beloved disciple, Vipula of Bhṛgu's line, and spoke to him.

**13.40.22**  'I shall go to perform a sacrifice; and this Ruci the lord of the gods forever woos. My son, guard her to the best of your power.'

**13.40.23**  'You must remain ever vigilant against Puraṃdara, for he assumes shapes of many kinds, O scion of Bhṛgu.'

**13.40.24**  Thus addressed by him, Vipula the ascetic—his senses subdued, ever fierce in penance, O king, radiant like fire and the sun,

**13.40.25**  knower of dharma and speaker of truth—answered, 'So be it'; and then, O great king, he further questioned his renowned preceptor in these words.

**13.40.26**  What forms does Śakra assume when he comes, O sage? Of what kind is his body and his splendor? This you ought to expound to me.

**13.40.27**  Then that blessed one, O Bhārata, declared to the great-souled Vipula, according to the truth, the magic art of Śakra.

**13.40.28**  Rich in illusions, O brahmin-seer, is the slayer of Bala, the chastiser of Pāka; this form and that he conjures, manifold, again and again.

**13.40.29**  Diademed, wielder of the thunderbolt, bearing a bow, crowned, with fastened earrings he appears; and in a moment he looks like a caṇḍāla.

**13.40.30**  With a topknot, with matted locks, clad in bark, he becomes again, my son; now huge of body, now stout, now lean.

**13.40.31**  Fair, dusky, and dark of hue he becomes by turns; misshapen and again comely, young and likewise old.

**13.40.32**  Wise and dull and mute, short and likewise tall; a brāhmaṇa, a kṣatriya, a vaiśya, and likewise a śūdra, born against the grain and with it—so does the lord of a hundred sacrifices become.

**13.40.33**  In the form of a parrot and a crow, in the form of a goose and a cuckoo, and again he takes on the shape of lions, tigers, and elephants.

**13.40.34**  The body of a god, of a daitya, and of kings he bears as well; very lean, his limbs broken by the wind, a misshapen bird likewise.

**13.40.35**  Four-footed and of many forms he again becomes a fool; and he takes on too the body of flies, gnats, and the like.

**13.40.36**  None can lay hold of him, O Vipula—not even by the Maker of all, dear son, by whom this world was created.

**13.40.37**  Now Śakra, hidden, is seen only by the eye of wisdom; and having become wind, that king of the gods becomes himself once more.

**13.40.38**  Thus does the chastiser of Pāka ceaselessly take on these forms; therefore, Vipula, guard with all effort this slender-waisted one.

**13.40.39**  See that the king of the gods does not lap up Ruci, O best of the Bhṛgus, as an evil-natured dog laps the oblation set down and placed at the sacrifice.

**13.40.40**  Having thus spoken, that sage, the performer of the sacrifice, then departed—the greatly fortunate Devaśarman, O best of the Bhāratas.

**13.40.41**  But Vipula, having heard his teacher's word, fell to brooding, and devised the utmost guard against the king of the gods of great might.

**13.40.42**  "What can I do to guard my teacher's wife? For that lord of the gods is a master of illusion, unassailable, and mighty in valor.

**13.40.43**  Not by shutting up the hermitage can the chastiser of Pāka be warded off, nor the leaf-hut, for his forms are of every kind.

**13.40.44**  In the form of the wind Śakra might assail my teacher's wife; therefore, entering into this Ruci, I shall this very day take my station within her.

**13.40.45**  Or else by mere manly strength she cannot be guarded by me, for the blessed one borne by bays is heard to be of many forms.

**13.40.46**  Therefore by the power of yoga I shall guard her from the chastiser of Pāka; I shall enter limb by limb into her limbs to keep her safe.

**13.40.47**  Yet if my teacher should see this wife Ruci defiled, then beyond doubt he, of divine knowledge and great austerity, will curse me in his wrath.

**13.40.48**  And she cannot be guarded as other women are guarded by men, for that lord of the gods is a master of illusion—alas, I have come into peril!"

**13.40.49**  "The teacher's command must surely be carried out; yet if I were to do this, a marvel would be wrought by me.

**13.40.50**  Entering by yoga here into the body of my teacher's wife, free from any form of passion, no fault would be mine.

**13.40.51**  As a wayfarer upon the road might lodge in an empty hall, so this day shall I lodge within my teacher's wife's body.

**13.40.52**  As a drop of water resting on a lotus leaf clings not, but trembles free, even so, composed, shall I dwell within her body."

**13.40.53**  Thus having looked upon dharma and upon the Vedas and their lore in every part, and having regarded the abundant austerity of his teacher and of himself,

**13.40.54**  having so resolved in his mind concerning the guarding, that descendant of Bhṛgu set himself to the utmost effort—hear how, O lord of earth.

**13.40.55**  Seated beside his teacher's wife, Vipula of great austerity beguiled with stories that seated one of faultless limbs.

**13.40.56**  Joining with his two eyes the beams of her eyes, beam to beam, Vipula entered her body as the wind enters the sky.

**13.40.57**  Mark upon mark, face within face, the sage stood unmoving, gone within her like a shadow.

**13.40.58**  Then Vipula, holding fast the body of his teacher's wife, abode there intent on guarding, and she was not aware of him.

**13.40.59**  For all the while, O king, that the great-souled teacher had not returned to his own house, his sacrifice concluded, for all that while did he keep watch.

**13.41.1**  Bhīṣma said: Then on a certain day the king of the gods, bearing a body of divine form, thinking "this is the moment," came thereupon to the hermitage.

**13.41.2**  Having made for himself a peerless, alluring form, O ruler of men, becoming most fair to behold, he entered that hermitage.

**13.41.3**  He beheld there, seated, the body of Vipula, motionless, with fixed and staring eyes, like a figure set down in a painting.

**13.41.4**  And Ruci of lovely sidelong glance, full of hip and breast, wide-eyed as the petals of a lotus, her face like the full moon.

**13.41.5**  Seeing him, she suddenly sought to rise to greet him, amazed at his beauty, wishing then to ask, "Who are you?"
