**13.41.6**  Though she wished to rise, she stayed still, held fast by Vipula, O lord of men, and could not stir.

**13.41.7**  The king of the gods addressed her with words most soft and winning: "Know that I, the king of the gods, have come for your sake, O bright-smiling one.

**13.41.8**  Tormented by the bodiless god of love, born of longing for you—therefore accept me, fair-browed one, before the time slips away."

**13.41.9**  Vipula the sage, dwelling within the body of his teacher's wife, heard Śakra speaking thus, and beheld the lord of the gods.

**13.41.10**  And the blameless one could not rise, O king, nor could she speak, O king, held fast as she was by Vipula.

**13.41.11**  But that scion of Bhṛgu, perceiving the bearing of his teacher's wife, restrained her—he of great splendor—forcefully by yoga, O lord, and with the bonds of yoga he bound all her senses.

**13.41.12**  Seeing her unmoved, the lord of Śacī once again, abashed, O king, spoke to her who was overcome by the power of yoga.

**13.41.13**  "Come, come," he said; and then she sought to answer him, but Vipula turned aside that speech of his teacher's wife.

**13.41.14**  "Sir, what is the purpose of your coming?"—thus from her mouth, like unto the moon, came forth speech adorned with refinement.

**13.41.15**  Abashed, having spoken that word against her own will, she fell silent; and Puraṃdara then grew alarmed and dismayed.

**13.41.16**  Marking that strangeness, the king of the gods, O lord of peoples, the thousand-eyed one, then looked with his divine eye.

**13.41.17**  And he beheld the sage moving within her body, lodged in his teacher's wife's frame like a reflection in a mirror.

**13.41.18**  Seeing him endowed with terrible austerity, Puraṃdara trembled, sorely afraid, fearing a curse then, O mighty one.

**13.41.19**  Then Vipula of great austerity, releasing his teacher's wife, entered his own body and spoke to the frightened Śakra:

**13.41.20**  "O you of unconquered senses, evil-souled, lustful Puraṃdara! Not for long shall the gods, nor men likewise, honor you.

**13.41.21**  Have you forgotten this, Śakra? Does it not stand in your mind—how by Gautama you were marked over with the signs of a woman's parts?

**13.41.22**  I know you to be childish of mind, undisciplined of self, and fickle. By me is she guarded, O fool; go, O wicked one, as you came.

**13.41.23**  I would this day burn you to ashes by my own splendor, O dull-souled one; yet out of compassion I do not wish to burn you, Vāsava.

**13.41.24**  And that wise teacher of mine, of terrible austerity, seeing you of wicked heart, would this day burn you utterly with an eye blazing with wrath.

**13.41.25**  Never act thus again, Śakra; the twice-born are to be honored by you. Go not, with your sons and ministers, to ruin, stricken by the might of brahman.

**13.41.26**  Holding to the thought, 'I am immortal,' you conduct yourself so; do not despise it—there is nothing whatsoever unattainable by austerities.

**13.41.27**  Hearing that speech of the great-souled Vipula, Śakra, saying nothing, ashamed, vanished then and there.

**13.41.28**  When but a moment had passed since Śakra's going, Devaśarman of great austerity, having performed his sacrifice as he wished, came home to his hermitage.

**13.41.29**  When the teacher had come, O king, Vipula, doer of welcome deeds, presented to him the blameless wife he had guarded.

**13.41.30**  And having saluted him, that tranquil-souled Vipula, devoted to his teacher, attended upon his teacher as before, untroubled.

**13.41.31**  Then to him, rested and seated together with his wife, Vipula reported that deed of Śakra.

**13.41.32**  Hearing this, that majestic sage grew pleased with Vipula for his character and conduct, his austerity and his self-restraint.

**13.41.33**  Seeing Vipula's conduct toward his teacher, his devotion to him, and his steadfastness in dharma, the lord said, "Well done, well done!"

**13.41.34**  And the righteous one, applauding his disciple who was devoted to dharma, offered to gratify him with a boon; and he, devoted to his teacher and so permitted by him, practiced unsurpassed austerity.

**13.41.35**  So too Devaśarman of great austerity, together with his wife, fearless of the slayer of Bala and Vṛtra, roamed in the lonely forest.

**13.42.1**  Bhīṣma said: But Vipula, having done his teacher's bidding, performed fierce austerity; and the valiant one then deemed himself accomplished in austerity.

**13.42.2**  Vying through that deed with the earth itself, O lord of earth, he roamed fearless and content, having won renown, foremost among men.

**13.42.3**  And the lord deemed that both worlds had been won by him likewise, O Kaurava, through that deed and through his abundant austerity.

**13.42.4**  Then when some time had passed, O delight of the Kurus, there was a giving in marriage of Ruci's sister, with wealth and grain.

**13.42.5**  At that very time a certain divine and lovely woman, bearing surpassing beauty, passed through the air.

**13.42.6**  From her body flowers fell to the earth, not far from that hermitage, fragrant with a divine scent, O Bhārata.

**13.42.7**  These then Ruci of lotus eyes gathered up, O king; and just then a summoner came swiftly on her sister's behalf.

**13.42.8**  For her elder sister, dear son, Prabhāvatī by name, had become the wife of Citraratha, the lord of the Aṅgas.

**13.42.9**  Having bound those flowers in her hair, the fair-complexioned one, being invited, then went, that Ruci, to the house of the lord of the Aṅgas.

**13.42.10**  Seeing those flowers, the lovely consort of the Aṅga lord, the fair-eyed one, then urged her sister to obtain such flowers.

**13.42.11**  Ruci of most lovely face told all to her husband; and the sage approved of all that had been spoken by her sister.

**13.42.12**  Then, O Bhārata, Devaśarman of great austerity summoned Vipula and urged him on for the sake of the flowers, saying, "Go, go."

**13.42.13**  And Vipula, of great austerity, without questioning his teacher's word, said "So be it," O king, and went to that region.

**13.42.14**  In the region where those blossoms had fallen from the vault of the sky, other unwithered flowers also lay there.

**13.42.15**  Then he gathered up those flowers, celestial and lovely, won by his own austerity and divine in fragrance, O Bhārata.

**13.42.16**  Having obtained them, glad of heart and obedient to his teacher's word, he then swiftly set out for Campā, garlanded with campaka trees.

**13.42.17**  In a deserted forest, my son, he saw a pair of beings turning round and round like a wheel, each grasping the other's hand.

**13.42.18**  There one of them moved swiftly, wheeling about in step, but the other did not do so likewise, O king; and thereupon the two fell to quarrelling.

**13.42.19**  "You go too fast," said the one; "No," said the other; and "No, no!" the two of them, my son, then said to each other.

**13.42.20**  As the two thus contended, this oath then arose; fixing their minds upon Vipula, they spoke these words:

**13.42.21**  "Whichever of us two has spoken falsely, may his lot in the world beyond be that of the brahmin Vipula!"

**13.42.22**  Hearing this, Vipula grew downcast of face, thinking: "I, of such fierce austerity—and yet this fate they invoke is a grievous burden."

**13.42.23**  "What sin of mine toward this pair could there be, that a destiny abhorred by all creatures has today been proclaimed for me by them?"

**13.42.24**  Pondering thus, O best of kings, Vipula, his face downcast and his head bowed, brooded upon his own misdeed.

**13.42.25**  Then he saw six other men gambling with dice of gold and silver, filled with greed and glee.

**13.42.26**  As they swore that very oath which the pair had sworn, they too, with Vipula in mind, then spoke these words:

**13.42.27**  "Whoever among us, yielding to greed, should venture to play foul, may he attain that lot which in the world beyond is Vipula's!"

**13.42.28**  Hearing this, Vipula could find no breach of dharma committed by himself before, from his very birth onward, O scion of the Kurus.

**13.42.29**  He brooded then, O king, like fire laid upon fire, his mind consumed with burning at having heard such a curse.

**13.42.30**  While he brooded, my son, many days and nights passed by; and this lay upon his mind—the guarding he had done in the matter of Ruci.

**13.42.31**  "By matching feature with feature and face with face I wrought the deed, and I did not then tell my teacher the truth of it."

**13.42.32**  This, O Kaurava, Vipula then reckoned a misdeed in himself, O illustrious one—and so indeed it was, beyond doubt.

**13.42.33**  Reaching the city of Campā, he gave the flowers to his teacher and, dear to his teacher as he was, honored him duly according to rite.

**13.43.1**  Bhīṣma said: Looking upon his disciple who had returned, Devaśarman of great splendor then spoke these words—hear them, O lord of men.

**13.43.2**  Devaśarman said: What did you see today, Vipula, in that great forest? They know you, O skillful one—your own self too, and Ruci as well.

**13.43.3**  Vipula said: O brahmin-sage, what was that pair, and who were those men, O mighty one, who know me in truth? You ought to tell me of them.

**13.43.4**  Devaśarman said: That pair, O brahmin, know to be day and night; wheeling round like a wheel, they know your misdeed.

**13.43.5**  And those men, O brahmin, who gamble joyously with dice—know them to be the seasons; they too know your misdeed.

**13.43.6**  Let no man of evil soul trust, thinking "None knows me," when he does a sinful deed in secret, O brahmin.

**13.43.7**  For the seasons forever behold a man doing a sinful deed in secret, and so too do day and night.

**13.43.8**  Seeing you smiling with joy yet not disclosing your deed to your teacher, they spoke thus to remind you, as you have heard.

**13.43.9**  Day and night know, and the seasons too know forever, the sinful deed in a man, or the auspicious deed of him who acts auspiciously.

**13.43.10**  Knowing that you did not declare to me that deed of yours, born of transgression and full of fear, they spoke to you thus, O brahmin.

**13.43.11**  And those worlds would befall you, as they befall the doer of sin, had you done that deed of yours and not disclosed it to me.

**13.43.12**  And thus an ill-conducted woman can be guarded, O brahmin; but you committed no offense at all—therein I am pleased with you.

**13.43.13**  But had I seen you ill-conducted, O best of brahmins, I would have cursed you in anger—of that I have no doubt.

**13.43.14**  Women cling to a man, and great is men's desire for them; had you guarded her otherwise, the curse and that fate would have been yours.

**13.43.15**  She was guarded by you, my son, and reported to me as well. I am pleased with you, dear child; blessings upon you—you shall go to heaven.

**13.43.16**  Bhīṣma said: Having spoken thus to Vipula, the pleased and great sage Devaśarman rejoiced, attaining heaven together with his wife and his disciple.

**13.43.17**  This tale, O king, the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya once told me long ago, in the course of a discourse on the bank of the Gaṅgā.

**13.43.18**  Therefore I tell you, O Pārtha, concerning all women: in them both are ever to be seen, the good and the bad alike.

**13.43.19**  Virtuous women, illustrious, esteemed as the mothers of the world, uphold this earth, O king, with its forests and groves.

**13.43.20**  But the unvirtuous, ill-conducted, ruinous to their families and bent on evil, are to be known by the evil marks inborn in their own bodies, O king.

**13.43.21**  Thus by great souls women can be guarded; otherwise, O tiger among kings, women cannot be guarded at all.

**13.43.22**  For these, O tiger among men, are fierce and of fierce vigor; there is none truly dear to them in union and intercourse with men.

**13.43.23**  These are to be wooed and to be won and to be possessed, O bull of the Bhāratas; yet these find no lasting delight in any single man, O joy of the Pāṇḍus.

**13.43.24**  No fondness, and likewise no jealousy, should be shown toward them by men, O lord of people; resting in patience and resting in dharma, let a man enjoy his lot.

**13.43.25**  A man who acts otherwise comes to ruin, O joy of the Kurus; in every case, O tiger among kings, sound judgment is everywhere to be honored.

**13.43.26**  By Vipula alone was the guarding of a woman accomplished; no other in this world of men, O king, has been able to guard women.

**13.44.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: That which is the root of all duties, of offspring and of the household, and of the rites to ancestors, gods, and guests—of this tell me, O grandfather.

**13.44.2**  Bhīṣma said: This indeed, of all duties, is held the most to be pondered, O lord of the earth—namely, to what kind of man a maiden should be given.

**13.44.3**  Having well examined his character and conduct, his learning, his lineage, and his deeds, a maiden should be given, with the pouring of water, to a worthy suitor of good qualities. This, O Yudhiṣṭhira, is the eternal duty of righteous brahmins.

**13.44.4**  He should take in marriage from one fit to give in marriage, and he who gives should give willingly—this is the eternal duty of cultivated kṣatriyas.

**13.44.5**  Setting aside his own preference, when a man is the maiden's own choice, and she who is desired by him is given to him, O Yudhiṣṭhira—that rite those versed in dharma call the gāndharva.

**13.44.6**  Buying her with much wealth and enticing her kinsmen—this, O king, the wise declare to be the rite of the asuras.

**13.44.7**  Slaying and cleaving the heads of those who weep, and carrying off by force the weeping maiden from her home, my son—that is the mark of the rākṣasa rite.

**13.44.8**  Of the five, three are lawful and two unlawful, O Yudhiṣṭhira; the paiśāca and the āsura should never be practiced in any way.

**13.44.9**  The brāhma, the kṣātra, and the gāndharva—these are lawful, O bull among men; whether singly or combined, they may be practiced, herein is no doubt.

**13.44.10**  Three wives may a brahmin have, but two wives a kṣatriya; a vaiśya should take a wife of his own caste; among these the offspring rank equal.

**13.44.11**  The brahmin wife should be foremost, and the kṣatriya wife of a kṣatriya; a śūdra wife may be taken for pleasure—though others say, "No."

**13.44.12**  The good do not approve the begetting of offspring upon a śūdra woman; a brahmin who begets children upon a śūdra woman is enjoined to perform expiation.

**13.44.13**  A man of thirty years should take to wife a girl of ten, still a maiden; or one of twenty-one should win one of seven years.

**13.44.14**  But her who has neither brother nor father, O bull of the Bhāratas, one should never marry, for she is bound by the law of the appointed daughter.

**13.44.15**  A maiden who has reached her courses should wait three years; but when the fourth has come, she may herself win a husband.

**13.44.16**  Her chance of offspring is lost, and her pleasure too, O bull of the Bhāratas; one who acts otherwise becomes blameworthy before Prajāpati.

**13.44.17**  One who is not a sapiṇḍa of his mother and not of the same gotra as his father—such a one should he take; that law Manu has declared.

**13.44.18**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: One man may have paid the bride-price; another may say, "I shall pay it"; another may speak with force; and another may display his wealth.

**13.44.19**  And yet another may be the one who takes her hand—whose, then, is the maiden, O grandfather? For us who seek to know the truth, may you be our eye.

**13.44.20**  Bhīṣma said: Whatever human act is carried forward to its conclusion, its sealing with sacred words is as with a binding formula; but a false utterance therein is a sin.

**13.44.21**  Wife, offspring, officiating priest, and teacher, and disciple and instructor too, deserve punishment when falsely addressed—though others say, "No."

**13.44.22**  For Manu does not commend an agreement made unwillingly; what is false is inglorious and unlawful and provokes the wrath of dharma.

**13.44.23**  There is no fault wholly fixed upon any one man, where such a gift is not properly obtained—she whom they bestow according to dharma, and she whom they buy, O Bhārata.

**13.44.24**  With the kinsmen's consent, let him perform the sacred words and the oblation; thus those formulas avail—never in the case of one not duly given.

**13.44.25**  That compact of sacred words which is made mutually between wife and husband—that, and the one made with the kinsmen, they declare the weightier.

**13.44.26**  By the ordinance of dharma a husband knows his wife as given by the gods; she casts off as false all other speech, divine or human.

**13.44.27**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: When a maiden's bride-price has been received, if a better suitor should come, endowed with dharma, desire, and wealth—should an untruth be spoken here, or not?

**13.44.28**  When fault lies on both sides in that matter, let a man do and practice the better course. This, of all our duties, we hold the most to be pondered.

**13.44.29**  For us who seek to know the truth, may you be our eye; tell us all of this, for I am not sated—let it be told.

**13.44.30**  Bhīṣma said: Knowing that bride-price is not what makes the marriage final, no good man ever exacted it; for the good, intent on a bride-price, never give a maiden at all.

**13.44.31**  But the kinsmen ask, as it were, a bride-price consisting of other good qualities—"Adorn her and take her away," says he who gives willingly.

**13.44.32**  He gives both that gift and her as well; it is no bride-price, and that is no sale. What is received in turn should be given back—this is the eternal law.

**13.44.33**  "I shall give the maiden to you" — when this has not been declared beforehand, there are some who say it, some who do not, and some who must say it of necessity.

**13.44.34**  Therefore, up until the taking of the hand, the two parties make request of one another. We have heard it told that in ancient times the bridegroom for a maiden was bestowed by the Maruts.

**13.44.35**  "A maiden is not to be given to one undesired" — so the sages have enjoined. That, in my judgment, is the root of procreation, which itself is rooted in desire.

**13.44.36**  Having weighed well the many evils that arise from the cohabitation of two who hate each other, hear now how the bride-price never came to be a thing that settles the matter.

**13.44.37**  For Vicitravīrya I brought home two maidens, after I had vanquished all the Māgadhas, the Kāśis, and the Kosalas. One had already had her hand taken in pledge, and being thus claimed, she met with rebuff.

**13.44.38**  "She whose hand has been taken must there and then be released," so my father said; and that scion of the Kurus took home only the other maiden.

**13.44.39**  He inquired further about the other as well, being uncertain of his father's word; for his longing after dharma was exceedingly great — greater even than my father's.

**13.44.40**  Then I myself, O king, desiring to know the right usage, spoke these words again and again: "I wish to understand the established practice in its very truth."

**13.44.41**  When I had spoken thus, O great king, my father Bāhlīka, foremost of those who uphold dharma, made this reply.

**13.44.42**  "If for you the matter is settled by the bride-price and not by the taking of the hand, then let her for whom the price has been received attend upon the husband she has chosen, even up to the parched-grain rite."

**13.44.43**  "For those who know dharma do not declare that to be authoritative which rests on mere words alone — those, that is, for whom the matter is settled by the bride-price and not by the taking of the hand."

**13.44.44**  "What is openly spoken at the giving away is their rejoinder besides; but those who reckon the bride-price as a purchase — those folk do not know dharma."

**13.44.45**  "To such men a maiden is not to be given, nor by them is one of that sort to be wedded; for a wife is in no wise to be bought, nor ever to be sold."

**13.44.46**  "Those folk who buy a woman as one buys a slave-girl, and those who sell — for such greedy men of sinful mind let the matter be settled in that fashion."

**13.44.47**  On this point of dharma the people questioned Satyavān: "In the case of a maiden for whom the price has been received, the one who paid the price has died."

**13.44.48**  "And another would be the one to take her hand — herein lies our doubt concerning dharma. Resolve it for us, O greatly wise one, for you are esteemed among the wise; be you the eye for us who seek to know the truth."

**13.44.49**  To all of them speaking thus Satyavān made reply: "She is to be given where it is desired; herein no debate need be made. Men act so even while the man yet lives; when he is dead, there is no doubt at all."

**13.44.50**  "Let the maiden go in unto the husband's brother, or else let her practice great austerity; remaining ever faithful to him alone, she bears the name of the one who took her hand."

**13.44.51**  "For some it is set down plainly in writing, for others only by degrees" — those who hold discourse together on this matter know this to be the settled conclusion.

**13.44.52**  Where a reply is given before the taking of the hand, that is indeed the all-auspicious sacred formula; but a false utterance is a cause of downfall.

**13.44.53**  The consummation of the hand-taking formulas comes at the seventh step; she becomes the wife of the man who takes her hand, the man to whom she is given with the pouring of water.

**13.44.54**  Having circled the fire according to rule, the foremost of the twice-born wins as his wife one who is compliant, of suitable lineage, given by her brother, and led before the sacred fire.

**13.45.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: If, for a maiden whose price has been received, there is no husband at all, what then should be the right procedure? Tell me that, O grandfather.

**13.45.2**  Bhīṣma said: She would then have the standing of one without a son and without inheritance.

**13.45.3**  But if she should take the bride-price, she becomes, being bought, the woman of the one who paid it; for his sake let her seek to bear offspring by whatever lawful means she can.

**13.45.4**  For her let no one perform any rite whatsoever with sacred formulas.

**13.45.5**  "She chose for herself" — thus Sāvitrī was accepted by her father; this some who know dharma commend, but other folk do not.

**13.45.6**  Yet others did not do this, nor ever did the good men of old; and the conduct of the good is, moreover, the weightier mark of dharma.

**13.45.7**  On this very topic Sukratu spoke his word — the grandson of the great-souled Janaka, king of Videha.

**13.45.8**  "Upon a course of conduct that is wrong, how should there be praise, or further inquiry, or doubt? This the good would censure."

**13.45.9**  "A lapse from dharma is itself a thing unworthy — a demonic dharma. Never have we heard of this manner of thing among men of bygone births."

**13.45.10**  "For the bond of wife and husband, of woman and man, is one of equals; their delight is a dharma shared in common" — so spoke that prince.

**13.45.11**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: Now by what rule is the wealth of men inherited? For a daughter ought to be to her father even as a son.

**13.45.12**  Bhīṣma said: As is one's own self, so is the son; and equal to the son is the daughter. While she, who is one's very self, yet stands, how should another carry off the wealth?

**13.45.13**  Whatever was the mother's marriage gift, that is the unmarried daughter's portion; or else the daughter's son may take the inheritance of a maternal grandfather who has no son.

**13.45.14**  For he offers the funeral rice-ball both to his own father and to his maternal grandfather; between a son and a daughter's son no distinction is here declared in point of dharma.

**13.45.15**  For by offspring born elsewhere a man seeks as it were a son; and a daughter, through a son born elsewhere of her, is even more distinguished.

**13.45.16**  By the rule of the daughter's son I see herein no cause for distinction; and the sons born of women who have been sold belong to the father alone.

**13.45.17**  But envious, most unrighteous, seizers of others' goods, and deceitful are they — sprung from the demonic mode of marriage, crooked of conduct in matters of dharma.

**13.45.18**  On this point those versed in ancient lore, knowers of dharma, recite the verses chanted by Yama, set down in the treatises of dharma, in the bulwarks of dharma.

**13.45.19**  Whatever man sells his own son and desires wealth thereby, or who for the sake of a livelihood gives away his daughter for a price —

**13.45.20**  in the seventh and lowest, most terrible hell called Kāla, that departed one feeds, in that place, on sweat, urine, and dung.

**13.45.21**  In the sage's marriage some call the pair of cattle a bride-price; but that is false. Whether little or much, O king, such a thing is just so much a sale.

**13.45.22**  Even though it has been practiced by some, this is in no wise dharma; and the practices of still others too are seen to spring from greed.

**13.45.23**  And those who enjoy a maiden who is set apart as their dependent — these are doers of sin, and they lie thereafter in blind darkness.

**13.45.24**  Nay, any other human being too is not to be sold — how much less one's own offspring! For of wealth rooted in unrighteousness there is no profit whatsoever.

**13.46.1**  Bhīṣma said: Those versed in ancient lore recite the saying of Pracetas' son: where the kinsmen take nothing for a maiden, that is no sale.

**13.46.2**  That is the honoring due to maidens, and that the most free from cruelty; and all of it should be given back to the maiden, without remainder.

**13.46.3**  By fathers and brothers, by fathers-in-law and husbands' brothers, women should be honored and cherished by those who desire great welfare.

**13.46.4**  If a woman take no pleasure and do not gladden the man, then from the man's lack of gladness procreation does not increase.

**13.46.5**  Women are ever to be honored and cherished, O ruler of men; and where they go unhonored, there all rites are fruitless. That house ceases to be a house in the very hour when its women grieve.

**13.46.6**  Houses cursed by their women, as though cut down by a sorcerer's spell, neither shine nor prosper, being bereft of fortune, O prince.

**13.46.7**  Manu, when about to depart for heaven, entrusted women to the keeping of men — the weak ones, scant in covering, kindly, ever winning by their truth.

**13.46.8**  Jealous, eager for honor, fierce, unfriendly, and unknowing though they be — women deserve honor; honor them, O men.

**13.46.9**  For your dharma rests upon women, and your delights and enjoyments wholly so; let the service, the food, and the consecrations be dependent upon them for you.

**13.46.10**  The begetting of offspring, the rearing of what is born, and the daily course of the world for the sake of joy — behold, all this is bound up with women.

**13.46.11**  And by these, when they are duly honored, you shall attain all your aims. On this the daughter of the king of Videha sang a verse.

**13.46.12**  "For a woman there is no sacrifice, no rite for the ancestors, no fasting; her dharma is service to her husband, and by that she wins heaven."

**13.46.13**  "The father protects her in girlhood, the husband protects her in youth, and the sons in old age; a woman is not fit for independence."

**13.46.14**  These women are very Fortune herself; they are to be well treated by one who desires prosperity. A woman, when cherished and yet held in check, becomes Śrī, O Bhārata.

**13.47.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: O you who know the ordinances of all the treatises, best knower of the duties and aims of kings, you are renowned throughout the earth as one who cuts away doubt utterly.

**13.47.2**  A certain doubt is mine; tell me of it, O grandfather. In this grievous time of distress, whom else should we ask?

**13.47.3**  What a man ought to do, and what is the eternal dharma — all this, O mighty-armed one, you are able to expound.

**13.47.4**  Four wives are ordained for a brāhmaṇa, O grandfather, if he desires their company — a brāhmaṇī, a kṣatriyā, a vaiśyā, and a śūdrā.

**13.47.5**  Among the sons born of all these, O best of the Kurus, which of them, in due order, is entitled to the paternal inheritance?

**13.47.6**  And by which of them, and how much, is to be taken from the father's wealth, O grandfather? I wish this to be told — what division among them is laid down.

**13.47.7**  Bhīṣma said: The brāhmaṇa, the kṣatriya, and the vaiśya — these three varṇas are the twice-born; among these is the rule ordained for the brāhmaṇa, O Yudhiṣṭhira.

**13.47.8**  Through irregularity, or through greed, or through desire, O scorcher of foes, a brāhmaṇa may come to have a śūdra wife; but she is not approved by any sound precedent.

**13.47.9**  A brāhmaṇa who raises a śūdra woman to his bed becomes thereby defiled, and must perform expiation by a means prescribed in the rules.

**13.47.10**  And if children are born of her, the expiation would be twofold, O Yudhiṣṭhira. Hence I shall now declare to you the rule concerning the wealth, O Bhārata.

**13.47.11**  An auspicious bull marked with good signs, and whatever conveyance is most excellent — these the son of the brāhmaṇī shall take as a single share, over and above, from the father's wealth.

**13.47.12**  But the remainder of the brāhmaṇa's property is to be made into ten parts, O Yudhiṣṭhira; and of these the same son shall take four shares of the father's wealth.

**13.47.13**  The son of the kṣatriyā wife is also a brāhmaṇa, beyond all doubt; but by reason of the difference in his mother he is entitled to take three shares.

**13.47.14**  And he who is born in the third varṇa, of a vaiśyā by a brāhmaṇa, shall take two shares of the brāhmaṇa's property, O Yudhiṣṭhira.

**13.47.15**  The one born of a śūdra woman by a brāhmaṇa is declared to be one whose share of wealth is not fixed by right; yet at least a little is to be given to the son of the śūdra woman, O Bhārata.

**13.47.16**  This would be the order for wealth divided into ten parts. But for sons born of wives of the same varṇa one should allot equal shares.

**13.47.17**  The son of a śūdra woman they reckon, owing to his lack of fitness, as no brāhmaṇa; for one born of a brāhmaṇa in the three varṇas becomes a brāhmaṇa.

**13.47.18**  Four varṇas are declared, and no fifth is recognized; yet the son of a śūdra woman may take a tenth part of the father's wealth.

**13.47.19**  But that he may take only if it has been given by the father; what is not given he is not entitled to take. Yet of necessity some wealth must be given to the son of the śūdra woman, O Bhārata.

**13.47.20**  "Freedom from cruelty is the highest dharma" — therefore it is given to him; and wherever he may have been born, it serves only to his benefit.

**13.47.21**  Even if he have but a single son, O Bhārata, or no son at all, to the son born of a Śūdra woman let him give no more than a tenth share.

**13.47.22**  When a twice-born man has a store of food beyond three years' sustenance, with that wealth let him perform sacrifice; he should not amass riches to no purpose.

**13.47.23**  To a woman a portion of wealth amounting to at most three thousand may be given; and that wealth which is bestowed upon her by her husband she may enjoy, but not what is not so given.

**13.47.24**  What women receive as their husband's gift is held to be theirs for enjoyment as its fruit; yet women must in no wise make off with anything from their husband's substance.

**13.47.25**  But whatever wealth has been given by her father to a woman, O Yudhiṣṭhira, the unmarried daughter of a Brāhmaṇa woman shall inherit it; for she is even as a son, O king. She indeed is ordained to be the equal of a son, O delight of the Kurus.

**13.47.26**  Thus has this been set forth among the laws, O bull of the Bhāratas. Mindful of this law, a man should not amass wealth to no purpose.

**13.47.27**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: If the son born of a Brāhmaṇa upon a Śūdra woman is declared to have no claim to inheritance, on what distinction is even a tenth share assigned to him?

**13.47.28**  A son begotten by a Brāhmaṇa upon a Brāhmaṇa woman is, beyond doubt, a Brāhmaṇa; and so too is the son begotten upon a Kṣatriya woman, and likewise upon a Vaiśya woman.

**13.47.29**  Why then should they receive unequal shares, O best of kings, when all three of these classes have been declared by you to be Brāhmaṇas?

**13.47.30**  Bhīṣma said: Though by one and the same name 'wife' is wives spoken of in the world, O scorcher of foes, even under that single name there exists a very great distinction.

**13.47.31**  Should a man, having first taken three wives, afterward wed a Brāhmaṇa woman, she shall be the foremost, she the one to be honored, and she the worthiest of them all.

**13.47.32**  The husband's bathing and adorning, the cleansing of his teeth and the anointing of his eyes, the offerings to gods and to the ancestors, and whatever else of sacred duty may arise in the house—

**13.47.33**  so long as she is present, no other wife may ever perform these; the Brāhmaṇa woman alone shall do them for the Brāhmaṇa, O Yudhiṣṭhira.

**13.47.34**  Food and drink, garlands, garments, and ornaments—these should be given by the husband to the Brāhmaṇa wife, for she is the worthiest of all.

**13.47.35**  And in the treatise declared by Manu, O delight of the Kurus, there too, O great king, this eternal law is seen to hold.

**13.47.36**  But should a man act otherwise, out of mere desire, O Yudhiṣṭhira, then he becomes like that Brāhmaṇa-Caṇḍāla seen of old—even so does he become.

**13.47.37**  The son who is of equal standing born of a Brāhmaṇa woman and the son born of a Kṣatriya woman—between these, O king, there is no difference of class, in respect of either.

**13.47.38**  Yet by birth the Kṣatriya woman is not in the world the equal of the Brāhmaṇa woman. The eldest son of the Brāhmaṇa woman shall receive the greater portion, O best of kings; and a yet greater portion shall be taken by him out of the father's wealth, O Yudhiṣṭhira.

**13.47.39**  As the Kṣatriya woman can never be the equal of the Brāhmaṇa woman, so the Vaiśya woman can never be the equal of the Kṣatriya woman.

**13.47.40**  Prosperity and sovereignty and the treasury are ordained for the Kṣatriyas, O Yudhiṣṭhira; and to them, O king, is the earth seen allotted, bounded by the sea.

**13.47.41**  For the Kṣatriya, by his own proper duty, attains abundant prosperity. The king is the wielder of the rod of justice, O king; protection lies nowhere but with the Kṣatriya.

**13.47.42**  For the Brāhmaṇas are most blessed, the very deities of the gods themselves. Toward them let the king conduct himself with worship, as the ordinance prescribes.

**13.47.43**  Knowing the everlasting, imperishable law laid down by the sages, the Kṣatriya, by his own proper duty, protects the people when their rights are being violated.

**13.47.44**  When wealth and wives are being carried off on every side by robbers, the king becomes the deliverer of all the classes alike.

**13.47.45**  The son of the Kṣatriya woman shall be the greater, without doubt, over the son of the Vaiśya woman; and by him too a greater share is to be taken out of the father's wealth, O Yudhiṣṭhira.

**13.47.46**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: You have duly spoken, O king, concerning the property of a Brāhmaṇa, O grandsire; but for the other classes, how is the division ordained?

**13.47.47**  Bhīṣma said: For a Kṣatriya too, two wives are ordained, O delight of the Kurus; a third may be a Śūdra woman, though she is not held to be such by the rule of precedent.

**13.47.48**  This same order shall hold for the Kṣatriyas, O Yudhiṣṭhira; the property of a Kṣatriya is to be divided in eight parts, O Yudhiṣṭhira.

**13.47.49**  The son of the Kṣatriya woman shall take four shares of the father's wealth; and whatever of the father's belongs to the spoils of war, that too he shall take.

**13.47.50**  The son of the Vaiśya woman shall take three shares, and the son of the Śūdra woman the eighth; he too may take what was given by the father, but he is not entitled to take what was not given.

**13.47.51**  For a Vaiśya there shall be but one wife, O delight of the Kurus; or a second may be a Śūdra woman, though she is not held to be such by the rule of precedent.

**13.47.52**  For a Vaiśya who lives with a Vaiśya woman, O bull of the Bhāratas, and with a Śūdra woman as well, O son of Kuntī, the division between their offspring is thus declared.

**13.47.53**  The property of a Vaiśya is to be divided fivefold, O bull of the Bhāratas; and the apportionment among the offspring of those two I shall declare, O lord of men.

**13.47.54**  By the son of the Vaiśya woman four shares of the father's wealth are to be taken; the fifth share shall fall to the son of the Śūdra woman, O Bhārata.

**13.47.55**  He too may take what was given by the father, but he is not entitled to take what was not given. Thus a Śūdra born of the three higher classes becomes one to whom wealth must be apportioned.

**13.47.56**  For a Śūdra the wife shall be of his own class alone, and none other in any wise. For a Śūdra the shares shall be equal, even were there a hundred sons.

**13.47.57**  Among sons born of wives of the same class, without distinction, in every one of the classes an equal share in the wealth is ordained.

**13.47.58**  The eldest's portion shall be the foremost—the one share that is preeminent. This is the rule of inheritance, O Pārtha, declared of old by the Self-existent One.

**13.47.59**  Among sons born of wives of the same class there is yet another distinction, O king, arising from the precedence of the marriage: the earlier-born, the earlier, is held the superior.

**13.47.60**  Even among sons of equal standing the eldest shall take the one preeminent share, the middle son a middling portion, and the youngest the least.

**13.47.61**  Thus, in all the births, those of the same class as the father have attained the foremost rank. This too the great sage Kāśyapa, son of Marīci, declared.

**13.48.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: Whether from the pursuit of gain, or from desire, or from uncertainty regarding the classes, or even from ignorance of the classes, there arises a confusion of classes.

**13.48.2**  For those born in this manner in the confusion of classes, what is their duty, what their occupations? Tell me that, O grandsire.

**13.48.3**  Bhīṣma said: In the very beginning, for the sake of sacrifice, Prajāpati brought forth the four classes alone, and the occupations belonging to those four classes.

**13.48.4**  Four are the wives of a Brāhmaṇa; of two of them a son of his own self is born, while of the two lower, in order of rank, are born sons taking the class of the mother.

**13.48.5**  This son of the Brāhmaṇa, sprung as it were from a living corpse, the son of the Śūdra woman, they call a Pāraśava. Let him be a servant of his own family, and let him never forsake his own proper conduct.

**13.48.6**  Weighing well every means, he should uphold the lineage of his own family—whether elder or younger, whoever of the twice-born be devoted to service and given to charity.

**13.48.7**  By a Kṣatriya's union there are three wives; of two of them a son of his own self is born, while of the third, a lower-class son is begotten, a Śūdra known as the Ugra.

**13.48.8**  And of a Vaiśya there are two wives; of both of them a son of his own self is born. The Śūdra has but one wife, a Śūdra woman, and of her a Śūdra alone is born.

**13.48.9**  But baser than these is the lowest, the violator of his elders' wives, who begets an outcast class, despised by the four classes.

**13.48.10**  A degraded Kṣatriya, fallen from his sacraments, begets the Sūta, intent on the chanting of hymns, who is unfit to have sacrifices offered for him; a degraded Vaiśya begets the Vaidehaka, a discarded Maudgalya.

**13.48.11**  A Śūdra begets upon a Brāhmaṇa woman the Caṇḍāla, exceedingly fierce, the slayer of the condemned, who dwells beyond the village—such are these defilers of their lineage. These, O best of the wise, O lord, are born of the confusion of classes.

**13.48.12**  From a Vaiśya is born of a Kṣatriya woman, through transgression, the Māgadha, a bard who lives by his words; from a Śūdra is born the Niṣāda, a slayer of fish.

**13.48.13**  From a Śūdra upon a Vaiśya woman is born the Āyogava, of village calling, a carpenter who lives in the forest, from whom no Brāhmaṇa may accept a gift.

**13.48.14**  These too beget, within their own kind, offspring of like class; but upon women of lower womb the higher beget offspring taking the mother's class.

**13.48.15**  As among the four classes a son of one's own self is born of two of the wives, so the outcast classes too are chiefly born from union with the class next adjoining.

**13.48.16**  They too beget, within their own kind, offspring of like class; but consorting one with another, they beget the despised.

**13.48.17**  And as a Śūdra begets upon a Brāhmaṇa woman an outcast creature, so from one more outcast still is an outcast born, sprung from beyond the four classes.

**13.48.18**  Living thus against the grain, from the outcast is begotten the yet more outcast; from the low are born the lower classes, fifteen in number are they.

**13.48.19**  And by union with the forbidden the confusion of classes proceeds. Among the fallen here are born the Sairandhras and, among the Māgadhas, one skilled in adorning and attendance, no slave yet living by a slave's labor.

**13.48.20**  From this is begotten the Āyogava, living in the forest by snares; and the Vaidehaka begets the Maireyaka, a brewer, and likewise the Mādhuka.

**13.48.21**  The Niṣāda begets the Mudgara and the Dāśa, who lives by the boat; and the Caṇḍāla begets the Mṛtapa and the Śvapāka, exceedingly abhorred.

**13.48.22**  The Māgadhī bears four sons, cruel ones living by deceit; and a cook who makes flesh savory, called the Saugandha.

**13.48.23**  From the Vaidehaka is born one most sinful, cruel, who lives off his wife; and from the Niṣāda the Madranābha, who journeys in carts drawn by asses.

**13.48.24**  And from the Caṇḍāla is born the Pulkasa, who feeds on asses, horses, and elephants, who is clad in the garments of the dead, and who eats from broken vessels.

**13.48.25**  Upon women of the Āyogava and other lower classes are born those three; from the Vaidehaka, the Kṣudra and the Andhra, whose dwelling lies outside the village.

**13.48.26**  The Kārāvara is begotten by a Carmakāra upon a Niṣāda woman; and from a Caṇḍāla is born the Pāṇḍusaupāka, who deals in hides and pith.

**13.48.27**  The Āhiṇḍika is begotten by a Niṣāda upon a Vaidehī woman; and by a Caṇḍāla the Saupāka, whose mode of living is like the Maudgalya's.

**13.48.28**  And a Niṣāda woman bears by a Caṇḍāla a son, the Antāvasāyin, who haunts the cremation ground, cast out even by the outcasts.

**13.48.29**  Thus these are the castes born of confusion, through the transgression of father and mother; whether concealed or manifest, they are to be known by their own deeds.

**13.48.30**  There is a law for the four classes alone, and for no other; among those of the classes who are devoid of law, there exists here no settled name for any.

**13.48.31**  By chance unions, with those excluded from sacrifice and from the company of the good, outcasts are begotten of outcasts, according to their occupation and their station.

**13.48.32**  Crossroads and cremation grounds, mountains and other great trees, they make their own, and ornaments too, and the implements of their craft.

**13.48.33**  Rendering their help, beyond doubt, for the sake of cows and Brāhmaṇas—freedom from cruelty, compassion, truthful speech, and forbearance,

**13.48.34**  and the protection of others with their own bodies—these bring fulfillment even to the outcasts, O tiger among men; of this I have no doubt.

**13.48.35**  A man of understanding should beget offspring only upon women duly proclaimed, according to the teaching, after careful reflection; for a son of base womb drags a man down, as a stone drags down one who would cross the water.

**13.48.36**  Whether a man be unlearned, or again though he be learned, women in this world surely lead astray onto the wrong path him who is the slave of desire and wrath.

**13.48.37**  And the very nature of women is, in this world, a corrupter of men; for this reason the wise do not cleave attached to women.

**13.48.38**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: A man fallen from his class, unrecognized, born of a tainted womb, ignoble though noble in seeming—how, O king, are we to know him?

**13.48.39**  Bhīṣma said: Though one be born of a tainted womb and beset by manifold conduct, purity of birth is to be discerned by his deeds—by the practices observed among the good.

**13.48.40**  Ignobility, lack of right conduct, cruelty, and a nature averse to duty—these reveal, here in the world, the man born of a tainted womb.

**13.48.41**  He takes up either the disposition derived from his father, or that from his mother, or both alike; but one of mixed origin can in no way hold his own true nature in check.

**13.48.42**  Just as a tiger is born resembling its mother and father in form, with its markings, so too a man conforms to his own womb of origin.

**13.48.43**  Though the lineage's stream be concealed, the man whose origin is of mixed birth still cleaves to that disposition, whether in small measure or great.

**13.48.44**  Even of one who walks a counterfeit path, bearing the appearance and conduct of the noble, his own innate character determines for certain whether he belongs to his own class or another.

**13.48.45**  Among beings of varied conduct, devoted to varied works, that which is well-joined in the world—where birth and conduct match—does not fall away.

**13.48.46**  Here a man's body is drawn along by its inner nature—be that nature highest, middling, or lowest; and like delights in like nature.

**13.48.47**  One should not honor even a person of higher standing who is wanting in good character; but a Śūdra of virtuous conduct, knowing dharma, one should indeed honor.

**13.48.48**  A man proclaims himself by his deeds, good and ill, wrought by his own disposition and conduct; and so a man, though his own lineage be lost to sight, brings it again to light by his own actions.

**13.48.49**  Among all these wombs of origin, both the mixed and the others, the wise man should shun those in which he ought not to beget himself.

**13.49.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: Tell me, O best of the Kurus, of the sons of the several classes, each apart—from what kind of woman, and of what kind, are the sons of whom, and who are they?

**13.49.2**  Many conflicting opinions are heard concerning the matter of sons; here, O king, you must cut away the doubt of those who are bewildered.

**13.49.3**  Bhīṣma said: The son born of oneself is to be known, and he who is born next after him; and the son begotten under appointment is to be known, and likewise the son born of one cast off.

**13.49.4**  And the son born to the wife of a fallen man, lawfully united by a husband; and the two sons, the given and the made; and yet another, the son brought with a married bride.

**13.49.5**  And the six born of degradation, and the son of an unwed maiden, and the lowborn—these have thus been declared to you; know them, O Bhārata.

**13.49.6**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: Who are the six born of degradation, and who again are the lowborn? All this, in accordance with the truth, you must expound to me.

**13.49.7**  Bhīṣma said: The sons whom a Brāhmaṇa begets upon the three other classes, O Yudhiṣṭhira, and the two whom a Kṣatriya begets upon the two classes, O Bhārata—

**13.49.8**  and the one whom the man of two classes begets—thus reckoned here, these are the six born of degradation. Now hear likewise of the lowborn.

**13.49.9**  The Caṇḍāla, and the Vrātya and the Vena—the three lowborn of a Śūdra are marked out, born respectively upon a Brāhmaṇa woman, upon a Kṣatriya woman, and upon a Vaiśya woman.

**13.49.10**  The Māgadha and the Vāmaka, the two reckoned as a Vaiśya's, born upon a Brāhmaṇa woman and a Kṣatriya woman; and the Kṣatriya's is but one—

**13.49.11**  the Sūta, marked out as born upon a Brāhmaṇa woman. These are remembered as the lowborn; for the seed that makes a son cannot be made false, O ruler of men.

**13.49.12**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: Some declare the son to be the field-born, others the seed-born; of which of the two are these equally sons? Tell me that, O grandsire.

**13.49.13**  Bhīṣma said: A son may be born of the seed, or, being abandoned, may be field-born; or he may be the adhyūḍha, born when a compact is broken—learn this from me.

**13.49.14**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: The son born of the seed we know; but how comes the field-born to be? And how do we know the adhyūḍha son, born when a compact has been set aside?

**13.49.15**  Bhīṣma said: When a man, having begotten his own son, abandons him for some other cause, the seed is no longer the deciding factor there; that son belongs to the lord of the field.

**13.49.16**  For when a man desiring a son, for a son's sake, takes a woman, O lord of peoples, there the field is the measure, and the son is not reckoned as begotten of his own seed.

**13.49.17**  In another case the son is marked as field-born, O bull of the Bhāratas; for one's own self cannot be slain—this is borne out by the established example.

**13.49.18**  And some son is the made one, recognized merely by adoption; there neither seed nor field is the measure, O Yudhiṣṭhira.

**13.49.19**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: Of what kind is the made son, recognized merely by adoption, where neither seed nor field is found to be the measure, O Bhārata?

**13.49.20**  Bhīṣma said: One whom a man finds abandoned by mother and father upon the road, and whose mother and father are not known—he is the made son.

**13.49.21**  In whom one establishes ownership over the ownerless, and a man of the same class rears him, that son becomes of the same class as his rearer.

**13.49.22**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: How is the sacrament to be performed for him, and after whose manner, and how? And how is a maiden to be given to him? Tell me that, O grandsire.

**13.49.23**  Bhīṣma said: One should perform the sacrament for him as for one's own son, and so according to the rearer's standing.

**13.49.24**  He who, abandoned by mother and father, comes to a man of the same class—for him one should perform the sacrament according to that man's lineage and class, O unfaltering one.

**13.49.25**  Then the maiden is to be given according to that man's class, O Yudhiṣṭhira; and where the mother's class is determined, the rites are to be done by the mother's lineage.

**13.49.26**  The son of an unwed maiden and the son brought with a married bride are likewise to be known as flawed sons; yet the settled rule is that these two also are to be consecrated as though they were one's own sons.

**13.49.27**  And whether field-born or lowborn, those who are the adhyūḍhas—for these too the Brāhmaṇas and the rest should perform the sacrament as for their own sons.

**13.49.28**  This is the settled rule concerning the classes as shown in the books of dharma. All this has been declared to you; what more do you wish to hear?

**13.50.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: What sort of affection arises in the seeing of cattle and in dwelling with them, O grandsire, and what is the great blessedness of cows? Tell me that, O grandsire.

**13.50.2**  Bhīṣma said: Come then, I shall relate to you an event of olden days, O greatly radiant one—the colloquy between Nahuṣa and the great sage Cyavana.

**13.50.3**  Of old, O bull of the Bhāratas, the great sage Cyavana of Bhṛgu's line, having undertaken a dwelling in the waters, became one of mighty vow.

**13.50.4**  Having slain pride and anger, and elation and grief as well, the sage held fast to his vow of dwelling in the water for twelve years.

**13.50.5**  He bestowed upon all beings the highest, most blessed trust, even upon the creatures that move in the water, like the cool-rayed lord the moon.

**13.50.6**  Becoming still as a post, and pure, and bowing to the gods, he entered the water between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā.

**13.50.7**  The most terrible current of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, with its dreadful roar and a swiftness like the rush of the wind, he received upon his head.

**13.50.8**  The Gaṅgā and the Yamunā, and the streams that follow after them, made their reverent circuit around the sage and did not afflict him.

**13.50.9**  Beneath the water the great sage slept, become like a log of wood; and thereafter the wise one stood upright, O bull of the Bhāratas.

**13.50.10**  He became a delight to behold for the creatures that dwell in the water, and the fishes, joyful in heart, came then and nuzzled him; and as he abode there a great span of time passed by.

**13.50.11**  Then, at one time, on a certain occasion, men who lived by fishing came to that region, nets in hand, O greatly radiant one.

**13.50.12**  Many Niṣādas, resolved upon hauling up fish, tall, strong, and bold, never turning back in the waters, came to that region, set upon the work of the net.

**13.50.13**  And they fastened together their net with special care, O lord of men, having reached the fish-filled water, O best of the Bhāratas.

**13.50.14**  Then those fishermen, craving fish, by many contrivances cast their nets over the waters of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.

**13.50.15**  Their net was well-spread, made of new cord, and so fashioned in breadth and length as to be fit for that water.

**13.50.16**  Then, having cast it out on every side—that net so very great, so strong, and so well-woven—they all hauled it in together.

**13.50.17**  Fearless in aspect and full of joy, working in concert one with another, they ensnared therein the fishes and other water-roving creatures as well.

**13.50.18**  And Cyavana, the delight of Bhṛgu's line, surrounded by the fishes, they drew up by chance in their net, O great king.

**13.50.19**  His limbs smeared with the river's moss, wearing a tawny beard and matted locks, his body clung about with clusters of shells, as if covered with strange chambered casings.

**13.50.20**  Seeing him drawn up in the net, that master of the Vedas, all the fishermen then, with joined palms, fell to the ground with their heads bowed.

**13.50.21**  From exhaustion and terror, and from the dragging of the net, and from being hauled onto dry land, the fishes perished.

**13.50.22**  That sage, beholding the slaughter wrought of the fishes, was overcome with compassion and sighed again and again.

**13.50.23**  The Niṣādas said: For the sin that we have done in ignorance, grant us your grace therein. What may we do to please you? Tell us that, O great sage.

**13.50.24**  Bhīṣma said: Thus addressed, Cyavana, standing amid the fishes, spoke these words: Hear with attentive minds what is now my highest wish.

**13.50.25**  Either to the giving up of life, or to being sold, will I go along with these fishes; for I cannot bear to forsake my companionship with these dwellers in the water.

**13.50.26**  Thus addressed, those Niṣādas, trembling exceedingly with fear, all of them with downcast faces, made it known to Nahuṣa.

**13.51.1**  Bhīṣma said: And Nahuṣa, hearing then that Cyavana had come to such a pass, set out thither in haste, together with his ministers and his household priest.

**13.51.2**  Having performed his purification as the rule requires, with palms joined and self subdued, the king announced himself to the great-souled Cyavana.

**13.51.3**  And that king's household priest also honored him—true to his vow, greatly blessed, and godlike, O lord of peoples.

**13.51.4**  Nahuṣa said: What may I do to please you? That you must explain to me. I shall do it all, O blessed one, even though it be most hard to accomplish.

**13.51.5**  Cyavana said: The fishermen who live by fish are joined to great toil; pay them my price, together with the price of the fishes.

**13.51.6**  Nahuṣa said: Let a thousand be given as the price to the Niṣādas, O priest, for the ransom of the blessed one, even as the delight of Bhṛgu's line has said.

**13.51.7**  Cyavana said: I am not worth a thousand—or how do you reckon it, O king? Let a fitting price be given; make your determination by your own judgment.

**13.51.8**  Nahuṣa said: Let a hundred thousand be given at once to the Niṣādas. Might this then be the price? Or does your honor reckon otherwise?

**13.51.9**  Cyavana said: I am not to be valued at a hundred thousand, O bull among rulers. Let a fitting price be given; consider it together with your ministers.

**13.51.10**  Nahuṣa said: Let a crore be given as the price to the Niṣādas, O priest; and if even this is no fit measure for you, let yet more than this be given.

**13.51.11**  Cyavana said: O king, I am not worth a crore, nor even more, O greatly radiant one. Let a fitting price be given; consider it together with the Brāhmaṇas.

**13.51.12**  Nahuṣa said: Let half the kingdom, or the whole of it, be given to the Niṣādas. This I deem to be the price—or do you reckon otherwise, O twice-born?

**13.51.13**  Cyavana said: I am not worth half the kingdom, nor the whole, O ruler. Let a fitting price be given; let it be pondered together with the sages.

**13.51.14**  Bhīṣma said: Hearing the great sage's words, Nahuṣa, worn with distress, then fell to pondering, together with his ministers and his household priest.

**13.51.15**  But there a certain other forest-dweller, who lived on roots and fruits, came to stand near Nahuṣa—a sage born of a cow.

**13.51.16**  That best of the twice-born, addressing the king, said: I shall satisfy the Brāhmaṇa, so that he shall be content.

**13.51.17**  "I would not speak a false word even in jest, much less in a grave matter. Whatever I shall say to you must be carried out without any hesitation."

**13.51.18**  Nahuṣa said: "Let the holy one name a price befitting the great sage, the son of Bhṛgu. Deliver me from this peril, and my kingdom, and my lineage."

**13.51.19**  "For the holy one, when angered, could destroy even the entire threefold world—how much more easily me, who am devoid of austerity and rely only on the strength of my arms."

**13.51.20**  "To one sunk in fathomless waters, together with his ministers and his priests, be you a raft, O great sage. Determine the price."

**13.51.21**  Bhīṣma said: Having heard the words of Nahuṣa, the majestic sage born of a cow spoke, gladdening all the ministers and that king as well.

**13.51.22**  "Beyond all price, O great king, are the twice-born, highest among the social orders, and so too are cows, O protector of the earth. Let a cow be reckoned as the price."

**13.51.23**  And then, O king, hearing the great sage's word, Nahuṣa was filled with great joy, together with his ministers and his household priest.

**13.51.24**  Approaching Cyavana, the son of Bhṛgu, firm in his vows, he spoke these words, O lord of men, as if soothing him with his speech.

**13.51.25**  "Rise, rise, O sage among brahmins! With a cow you have been purchased, O scion of Bhṛgu. This I deem your price, O best of the upholders of dharma."

**13.51.26**  Cyavana said: "I rise, O lord of kings; rightly have I been bought by you, O sinless one. No wealth do I see in this world that is equal to cows, O unfailing one."

**13.51.27**  "To celebrate cows, to hear of them, to give them, and even to behold them, O king—all this is praised, O hero, as auspicious and the remover of every sin."

**13.51.28**  "Cows are ever the root of prosperity; in cows no evil is found. Cows are always food itself, and the highest oblation of the gods."

**13.51.29**  "The sacred utterances svāhā and vaṣaṭ are eternally established in cows. Cows are the very bearers of the sacrifice, and they are the mouth of the sacrifice."

**13.51.30**  "They yield and they bear the nectar, imperishable and divine; they are the abode of immortality, revered by all the worlds."

**13.51.31**  "In radiance and in form, cows are like fire upon the earth; cows are a great splendor indeed, and bestowers of happiness upon living beings."

**13.51.32**  "Wherever a herd of cattle, settled and at ease, breathes freely without fear, it makes that land shine and draws away its evil."

**13.51.33**  "Cows are the stairway to heaven; cows are honored even in heaven. Cows are goddesses who yield every desire; nothing else is held to be higher."

**13.51.34**  "Thus has the glory of cows been proclaimed by me, O bull among kings—yet this is but the telling of a portion of their virtues; their full account cannot be exhausted."

**13.51.35**  The Niṣādas said: "A meeting and a converse with us you have had, O sage; among the good, seven steps together make friendship. Show us your favor, O lord."

**13.51.36**  "As the fire devours all oblations, so are you too, O righteous soul, a fire in the form of a man, blazing with power."

**13.51.37**  "We seek to win your favor, O learned one; bowed low are we. For the sake of grace toward us, let this cow be accepted."

**13.51.38**  Cyavana said: "The glance of one who is wretched, of a sage, and of a venomous serpent burns a man down to the root, as a blazing fire consumes the dry brushwood."

**13.51.39**  "I accept your milch-cow, O fishermen; freed from your sins are you. Go swiftly to heaven, together with the fish drawn up in your net."

**13.51.40**  Bhīṣma said: Then, by the grace of that great sage of purified soul, the Niṣādas, through that word, ascended to heaven together with the fish.

**13.51.41**  Then King Nahuṣa was struck with wonder, beholding the fishermen, and the fish too, ascending to the threefold heaven, O bull of the Bhāratas.

**13.51.42**  Then both the one born of a cow and Cyavana, the upholder of Bhṛgu's line, offered the king his choice of two fitting boons.

**13.51.43**  Then the mighty King Nahuṣa, lord of the earth, well pleased, said "It is excellent," O best of the Bhāratas.

**13.51.44**  Then that king, equal to Indra, took up a firm standing in dharma; urged "So be it," he, well pleased, paid honor to those two sages in return.

**13.51.45**  Then Cyavana, his consecration completed, went to his own hermitage, and the one born of a cow, of great splendor, returned to the site of his own hermitage.

**13.51.46**  And the Niṣādas went to heaven, and so did the fish, O lord of men; and Nahuṣa too, having obtained his boon, entered his own city.

**13.51.47**  "This has been told to you, my son, that which you asked of me: what kind of affection arises in beholding one, and in dwelling together, O Yudhiṣṭhira."

**13.51.48**  "And the great blessedness of cows, and likewise the determination of dharma. What more shall be told, O hero? What is it that you wish to ask in your heart?"

**13.52.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: "A doubt I have, O greatly wise one, vast as the ocean. Hear it from me, O mighty-armed one, and having heard, be pleased to explain it."

**13.52.2**  "Great is my curiosity, O lord, concerning the son of Jamadagni—Rāma, the foremost of the upholders of dharma. Be pleased to explain it to me."

**13.52.3**  "How was this Rāma, whose valor is truth, brought forth? And how, in a line of brahmin-sages, was he born with the dharma of a kṣatriya?"

**13.52.4**  "Recount his origin in full, O king; and how it was that from the Kauśika line, a kṣatriya line, there came to be a brahmin."

**13.52.5**  "Ah, how very great was the power of those two great souls—of Rāma, O tiger among men, and of Viśvāmitra indeed."

**13.52.6**  "How was it that, passing over their sons, this defect arose among their grandsons, leaving the sons aside? Be pleased to explain this to me."

**13.52.7**  Bhīṣma said: On this too they recount an ancient tale—the dialogue of Cyavana and of Kuśika, O Bhārata.

**13.52.8**  Foreseeing this defect of old as it was to come upon his own line, Cyavana the son of Bhṛgu, that bull among sages of great wisdom—

**13.52.9**  —pondering in his mind the whole of it, its merits and defects, its strength and weakness, that ascetic resolved to burn down the entire family of the Kuśikas.

**13.52.10**  Cyavana, coming to that Kuśika, spoke these words: "A wish has arisen in me to dwell together with you, O sinless one."

**13.52.11**  Kuśika said: "Holy one, this is a duty to be shared in marriage, upheld here by the learned; it is spoken of by the wise always at the time of the giving of maidens."

**13.52.12**  "But as for that door of duty which has so far been passed by, O ascetic, that task I shall perform; be pleased to grant me leave for it."

**13.52.13**  Bhīṣma said: Then, taking up a seat for Cyavana the great sage, Kuśika, together with his wife, came to where the sage was.

**13.52.14**  Taking up a water-vessel, the king offered him water for his feet, and performed all the rites of welcome for that great soul.

**13.52.15**  Then that king, the great-souled one, steadfast in his vows and unperturbed, had Cyavana receive the honey-and-curd offering according to rule.

**13.52.16**  Having thus honored the brahmin, he spoke these words: "Holy one, the two of us are at your command. Tell us, what shall we do?"

**13.52.17**  "Whether the kingdom, whether wealth, whether cows, O you of stern vows, and likewise sacrifices and gifts—say the word, and I shall give you all."

**13.52.18**  "This house, this kingdom, and this seat of dharma are yours. You are the king; govern the earth. I am your servant, dependent upon you."

**13.52.19**  When these words were spoken, then Cyavana the son of Bhṛgu, filled with the highest gladness, replied thus to Kuśika:

**13.52.20**  "I desire not the kingdom, O king, nor wealth, nor women, nor cows, nor your lands, nor sacrifices. Let this be heard:"

**13.52.21**  "I shall undertake a certain observance, if it pleases the two of you; and that you both should attend upon me without hesitation."

**13.52.22**  When this was spoken by him, the wedded pair rejoiced, and they answered that sage, "So be it," O Bhārata.

**13.52.23**  Then Kuśika, delighted, led him into a most excellent quarter of the house, and there showed him a beautiful spot.

**13.52.24**  "This is your couch, holy one; dwell here as you please. We two shall strive to bring you delight, O ascetic."

**13.52.25**  Now the sun passed onward while they were thus conversing, and the sage then called for drink and likewise for food.

**13.52.26**  Then King Kuśika, bowing low, asked him: "What kind of food is desired by you? What shall I set before you?"

**13.52.27**  Then he, with the utmost pleasure, replied to the lord of men: "Give me whatever food comes ready to hand," O Bhārata.

**13.52.28**  Honoring that word, the king said "So be it," and the lord of men gave him such food as was at hand.

**13.52.29**  Then that holy one, knower of dharma, having eaten, said to the wedded pair: "I wish to sleep; drowsiness oppresses me, O lord."

**13.52.30**  Then, reaching the sleeping-chamber, the holy one, best of sages, lay down; but the king, together with his wife, remained standing.

**13.52.31**  "I am not to be wakened once asleep," said the son of Bhṛgu then; "my feet are to be massaged, and you two must keep watch through the night."

**13.52.32**  And Kuśika, the knower of dharma, without hesitation said "So be it," and the two did not waken him even at the closing of the night.

**13.52.33**  According to the great sage's command, the wedded pair, intent on his service and self-restrained, then remained so, O great king.

**13.52.34**  Then that holy brahmin, having so instructed the king, slept upon a single side for twenty-one days.

**13.52.35**  But that king, taking no food, together with his wife, O delight of the Kurus, attended upon him with gladness, devoted to the propitiation of Cyavana.

**13.52.36**  But the son of Bhṛgu, the ascetic, rose up of his own accord, and saying nothing at all, that great ascetic walked out of the house.

**13.52.37**  The two of them followed after him, hungry and worn with toil, husband and wife; but the best of sages did not so much as look upon them.

**13.52.38**  Even as the two of them looked on, the upholder of the line of the Bhārgavas vanished, O lord of kings; thereupon the king fell to the ground.

**13.52.39**  After resting a moment, that king of great splendor, together with his queen, then made the utmost effort to search for him once again.

**13.53.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: "When that brahmin had vanished, what did the king do then, and his greatly blessed wife? Tell me that, O grandsire."

**13.53.2**  Bhīṣma said: Not finding that sage, the protector of the earth, together with his wife, utterly spent, turned back, abashed and bereft of his senses.

**13.53.3**  Entering the city, downcast, he spoke not a single word; he brooded only upon that conduct of Cyavana.

**13.53.4**  Then with a vacant mind the king entered his house, and he beheld, upon that very couch, the son of Bhṛgu lying asleep.

**13.53.5**  The two of them, astonished, beholding him and pondering that marvel, became refreshed at the very sight of that sage.

**13.53.6**  Taking their proper places, the two once more massaged him; and then that great sage slept upon his other side.

**13.53.7**  And after that same span of time the mighty one awoke; yet the two, anxious with fear, showed no change of countenance at all.

**13.53.8**  Now the sage, having awakened, said to the two, O lord of peoples: "Let an anointing with oil be given me; I shall bathe," O Bhārata.

**13.53.9**  Promising "So be it," the two, hungry and worn with toil, attended upon him with hundred-times-refined oil of great value.

**13.53.10**  Then, holding their speech in check, the two attended upon the sage as he sat at his ease; yet Bhārgava, of mighty austerities, said it was not enough.

**13.53.11**  When Bhārgava observed that the two remained unmoved, he rose all at once and entered the bathing-chamber; there the bathing appointments, befitting a king, stood already made ready.

**13.53.12**  But the sage, scorning all that, vanished from the very spot once more before the king's eyes; and the royal couple, O bull of the Bhāratas, harbored no resentment.

**13.53.13**  Then, having bathed, the venerable lord, the delight of the Bhṛgus, seated upon a lion-throne, showed himself to Kuśika and his wife.

**13.53.14**  With a glad countenance, King Kuśika, together with his wife, bowed low and unperturbed announced to the sage that the meal was prepared.

**13.53.15**  "Let it be brought," the sage said to that lord of men; and the king, together with his wife, fetched forth that food.

**13.53.16**  Many kinds of meat dishes, and vegetables of many kinds, and preparations richly spiced, and light beverages,

**13.53.17**  varied sweet cakes, and sweetmeats, and the six-flavored relishes, and juices of every sort, and the wild forest fare fit for a sage.

**13.53.18**  And fruits of many kinds, and other foods in abundance—jujubes, iṅgudas, kāśmarya berries, marking-nuts, and banyan figs—

**13.53.19**  whatever food belongs to householders and whatever belongs to forest-dwellers—the king had all of it brought, in dread of the sage's curse.

**13.53.20**  Then all of it was set out before Cyavana; whereupon the sage gathered up the whole of it, along with the couch and the seat,

**13.53.21**  and, having covered it over with fine garments together with the vessels of the meal, Cyavana, the delight of the Bhṛgus, set the whole of it ablaze.

**13.53.22**  Yet the couple, steadfast in their great vow, gave way to no anger; and even as the two looked on, he vanished once again.

**13.53.23**  And in that very place the royal sage stood through that night, with his wife, silent and glorious; nor did anger enter into him.

**13.53.24**  Day after day the dressed food of many kinds, and the finest couches, and lavish baths were furnished in the royal dwelling,

**13.53.25**  and garments of every fashion were procured; and Cyavana could find no flaw therein to seize upon.

**13.53.26**  Then once more the brahman-sage said to King Kuśika: "With your wife, convey me swiftly by chariot to wherever I direct."

**13.53.27**  "So be it," said the king, without misgiving, to that ascetic rich in penance. "Shall it be a pleasure-chariot, O venerable one, or a war-chariot?"

**13.53.28**  Thus addressed by that gladdened king, the sage Cyavana, well pleased, made this reply to the conqueror of hostile cities:

**13.53.29**  "Make ready at once the chariot that you reckon a war-chariot—furnished with weapons, with banners, with a lance, and with a barbed javelin,

**13.53.30**  resounding with a hundred bells, fitted with arrays of pikes, bound about with mace and sword, and supplied with hundreds of choice arrows."

**13.53.31**  Then he, saying "So be it," made ready the great chariot, and set his wife at the left of the yoke and himself at the right,

**13.53.32**  and took up there a goad three-pronged and sharp as an adamant needle at its point. Having given all this over, the king then spoke these words:

**13.53.33**  "Venerable one, where shall the chariot go? Let the delight of the Bhṛgus declare it. Wherever you shall say, O brahman-sage, there shall your chariot go."

**13.53.34**  Thus addressed, the venerable one replied to that king: "From here onward you must go step by step, slowly,

**13.53.35**  so that no fatigue may come to me. Move at my pleasure, you two; I am to be drawn in comfort, and let all the people look on."

**13.53.36**  "No traveler is to be thrust aside; to them I shall give wealth—to the brahmans too who shall beg of me their desires along the way.

**13.53.37**  I shall give it all without remainder, the wealth and the jewels alike. Let this be done in full; do not deliberate, O king."

**13.53.38**  Hearing that word of his, the king then said to his servants: "Whatever the sage may ask, all of it is to be given without hesitation."

**13.53.39**  Then jewels beyond number, women, draught-teams, goats and sheep, gold both wrought and unwrought, and lordly elephants like mountains,

**13.53.40**  and the king's ministers, all of them, followed after that sage; and the whole city became a tumult of grief, struck with anguish.

**13.53.41**  Goaded all at once by the sharp-pointed prod, pierced upon the back and on the hip, the two, unmoved, drew him along.

**13.53.42**  Trembling, gone without food, wasted by fifty nights, the heroic couple drew that surpassing chariot with utmost difficulty.

**13.53.43**  Pierced again and again and grievously, oozing the blood sprung from their wounds, they appeared, O great king, like two kiṃśuka trees in flower.

**13.53.44**  Beholding the two, the townsfolk were utterly given over to grief; yet, terrified by the dread of his curse, they said nothing at all.

**13.53.45**  And all of them said, two by two: "Behold the power of penance! Though wrathful, we cannot so much as look upon this best of sages."

**13.53.46**  "Ah, the might of the venerable great sage of perfected soul! And behold too what fortitude the king, with his wife, displays!"

**13.53.47**  For though spent, with great hardship they drew this chariot onward; yet the delight of the Bhṛgus saw in the two no change of heart.

**13.53.48**  Bhīṣma said: Then, seeing the two unmoved, the upholder of the Bhṛgu line dispensed wealth as Vaiśravaṇa himself might do.

**13.53.49**  In that too the king, glad of heart, did as he was bidden; whereupon the venerable one, that best of sages, grew pleased with him.

**13.53.50**  Descending from that finest of chariots, he released the couple; and having freed them duly, he then spoke these words.

**13.53.51**  In a voice tender, deep, and most serene, Bhārgava said: "Let me grant the two of you a choicest boon; name it," O Bhārata.

**13.53.52**  And that best of sages, the knowing one, touched the two tender ones with his hands, hands like ambrosia, out of affection, O best of the Bhāratas.

**13.53.53**  Then the king spoke: "There is no weariness in us two here; by your power, O Bhārgava, by your very meditation, we are wholly rested."

**13.53.54**  Then the venerable Cyavana, greatly delighted, said to the two: "What I declared before was not spoken in vain; it shall come to pass.

**13.53.55**  Delightful is this spot, this fair bank of the Gaṅgā; for some time, intent upon my vow, I shall dwell here, O king.

**13.53.56**  Go to your own city, my son; rested, you shall return. Tomorrow, with your wife, you shall behold me abiding here, O lord of men.

**13.53.57**  Nor should you give way to wrath: a blessing has drawn near to you. Whatever is wished for, set in your heart, all of it shall come to be."

**13.53.58**  Thus addressed, Kuśika, with inmost soul rejoicing, spoke to that tiger among sages this word fraught with meaning:

**13.53.59**  "I bear no wrath, O greatly fortunate one; by you, venerable lord, I am made pure. We two have become young again, full of beauty and of strength.

**13.53.60**  The wounds you made upon me and my wife with the goad—I see them no longer upon our limbs; I am whole again, together with my wife.

**13.53.61**  And this lady I behold, O sage, like a celestial apsaras, endowed with surpassing beauty, even as I saw her of old.

**13.53.62**  By your grace has all this come to pass, O great sage; yet this is no wonder in you, O venerable one whose valor is truth."

**13.53.63**  Thus addressed, Cyavana then replied to Kuśika: "You shall come here, and with your wife," O lord of men.

**13.53.64**  Thus addressed and given leave, the royal sage saluted him and set forth, endowed with beauty, toward the city, like the king of the gods.

**13.53.65**  Then there came forth to meet him the ministers with the household priests, the men of the army, the courtesans, and all the orders of the realm as well.

**13.53.66**  Encircled by them, King Kuśika, blazing with surpassing splendor, entered the city, gladdened, honored by the bards.

**13.53.67**  Then, having entered the city and performed all the rites of the day, that lord of earth, with his wife, dined and passed the night.

**13.53.68**  Then the two, beholding their renewed youth in each other, rejoiced like immortals freed of age, beautiful of form upon their couch, endowed with that splendor bestowed by the best of brahmans.

**13.53.69**  And that sage too, the increaser of the Bhṛgu line's renown, rich in penance, fashioned by the power of his mind a delightful, flourishing forest, adorned with jewels of many kinds, such as is not found even with the lord of a hundred sacrifices.

**13.54.1**  Bhīṣma said: Then that high-minded king, awakened at the close of night, having performed the morning rites, set out with his wife toward that forest.

**13.54.2**  Then the king beheld a palace all of gold, rich with a thousand jeweled pillars, like a city of the gandharvas; and there Kuśika beheld marvels of celestial design.
