**13.54.3**  Mountains with lovely peaks, and lotus-pools bearing their blossoms, and picture-galleries of many kinds, and gateways, O Bhārata, and ground heaped with fresh turf, paved too with gold.

**13.54.4**  Mango trees in full bloom, ketakas, uddālakas, dhavas, aśokas, and mucukundas, and atimuktakas all flowering,

**13.54.5**  campakas, splendid tilakas, jackfruit trees, and vañjulas too, and karṇikāras in flower—these he beheld here and there.

**13.54.6**  The śyāmā creeper, the vāraṇapuṣpī, and the aṣṭāpadikā vine, set out here and there—these that lord of earth beheld.

**13.54.7**  Trees bearing lotuses and water-lilies, and others blossoming in every season, and palaces shaped like celestial cars, mansions resembling lotuses,

**13.54.8**  and waters cool, and in some places warm, O Bhārata, and seats of varied work, and couches of the choicest kind,

**13.54.9**  divans all of gold, spread over with coverlets of priceless worth, and food to be eaten and to be enjoyed without end, made ready here and there.

**13.54.10**  Sweet-voiced parrots too, and śārikā mynas and bhṛṅgarāja birds, cuckoos and woodpeckers, sandpipers and jungle-fowl,

**13.54.11**  peacocks and wild-cocks, putraka birds and jīvaṃjīvakas, cakora partridges, monkeys, swans, sārasa cranes, and the birds named after the cakravāka,

**13.54.12**  crying out on every side, most charming—these he beheld, and in some places throngs of apsarases and of gandharvas, O king.

**13.54.13**  Others he beheld there embraced by their beloved ones; and then he saw them no more, and again the king saw them once more.

**13.54.14**  The sweet sound of song, and likewise the sound of recitation, and the swans most sweet of voice—these the king heard there.

**13.54.15**  Beholding that exceeding marvel, the king then pondered within his mind: "Is this a dream, a derangement of the mind, or is it truly real?

**13.54.16**  Ah, in this very body have I reached the supreme abode—the holy Northern Kurus, or else Amarāvatī itself!

**13.54.17**  Yet what is this great wonder that I behold?"—so he mused. And even as he mused thus, he beheld the bull among sages,

**13.54.18**  the delight of the Bhṛgus, reclining in that golden car thronged with jeweled pillars, upon a precious, celestial couch.

**13.54.19**  Toward him the lord of men, with his wife, drew near in great joy; whereupon Cyavana vanished once again, and that couch as well.

**13.54.20**  Then in another quarter of the forest he beheld him once more, seated upon a couch of kuśa grass, murmuring his prayers, steadfast in his great vow. Thus, by the power of yoga, the brahman bewildered the king.

**13.54.21**  In an instant that forest, and the throngs of Apsarases, and the Gandharvas, and the trees as well—all of it vanished away.

**13.54.22**  The bank of the Gaṅgā fell silent once more, O king, and became thick with kuśa-grass and anthills, just as it had been before.

**13.54.23**  Then king Kuśika, together with his wife, beholding that great marvel, was struck by that deed with the utmost astonishment.

**13.54.24**  Then Kuśika, filled with delight, said to his wife: "Behold, good lady, what wondrous, exceedingly rare splendors we have seen!

**13.54.25**  By the grace of the foremost of the Bhṛgus—whence else but from the power of austerity? For by austerity is attained that which cannot be won by mere wishing.

**13.54.26**  Austerity surpasses even the sovereignty of the three worlds; for through austerity well practiced this man, whose wealth is austerity, sports as he pleases.

**13.54.27**  Ah, the might of the great-souled Brahmā-sage Cyavana! Should he so wish, by the force of his austerity he could even create other worlds.

**13.54.28**  Brāhmaṇas alone would be born—holy in speech, in thought, and in deed; for who else but Cyavana could here have the power to do such a thing?

**13.54.29**  Brāhmaṇhood is hard to attain in this world, while sovereignty is easily gained by men; for through the power of his Brāhmaṇhood we two were yoked to his chariot like well-matched draught-horses.

**13.54.30**  As the king mused thus, he became known to Cyavana, who, looking upon him, said to him: "Come hither at once."

**13.54.31**  Thus addressed, the king together with his wife approached the great sage, and bowed with his head to that one worthy of reverence.

**13.54.32**  Then the wise sage, having pronounced his blessings upon the lord of men, said to him, "Be seated," speaking gently to him, O bull among men.

**13.54.33**  Then the descendant of Bhṛgu, returned to his natural calm, O king, addressed the monarch in smooth speech, as if refreshing him, O Bhārata.

**13.54.34**  "O king, since you have here rightly conquered the five senses among the five objects, with the mind as the sixth, by that very feat you are released from peril.

**13.54.35**  You have rightly propitiated me, my son, O best of speakers; not the slightest fault, however subtle, is found in you.

**13.54.36**  Give me leave, O king; I shall depart as I came. I am pleased with you, O lord of kings; let a boon be accepted from me."

**13.54.37**  Kuśika said: O blessed one, it was as one standing amid fire that I conducted myself in your presence, O tiger of the Bhṛgus; that I was not burned up—that is boon enough.

**13.54.38**  This is the chief boon I have gained, O joy of the Bhṛgus: that you are pleased with my conduct, and my line is made pure, O sinless one.

**13.54.39**  This is grace enough for me, O brāhmaṇa, and the very purpose of my life; this is the fruit of my kingship, and this my highest austerity.

**13.54.40**  But if you are well pleased with me, O brāhmaṇa, joy of the Bhṛgus, there is a certain doubt in me; that you ought to explain to me.

**13.55.1**  Cyavana said: Let a boon be taken from me; and whatever doubt is in your heart, declare it, O best of men—all of it I shall resolve for you.

**13.55.2**  Kuśika said: If you are pleased, O blessed one, then tell me, O descendant of Bhṛgu—I wish to hear the reason for the dwelling you made in my house:

**13.55.3**  your lying on one side for twenty-one days, your going outside without saying a word, O bull among sages,

**13.55.4**  your sudden disappearance and again your reappearance, and once more your lying down, O brāhmaṇa, for twenty-one days;

**13.55.5**  your departure when anointed with oil, and your eating in my house; and how, when manifold food had been brought together, it was burned by Jātavedas the fire; and how you suddenly set out swiftly in the chariot;

**13.55.6**  and the squandering of my riches, and the apparition of the forest, and of the many golden palaces, O great sage,

**13.55.7**  and the sight of couches with legs of gem and coral, and then again the vanishing of all that—I wish to hear the reason.

**13.55.8**  For in this I am utterly bewildered, brooding day and night, and I cannot arrive at any certainty about all of it; this I wish to hear in full and truly, O you whose wealth is austerity.

**13.55.9**  Cyavana said: Hear all of it without remainder—this thing, and the reason for it; for being so questioned, O king, I cannot leave it untold.

**13.55.10**  What I once heard the Grandsire say at an assembly of the gods, that, O king, hear from me as I relate it.

**13.55.11**  "Through the strife of Brāhmaṇa and Kṣatriya there shall come a mingling of lines; a grandson shall be born to you, O king, endowed with brilliance and might.

**13.55.12**  Therefore, to safeguard my own line, I came to you, O Kuśika, seeking to bring about your extinction, longing to burn up your house.

**13.55.13**  So, having come to you then, O lord of the earth, I said: "I shall undertake a certain observance; let attendance be rendered to me."

**13.55.14**  But I found no fault whatever in your house; by that you live, O royal sage—otherwise it would have been far otherwise with you.

**13.55.15**  With this intent I slept for twenty-one days, thinking, "If anyone should wake me…," O king.

**13.55.16**  When neither you nor your wife roused me from sleep, at that very moment I was pleased with you in my heart, O best of kings.

**13.55.17**  And I rose and went out, thinking, "If you, O lord of the earth, should ask me, 'Where are you going?'—then I would curse you," O lord.

**13.55.18**  And I made myself vanish, and again and again, in your house, taking up yoga, I lay down for twenty-one days.

**13.55.19**  Thinking, "Perhaps, hungry or worn with toil, he will resent me," O lord of men—with this intent I wasted you both with hunger.

**13.55.20**  Yet not the slightest anger arose in your mind, O king, nor in your wife's, O best of men; therefore I am pleased with you.

**13.55.21**  And when I gathered the food and set it ablaze—thinking, "Perhaps out of resentment he will grow wrathful"—that too you endured.

**13.55.22**  Then I mounted the chariot and said to you, O lord of men, "Together with your wife, draw me along"—and that too you did.

**13.55.23**  Without misgiving, O lord of men—and by that too I was pleased with you; even when the squandering of your wealth was done, no anger overcame you.

**13.55.24**  Then, being pleased, O king, I did this once more for you and your wife—that forest; know it for what it was, O ruler of men.

**13.55.25**  And for your delight this showing of heaven was made by me—that divine vision which you beheld in this forest, O king.

**13.55.26**  That region of heaven, O king, you experienced in your own body for a moment, together with your wife, O best of kings.

**13.55.27**  It was to give a glimpse of austerity and of dharma, O lord of men; the longing that arose in you there, O king, that too is known to me.

**13.55.28**  For you long for Brāhmaṇhood and for austerity, O lord of the earth, disdaining the rank of a king and even the rank of Indra of the gods, O monarch.

**13.55.29**  It is as you say, my son: Brāhmaṇhood is hard to attain; where there is Brāhmaṇhood there comes seerhood, and in seerhood the life of austerity.

**13.55.30**  This desire of yours shall be fulfilled: from Kuśika a Kauśika brāhmaṇa shall arise, who, reaching the third generation, shall attain Brāhmaṇhood.

**13.55.31**  Your line, O best of kings, shall through the very brilliance of the Bhṛgus—your grandson shall become a brāhmaṇa, an ascetic, with the splendor of fire,

**13.55.32**  who shall strike fear into gods and men and into the three worlds alike—this I tell you in truth.

**13.55.33**  Take the boon, O royal sage, that lies in your heart; I shall set out on a pilgrimage to the sacred fords, for the time slips by.

**13.55.34**  Kuśika said: This is my very boon today—that you are pleased, O great sage. May it be as you have said: let there be austerity in my grandson, O sinless one, and Brāhmaṇhood for my line, O blessed one; this is the boon I ask.

**13.55.35**  And again I wish you to explain in full, O blessed one: how shall my line come to brāhmaṇa-hood, O joy of the Bhṛgus? And who shall be that kinsman of mine, and who the one esteemed among them?

**13.56.1**  Cyavana said: This must surely be told to you, O bull among men—the very reason for which I came to destroy you, O ruler of men.

**13.56.2**  The Kṣatriyas are ever the patrons whose sacrifices the Bhṛgus perform, O lord of men; yet they shall fall into discord through a cause ordained by fate.

**13.56.3**  And the Kṣatriyas shall slay all the Bhṛgus, O lord of men, cutting them down even to the embryo in the womb, driven by the rod of destiny.

**13.56.4**  Then in our line shall be born one who shall increase the lineage, named Aurva, of great brilliance, with a radiance like blazing fire and sun.

**13.56.5**  He shall give birth to a fire of wrath to destroy the three worlds—a fire that would reduce the earth, with its mountains and forests, to ashes.

**13.56.6**  But after some time that best of sages shall himself quell that fire, casting it into the ocean within the mare's mouth.

**13.56.7**  Upon his illustrious son Ṛcīka, joy of the Bhṛgus, the whole science of archery shall present itself in visible form, O sinless one,

**13.56.8**  for the undoing of the Kṣatriyas, through a cause ordained by fate; and he, having received it, shall pass it on to his son.

**13.56.9**  To Jamadagni, the illustrious, his soul refined by austerity; and that tiger of the Bhṛgus too shall hold that science.

**13.56.10**  And from your line, O righteous one, he shall obtain a maiden, for the raising up of your house, O best of kings.

**13.56.11**  Gaining the daughter of Gādhi, your granddaughter, that great ascetic shall beget Rāma, a brāhmaṇa with the ways of a Kṣatriya.

**13.56.12**  And in your line he shall bring forth Viśvāmitra, son of Gādhi—a Kṣatriya with the works of a brāhmaṇa, in might like Bṛhaspati, deeply righteous, endowed with great austerity, O you of great splendor.

**13.56.13**  Two women shall be the cause of this exchange; by the ordinance of the Grandsire it shall not be otherwise.

**13.56.14**  In the third generation Brāhmaṇhood shall come to you, and you shall become a kinsman of the Bhṛgus, whose souls are refined.

**13.56.15**  Bhīṣma said: When king Kuśika heard the words of the great-souled sage Cyavana, he was filled with joy, and that righteous one spoke this word: "So be it," O best of the Bhāratas.

**13.56.16**  But Cyavana of great brilliance again urged the lord of men to take a boon; and the king said to him:

**13.56.17**  "Surely, even so I shall gladly accept it from you, O great sage: let my line become brahman-like, and let its mind be set upon dharma."

**13.56.18**  Thus addressed, the sage Cyavana answered, "So be it," and, taking leave of the king, then set out upon his pilgrimage to the sacred fords.

**13.56.19**  All this I have told you without remainder, O king—the cause of the kinship between the Bhṛgus and the Kuśikas.

**13.56.20**  And just as it was foretold by the sage, so it came to pass, O king—the birth of the sage Rāma and of Viśvāmitra as well.

**13.57.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: I seem to swoon today as I hear, brooding again and again over this earth bereft of its bands of glorious kings.

**13.57.2**  Having gained kingdoms by the hundred and conquered the earth, O Bhārata, having slain men by the tens of millions, I am consumed with anguish, O grandfather.

**13.57.3**  What shall now be the lot of those noble women who are bereft of husbands, of sons, of maternal uncles, and of brothers?

**13.57.4**  For we, having slain our elders and kinsmen and friends as well, shall surely fall headlong into hell; of this there is no doubt.

**13.57.5**  I wish to yoke this body to fierce austerity, O Bhārata; I wish to be instructed herein according to the truth, O lord of men.

**13.57.6**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard those words of Yudhiṣṭhira, the great-souled Bhīṣma, after examining Yudhiṣṭhira keenly with his discerning mind, spoke to him.

**13.57.7**  Hear the secret and the wondrous thing that I shall declare to you, O descendant of Bharata—by what means a man attains his destined state in the conditions that follow death.

**13.57.8**  By austerity heaven is won, by austerity fame is won; length of life and enjoyments too are gained by austerity, O mighty one.

**13.57.9**  Knowledge, discernment, health, beauty, prosperity, and good fortune as well—all these are attained by austerity, O bull of the Bhāratas.

**13.57.10**  By austerity one obtains wealth; silence bestows knowledge; enjoyments come through giving, and long life through chastity.

**13.57.11**  Beauty is the fruit of non-injury; birth in a noble lineage the fruit of sacred vows; a kingdom befalls those who feed on fruits and roots, and heaven those who feed on leaves.

**13.57.12**  He who lives on milk goes to heaven; by ritual bathing one grows rich in possessions; by service to the teacher comes learning, and by constant offerings to the ancestors comes progeny.

**13.57.13**  By vows of eating only herbs a man becomes rich in cattle; from feeding on grass, they say, comes heaven; from bathing at the three pressings come women, and by drinking only air one gains the merit of a sacrifice.

**13.57.14**  By bathing daily one becomes capable; the twice-born who murmurs his prayers at the two twilights wins a kingdom by mastering the desert wilds, and the vault of heaven by total fasting.

**13.57.15**  For those who sleep upon the bare ground there come houses and couches; through garments of rags and bark come fine robes and ornaments.

**13.57.16**  For the ascetic rich in penance and joined to discipline come beds, seats, and chariots; for one who enters the fire, the world of Brahmā is surely ordained.

**13.57.17**  By renouncing savory delicacies one finds good fortune here; by abstaining from flesh one's offspring become long-lived.

**13.57.18**  He who dwells standing in water becomes a lord of men; the truth-speaker, O best of men, rejoices in the company of the gods.

**13.57.19**  Renown comes through giving, and health through non-injury; by service to the twice-born comes a kingdom, or else abundant twice-born status itself.

**13.57.20**  By the gift of water one's fame becomes everlasting; by the gift of food and drink one is sated to the full in the enjoyment of one's desires.

**13.57.21**  He who speaks gently to all beings is freed from every sorrow; service to the gods bestows a kingdom and a celestial beauty.

**13.57.22**  By the gift of lamplight a man becomes endowed with keen sight; by the gift of fair spectacles he attains memory and intelligence.

**13.57.23**  By abstaining from perfumes and garlands one's renown grows abundant; for those who let their hair and beard grow there comes excellent progeny.

**13.57.24**  He who keeps fasting, the sacred vow, and ablution for twelve years, O king, surpasses even the abode of heroes.

**13.57.25**  By giving a daughter in righteous marriage—along with maidservants and menservants, ornaments, fields, and houses—a man obtains them all in turn, O bull among men.

**13.57.26**  By sacrifices and fasts a man goes to the triple heaven, O descendant of Bharata; and the man who offers oblations and flowers gains an enduring station.

**13.57.27**  The man who bestows a thousand cows adorned with golden horns attains the blessed world of the gods in heaven—so declare the assembled sages and deities.

**13.57.28**  To him who gives a tawny cow draped in cloth, with a bronze milking-vessel and gold-tipped horns, that cow—becoming for him a fulfiller of every wish by all those virtues—returns to the man who gave her.

**13.57.29**  As many as are the hairs upon the cow, so great is the reward the giver of cattle obtains; and he delivers his sons, his grandsons, and his whole line down to the seventh generation in the world beyond.

**13.57.30**  For one who gives to a twice-born a cow of sesame, complete with priestly fee, with fair golden horns, a bronze milking-vessel, and a covering of wealth, the worlds of the Vasus become easy to win.

**13.57.31**  As a ship driven by the wind across the great ocean, so the gift of cattle carries a man across to the world beyond—a man bound fast by his own deeds and falling into a hell of dense darkness.

**13.57.32**  He who gives a maiden in righteous marriage, who bestows land upon a brāhmaṇa, and who gives food according to the rite—he attains the world of Puraṃdara.

**13.57.33**  The man who gives a dwelling endowed with every comfort to a twice-born adorned with the virtues of sacred study and good conduct—for him too the worlds in the northern Kurus are won.

**13.57.34**  By the gift of draught-oxen and likewise of cattle and horses, a man attains the worlds of the Vasus; and they say the gift of silver leads to heaven, while the gift of gold is more excellent still.

**13.57.35**  By the gift of a parasol comes an excellent house; by the gift of footwear, a chariot; by the gift of garments, the fruit of beauty; and by the gift of perfumes a man becomes fragrant.

**13.57.36**  He who bestows upon a twice-born a tree laden with flowers or with fruit gains, without effort, a house rich in women and filled with many jewels.

**13.57.37**  The giver of food, drink, water, and savory dishes obtains all delights to his heart's content; and the giver of shelter and clothing obtains those very same—of this there is no doubt.

**13.57.38**  The man who gives to the twice-born wreaths, incense, perfumes, unguents, bathing-materials, and garlands becomes free from disease, and likewise comely, in the world of kings.

**13.57.39**  The man who gives to a twice-born a house not empty of seed and furnished with couches gains, O king, an excellent abode, holy and delightful and filled with many jewels.

**13.57.40**  The man who gives to a twice-born a bed furnished with fragrant and richly patterned coverings gains, without effort, a wife endowed with beauty, well-supported by kin, and pleasing to the heart.

**13.57.41**  The man who lies down to die as a hero becomes a follower of the Grandsire; than this there is nothing higher—so declare the supreme seers.

**13.57.42**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard those words of his, the delighted son of the Kurus no longer favored dwelling in a hermitage, longing instead for the path of the hero.

**13.57.43**  Then Yudhiṣṭhira, the bull of the Bhāratas, that lord addressed the Pāṇḍavas: "Let the words of the Grandsire find favor with you."

**13.57.44**  Thereupon all the Pāṇḍavas, and the illustrious Draupadī, honored those words of Yudhiṣṭhira, saying, "So be it."

**13.58.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: Among those gifts that are reckoned as made outside the sacrificial altar, which gift do you hold to be the most excellent, O foremost of the Kurus?

**13.58.2**  For my curiosity in this matter is very great, O lord: declare to me that gift whose merit follows after the giver.

**13.58.3**  Bhīṣma said: Freedom from fear granted to all beings, and aid given in time of distress; and that which one gives, the very thing he longs for, to a thirsting suppliant who begs—

**13.58.4**  that gift, after giving which one feels he has truly given, is called the best; for it is the gift whose merit follows after the giver, O bull of the Bhāratas.

**13.58.5**  The gift of gold, the gift of cattle, and the gift of land—these indeed are purifying, and they carry across even the doer of evil.

**13.58.6**  Give these always to the virtuous, O tiger among men; for gifts release a man from sin—of this there is no doubt.

**13.58.7**  Whatever is most cherished in the world, and whatever is most beloved in one's own house—that should be given to a worthy man by one who desires it to become imperishable.

**13.58.8**  He who gives what is dear and does what is dear obtains dear things in the world, and becomes beloved of all beings both here and hereafter.

**13.58.9**  He who, out of pride, does not honor to the best of his power a suppliant who begs—one full of hope and possessing nothing—that man is cruel, O Yudhiṣṭhira.

**13.58.10**  He who shows favor in time of distress even to an enemy who comes wretched and seeking refuge—he indeed is the best of men.

**13.58.11**  To the gaunt and modest man, my son, ruined in his livelihood and sinking down—he who drives away that man's hunger, no other man is his equal.

**13.58.12**  The virtuous who are held back by modesty, worn thin with the care of wives and children, and who do not beg—these, O son of Kuntī, invite by every means.

**13.58.13**  Those who make no entreaty either to the gods or to mortals—worthy men, ever fixed in goodness, living on whatever they happen to obtain—

**13.58.14**  guard yourself against such men, who are like venomous serpents, O descendant of Bharata; sound out those most excellent of the twice-born with respectful words.

**13.58.15**  Invite them ever, O scion of Kuru, with dwellings made ready, complete with servants and furnishings, that bring every desire and comfort.

**13.58.16**  If those righteous men of holy deeds should accept what is hallowed by faith, O Yudhiṣṭhira, deeming it merely a duty to be done—

**13.58.17**  those brāhmaṇas accomplished in learning, accomplished in vows, who live without dependence on others, whose private study and austerity are hidden, and whose vows are firmly held—

**13.58.18**  whatever good you do to them—the pure, the self-controlled, devoted to their own wives—that will establish you in the higher worlds.

**13.58.19**  As the fire-oblation well offered evening and morning by the twice-born, so does the gift given to the twice-born by a man of disciplined soul become.

**13.58.20**  This is your sacrifice spread out, hallowed by faith and furnished with priestly fees—surpassing all other sacrifices. Let it proceed, my son, as you give.

**13.58.21**  An offering to the ancestors is like a gift when made to such men, O Yudhiṣṭhira; by making such offerings and honoring them, one is freed of his debt to them.

**13.58.22**  Those who are never angry with us and never covet even so much as a blade of grass—they are the most worthy of our reverence, and likewise the others who speak kindly.

**13.58.23**  Those others who do not think much of us and do not press themselves forward—they too are to be cherished like one's own sons; reverence to them, and to them freedom from fear.

**13.58.24**  The officiating priest, the household chaplain, and the teacher—these bear the sacred power gently; for even the splendor mingled with kṣatriya might is quenched in the twice-born.

**13.58.25**  Thinking "I have wealth, I am mighty, I am king," do not, O Yudhiṣṭhira, slight the brāhmaṇas in the matter of garments and of food.

**13.58.26**  Whatever wealth you have for the sake of splendor or of strength, O sinless one, with it the brāhmaṇas are to be honored by you who follow your own duty.

**13.58.27**  The brāhmaṇas, living rightly according to truth, are to be saluted by you; let them take their pleasure in you to their ease and to their delight, as sons do with a father.

**13.58.28**  For who else but you, O best of the Kurus, is fit to provide the maintenance of these gracious friends who are content with little?

**13.58.29**  As the duty of women in the world is eternally to take refuge in their husband—he is their god, he their sole recourse and no other—so are the twice-born to us.

**13.58.30**  If the brāhmaṇas, dishonored, should forsake us, my son—seeing the cruel deeds that ever attend the kṣatriya—

**13.58.31**  then, bereft of the Veda, of fame, of the higher worlds, and of sacrifice, what use is life to us? For that all rests upon our recourse to the brāhmaṇas.

**13.58.32**  On this I shall expound to you what the eternal law is. In olden days the kṣatriya waited upon the brāhmaṇa, O king, the vaiśya upon the kṣatriya, and the śūdra upon the vaiśya—so runs the sacred tradition.

**13.58.33**  The brāhmaṇa, blazing like fire, is to be served by the śūdra from a distance, but he may be served with touch by the vaiśya and by the kṣatriya.

**13.58.34**  Attend upon those twice-born, who are gentle of nature, truthful in conduct, and guardians of the law of truth, yet who when angered are like venomous serpents.

**13.58.35**  The fiery energies and austerities of the kṣatriyas who burn with splendor and might—surpassing some, surpassing others, surpassing even those beyond the rest—are quelled in the brāhmaṇas alone.

**13.58.36**  Not my father is dearer to me, nor are you, my son, so dear, nor my father's father, O king, nor my own self, nor my life—

**13.58.37**  and though there is none on earth dearer to me than you, yet even dearer to me than you, O bull of the Bhāratas, are the brāhmaṇas.

**13.58.38**  This truth I speak, O joy of Pāṇḍu, just as it is; and by that truth may I go to those worlds where Śaṃtanu dwells.

**13.58.39**  And may I behold the pure worlds of the good, with the sacred power set foremost; thither, my son, I must go, both soon and for long to come.

**13.58.40**  And I, having beheld such worlds, O best of the Bhāratas, do not repent of what I have done for the brāhmaṇas, O son of Pṛthā.

**13.59.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: Of two men who are alike endowed with good conduct, and equal in learning and in birth—to which of these is the gift more excellent, to the one who does not beg or to the one who begs?

**13.59.2**  Bhīṣma said: A gift bestowed upon one who does not beg is held more meritorious than one given to a beggar, O Pārtha; for the steadfast man is far worthier of honor than the wretch whose soul lacks self-command.

**13.59.3**  The kṣatriya is steadfast in protection, the brāhmaṇa steadfast in not soliciting; the learned and contented brāhmaṇa, firm of resolve, gives delight to the gods.

**13.59.4**  Begging, O Bhārata, they call the resort of the powerless, a kind of seizing; for he who begs ever distresses living beings, like a robber.

**13.59.5**  The one who begs is as good as dead, and the giver dies along with him if he refuses; but by giving, O Yudhiṣṭhira, he keeps that suppliant alive, and himself as well.

**13.59.6**  Freedom from cruelty is the supreme dharma, which is fulfilled in what is given to one who begs; but those who suffer in silence and do not ask, invite them by every means.

**13.59.7**  If such foremost of the twice-born should dwell within your realm, take pains to recognize them, like fires hidden beneath their ashes.

**13.59.8**  Blazing with their austerity, they could consume even the earth; for they are worthy of worship, endowed with knowledge, discernment, austerity, and yoga.

**13.59.9**  Offer worship to those brāhmaṇas, O scorcher of foes, bestowing gifts of many kinds, and coaxing forth those who do not ask.

**13.59.10**  Whatever fruit accrues from the agnihotra well-offered at evening and at dawn, that same fruit is declared to belong to a gift made to one possessed of learning, Veda, and vows.

**13.59.11**  Those brāhmaṇas who have bathed in the close of learning, Veda, and vows, who live without dependence on others, whose private study and austerity are hidden, who are firm in their vows—

**13.59.12**  with pleasing dwellings built for them, furnished with servants and appointments, you should invite those foremost of the twice-born, O son of Kuntī, and with other things they desire.

**13.59.13**  Perhaps they will accept what is hallowed by faith, O Yudhiṣṭhira, thinking only that it must be done—knowers of dharma, seers of the subtle.

**13.59.14**  Perhaps those brāhmaṇas, having eaten, will return to homes with stores laid by, whose wives await them as farmers await the rain-cloud.

**13.59.15**  Let the brāhmaṇas, disciplined celibates, partaking of food at the morning pressing, my child, give delight thereby to your three sacred fires.

**13.59.16**  Let your midday pressing proceed, my child, as you give cattle, gold, and garments; by that may Indra be pleased with you.

**13.59.17**  That is your third, the Vaiśvadeva pressing, O Yudhiṣṭhira, in what you bestow upon the gods, the ancestors, and the brāhmaṇas.

**13.59.18**  Non-injury toward all beings, sharing in every way, self-restraint, renunciation, steadfastness, and truth—let these serve as your concluding bath of the sacrifice.

**13.59.19**  This is your sacrifice spread wide, hallowed by faith, attended with its offerings, surpassing all sacrifices; may it ever go forward, my child.

**13.60.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: Of giving and the rite of sacrifice here, which yields the greater fruit hereafter? Whose fruit is declared the loftier—and to what kind of recipients, how, and when?

**13.60.2**  This I wish to know truly as it is, O Bhārata; learned one, to me who seeks to understand, expound the laws of giving.

**13.60.3**  What is given within the altar-ground, with faith and without cruelty—which of these brings the highest good, my father? Tell me that, grandsire.

**13.60.4**  Bhīṣma said: The work of the kṣatriya is forever fierce, my child; for him the rite of the sacred fires and giving are the purifiers in this world.

**13.60.5**  But the good do not accept gifts from kings who do evil; for this reason a king should worship with sacrifices furnished with well-earned offerings.

**13.60.6**  But if they do accept, let the king give day after day, taking his stand on the highest faith; for this is the supreme purification.

**13.60.7**  Let him, his vows controlled, satisfy with gifts the brāhmaṇas at the sacrifice—the friendly, the good, the knowers of the Veda, endowed with character, conduct, and austerity.

**13.60.8**  Whatever they shall accomplish thereby will become an accomplished deed for you; bring sacrifices to fulfillment for the good, with savory food and ample offerings.

**13.60.9**  Deem yourself to have sacrificed and given; by the act of giving honor those constant in sacrifice, that a share thereof may be yours as well.

**13.60.10**  Support too the brāhmaṇas blessed with offspring and burdened with many to feed; by this one becomes rich in progeny, even as the begetter himself.

**13.60.11**  As many righteous observances as the good keep alive, so many of those men who bear heavy burdens of dependents must likewise be maintained.

**13.60.12**  Prosperous as you are, bestow upon the brāhmaṇas, O Yudhiṣṭhira, milch-cows, oxen, food, a parasol, garments, and sandals.

**13.60.13**  Clarified butter to the sacrificers, and food and viands, O Bhārata, and conveyances drawn by horses, dwellings, and beds.

**13.60.14**  These are to be given—fruitful and easily come by, O Bhārata—once you have marked out the blameless brāhmaṇas worn thin by want of livelihood.

**13.60.15**  Whether in secret or in the open, provide them with a livelihood; for a kṣatriya that is more excellent than the Rājasūya and the Aśvamedha.

**13.60.16**  Thus freed from your sins and made pure, you shall attain heaven, when, having loosed your treasury again, you shall protect your realm.

**13.60.17**  And thereafter you shall attain oneness with Brahman, and wealth besides; guard well the livelihood of yourself and of others, O Bhārata.

**13.60.18**  Cherish your servants and your subjects as you would your sons; and let your care for their welfare and security ever rest upon the brāhmaṇas, O Bhārata.

**13.60.19**  A king who does not protect but seizes, who plunders and gives nothing—that disgrace among kings, that pitiless one, the people, banding together, would do well to slay.

**13.60.20**  The lord of earth who says 'I am your protector' yet does not protect—him should the people unite to kill, like a mad and rabid dog.

**13.60.21**  Whatever evil the subjects commit when left unprotected by the king, a fourth part of that evil the king incurs, O Bhārata.

**13.60.22**  Some say it is the whole; others fix it firmly at a half; but a fourth is our own view, having heard the teaching of Manu.

**13.60.23**  And whatever good the subjects do when well protected by the king, a fourth part of that merit the king obtains, O Bhārata.

**13.60.24**  May all your subjects live in dependence on your life, O Yudhiṣṭhira, as living beings on the rain-cloud, as birds upon a mighty tree.

**13.60.25**  As the rākṣasas live in dependence on Kubera, as the immortals on Indra of the hundred sacrifices, so may your kinsmen and friends live in dependence on you, O scorcher of foes.

**13.61.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: 'This is to be given, this is to be given'—so runs the injunction of scripture, and kings have many things to give; but what gift is the most excellent of all?

**13.61.2**  Bhīṣma said: Surpassing all gifts, the gift of land is proclaimed supreme; for the earth is unmoving and imperishable, yielding desires that have no equal.

**13.61.3**  She yields garments, gems, cattle, rice, and barley; the giver of land flourishes among all beings for everlasting years.

**13.61.4**  As long as the life of the earth endures, so long does the giver of land flourish; there is nothing here higher than the gift of land, O Yudhiṣṭhira.

**13.61.5**  Even a little of the earth the ancients gave, so we have heard; all those people who enjoy the use of land have in truth given land.

**13.61.6**  By their own deeds alone do men live, here and hereafter; the earth, prosperity itself, the great goddess, makes the giver dear to her.

**13.61.7**  That lord of earth who bestows this imperishable gift, on attaining human birth once more, shall himself become a lord of earth.

**13.61.8**  As the gift, so the enjoyment—such is the settled rule in the codes of dharma; let a man either yield up his body in battle or give away this earth.

**13.61.9**  This they declare to be the highest blessing of the warrior kinsmen; the earth, once given, purifies the giver—so have we heard.

**13.61.10**  Even him whose conduct is sinful, even a slayer of a brāhmaṇa or a speaker of falsehood—she alone cleanses of that sin, she alone can release from sin.

**13.61.11**  Even from kings who do evil the good accept the earth, and desire nothing else; for she purifies like a mother.

**13.61.12**  'Priyadattā'—'Dear when given'—is the secret, eternal name of this goddess; either gift or knowledge is dearest to that name of hers. Therefore, no sooner has a king won the earth than he should give it to a brāhmaṇa.

**13.61.13**  By no means may the earth be held by one who is not a lord of the soil; nor should one conceal it through a worthy proxy, nor proceed by stealth. And whoever else might covet land should act in this same way, beyond all doubt.

**13.61.14**  He who takes away a good man's land—he wins no land at all; but he who gives land to the good wins land indeed, and that righteous soul gains great renown both here and hereafter.

**13.61.15**  He whose land the brāhmaṇas, being good, ever govern—his enemies, O king, never come to rule the earth.

**13.61.16**  Whatever sin a man commits, worn thin by want of livelihood, he is cleansed of it by the gift of land—even of land no larger than a cowhide.

**13.61.17**  Even for those kings whose deeds are mixed and whose works are cruel, the supreme gift of land is to be proclaimed a means of purity.

**13.61.18**  That the difference is ever but slight, the men of old held: between one who sacrifices with the Aśvamedha and one who gives the earth to a good man.

**13.61.19**  Even when they have done a good deed, the wise may yet harbor misgiving; this one thing alone is beyond such doubt—the supreme, irreproachable gift of land.

**13.61.20**  Gold, silver, garments, jewels, pearls, and riches—all this, O greatly wise one, the giver of the earth bestows in giving it.

**13.61.21**  Austerity, sacrifice, sacred learning, character, freedom from greed, truthfulness, and worship of teachers and gods—none of these surpasses the giver of land.

**13.61.22**  Those who, devoted to their lord's highest good, give up their lives and are slain in battle, the perfected who have gone to the world of Brahman—even they do not outstrip the giver of land.

**13.61.23**  As a mother ever nourishes her own son with her milk, so does the earth favor the giver with all her savors.

**13.61.24**  The rod that is Death's servant, the most dreadful burning of fire, and the terrible nooses of Varuṇa—none of these draws near the giver of land.

**13.61.25**  The ancestors abiding in the world of the fathers and the gods in the world of the gods—both does that serene soul satisfy who gives away the earth.

**13.61.26**  To the gaunt, the dying, the man wasted in his livelihood and sinking down, a man who gives sustaining land becomes as one who has performed a sacrificial session.

**13.61.27**  As a cow runs to her calf, letting her milk flow freely, so, O highly blessed one, does the earth come to the giver of land.

**13.61.28**  By giving land plowed and sown, bearing seed and yielding fruit, or by giving a noble refuge, a man becomes a granter of desires.

**13.61.29**  The man who makes a brāhmaṇa accept land—one perfect in conduct, who has set up his sacred fires, pure in his vows—does not go to the abode of Yama.

**13.61.30**  As the waxing of the moon comes day by day, so does the gift made of land increase with every crop.

**13.61.31**  On this the knowers of old recite the songs sung by the Earth herself, on hearing which the son of Jamadagni gave the earth to Kāśyapa.

**13.61.32**  'Receive me, give me; having given me, you shall win me again—in this world and in the next, and thereafter once more in birthlessness.'

**13.61.33**  The brāhmaṇa, devoted to Brahman, who knows this utterance, at a śrāddha whose oblations are being offered attains oneness with Brahman.

**13.61.34**  'A mighty quelling am I of malign rites and curses, the calmer of ill-offered sacrifices; once a man has performed the expiation that I am, it purifies ten on either side.'

**13.61.35**  'Whoever knows this is purified, and I myself am likewise the Veda; the source of all beings, the everlasting earth—so am I held.'

**13.61.36**  As soon as a king is consecrated, let this sacred lore be recited to him, that on hearing it he may give the earth and not take it from the good.

**13.61.37**  This, then, is the whole matter, both of the brāhmaṇa and of the king, beyond all doubt; for a king skilled in dharma is the foremost mark of prosperity.

**13.61.38**  Now those whose king is ignorant of dharma and a denier of the sacred order—they neither wake in comfort nor sleep in peace.

**13.61.39**  The people are forever distressed by his misdeeds; and many who would have brought security and prosperity refuse to enter his realm.

**13.61.40**  But those whose king is wise and righteous—they wake in happiness and sleep in deep contentment.

**13.61.41**  Contented by that king's auspicious and noble deeds, his subjects flourish through their own labors, through prosperity and through the rains.

**13.61.42**  He is well-born, he is a true man, he is a kinsman, he is a doer of merit, he is a giver and he is valorous—the one who gives away the earth.

**13.61.43**  Like the Ādityas, those mortals blaze with splendor upon the earth who bestow rich land upon a brāhmaṇa learned in the Veda.

**13.61.44**  As seeds scattered upon the ground spring up, so do desires sprout forth when they are won by the gift of land.

**13.61.45**  Āditya, Varuṇa, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Soma, the fire-eater Agni, and the blessed Lord who bears the trident—all rejoice in the giver of land.

**13.61.46**  Upon the earth men are born, and upon the earth they come to their end; for this fourfold world is constituted of the qualities of the earth.

**13.61.47**  She is the mother and the father of the world, O lord of the earth; there exists no being equal to her, O ruler of men.

**13.61.48**  And on this matter they recount an ancient tale, the dialogue between Bṛhaspati and Indra, O Yudhiṣṭhira.

**13.61.49**  Having sacrificed with a hundred great rites richly endowed with priestly fees, Maghavat questioned Bṛhaspati, foremost of those skilled in speech, on this very matter.

**13.61.50**  O blessed one, by which gift does a man who has gone to heaven thrive in happiness? Tell me that gift which is imperishable and of great worth, O best of speakers.

**13.61.51**  Thus addressed by the lord of the gods, the priest of the celestials, the mightily resplendent Bṛhaspati, replied to him of the hundred sacrifices.

**13.61.52**  The gift of gold, the gift of cattle, and the gift of land, O slayer of Vṛtra—the man of great wisdom who bestows these is released from all his sins.

**13.61.53**  There is nothing higher than the gift of land, O lord of the gods, O master; I hold it to be the most excellent, even as the wise have declared.

**13.61.54**  Those heroes slain in battle who, eager for giving, have gone to heaven—not one of them, O best of the gods, surpasses the giver of land.

**13.61.55**  The heroes devoted to their lord's supreme good, who lay down their lives and are slain in battle and attain the world of Brahmā—even they do not surpass the giver of land.

**13.61.56**  Five forefathers and six who have gone before—the man who gives land delivers all eleven of his line here in this world.

**13.61.57**  He who gives away land strewn with jewels, O Puraṃdara, is freed from all his impurities and is honored in the world of heaven.

**13.61.58**  A king who gives away a flourishing land endowed with all that the heart desires becomes a king of kings; that indeed is the gift unsurpassed.

**13.61.59**  He who bestows the earth of Kaśyapa, furnished with every object of desire—all beings think, 'It is to me that he gives,' O Vāsava.

**13.61.60**  The mortal who gives a cow that yields every wish and grants every desire, O thousand-eyed one, goes to heaven.

**13.61.61**  Rivers that flow with honey and clarified butter, and that bear milk and curds, refresh here, O lord of the gods, the giver of land.

**13.61.62**  By the gift of land a king is freed from the guilt that clings to kingship; for no other gift surpasses the gift of land.

**13.61.63**  He who gives away the earth bounded by the oceans, won by the sword—men tell of him here for as long as this earth shall endure.

**13.61.64**  He who gives a holy land rich in sap, O Puraṃdara—the worlds he has won by the merit of the gift of land never wane for him.

**13.61.65**  By every means should a ruler who ever desires prosperity, who longs for happiness, O Śakra, give land according to the prescribed rite to a worthy recipient.

**13.61.66**  Even a man who has committed a sin, by giving land to a twice-born, casts off that sin as a serpent casts off its worn-out skin.

**13.61.67**  Oceans, rivers, mountains, and forests in their entirety—all this a man gives, O Śakra, when he gives away the earth.

**13.61.68**  Ponds and wells, streams and lakes, oils and every kind of sap—all these he gives when he gives away the earth.

**13.61.69**  Herbs abounding in milky sap, trees laden with flowers and fruit, and forests, stones, and crags—all these he gives when he gives away the earth.

**13.61.70**  Though one sacrifice with the Agniṣṭoma and other rites, complete with their proper priestly fees, he does not attain the fruit that he enjoys from the gift of land.

**13.61.71**  The giver favors ten generations; he who reviles a gift destroys ten; and he who takes back land once given goes down to hell.

**13.61.72**  He who, having promised, does not give, or who takes back what he has given, is bound in the nooses of Varuṇa and tormented by the decree of death.

**13.61.73**  Those who support a brāhmaṇa of the highest order—one who has kindled the sacred fire, ever offers sacrifice, keeps but scant retinue, and loves his guests—do not come near Yama.

**13.61.74**  It should be regarded as a debt owed by the king to the brāhmaṇas, O Puraṃdara; but of the other castes too he should rescue the lean and the feeble.

**13.61.75**  Let no one wrest away land once made over by another, O lord of the thirty gods, to a brāhmaṇa of scant means, O best of the celestials.

**13.61.76**  And the tears that fall from those wretched, sinking brāhmaṇas when their field is seized destroy three generations of the despoiler's line.

**13.61.77**  But he who restores once more a ruler fallen from his realm—his dwelling, O thousand-eyed one, is honored upon the vault of heaven.

**13.61.78**  Land covered over with sugarcane, thick with barley and wheat, abounding in cattle, horses, and beasts of burden, won by the strength of his own arm—

**13.61.79**  —land whose womb holds treasures and which is adorned with every jewel: the man who gives it attains imperishable worlds, for that is to him a very sacrifice of land.

**13.61.80**  Having shaken off all his impurity, cleansed of passion and esteemed by the good, he who gives away the earth is honored in the world by the virtuous.

**13.61.81**  As a drop of oil fallen upon water spreads, O Śakra, so does a gift made in land spread out in crop after crop.

**13.61.82**  Those kings, heroes resplendent in the assembly of battle, who are slain facing the foe at the front of combat, O Śakra—they go to the world of Brahmā.

**13.61.83**  Women given to dance and song, adorned with celestial garlands, attend forever upon the giver of land in heaven, O lord of the gods.

**13.61.84**  He who duly, by the prescribed rite, gives land here to a twice-born rejoices in happiness in heaven, honored by gods and gandharvas.

**13.61.85**  A hundred apsarases, adorned with celestial garlands, attend forever upon the man who is a giver of land, O lord of the gods.

**13.61.86**  The conch, the throne of state, the parasol, fine horses and noble elephants, and heaps of gold—these are the blossoms that spring from the gift of land.

**13.61.87**  Command forever unopposed and the cry of victory besides—these are the flowers of the gift of land; its fruit is heaven, O Puraṃdara.

**13.61.88**  Herbs with blossoms of gold, and lawns of kuśa grass and gold—the man who gives land attains a land that brings forth ambrosia.

**13.61.89**  There is no gift like the gift of land, no elder like a mother, no dharma like truth, and no treasure like giving.

**13.61.90**  Having heard this from the son of Aṅgiras, Vāsava then gave to that son of Aṅgiras this very earth strewn with wealth and jewels.

**13.61.91**  He who recites this hymn in praise of the gift of land at a śrāddha rite—no portion of his offering falls to the rākṣasas or to the asuras.

**13.61.92**  And what is given to the ancestors becomes imperishable—of this there is no doubt; therefore at śrāddhas let a brāhmaṇa recite this to the twice-born as they dine.

**13.61.93**  Thus have I declared to you, O sinless one, that which is the foremost of all gifts, O tiger of the Bhāratas; what more do you wish to hear?

**13.62.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: What gifts in this world should a king desirous of giving bestow upon brāhmaṇas of surpassing merit, O best of the Bhāratas?

**13.62.2**  By what are they at once made content, and what, when content, do they grant in return? Tell me this, O mighty-armed one—the great and holy fruit of such merit.

**13.62.3**  What gift, O king, bears fruit both in this world and in the next? I wish to hear it from you; tell me that in full detail.

**13.62.4**  Bhīṣma said: On this very matter Nārada, who beholds the gods, was once questioned; hear from me as I tell what he then declared, O descendant of Bharata.

**13.62.5**  Nārada said: It is food above all that the gods, together with the hosts of sages, praised of old; for the order of the world and the sacrifices—all rest upon food.

**13.62.6**  No gift equal to food has been or shall ever be; therefore men desire above all to give food.

**13.62.7**  Food gives strength in the world, and the vital breaths are established in food; by food this whole universe is upheld, O lord.

**13.62.8**  From food the householders in this world subsist, and the mendicants likewise; from food springs the breath of life—this is plain to see, and herein is no doubt.

**13.62.9**  Even at the cost of straitening his own household, a man who desires his own welfare should give food to a great-souled brāhmaṇa and to a mendicant.

**13.62.10**  He who gives food to a worthy brāhmaṇa in need lays up for himself the finest of treasures, a treasure for the world beyond.

**13.62.11**  The householder who desires prosperity should honor the weary traveler on the road, the aged and worthy man who has come to his door.

**13.62.12**  Casting off rising anger, well-conducted and free from grudging, the giver of food attains, O king, whatever happiness there is both in heaven and here.

**13.62.13**  Let him never slight one who has come, nor turn him away by any means; even when given to an outcaste or to a dog, a gift is never lost.

**13.62.14**  He who ungrudgingly gives food to a weary man upon the road, one never seen before, attains a great measure of dharma.

**13.62.15**  The man who gratifies with food the ancestors, the gods, the sages, the brāhmaṇas, and his guests, O ruler of men—great is the fruit of his merit.

**13.62.16**  Even one who has done an evil deed, if he gives food to a needy man—and above all to a brāhmaṇa—is not bound by his sin.

**13.62.17**  A gift to brāhmaṇas is imperishable; food given to a śūdra bears great fruit; the giving of food, whether to a śūdra or to a brāhmaṇa, is preeminent.

**13.62.18**  When food is begged of him here by a brāhmaṇa, let him not inquire into the lineage, the conduct, the sacred study, the homeland, or the birth of the one who asks.

**13.62.19**  For the giver of food there grow trees of food laden with the fruit of every desire, whether here or in the world beyond, O king; herein is no doubt.

**13.62.20**  For the ancestors yearn, as farmers yearn for good rain: 'Will our son too, or our grandson, give food on our behalf?'

**13.62.21**  For the brāhmaṇa is a great being who himself begs, saying 'Give'; and whether one gives unwillingly or willingly, by giving one attains merit.

**13.62.22**  The brāhmaṇa is the guest of all beings, the one who eats the first portion offered; he it is to whose house the twice-born come ever, begging alms.

**13.62.23**  And when they depart honored, that household prospers exceedingly; and after death one attains birth in a family of great abundance, O descendant of Bharata.

**13.62.24**  Having given food, a man attains in this world an unsurpassed station; and he who gives the most delicate of foods dwells honored in heaven.

**13.62.25**  Food is the very life-breath of men, for all things rest upon food. The giver of food becomes rich in cattle, blessed with sons, abounding in wealth, and full of enjoyments.

**13.62.26**  He becomes vigorous in life and comely in form as well, O king. The giver of food is in this world a giver of life, and he is called the giver of all things.

**13.62.27**  For when one bestows food, according to the ordinance, upon a guest who is a brāhmaṇa, the giver attains happiness and is honored even by the gods.

**13.62.28**  The brāhmaṇa is indeed a great being who roams about as a field on foot; and whatever seed is sown therein yields a mighty fruit of merit.

**13.62.29**  The gift of food brings joy at once, plainly visible, both to him who eats and to him who gives; whereas all other gifts bear their fruit only out of sight.

**13.62.30**  Know that procreation springs from food, and from food too comes delight, O Bhārata. Know that dharma and prosperity arise from food, and likewise from food comes the destruction of disease.

**13.62.31**  In the ancient age Prajāpati declared that food is verily ambrosia. Food is the earth, the heaven, and the sky; all things rest upon food.

**13.62.32**  When food is wanting, the five elements within the body fall asunder; and the strength even of the strong perishes in this world through lack of food.

**13.62.33**  Receptions and weddings and sacrifices cannot proceed without food, O best of men, and the recitation of the Veda too dissolves away for want of it.

**13.62.34**  For all this, whatever is fixed or moving, arises from food. Therefore, throughout the three worlds, food should be given by the wise for the sake of dharma.

**13.62.35**  For the man who gives food, his strength, vigor, glory, happiness, and renown grow forever throughout the three worlds, O lord of the earth.

**13.62.36**  The auspicious wind, the very breath of living things, gathers water in the clouds; and that water lodged within the clouds Śakra rains down, O Bhārata.

**13.62.37**  And Āditya, the sun, draws up the moisture of the earth with his own rays; and from the sun the wind, the god Prajāpati, draws those essences.

**13.62.38**  And when the water has fallen from the cloud upon the ground, then the goddess Earth, bearer of treasures, grows moist and rich, O Bhārata.

**13.62.39**  Thereupon the crops spring up, by which the world is sustained; and from that, in turn, arises the production of flesh, fat, bone, and seed.

**13.62.40**  Then from that seed living creatures come into being, O lord of the earth; for Agni and Soma are that generative seed, and they nourish the begetting of offspring.

**13.62.41**  Thus food, and the sun, and the wind, and the seed are remembered as one single mass, from which all beings have been born.

**13.62.42**  He who promptly gives food to a needy one come to his house bestows life-breath upon living beings, and splendor as well, O bull of the Bhāratas.

**13.62.43**  Bhīṣma said: Thus addressed by Nārada, I gave food always, O king. Do you too, free of envy and freed of all fever of heart, give food therefore.

**13.62.44**  Having given food according to the ordinance, O king, to brāhmaṇas worthy of it and as is fitting, O lord, you too shall thereby attain heaven.

**13.62.45**  Now hear of those worlds that belong to the givers of food, O ruler of men. In heaven there shine the mansions of those great-souled ones, of manifold shapes and forms and furnished with manifold pillars.

**13.62.46**  White as the orb of the moon, hung with nets of little bells, of the hue of the young rising sun, some standing fixed and some that move.

**13.62.47**  Rising in many hundreds of storeys, having within them pools of water and groves, gleaming like beryl and the sun, and wrought of silver and gold.

**13.62.48**  And trees yielding the fruit of every desire stand set within those mansions, with tanks, avenues, halls, wells, and long ponds on every side.

**13.62.49**  And resounding chariots stand ready harnessed by the thousand; there are mountains made of dainties and viands, and garments and ornaments too.

**13.62.50**  There are rivers streaming with milk, and mountains of food, palaces gleaming like pale white clouds, and couches bright with gold. To these the givers of food attain; therefore be a giver of food.

**13.62.51**  These are the worlds of those great-souled doers of meritorious deeds, the givers of food. Therefore food above all should be given by men upon the earth.

**13.63.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: I have heard your words on the rule for the giving of food. Now tell me of the manner of giving according to the conjunction of the lunar mansions.

**13.63.2**  Bhīṣma said: On this point too they recount this ancient tale, the dialogue between Devakī and the divine sage Nārada.

**13.63.3**  When Nārada, who beheld the gods, had come to Dvārakā, Devakī, who looked upon dharma, then put this question to him.

**13.63.4**  To her as she questioned, the divine sage Nārada then expounded all duly, according to the ordinance. Hear that, O lord of peoples.

**13.63.5**  Nārada said: Under the asterism Kṛttikā, O blessed lady, by satisfying worthy brāhmaṇas with milk-rice mixed with ghee, one attains worlds most excellent.

**13.63.6**  Under Rohiṇī one should give to a twice-born, for the sake of discharging one's debt, choice meats, beans, cooked food, and ghee, with milk to drink afterward.

**13.63.7**  Having given a milch cow together with her calf under the asterism whose deity is Soma, men pass from the world of men to the most excellent world of heaven.

**13.63.8**  Having fasted and given, under Ārdrā, a dish of rice and sesame mingled with oil, a man crosses over difficult straits and mountains sharp as razors' edges.

**13.63.9**  Having given cakes and likewise foods under the fair asterism Punarvasu, one is born renowned and endowed with beauty in a house abounding in food.

**13.63.10**  Having given gold under Puṣya, whether wrought or unwrought, he shines like the moon in worlds that are otherwise without light.

**13.63.11**  He who under Āśleṣā gives silver or a bull becomes freed from every fear and stands triumphant over his foes.

**13.63.12**  Having presented under Maghā vessels filled with sesame, brimming over, a man, blessed with sons and cattle, rejoices both here and in the world to come.

**13.63.13**  At the season of the Pūrvā Phālgunī, having fasted and given to brāhmaṇas dainties prepared with raw sugar, one attains good fortune.

**13.63.14**  Having given duly, in the domain of the Uttarā asterism, rice of the sixty-day kind dressed with ghee and milk, one is exalted in the world of heaven.

**13.63.15**  Whatever gift is bestowed by men in the domain of the Uttarā asterism becomes of great and endless fruit: such is the settled truth.

**13.63.16**  Having fasted and given under Hasta an elephant-chariot drawn by four, one attains the highest worlds, fulfilled in merit and in desire.

**13.63.17**  Having given under Citrā a bull and holy perfumes, O Bhārata, one roams in the world of the apsarases and takes delight in the grove of Nandana.

**13.63.18**  And having given under Svāti the wealth that is dearest to himself, he attains auspicious worlds, and great renown even here.

**13.63.19**  Under Viśākhā, having given an ox and a milch cow yielding milk, and a cart with its yoke-pole, laden with grain and furnished with cloth—

**13.63.20**  —he gladdens the ancestors and the gods, and after death enjoys the endless; he meets with no hard straits and goes to the world of heaven.

**13.63.21**  Having given to brāhmaṇas as prescribed, he obtains the livelihood he desires, and does not meet with hell and other torments: such is the settled truth.

**13.63.22**  Having fasted and given under Anurādhā an outer wrap and another garment, a man is exalted in heaven for even a hundred ages.

**13.63.23**  A mortal who under Jyeṣṭhā gives to brāhmaṇas dark pot-herbs together with their roots gains the prosperity he wishes for and the destiny he desires.

**13.63.24**  Having given roots and fruits to brāhmaṇas under Mūla with a composed mind, he gladdens the ancestors and goes to the destiny he desires.

**13.63.25**  And under the Pūrvā Aṣāḍhā, having fasted, by presenting bowls of curds to a brāhmaṇa endowed with good family conduct and versed to the end in the Veda, one is born after death into a house rich in herds of cattle.

**13.63.26**  Having given under the Uttarā Aṣāḍhā a barley-and-water gruel with ghee and abundant honey and raw sugar, one would attain all desires.

**13.63.27**  And one ever devoted to dharma who, under the conjunction of Abhijit, gives to the wise milk drenched with honey and ghee is exalted in the world of heaven.

**13.63.28**  Having given under Śravaṇa a woolen blanket together with another garment, one journeys in a white chariot through all the unobstructed worlds.

**13.63.29**  Having given under Dhaniṣṭhā with composed mind an ox-drawn carriage fitted with cloth and reins, he straightway attains sovereignty after death.

**13.63.30**  Having given under the conjunction of Śatabhiṣaj perfumes together with aloe-wood and sandal, one attains after death the worlds of the apsarases and fragrances everlasting.

**13.63.31**  And having presented kidney-beans under the conjunction of Pūrvā Bhādrapadā, endowed with the fruit of every kind of food, he is verily happy after death.

**13.63.32**  He who under the conjunction of Uttarā Bhādrapadā gives the flesh of a ram gladdens the ancestors and after death enjoys the endless.

**13.63.33**  He who under Revatī gives a milch cow milked into a bronze vessel—after death she comes, bearing his desires, and waits upon the giver.

**13.63.34**  Having given under Aśvinī a chariot yoked with horses, the best of men is born radiant in a house rich in elephants, horses, and chariots.

**13.63.35**  Having presented under Bharaṇī to twice-born ones a cow made of sesame, a man obtains cattle in great abundance, and renown likewise, after death.

**13.63.36**  Bhīṣma said: Thus was this summary of the marks declared, according to the conjunction of the lunar mansions, by Nārada to Devakī; and she spoke this to her daughters-in-law.

**13.64.1**  Bhīṣma said: Those who give gold give all desires—thus spoke the venerable Atri, the son of the Grandsire.

**13.64.2**  Gold is purifying, pure, life-giving, and, for the ancestors, imperishable—so it was extolled by Hariścandra, the lord of men.

**13.64.3**  The gift of water is the highest of gifts, Manu declared. Therefore one should have tanks and wells and pools dug out.

**13.64.4**  A well whose water flows freely and ever flows well carries away here half the sin of a man's deeds.

**13.64.5**  He whose dug-out reservoir is one where cattle and brāhmaṇas and good men ever drink saves his whole lineage.

**13.64.6**  He at whose place water stands unstinted in the season of summer's heat never meets with hardship, peril, or distress.

**13.64.7**  By the gift of ghee there comes the favor of the venerable Bṛhaspati, of Pūṣan, of Bhaga, of the two Aśvins, and of the Fire.

**13.64.8**  For this ghee is the supreme medicine; this is the best of offerings in sacrifice; this is the best of savory things and the best of fruits.

**13.64.9**  He who desires fruit, who desires fame, and who desires thriving—such a man, pure and self-possessed, should ever give ghee to the twice-born.

**13.64.10**  For him who gives ghee to brāhmaṇas in the month of Āśvayuja, the two Aśvin gods, well pleased, bestow beauty in this world.

**13.64.11**  He who gives to the twice-born milk-rice mixed with ghee—his house the rākṣasas never assail at any time.

**13.64.12**  He who gives waterpots does not die of thirst, is seen to be pleasing of speech, and meets with no calamity.

**13.64.13**  The man who, self-restrained and filled with supreme faith, gives to the foremost of brāhmaṇas obtains ever a sixth share of the merit of their ritual sippings of water.

**13.64.14**  The man who, for the sake of their rites and for warmth, ever gives firewood to brāhmaṇas of good conduct, O king of kings—

**13.64.15**  —for him his aims ever prosper and his manifold undertakings as well; and he blazes in splendor of form higher and higher above his foes.

**13.64.16**  And the venerable Fire is ever well pleased with him; the herds do not forsake him, and in battle too he is victorious.

**13.64.17**  He who gives a parasol obtains sons and prosperity; he contracts no disease of the eyes, and he partakes of a share in the sacrifice.

**13.64.18**  Whoever bestows an umbrella in the hot season or in the rains, no anguish of mind ever arises in him; and from hardship and from peril, O brāhmaṇa, he wins deliverance.

**13.64.19**  Of all gifts, the gift of a cart is the most excellent—thus declared the greatly blessed and venerable seer Śāṇḍilya.

**13.65.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: When a man gives a pair of sandals to a brāhmaṇa whose feet are scorched, what fruit accrues to him—tell me that, O grandfather.

**13.65.2**  Bhīṣma said: He who, with collected mind, bestows a pair of sandals upon brāhmaṇas tramples down all thorns and crosses over every rough place; and he stands triumphant above his foes, O Yudhiṣṭhira.

**13.65.3**  A gleaming carriage yoked with she-mules, adorned with silver and gold, attends upon him, O lord of peoples, O son of Kuntī; and it is as though he had given a cart yoked with trained oxen.

**13.65.4**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: The fruit that is proclaimed in the gift of sesame and the gift of land, in the gift of a cow and the gift of food—tell me of that once more, O Kaurava.

**13.65.5**  Bhīṣma said: Hear from me, O son of Kuntī, what fruit the gift of sesame yields; and having heard it, bestow it duly, O best of the Kurus.

**13.65.6**  Sesame seeds were created by the Self-Existent as the foremost food of the ancestors; therefore by the gift of sesame the company of the fathers rejoices.

**13.65.7**  He who in the month of Māgha gives sesame to brāhmaṇas does not behold the hell thronged with every kind of creature.

**13.65.8**  He who honors the ancestors with sesame worships them with all desired things fulfilled; yet the sesame śrāddha must never be offered grudgingly, against one's will.

**13.65.9**  These sesame seeds sprang forth from the limbs of the great seer Kaśyapa; thence, O lord, sesame attained a divine nature among the offerings of gifts.

**13.65.10**  They give nourishment, they bestow beauty, and they are destroyers of sin; therefore, of all gifts, the gift of sesame is the most excellent.

**13.65.11**  The sagacious Āpastamba, and Śaṅkha, and Likhita, and the great seer Gautama too—all went to heaven by gifts of sesame.

**13.65.12**  Brāhmaṇas devoted to the sesame oblation, all restrained in their pleasures, are reckoned the equals of those who offer the oblation of cow's products and who abide steadfast in their observances.

**13.65.13**  Of all gifts whatsoever, the gift of sesame is held to be supreme; among all gifts, the gift of sesame is here declared imperishable.

**13.65.14**  And of old, when the oblation had been produced, the seer Kuśika, O scorcher of foes, having offered into the three fires with sesame, attained the highest goal.

**13.65.15**  Thus has the unsurpassed gift of sesame been declared, O foremost of the Kurus, together with the rite by which the offering of sesame is here commended.

**13.65.16**  Hereafter learn of this, O great king—how the gods, desiring to perform a sacrifice, came together with the Self-Existent Brahmā.

**13.65.17**  The gods, having assembled before Brahmā and wishing to sacrifice, begged for a portion of earth, an auspicious tract: "Let us perform the sacrifice," O son of Pṛthā.

**13.65.18**  The gods said: O Blessed One, you are the lord of all the earth and of the threefold heaven; with your leave, O greatly blessed one, let us perform the sacrifice, for on unsanctioned ground no one wins the fruit of a sacrifice.

**13.65.19**  For you are the lord of the whole world, both the moving and the unmoving; therefore it is fitting that you grant us your sanction.

**13.65.20**  Brahmā said: I give you a portion of the earth, O bulls among the gods, the tract whereon you shall perform your sacrifice, O sons of Kaśyapa.

**13.65.21**  The gods said: O Blessed One, our wish is fulfilled; we shall sacrifice with the prescribed fees duly rendered—and this very tract the sages have ever frequented and revered.

**13.65.22**  Bhīṣma said: Then Agastya and Kaṇva, Bhṛgu, Atri, Vṛṣākapi, and Asita Devala came to the gods' sacrifice.

**13.65.23**  Then the high-souled gods performed the sacrifice, O unfailing one, and the bulls among the gods brought it to its completion in due season.

**13.65.24**  Having performed their sacrifice, the thirty gods upon Himavat, that loftiest of mountains, made the gift of land a sixth part of that rite.

**13.65.25**  Whoever gives even a span's measure of land, unencumbered, does not sink in times of hardship nor fall into straits.

**13.65.26**  Having given a well-prepared plot for a dwelling, proof against cold, wind, and heat, a man dwells in the world of the gods and is not dislodged even when his merit is spent.

**13.65.27**  The wise man dwells in joy together with Śakra, O son of Pṛthā; and the giver of shelter, he too is exalted in heaven.

**13.65.28**  He in whose house a man born in a line of teachers, learned in the Vedas and of subdued senses, dwells contented—that giver attains the foremost world.

**13.65.29**  Likewise, a great shelter for the sake of cattle, proof against cold and rain, redeems one's line down to the seventh generation, O best of the Bhāratas.

**13.65.30**  By giving farmland in this world, my son, a man would gain prosperity; and by bestowing a tract rich in gems, he would cause his family line to flourish.

**13.65.31**  But one should never give land that is barren and salt, nor land scorched and burnt, nor land bordered by a cremation ground, nor land used for wicked deeds.

**13.65.32**  When a man makes an offering to the ancestors upon a tract of land belonging to another, that funerary rite is despoiled by the fathers of the land's owner.

**13.65.33**  Therefore let the discerning man first buy the land, even a little, and then give it; for the rice-ball offered to the fathers upon such ground becomes everlasting.

**13.65.34**  Forests and mountains, and whatever river-fords there be—all these, they say, are ownerless, for there is no private possession of them.

**13.65.35**  Thus has the fruit of the gift of land been told, O lord of peoples; and now, after this, I shall proclaim to you the gift of a cow, O sinless one.

**13.65.36**  Since cows are higher than all ascetics whatsoever, therefore the god Maheśvara undertook his austerity in their company.

**13.65.37**  These cows dwell in the world of Brahmā together with Soma, O Bhārata; from their midst the perfected brahman-seers seek the supreme goal.

**13.65.38**  With milk, with the clarified offering, with curd, and even with their dung, with their hide, with their bones, with their horns and their hair do they render service, O Bhārata.

**13.65.39**  Neither cold nor heat afflicts them; ever do they do their work; neither rain nor rough weather brings them any distress.

**13.65.40**  United with the brāhmaṇas they go to the highest station; therefore the wise speak of cow and brāhmaṇa as one.

**13.65.41**  At the sacrifice of Rantideva they were appointed as sacrificial victims; thence, O king, the river Carmaṇvatī came to flow from the hides of the cattle.

**13.65.42**  Released thereafter from the state of sacrificial victims, they were ordained for giving away; and whoever gives these to the foremost of brāhmaṇas, O lord of earth, would cross over grievous calamity, even though set in dire straits, O son of Pṛthā.

**13.65.43**  He who gives a thousand cows beholds no hell after death and wins victory everywhere, O ruler of men.

**13.65.44**  "The milk of cows is verily the nectar of immortality," so said the lord of the thirty gods; therefore he who gives a milch-cow gives the nectar itself.

**13.65.45**  The knowers of the Veda know this to be the imperishable oblation-stuff of the fires; therefore he who gives a milch-cow bestows the very means of the offering.

**13.65.46**  This bull, the lord of the cows, is heaven in bodily form; whoever gives him to a brāhmaṇa endowed with virtues is himself exalted in heaven.

**13.65.47**  These are declared to be the very life-breaths of living beings, O bull of the Bhāratas; therefore he who gives a milch-cow gives life-breath itself.

**13.65.48**  "Cows are the refuge of creatures," thus the knowers of the Veda know; therefore he who gives a milch-cow bestows refuge itself.

**13.65.49**  A cow must not be given to be slaughtered, nor to a miser, nor to an unbeliever; nor should a cow be given to one who lives by trafficking in cattle, O bull among men.

**13.65.50**  The man who gives cows to such evildoers goes to the imperishable hell—so the wise have declared.

**13.65.51**  One should not give to a brāhmaṇa a cow that is emaciated, or one whose calf has come to harm, or one that is barren or diseased, or one that is maimed or worn out.

**13.65.52**  He who duly gives ten thousand cows rejoices together with Śakra; the man who gives a hundred thousand wins imperishable worlds.

**13.65.53**  Thus the gift of cattle, the gift of sesame, and the gift of land have been proclaimed; now hear concerning the gift of food, O Bhārata.

**13.65.54**  The gift of food they declare to be foremost, O son of Kuntī; for by the gift of food Rantideva went to heaven.

**13.65.55**  He who gives food to one weary and hungry, O lord of earth, beholds the greatly blessed son of the Self-Existent, O ruler of men.

**13.65.56**  Not by gifts of gold, nor of garments, nor by the gift of horses, O Bhārata, do men win such welfare as the givers of food win here, O lord.

**13.65.57**  Food is verily the supreme substance, and food is deemed the highest prosperity; from food springs life-breath, and likewise vigor, valor, and strength.

**13.65.58**  The man who gives food to the good, ever single-minded, does not fall into straits—thus declared Parāśara.

**13.65.59**  Having duly worshipped, one should present the food to the gods; for whatever food a man eats, O king, that same food belongs to his deities.

**13.65.60**  He who makes a gift of food on the full-moon day of Kārttika, in the bright fortnight, crosses over all straits and, after death, partakes of the infinite.

**13.65.61**  He who, with collected mind, gives food to a guest before he himself has eaten, would surely attain the worlds of those who know Brahman, O bull of the Bhāratas.

**13.65.62**  Though fallen into the direst calamity, the giver of food crosses over; he crosses beyond sin even here, and casts off his ill deeds.

**13.65.63**  Thus has the fruit of the gift of food, and of the gift of sesame, and of the gift of land, and of the gift of cattle been proclaimed.

**13.66.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: I have heard the fruit of giving that you have proclaimed, dear father; but food, in your account, is here especially praised, O Bhārata.

**13.66.2**  And how is the gift of water supreme here, and of great fruit? This I wish to hear in full, O grandfather.

**13.66.3**  Bhīṣma said: Come, I shall recount it to you faithfully, O bull of the Bhāratas; hearken now as I tell it, O you whose valor is truth; beginning with the gift of water, I shall declare it all to you, O sinless one.

**13.66.4**  When a man, having given food and water, then enjoys their fruit—there is, in my judgment, no gift higher than this.

**13.66.5**  From food, dear son, all that bear life come forth in every way; therefore food is called supreme in the world among all gifts.

**13.66.6**  From food the strength and the vital fire of living beings ever increase; therefore Prajāpati has declared the gift of food to be the best.

**13.66.7**  For from Sāvitrī herself, O son of Kuntī, you have heard the auspicious word, whence this is and how this is, at the sacrificial session of the gods, O greatly wise one.

**13.66.8**  When food is given by a man in this world, life-breaths too are given thereby; and than the gift of life-breath no higher gift is known here.

**13.66.9**  For you have heard, O mighty-armed one, that word of Lomaśa as well—what Śibi of old attained when he gave up his own life for the sake of a dove.

**13.66.10**  That same goal one wins by giving food to a brāhmaṇa, O lord of peoples; the givers of life-breath go to a most exalted goal—so have we heard.

**13.66.11**  And food itself arises from water, O best of the Kurus; for without that which is born of water, nothing whatsoever comes to be.

**13.66.12**  Water-born too is the blessed Soma, lord of the host of planets, and the nectar of immortality, and ambrosia, and Svāhā, and Vaṣaṭ as well.

**13.66.13**  Grains and healing herbs, O great king, and the creeping plants are sprung from water—whence the life-breaths of all that bear life come into being, O lord of peoples.

**13.66.14**  The food of the gods is the nectar of immortality, and that of the nāgas is ambrosia; the food of the fathers is declared to be svadhā, and that of the beasts the creeping plants.

**13.66.15**  Food, the wise declare, is the very life-breath of human beings; and all of this, O tiger among men, arises from water.

**13.66.16**  Therefore nowhere is there a gift higher than the giving of water; and the man who would seek his own well-being should give it without ceasing.

**13.66.17**  The giving of water brings fortune, fame, and length of days, O lord of peoples; and the giver of water, O son of Kuntī, stands ever superior even to his enemies.

**13.66.18**  He gains all his desires and undying renown in this world; after death he attains the endless realms and is set free from his sins.
