**13.66.19**  The giver of water, O tiger among men, O greatly resplendent one, having gone to heaven, attains the imperishable worlds — so said Manu.

**13.67.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: Of what kind is the gift of sesame seeds, and of lamps as well, and of food and of garments? Tell me of these once again.

**13.67.2**  Bhīṣma said: On this too they recount an ancient tale, the dialogue of a brāhmaṇa and Yama, O Yudhiṣṭhira.

**13.67.3**  In the Middle Country there was once a great village of brāhmaṇas, set between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā, below the Yamunā mountain.

**13.67.4**  It was renowned as Parṇaśālā and was a place of delight, O ruler of men; and learned brāhmaṇas in great numbers dwelt there in those days.

**13.67.5**  Then Yama spoke to a certain man clad in black garments, red-eyed, with hair standing on end, with the shanks, eyes, and nose of a crow.

**13.67.6**  "Go you to the village of the brāhmaṇas, and going there bring back the one of the Agastya line by gotra, and Śarman by name.

**13.67.7**  He is settled in tranquillity, learned, a teacher, yet little honored; and do not bring back another of his same gotra dwelling beside him.

**13.67.8**  For that other one is of like qualities, equal to him in study and in birth, in offspring, and in conduct — wholly his match in wisdom. Bring back the one I have appointed, for I must do him honor."

**13.67.9**  He went and did the contrary to Yama's command: he seized and brought back the very one whom Yama had forbidden.

**13.67.10**  To him the mighty Yama rose up and did honor, then declared, "Let this man be taken back, and let that other be brought instead."

**13.67.11**  When the King of Righteousness had spoken thus, that twice-born one, weary of his studies, said to the Dharmarāja: "Whatever span of life remains to me, let me dwell it out here, O imperishable one."

**13.67.12**  Yama said: "In no way can I overstep what Time has ordained; I only know who it is that practices righteousness.

**13.67.13**  Go, brāhmaṇa, this very day to your own home, O greatly resplendent one; or speak as you freely wish — what shall I do for you?"

**13.67.14**  The brāhmaṇa said: "Tell me that deed which, done back there, would bring the greatest merit; for you are the standard of all, even of the three worlds, O most excellent one."

**13.67.15**  Yama said: "Hear truly, O sage among brāhmaṇas, the supreme rule of giving. Sesame seeds are the highest gift, and their merit here is everlasting.

**13.67.16**  Sesame seeds should be given according to one's power, O bull among the twice-born; given without ceasing, sesame fulfills every desire.

**13.67.17**  They praise sesame at the rites for the ancestors, for this gift is unsurpassed; bestow it upon the brāhmaṇas with rites performed as the ordinance directs.

**13.67.18**  Sesame should be eaten always, and with it the touching of the body should be performed without fail by those who, with their whole heart, desire well-being in the home.

**13.67.19**  So too water should ever be given and offered to drink — of this there is no doubt; and here one should have lotus-pools, tanks, and wells dug out.

**13.67.20**  This is the rarest of all in the world, O best of the twice-born; water should ever be given by you, for this merit is unsurpassed.

**13.67.21**  And watering-sheds should ever be built by you for men to drink, O most excellent of the twice-born; and even after a meal you should especially offer water to drink."

**13.67.22**  When this had been spoken, he was then led home by that messenger of Yama, and he carried out in full all that command of Yama.

**13.67.23**  Having brought that man home, the messenger of Yama then took Śarman and went, and presented him to the King of Righteousness.

**13.67.24**  The majestic King of Righteousness honored that knower of dharma, and having made his compact with him, sent him back as he had come.

**13.67.25**  To him too Yama gave the whole instruction; and returning, that man did all that Yama had told.

**13.67.26**  Likewise Yama praises lamps, desiring the welfare of the ancestors; therefore the giver of lamps forever carries the fathers across.

**13.67.27**  Lamps should be given always, O most excellent of the Bhāratas; for they are held to abide in the eyes of the gods and of the fathers, O lord.

**13.67.28**  The gift of gems too is declared a very great merit, O ruler of men; for selling them, the brāhmaṇa, the giver of safety, performs sacrifice.

**13.67.29**  Whatever a brāhmaṇa, having himself received, gives to other brāhmaṇas becomes imperishable for both — for the giver and for the receiver alike.

**13.67.30**  He who, abiding in right conduct, gives a gift to be received by such a man — this Manu, the knower of dharma, declared an imperishable merit for both.

**13.67.31**  By the gift of garments, a man devoted to his own wife becomes well-clothed and well-adorned — so have we heard in turn.

**13.67.32**  Cows, and gold, and sesame too have been extolled again and again, O tiger among men, on the strength of the Vedas' authority.

**13.67.33**  And one should make marriages and beget sons; for the gaining of a son, O descendant of Kuru, surpasses every other gain.

**13.68.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: Once again, O best of the Kurus, recount the supreme rule of gifts, O greatly wise one, and the gift of land in particular.

**13.68.2**  A kṣatriya should give land, and a brāhmaṇa by his own proper office should duly receive it; but no other has the right to give it.

**13.68.3**  What may be given by all the varṇas who long for its fruit, or what is enjoined in the Veda — that you ought to expound to me.

**13.68.4**  Bhīṣma said: Three things to be given bear like names and like fruit, yielding here every desired reward — cows, the earth, and Sarasvatī (sacred speech).

**13.68.5**  And he who would impart to a pupil the righteous, sacred speech of Brahman enjoys a fruit equal to the giving of land and cows.

**13.68.6**  Likewise they praise cows, and nothing is to be given higher than they; for their fruit is close at hand and easily had, O Yudhiṣṭhira. Cows are the mothers of all beings, the bestowers of every happiness.

**13.68.7**  He who longs for increase should ever keep cows and circle them to the right; these goddesses are the abode of auspiciousness, and therefore are ever to be revered.

**13.68.8**  For those engaged in the work of tending cows, a god-given impulse is at hand; only that first imperishable syllable, and nothing else, should ever be uttered over them.

**13.68.9**  Whether at pasture or at the watering-trough, the wise man should not vex the cows; for thirsting and gazing upon him, they might destroy a man together with his kin.

**13.68.10**  The dwellings of the fathers and the temples of the gods are forever purified by their dung — what is purer than that?

**13.68.11**  He who for a full year gives a handful of fodder to another's cow before he has taken his own food — that vow grants every desire.

**13.68.12**  For he gains sons, and glory, and prosperity besides; he destroys what is inauspicious and drives away evil dreams.

**13.68.13**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: Of what marks are the cows that should be given, and which should one avoid? To what kind of man should they be given, and to what kind not?

**13.68.14**  Bhīṣma said: To a man of evil conduct, a sinner, a greedy man, a speaker of falsehood, one who has forsaken the offerings to gods and ancestors — to such a one a cow should never in any way be given.

**13.68.15**  But the giver who bestows ten cows upon a mendicant of many sons, a knower of the Veda who has kindled the sacred fire, attains the highest worlds.

**13.68.16**  And of whatever dharma that man performs, and whatever the meritorious fruit thereof, the giver shares a portion of it all; for through him these undertakings come to be.

**13.68.17**  He who begets a man, he who saves him from danger, and he who provides his livelihood — these three are all his fathers.

**13.68.18**  Service to one's elders destroys defilement; honor wins great fame; three sons remove childlessness, and ten milch-cows remove want of livelihood.

**13.68.19**  To one steadfast in the end of the Veda, deeply learned, content in wisdom, his senses conquered, refined, self-restrained and disciplined, who speaks ever kindly to all beings —

**13.68.20**  who out of fear of hunger would do no forbidden deed, who is gentle, self-controlled, and ever hospitable — to such a brāhmaṇa, of like virtue and with his sons and wife, one should grant a livelihood.

**13.68.21**  As great as are the merits of giving a cow to a worthy recipient, so great is the sin in stealing a brāhmaṇa's property; in every circumstance the seizing of a brāhmaṇa's goods, and their wives as well, must be shunned from afar.

**13.69.1**  Bhīṣma said: On this very matter the good recount how, in laying hands upon a brāhmaṇa's property, the great distress was met by Nṛga, O foremost of the Kurus.

**13.69.2**  Long ago, as Dvāravatī was being settled, O Pārtha — so the tradition runs — a great well was found, overgrown with grass and creepers.

**13.69.3**  Men in want of water, laboring there with great effort upon that well whose water was well concealed,

**13.69.4**  saw a lizard of huge body lodged within; and they strove by the thousands to draw it out.

**13.69.5**  Binding it with ropes and straps of leather — that creature like a mountain — they could not haul it up; then they went to Janārdana.

**13.69.6**  "A great lizard sits blocking the mouth of the well, and there is no drawing it out" — so they reported to Kṛṣṇa.

**13.69.7**  Drawn up by Vāsudeva, and asked of his desires, the king Nṛga then made himself known, declaring of old that he had offered a thousand sacrifices.

**13.69.8**  To him speaking thus Mādhava said: "Pure was the deed you did, and not sinful; how then did you come to so wretched a state, O lord of men? Tell me — what is this thing of such a kind?"

**13.69.9**  "A hundred thousand cows, a hundred again and again, eight hundred myriads — so we have heard that you of old gave to the twice-born, O king. Where then has that merit of yours gone?"

**13.69.10**  Then Nṛga said to Kṛṣṇa: "A single cow belonging to a brāhmaṇa, a keeper of the sacred fire who was away from home, had strayed into my herd of cattle.

**13.69.11**  Counted then by my herdsmen among a thousand cows, she was given by me to a brāhmaṇa, for I sought reward in the world beyond.

**13.69.12**  And the brāhmaṇa whose she had been, searching, spied her in another's house, and said, 'This cow is mine.'

**13.69.13**  The two of them came before me, disputing in great heat, and they said to me then: 'You are the giver — you are the thief!'

**13.69.14**  With an exchange of a hundred cows by the hundred I begged the one who had received her; but he said this to me:

**13.69.15**  'She is suited to time and place, a good milker, gentle, most loving, a giver of sweet milk, auspicious, and ever in my home.

**13.69.16**  And this cow nourishes my frail, unweaned son; her I cannot give up.' Having spoken thus, he went away.

**13.69.17**  Then I begged that other brāhmaṇa in exchange: 'Let a hundred thousand cows be taken in her stead.'

**13.69.18**  The brāhmaṇa said: 'I accept nothing from kings; I am able to seek out my own. Let that very cow be given back to me at once' — so he said, O slayer of Madhu.

**13.69.19**  Though I offered gold and horses, silver and chariots too, that bull among brāhmaṇas would take none of it, and then went his way.

**13.69.20**  At that very time, urged on by the law of Time, I reached the world of the fathers and came before the King of Righteousness.

**13.69.21**  Yama, having honored me, then spoke these words: 'No end can be reckoned, O king, to your meritorious deeds.

**13.69.22**  And yet a sin too has been committed — and that by you in ignorance. Undergo the penalty for that sin either afterward or before, as you please.'"

**13.69.23**  "'I shall be protected'—so it was promised you, yet your pledge proved false; and you took what belonged to a brāhmaṇa: thus your transgression is threefold."

**13.69.24**  "'First I shall undergo the hardship, and the bliss thereafter'—O lord, even as I was saying this to the King of Dharma, I fell upon the surface of the earth."

**13.69.25**  "And as I was tumbling down I heard Yama proclaiming aloud: 'Vāsudeva, Janārdana, shall be your deliverer.'"

**13.69.26**  "'When a full thousand years are ended and your evil deed is exhausted, you shall attain the eternal worlds, won by your own action.'"

**13.69.27**  "I beheld myself fallen headlong into the well, sunk into the womb of a beast; yet memory did not forsake me."

**13.69.28**  "Today I have been ferried across by you—by what else than the power of austerity? Give me leave, O Kṛṣṇa, that I may go this very day to heaven."

**13.69.29**  Granted leave by Kṛṣṇa, having bowed to Janārdana, he mounted a celestial chariot and went to heaven, O subduer of foes.

**13.69.30**  Then, when Nṛga had reached heaven, O best of the Bhāratas, Vāsudeva uttered this verse, O joy of the Kurus:

**13.69.31**  "A discerning man must never seize a brāhmaṇa's property; a brāhmaṇa's property, once seized, destroys, as the brāhmaṇa's cow destroyed Nṛga."

**13.69.32**  "Communion with the good, O Pārtha, is never fruitless for the good: behold how Nṛga was released from hell through fellowship with the holy."

**13.69.33**  "In this matter giving bears fruit, and so too does wrongdoing bear its fruit; therefore, Yudhiṣṭhira, one should shun any offence against cows."

**13.70.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: Tell me, O sinless one, of the fruit that comes from cows that are given away; tell it at length, O mighty-armed—let it be told, for I am not yet sated.

**13.70.2**  Bhīṣma said: On this too they recount an ancient tale, the words of both the seer Uddālaka and of Nāciketa.

**13.70.3**  The seer Uddālaka, having undertaken a consecration, said to his son Nāciketa, "Attend upon me"; and when that observance was completed, the great seer spoke to his son.

**13.70.4**  "While I was intent on my ablutions and absorbed in my recitation, I forgot the kindling, the darbha grass, the flowers, the water-pot, and the water all about. Fetch them and come here from the riverbank."

**13.70.5**  Going there, the young ascetic could not recover any of it, for it had been swept away by the river's current; and so he said to his father, "I do not see it."

**13.70.6**  Then the sage Uddālaka, overcome by hunger, thirst, and weariness—he of great austerity—cursed his son, saying, "Go behold Yama!"

**13.70.7**  Struck thus by his father with the thunderbolt of speech, with hands joined and saying only "Be gracious," the boy fell to the ground, his life gone out of him.

**13.70.8**  Seeing Nāciketa fallen, the father, swooning with grief and crying, "What have I done!", sank down upon the earth.

**13.70.9**  For him, encompassed by sorrow as he held his own son in his embrace, the remainder of that day passed, and a grim night came over him there.

**13.70.10**  By the falling of his father's tears, O foremost of the Kurus, Nāciketa stirred upon the bed of kuśa grass, like a crop revived when steeped in rain.

**13.70.11**  He questioned that worthy son returned to him once more, anointed with celestial fragrances, risen as if from a fading dream.

**13.70.12**  "Have you, my son, won the blessed worlds by your own deeds? By good fortune you are restored to me again—surely your form is no longer that of a mortal."

**13.70.13**  He who had beheld all with his own eyes, when questioned by his great-souled father, recounted it truthfully to that father in the midst of the great seers.

**13.70.14**  "Carrying out your command, I went swiftly forth, and reaching the vast and radiantly lustrous hall of Vaivasvata, I beheld it, its golden floor stretching for thousands of leagues."

**13.70.15**  "The moment he saw me hastening toward him, the son of Vivasvat showed me to his abode and assigned me a seat; and for your sake he honoured me with the welcome-offering and other tokens of reverence."

**13.70.16**  "Then softly I said to him, surrounded by his assessors and receiving their homage: 'O King of Dharma, I have come into your realm; ordain for me those worlds which I deserve.'"

**13.70.17**  "Yama said to me: 'You are not dead, gentle one; yet your father the ascetic, in splendour like a blazing fire, bade you behold Yama—and that, O brāhmaṇa, cannot be made false.'"

**13.70.18**  "'You have beheld me—go back, my child; he who gave you your body is grieving. And I grant whatever your heart desires: choose your wishes, O welcome guest.'"

**13.70.19**  "Thus addressed by him, I answered him: 'I have reached your realm, hard to come back from; I wish to behold the abounding worlds of those who have done good, if I am worthy of a boon from you.'"

**13.70.20**  "Then that god, setting me upon a radiant, sun-bright chariot yoked with steeds, showed me at that time all the worlds of those who have done good, O foremost of brāhmaṇas."

**13.70.21**  "There I beheld the gleaming mansions of the disciplined souls, of manifold shapes and forms and wrought all of jewels."

**13.70.22**  "White as the disc of the moon, festooned with networks of little bells, of many hundred storeys, set amid waters and groves within."

**13.70.23**  "Shining like beryl and the sun, fashioned of silver and gold, of the hue of the young morning sun, some fixed and some that moved at will."

**13.70.24**  "Mountains made of food hard and soft, and garments and couches, and trees bearing the fruit of every desire, standing about the dwellings."

**13.70.25**  "Rivers, avenues, assembly-halls, ponds, and long pools on every side, and chiming chariots ready-yoked by the thousand."

**13.70.26**  "Rivers flowing with milk, and mountains, and clarified butter, and water utterly clear; many regions sanctioned by Vaivasvata, never seen before, did I behold."

**13.70.27**  "Having seen all this, I said to the King of Dharma, the ancient and almighty one: 'These rivers of milk and of clarified butter, ever-flowing—for whose enjoyment are they ordained?'"

**13.70.28**  "Yama said: 'Know that these are to be enjoyed by those good men who are givers of the products of the cow; and there are still other worlds, eternal and free from sorrow, thronged with those devoted to the gift of cows.'"

**13.70.29**  "'Yet the mere giving of them is not what is praised; the worthy recipient, the time, the particular cow, and the rite all matter. Knowing these, O brāhmaṇa, should one give—for the true worth of a cow is as hard to discern as the nature of fire and the sun.'"

**13.70.30**  "'A brāhmaṇa rich in sacred recitation, exceedingly austere, established in the sacrificial fires, is the worthy recipient of these. Cows released in time of hardship, or come for their nurture—by such avenues are particular cows esteemed.'"

**13.70.31**  "'Having fasted three nights on water and lying on the bare ground, contented cows should be given to those who have been satisfied—cows glad with their calves, rich in offspring, attended with all due rites; and having given them, for three days one should live upon the cow's own products.'"

**13.70.32**  "'Having given a milch-cow of gentle ways, milked into bronze, with a fair calf and not given to straying—for as many hairs as are upon her, for so many years does the giver enjoy the world of heaven.'"

**13.70.33**  "'So too, having given to a brāhmaṇa an ox—tamed, fit for the yoke, strong and young, sustaining its lineage, vigorous and great—one enjoys worlds equal to those of the giver of a milch-cow.'"

**13.70.34**  "'One forbearing toward cows, a refuge to cows, grateful, and worn down in his livelihood—such a man they call a worthy recipient; whether in failing livelihood, in some great emergency, for the sake of ploughing, for an oblation, or at a birth—'"

**13.70.35**  "'—or for a teacher's sake, or out of concern for the nourishment of children: no particular place or time is required for giving cows. Such cows may be born among one's own herd, gained by fair purchase, acquired by sacrifice or knowledge, bought at the price of one's own life, won in battle, or received as a libation of water.'"

**13.70.36**  Nāciketa said: "Having heard the words of Vaivasvata, I asked him again: 'How does one who has no cow attain the worlds of the givers of cows?'"

**13.70.37**  "Then the wise Yama said: 'The gift of a cow leads to the highest goal; yet there are substitutes for the gift of a cow, and even without a cow there are those who count as cow-givers.'"

**13.70.38**  "'He who, lacking cows, gives a cow made of clarified butter, firm in his vow—for him these rivers of butter flow as tenderly as loving cows yielding their milk.'"

**13.70.39**  "'And he who, wanting butter, gives a cow made of sesame, firm in his vow, is borne across distress by that cow and rejoices in the river of milk.'"

**13.70.40**  "'And he who, wanting sesame, gives a cow made of water, firm in his vow, comes to enjoy this cool river that flows at his desire.'"

**13.70.41**  "Such things and more did the King of Dharma show me there; and beholding them I attained the highest joy, O Acyuta."

**13.70.42**  "And I announce to you a glad tiding: a great sacrifice, requiring but small wealth to perform, has come to me, dear father, sprung from me; conducted by the rule of the Veda, it shall come to fruition."

**13.70.43**  "For this curse of yours came to me as a grace, in which I beheld Yama; and having there seen the great reward of giving, I shall practise the duties of gift-giving beyond all doubt."

**13.70.44**  "And this the King of Dharma told me again and again, greatly pleased, O seer among brāhmaṇas: 'Be ever assiduous in giving, my child, and above all perform the gift of cows.'"

**13.70.45**  "'For wealth honestly come by must not be scorned: in accord with your own duty, it should be given to a worthy recipient at a fitting place and time. Therefore cows should ever be given by you; let no doubt of any kind arise in you here.'"

**13.70.46**  "'These men of old, of tranquil soul, set upon the path of giving, gave cows unceasingly; undertaking fierce austerities without misgiving, they too bestowed gifts to the full measure of their power.'"

**13.70.47**  "'Giving in due time according to their power, casting envy aside—pure of soul, faithful, of virtuous conduct—having given and having done penance, they have attained yonder world, and these men of virtuous conduct shine resplendent in heaven.'"

**13.70.48**  "'This gift, won by lawful means and given to brāhmaṇas, should be conferred upon a worthy recipient after due scrutiny; and on the desired eighth day one should pass ten days living on the products of the cow—its milk, its dung, or its yield.'"

**13.70.49**  "'The giver of a bull keeps the vow of the Veda; the gift of a yoke of cattle yields the attainment of the Veda; the gift of a yoked team yields the attainment of holy fords; and the gift of a tawny cow yields the casting-off of sin.'"

**13.70.50**  "'By bestowing even a single tawny cow, lawfully come by, one is wholly freed from defilement. Than the milk of cows there is nothing higher; the gift of cows, they declare, is a very great thing.'"

**13.70.51**  "'Cows, yielding their milk, sustain the worlds; cows bring forth food in the world. The man who, knowing this, does not give his heart to cows—that man of evil mind shall surely go to hell.'"

**13.70.52**  "'Whether you have a thousand cows to give, or a hundred, or fifty, or ten with goodly calves, or even one to a worthy brāhmaṇa—she shall be for that man a river of holy fords in the world beyond.'"

**13.70.53**  "'In their bounty, their nourishment, and their guarding of the world, cows on earth are the equals of the sun's rays: the name is the same, the lineage is the same, and the enjoyment is the same; therefore the giver of cows shines forth like the sun.'"

**13.70.54**  "'In the gift of cows the disciple should choose a teacher; he, the reciter of the rite, is assuredly the bestower of heaven. Great among those who know the rites is this duty; for all rites have recourse to that first ordinance.'"

**13.70.55**  "'This gift, won by lawful means, you should confer upon brāhmaṇas, giving it to a worthy recipient after due scrutiny. Upon you the immortals and men alike set their hopes, and we too, men of virtuous conduct, when the gift goes forth.'"

**13.70.56**  "Thus addressed by the King of Dharma, O great seer, bowing my head to that righteous one, and given leave by Vaivasvata, I came back to the feet of your reverence."

**13.71.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: You have spoken of the gift of cows in connection with the seer Nāciketa, and you have also told, by way of summary, the greatness of cows, O lord.

**13.71.2**  And how the great-souled Nṛga underwent suffering through a single offence committed in ignorance, O grandsire of mighty mind;

**13.71.3**  and how he was raised up at Dvāravatī while it was being settled, Kṛṣṇa becoming the cause of his deliverance—this too I have grasped.

**13.71.4**  But a doubt remains in me concerning the world of cows, O lord; I wish to hear truly into what region the givers of cows enter.

**13.71.5**  Bhīṣma said: On this too they recount an ancient tale, how Śatakratu put this very question to the Lotus-born.

**13.71.6**  Śakra said: Outshining by their own radiance the splendour of those who dwell in heaven, I behold the dwellers of the cow-world faring on; herein lies my doubt.

**13.71.7**  Of what nature, O blessed one, are the worlds of cows? Tell me that, O sinless one—those that the givers inhabit; this I wish to know.

**13.71.8**  Of what kind are they, what fruit do they bear, and what is the supreme excellence there? And how do men come thither, freed from all affliction?

**13.71.9**  For how long does the giver enjoy the fruit of his gift? And how is a gift made manifold, or how even a small one?

**13.71.10**  What is the giving of many cows like, and what the giving of few? And by what means are there those reckoned cow-givers who have given none? Tell me that as well.

**13.71.11**  And how may the giver of many be the equal of the giver of few, O lord? And how may the giver of little rank as a giver of much, O master here?

**13.71.12**  And what kind of sacrificial fee is esteemed highest in the gift of cows? All this, O blessed one, you ought to declare to me in truth.

**13.72.1**  Brahmā said: This question that you have asked, bearing upon the worthiness for the gift of cows—there is in this world no questioner of it other than you, O Śatakratu.

**13.72.2**  There exist worlds of many kinds, O Śakra, which you do not behold — worlds that I behold, and likewise the women who are faithful to a single husband.

**13.72.3**  By their wholly auspicious deeds the seers of firm vows, and the Brāhmaṇas of pure conduct, attain those worlds in their very bodies.

**13.72.4**  And those of firm vows, by laying down the body in release and through a mind made spotless, behold even here those worlds that are like a dream.

**13.72.5**  And those worlds, O thousand-eyed one — hear with what qualities they are endowed. There time does not advance, nor old age, nor any evil; nor anything else inauspicious, no disease there, and no fatigue.

**13.72.6**  And whatever the cattle there desire in their minds, O Vāsava, all that they obtain by beholding me directly; going where they wish, roaming where they please, at will they enjoy their every wish.

**13.72.7**  Tanks, lakes, rivers, and forests of many kinds, dwellings and mountains too, and whatever substance there may be —

**13.72.8**  all that is pleasing to every being is seen there. Know those worlds to be of such a kind; there is no world higher than that.

**13.72.9**  To that place go, O Śakra, the best of men — all-enduring, patient, affectionate, devoted to their elders, and wholly free of egotism.

**13.72.10**  The man who never eats flesh of any kind, ever devoted until his end, who honors his mother and father, joined to truth, a server of the Brāhmaṇas, blameless —

**13.72.11**  free of anger toward cattle and toward the twice-born, delighting in dharma, a servant of his elders, devoted lifelong to the practice of truth, given to charity, and forgiving of offense —

**13.72.12**  gentle, self-controlled, devoted to the gods, hospitable to all guests and full of compassion — a man endowed with such qualities proceeds to the world of cattle, eternal and imperishable.

**13.72.13**  No adulterer beholds this world, nor the slayer of a teacher, nor the babbler of falsehood, nor the forever-slandering Brāhmaṇa who has let his Vedic learning lapse, nor the evil-souled one yoked to other faults.

**13.72.14**  No betrayer of a friend, no deceiver, no ingrate, no rogue, no crooked man, no hater of dharma, no slayer of a Brāhmaṇa may even in his mind behold the world of cattle, the dwelling of those who have done meritorious deeds.

**13.72.15**  All this has been told you with precision, O lord of the gods; now hear the fruit that belongs to those devoted to the gift of cattle, O performer of a hundred rites.

**13.72.16**  He who, having bought cattle with wealth obtained as his rightful inheritance, gives them away, attains imperishable worlds purchased with righteously gained riches.

**13.72.17**  He who, having won wealth at dice, buys cattle and gives them away, enjoys, O Śakra, a divine reward lasting ten thousand years.

**13.72.18**  Cattle that are a man's inheritance, gained by lawful means and then bestowed, become for their givers imperishable and enduring.

**13.72.19**  And he who, having received cattle, gives them away with a wholly purified heart — know, O husband of Śacī, that for him too the worlds here are imperishable and enduring.

**13.72.20**  He who from birth speaks truth, his senses restrained, forbearing toward elders and the twice-born and patient — his attainment is equal to that won by the gift of cattle.

**13.72.21**  Never should a Brāhmaṇa be addressed with what ought not be spoken, O husband of Śacī; one should not even in mind do harm to cattle, but live by their ways and be compassionate to them.

**13.72.22**  For one devoted to truth and dharma — hear, O Śakra, his reward: his single cow becomes equal to a thousand.

**13.72.23**  Hear the reward of a Kṣatriya endowed with these same qualities: for him too one cow becomes equal to a hundred — such is the firm conclusion.

**13.72.24**  If these qualities belong to a Vaiśya, for him it becomes equal to fifty; and for a disciplined Śūdra too the reward is reckoned as a quarter of that.

**13.72.25**  And he who carries this out, ever devoted — joined to truth and to service of his elders, self-controlled, forbearing, a worshipper of the gods, serene, pure, awakened, of righteous disposition, free of self-assertion in speech —

**13.72.26**  that man attains a great reward by giving to a twice-born, according to this rule, a milch cow yielding milk. Let him give ever, taking but one meal a day, established in truth and a servant of his elders.

**13.72.27**  He who recites the Veda and is devoted to cattle, who ever rejoices at the sight of cows, and who bows to cattle from his very birth — mark, O Śakra, the reward that is his.

**13.72.28**  Whatever reward there is from performing the Rājasūya, whatever from sacrificing with abundant gold — equal and foremost to this, they declare his reward to be, all the holy ones and the seers and the perfected.

**13.72.29**  He who, without first tasting any morsel of his food, always offers the first portion to cattle — vowed to the cow, truth-speaking, serene, awakened — that man of meritorious character attains within a year the merit of a thousand cows.

**13.72.30**  He who eats but one meal a day and gives even one share to cattle — vowed to the cow and compassionate to it — gains ten endless years of merit.

**13.72.31**  And he who, taking but a single meal a day, buys a cow and gives it away — for as many days as are reckoned to him, O performer of a hundred rites, so many hundreds of cows' eternal reward does he obtain.

**13.72.32**  This is the reward of the Brāhmaṇa; now hear what is declared for the Kṣatriya. The Kṣatriya's reward is reckoned at five years' worth; the Vaiśya's at half of that, and the Śūdra's at half the Vaiśya's.

**13.72.33**  And he who, having even sold himself, buys cattle and gives them away, enjoys reward for as many cows as he can touch; for each hair upon them, O greatly blessed one, his worlds are reckoned imperishable.

**13.72.34**  But he who, having won cattle in battle, gives them away — know those gifts to be equal to selling oneself, and eternal, O Kauśika.

**13.72.35**  He who, when no cattle can be had, gives a cow made of sesame, his vows controlled, is carried by that cow across the hard passage and rejoices upon a river of milk.

**13.72.36**  Yet the mere giving of them is not praised; the worthy recipient, the time, the particular kind of cow, and the rite all matter. Knowledge of the right time, O Brāhmaṇa, and the differences among cattle are hard to know, being of the very nature of fire and the sun.

**13.72.37**  Rich in Vedic recitation, of pure birth, serene, settled in the sacrificial fires, fearful of sin, grateful, forbearing toward cattle, not over-harsh, a refuge for others, yet worn by want of livelihood — such a one they call a worthy recipient.

**13.72.38**  When a man is sorely worn by want and sinking utterly, whether for the sake of tillage, or for the oblation, at a birthing, for an elder's need, or for the raising of a child — let one give a cow at a fitting place and time.

**13.72.39**  Born within one's own herd, gained by a good purchase, bought at the cost of one's life, won in battle, born together as a single litter, released from peril, or come to one for their nurture — by these means the choicest cattle are approved.

**13.72.40**  Strong, of good temper and fit age, sweet-smelling — all such are praised; for as the Gaṅgā is the best among rivers, so the tawny cow is the best among the white.

**13.72.41**  Having fasted three nights upon water and lain upon the ground, well-satisfied cattle should be given to satisfied recipients — cows with well-fed, milk-drinking calves, good in pasture; and for three days after the gift one should live on their milk-products alone.

**13.72.42**  Having given a cow of gentle disposition, with a fine calf, of auspicious habits and not given to straying, for as many hairs as are upon her, so many years does one dwell in the world beyond.

**13.72.43**  Likewise, having given to a Brāhmaṇa a draught-ox fit for the yoke — young, strong, well-broken, a bearer of the plough, of boundless vigor — one attains the worlds of a giver of ten milch cows.

**13.72.44**  He who in the wilderness rescues Brāhmaṇas and cattle, O Kauśika, and brings them safely free — hear the fruit of his merit: his reward becomes eternal and equal to that of the horse-sacrifice.

**13.72.45**  At the hour of death, O thousand-eyed one, whatever state of being he longs for, whatever manifold heavenly worlds, or whatever dwells within his heart —

**13.72.46**  all that the man attains by that deed, and, granted favor by the cattle, he is everywhere held in honor.

**13.72.47**  And he who by this very rite follows the cattle into the forests, eating grass, cow-dung, and leaves, free of craving, restrained and pure —

**13.72.48**  that man, desireless and glad, O performer of a hundred rites, must dwell in my world together with the gods, in whatever world he may also wish.

**13.73.1**  Indra said: He who knowingly carries off a cow, or sells it for the sake of gain — this I wish to understand: what indeed is his destiny?

**13.73.2**  Brahmā said: As for those who carry off a cow — whether to eat it, to sell it, or to give it to a Brāhmaṇa — hear in this matter what the fruit shall be.

**13.73.3**  He who, unbridled, would slay a cow to sell it or to eat it, and those self-seeking men who would consent to the one who has it killed —

**13.73.4**  the slayer, the eater, and likewise he who gives his consent — for as many hairs as are upon that cow, so many years does he sink in hell.

**13.73.5**  Whatever faults, and of whatever kind, attach to one who ruins a twice-born's sacrifice, those very faults are declared to attach to the selling and the carrying off of a cow, O lord.

**13.73.6**  But he who carries off a cow and then gives it to a Brāhmaṇa — for as long as the reward of that gift would last, so long does he descend into hell.

**13.73.7**  Gold, they say, is the sacrificial fee in the gift of a cow, O greatly resplendent one; gold is declared the supreme thing for the purpose of the fee, beyond all doubt.

**13.73.8**  The gift of a cow carries across seven ancestors and seven descendants; and when gold is given as the fee, the deliverance is said to be twofold.

**13.73.9**  Gold is the supreme gift, gold is the highest fee; gold is purifying, O Śakra, and is reckoned the foremost among purifiers.

**13.73.10**  Gold they declare to be the purifier of lineages, O performer of a hundred rites; thus has the matter of the fee been told by me in brief, O greatly resplendent one.

**13.73.11**  Bhīṣma said: This was spoken by the Grandsire to Indra, O bull of the Bhāratas; Indra told it to Daśaratha, and the father then told it to Rāma.

**13.73.12**  Rāghava in turn told it to his dear brother, the glorious Lakṣmaṇa; and by Lakṣmaṇa, dwelling in the forest, it was told to the seers, O lord.

**13.73.13**  And this, come down through the succession, the seers of strict vows held fast though it is hard to hold, and the righteous kings likewise; and this was told to me too by my teacher, O Yudhiṣṭhira.

**13.73.14**  The Brāhmaṇa who would ever recite this in an assembly of Brāhmaṇas, at sacrifices, at the giving of cattle, and at the meeting of the two —

**13.73.15**  for him, they say, the worlds are imperishable forever, together with the gods — thus spoke the blessed Brahmā, the supreme lord.

**13.74.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: I have been given confidence by you as you declare the dharmas, O lord; yet I shall set forth a doubt — resolve it for me, O Grandsire.

**13.74.2**  What reward is declared for vows, and of what kind, O greatly resplendent one? What is the reward of restraints, and what the reward of diligent study?

**13.74.3**  What here is the reward of self-restraint, and what in the retention of the Vedas? What is the reward in teaching them? All this I wish to know.

**13.74.4**  And what reward in the world is there for one who accepts no gifts, O Grandsire? And what reward, seen or heard of, for one who bestows them?

**13.74.5**  And what is the reward of those devoted to their own duty, and of the heroes as well? What reward is declared for truth, and what for chastity?

**13.74.6**  And what in the service of one's father, and likewise in the service of one's mother, in the service of preceptor and elder, in mercy and in compassion?

**13.74.7**  All this in full and exactly as it is, O Grandsire, I wish to know, O knower of dharma; for great is my curiosity.

**13.74.8**  Bhīṣma said: He who undertakes a vow exactly as it has been prescribed, unbroken and rightly begun — for him the worlds are everlasting.

**13.74.9**  The reward of the restraints, O king, is seen plainly here in this world; and this reward of the restraints and of the sacrifices has been won by you.

**13.74.10**  And the reward of diligent study too is seen both there and here; in this world he is ever possessed of substance, and in the world of Brahmā he rejoices.

**13.74.11**  But hear from me at length, O king, the reward of self-restraint: the self-restrained are happy everywhere, the self-restrained are everywhere at peace.

**13.74.12**  The self-restrained go wherever they wish and are slayers of all foes; and whatever the self-restrained seek, that they obtain — there is no doubt of it.

**13.74.13**  For the self-restrained are united with all desired things everywhere, O Pāṇḍava, and they rejoice in heaven through their austerity and their valor.

**13.74.14**  Just as the self-restrained, endowed with forbearance, prosper by gifts and by sacrifices of many kinds — yet the giver may grow angry, the self-restrained never does; therefore self-restraint is higher than giving.

**13.74.15**  But he who gives without growing angry — for him the worlds are everlasting; for anger destroys the gift, and therefore self-restraint is higher than giving.

**13.74.16**  There are unseen abodes by the tens of thousands in heaven, O great king — the abodes of the seers, to which the gods proceed throughout all the worlds.

**13.74.17**  To these, O lord of men, the supreme seers proceed through self-restraint, longing for that great abode; therefore self-restraint is higher than giving.

**13.74.18**  The teacher, through his toil, enjoys an imperishable reward, having duly offered oblation into the fire, in the world of Brahmā, O ruler of men.

**13.74.19**  And he who, having mastered the Vedas, imparts them to those versed in right reasoning, and who extols the duty owed to a teacher—he too is exalted in heaven.

**13.74.20**  The kṣatriya devoted to study, to sacrifice, and to the work of giving, who is a protector in battle—he too is exalted in heaven.

**13.74.21**  The vaiśya intent upon his own duty gains a great reward through giving; the śūdra intent upon his own duty attains heaven through dutiful service.

**13.74.22**  Heroes have been declared to be of many kinds; hear from me their meanings, and the reward set forth for those of heroic lineage and for the hero himself.

**13.74.23**  There are heroes in sacrifice, heroes in self-restraint, and others who are heroes in truth; men called heroes in battle, and likewise heroes in giving.

**13.74.24**  Others again are heroes in wisdom, and some heroes in forbearance; and there are men who are heroes in uprightness and who abide in tranquillity.

**13.74.25**  By this or that observance there are many other heroes besides: heroes in the study of the Vedas, and heroes devoted to teaching them.

**13.74.26**  Heroes in serving the teacher, others in serving the father, heroes in serving the mother, and others again heroes in the life of mendicancy.

**13.74.27**  Many are heroes in Sāṃkhya and others heroes in Yoga; heroes in the forest, in the household life, and in the honouring of guests—all of them attain the highest worlds, won by the fruit of their own works.

**13.74.28**  The retaining of all the Vedas, the bathing at every sacred ford—whether for him who ever speaks the truth these be equal or not equal.

**13.74.29**  A thousand horse-sacrifices and truth were weighed in the balance: truth alone outweighs a thousand horse-sacrifices.

**13.74.30**  By truth the Sūrya gives heat, by truth Agni blazes, by truth the wind blows; all things are established upon truth.

**13.74.31**  By truth one gladdens the gods, the ancestors, and the brāhmaṇas alike. Truth, they say, is the supreme dharma; therefore one should never transgress the truth.

**13.74.32**  The sages are devoted to truth, the sages have truth for their valour, the sages have truth for their vow; therefore truth is supreme. The truthful rejoice in the world of heaven, O bull of the Bhāratas.

**13.74.33**  The attainment of the fruit of self-restraint and of truth has been told by me with all my heart. Beyond doubt, every man of disciplined self is exalted in heaven.

**13.74.34**  Now hear from me the virtues of chastity, O lord of the earth. He who in this world remains a celibate from birth until death—know, O lord of men, that for him there is nothing unattainable.

**13.74.35**  Many tens of millions of seers dwell in the world of Brahmā—those ever delighting in truth, the self-restrained, the keepers of upward-flowing seed.

**13.74.36**  Chastity, when cultivated, burns away all sins, O king—especially when cultivated by a brāhmaṇa; for the brāhmaṇa is called a very fire.

**13.74.37**  This too is plain to your own eyes among the brāhmaṇas and the ascetics: how Śakra trembles when assailed by a celibate. Such is the fruit of chastity seen here among the seers.

**13.74.38**  Hear from me too the duty that lies in honouring mother and father. He who serves his father and never in any way speaks ill of his mother, who utters no proud word against his elder or his teacher—

**13.74.39**  —know, O king, that his reward is the highest station in the world of heaven; the self-possessed man who serves his elders shall never behold hell.

**13.75.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: I wish to hear truly the supreme ordinance concerning cows, by which we may attain in their entirety those everlasting worlds.

**13.75.2**  Bhīṣma said: There is nothing higher than the gift of a cow, O lord of the earth; for a cow righteously obtained and given away delivers one's whole line at once.

**13.75.3**  That which was rightly created for the good, fashioned aright and consecrated for the welfare of creatures—since the gift of cows has been in practice from the very first beginning, hear from me, O king, its ordinance.

**13.75.4**  Of old, when cows had been brought near, Bṛhaspati answered the question put to him by Māndhātṛ, who was in doubt as to what he should behold.

**13.75.5**  Having honoured the twice-born and having announced the time on the morrow, the man of steadfast vow should set apart a red cow for the purpose of the gift.

**13.75.6**  He should employ the call, 'O perfect-limbed one, O abundant one,' and entering into the midst of the cows he should recite this sacred utterance:

**13.75.7**  'The cow is my mother, the bull is my father; heaven is my shelter, the earth my support.' Taking refuge thus and passing the night among the cows, the silent one should let forth this speech at the giving of cows.

**13.75.8**  That man, for that one night a fellow and a vow-sharer of the cows, by reaching oneness with them is at once wholly freed from sin.

**13.75.9**  A cow whose bull and calf have been set free is to be given at the sight of the sun; and a threefold formula is to be observed—the explanatory praise, the benediction, and the hymns of laud.

**13.75.10**  'Rich in vigour and full of nourishing strength, they are the sacrifice, the womb of the nectar, and the support of the world; the source of prosperity upon the earth forever, born of Prajāpati'—such is the explanatory praise, comprising all.

**13.75.11**  'May these cows of the Sun drive away my sin, and may those of the Moon be for my journey to heaven; let those that are named grant me their shelter, and let all those unnamed be a blessing upon me.'

**13.75.12**  'At the giving away of all that remains, at the releasing of the body through rites, you Sarasvatī-cows are ever set toward the highest good; ever to be carried forth by holy works, grant me, you that have come, the goal I desire.'

**13.75.13**  'What you are, that am I—today of one single being; in giving you away I give my very self. Released from the mind yet endowed with mind, kindle me, O you of gentle form and terrible form.'

**13.75.14**  Thus, before him, the giver of cows should first speak the former half according to ordinance, as seen of old; and the twice-born one who knows the rite, in receiving at the gift of cows, should answer with the remaining half.

**13.75.15**  'I give the cow'—so should it be said by him who bestows the welcome-offering, garments, and wealth; the udder is to be kept filled, and he should declare her sacred to Viṣṇu.

**13.75.16**  He should proclaim her name, and reward upon reward accrues in order of number—twenty-six, and eight, and twenty thousand.

**13.75.17**  Thus the giver of cows wins all these growing merits of cows and the rest, in due order, complete at the eighth stage.

**13.75.18**  The giver of cows becomes virtuous; the giver of the welcome-offering becomes fearless; the giver of wealth ceases to be sorrowful and gains his desires; and the learned man who has borne the filled udder, O Bhārata—for all these the worlds of Viṣṇu and of the Moon are declared.

**13.75.19**  Having given cows, one should keep the cow-vow for three nights, and dwell here for one night among them; on the eighth day, sought of desire, one should pass three nights subsisting on the cow's juices, or on its dung, or on its milk.

**13.75.20**  The giver of a bull becomes a keeper of the Veda-vow; in the gift of a yoke of oxen lies the attainment of the Veda. So the sacrificer who follows the ordinance of cows wins the foremost worlds—but not he who knows not the rite.

**13.75.21**  He who gives away all earthly desires gathered into one, and a milch-cow that yields every wish—rightly do such cows abound in streams of offerings to gods and ancestors; and greater still is the bestowal of the bulls among them.

**13.75.22**  One should not impart this to a non-pupil, to one without vows, nor to the unbelieving, nor to the crooked of mind; for this is the secret dharma of all the world, and one should not babble this dharma here and there.

**13.75.23**  There are believing men in the world, and there are mean ones, very demons among men, to whom the giving of a gift is hateful; the unholy take refuge even in disbelief.

**13.75.24**  Hearing this counsel of Bṛhaspati, those kings who, having made gifts of cows, attained the worlds—holy in conduct and of good ways—hear of them, O king, as I recount them.

**13.75.25**  Uśīnara, Viṣvagaśva, and Nṛga; Bhagīratha, and the renowned son of Yuvanāśva; Māndhātṛ indeed, and King Mucukunda; Bhūridyumna, the lord of Niṣadha, and Somaka—

**13.75.26**  Purūravas, and Bharata the universal emperor, in whose line are all the Bhāratas; and the hero Rāma, son of Daśaratha; and whatever others renowned and glorious there were.

**13.75.27**  So too King Dilīpa of mighty deeds, knowing the ordinance of the gift of cows, attained heaven; and Māndhātṛ became great through sacrifices, gifts, austerity, the duties of kings, and through gifts of cows.

**13.75.28**  Therefore, O Pārtha, do you too hold fast to this teaching of Bṛhaspati that I have spoken; and gladly, having gained the kingdom of the Kurus, bestow holy cows upon the foremost of the twice-born.

**13.75.29**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: So the King of Righteousness did all this, as Bhīṣma had told him, duly in the gift of cows; that king rightly upheld the dharma of Māndhātṛ, which had been taught by the god of gods.

**13.75.30**  Thus, O king, ever intent upon the giving of cows, drinking barley-grains together with cow-dung, sleeping upon the bare ground, wearing the tuft, self-controlled—that bull among kings became then as a bull itself.

**13.75.31**  That king was ever devoted to them, with mind made pure, glorifying the cows; and he yoked no cow again to the burden of royal service, but went here and there with his choicest steeds.

**13.76.1**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then King Yudhiṣṭhira the wise, O king, full of humility, asked the son of Śaṃtanu yet further about the gift of cows in its fullness.

**13.76.2**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: Tell me once more, O Bhārata, the merits in the gift of cows, fully; for I am not sated, O hero, listening to such nectar as this.

**13.76.3**  Thus addressed by the King of Righteousness, the son of Śaṃtanu, O king, then duly recounted to him the unmixed merits of the gift of cows.

**13.76.4**  Bhīṣma said: Giving to a brāhmaṇa such a cow—affectionate, endowed with good qualities, young, and draped with cloth—a man is freed from all his sins.

**13.76.5**  There are worlds called 'sunless'; into them one goes who gives a cow whose water is drunk dry, whose grass is eaten up, whose milk has failed, and whose powers are spent—

**13.76.6**  —worn out with age, her usefulness already taken, decrepit like a waterless well; giving such a one, he enters darkness, for he would yoke the twice-born to mere trouble.

**13.76.7**  A cow that is vicious, ill-tempered, diseased, or feeble, and those for which the price has not been paid, are not to be given; he who yokes a brāhmaṇa to troubles that bear no fruit—his worlds too shall be without vigour and without fruit.

**13.76.8**  All praise cows that are strong, endowed with good temper and right age, and sweet of scent; for as the Gaṅgā is the best of rivers, so among the white cows the tawny one is the best.

**13.76.9**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: When the gift of a many-coloured cow is the same, why is the gift of a tawny one extolled by the good? I wish to hear the distinction, O great-souled one; for you are able to declare it.

**13.76.10**  Bhīṣma said: What I have heard from the elders as they spoke, that, my son, of which you ask, I shall tell you in full—how the red cows were fashioned.

**13.76.11**  Commanded of old by the Self-existent, 'Create creatures,' Dakṣa first of all created their very sustenance, desiring the welfare of beings.

**13.76.12**  For as the dwellers in heaven subsist depending on the nectar, even so do creatures subsist depending upon their sustenance, O mighty one.

**13.76.13**  Than motionless beings the moving are better, and than these, men; and than these, the brāhmaṇas are best; in them the sacrifices are established.

**13.76.14**  By sacrifices the Soma is nourished, and that is established in the cows; all the gods rejoice, and thence creatures fare as of old.

**13.76.15**  Now these very beings cried aloud in longing for sustenance, and athirst they came after the giver of sustenance as toward a father and mother.

**13.76.16**  Pondering this in his mind, Prajāpati then, for the sake of his own creation of beings, drank the nectar that bestows strength.

**13.76.17**  Having come to the contentment thereof, belching forth a fragrant odour, he beheld Surabhī, the daughter born from his mouth, brought forth from his eructation.

**13.76.18**  And Surabhī brought forth the daughters of Surabhī, the mothers of the world—tawny cows of golden hue, the milch-cows that are the sustenance of creatures.

**13.76.19**  As those of nectar-hue flowed forth on every side, there arose from them a foam born of the nectar, even as the wave-born foam of streaming rivers.

**13.76.20**  That foam, fallen from the mouth of a calf, lighted upon the head of Bhava as he stood upon the earth; thereat the Lord, enraged, gazed upon the red cows with the eye sprung from his forehead, as though to burn them up.

**13.76.21**  That fierce splendour, O lord of peoples, brought the tawny cows to many-coloured hues, as the sun colours the clouds.

**13.76.22**  But those that drew away from it and took refuge in the Soma, abiding in their own hue as they were born, were not brought to any other colour.

**13.76.23**  Then Prajāpati spoke to the angry Mahādeva: 'You have been besprinkled with nectar; there is no defilement among the cows.

**13.76.24**  For as the Soma, having taken up the nectar, flows forth again, so do these red cows, sprung from the nectar, pour forth their milk.

**13.76.25**  The wind is not defiled, nor fire, nor gold, nor the ocean; nectar drunk by nectar is no defilement, and the loving cow, drunk of by her calf, is not made impure.

**13.76.26**  These cows shall sustain the worlds with their oblation and their milk; partake of their sovereignty, auspicious and made wholly of nectar.'

**13.76.27**  And Prajāpati gave him a bull together with those cows, and by that he won over the mind of Rudra, O Bhārata.

**13.76.28**  And Mahādeva, well pleased, then made the bull both his banner and his mount; therefore is he the Bull-bannered one.

**13.76.29**  Then by the gods was Mahādeva made the Lord of Beasts, Paśupati; and he, the Sovereign, is called among the cattle Vṛṣāṅka, the one whose emblem is the bull.

**13.76.30**  Thus the first and foremost rite in the giving of tawny cows of unblemished hue and mighty splendour is proclaimed for all of them.

**13.76.31**  Eldest in the worlds, set in motion to sustain the life of the worlds, joined with Rudra, born of the overflowing of Soma, gentle, holy, granters of desires and givers of life — by bestowing such cows a man becomes a giver of every wish.

**13.76.32**  This supreme account of the origin of cattle, the man who recites it ever pure and devoted to the highest auspiciousness is freed from the taint of the Kali age, and obtains dear sons and wealth in cattle besides.

**13.76.33**  Oblations to the gods, offerings to the ancestors, the libation of refreshment, rites of peace, the means of conveyance, raiment, and the nourishing of the aged and the young — all these merits of the gift of cattle, O king, the giver attains forever.

**13.76.34**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard the words of the grandsire, the king of Ajamīḍha's line together with his brothers — Pārtha — then gave cattle whose milk was drawn into vessels of gold and bronze to the most excellent of brāhmaṇas.

**13.76.35**  In the same way he bestowed upon those twice-born thousands and hundreds of cattle, intending them as sacrificial gifts at the sacrifices, in order to conquer the worlds and the highest renown.

**13.77.1**  Bhīṣma said: At that very time, King Saudāsa, born of the line of Ikṣvāku, the best of givers, approached Vasiṣṭha, the most excellent of seers.

**13.77.2**  Having saluted his household priest — the perfected one who ranges through all the worlds, the eternal treasury of sacred knowledge — he began to put this question to him.

**13.77.3**  Saudāsa said: In the three worlds, O blessed and sinless one, what is declared to be purifying, by ever proclaiming which a mortal might obtain the highest merit?

**13.77.4**  Bhīṣma said: To him who bowed before him the learned sage then spoke a wholesome word — the secret doctrine of cattle — being pure and having made obeisance to the cattle.

**13.77.5**  Cattle are fragrant with sweet scent and breathe the perfume of guggulu; cattle are the support of all creatures, cattle are a great means of blessing.

**13.77.6**  Cattle are what has been and what shall be; cattle are nourishment eternal; cattle are the root of prosperity; what is given to cattle is never lost; cattle are ever food itself, and the highest oblation of the gods.

**13.77.7**  The utterances svāhā and vaṣaṭ are forever established in cattle; cattle are indeed the fruit of sacrifice, and in cattle the sacrifices are grounded.

**13.77.8**  At evening and at dawn, constantly at the hour of oblation, O great-minded one, the cattle yield what is to be offered to the seers, O bull among men.

**13.77.9**  Whatever hard straits there be, and whatever evil deeds have been done, those who bestow a milch-cow cross beyond them and beyond sin itself, O lord.

**13.77.10**  Let the owner of ten cows give one, the owner of a hundred give ten, and the owner of a thousand give a hundred — for all of these reap an equal fruit.

**13.77.11**  He who keeps no sacred fire though he owns a hundred cows, he who offers no sacrifice though he owns a thousand, and the wealthy man who is yet a miser — these three deserve no offering of honour.

**13.77.12**  Those who bestow a tawny cow together with her calf, milked into a bronze vessel, gentle of nature and draped with cloth, conquer both worlds.

**13.77.13**  A young and vigorous bull, lord of the herd, leading a hundred cows, a chief among cattle with broad horns and richly adorned, given to a foremost brāhmaṇa —

**13.77.14**  those who bestow such a bull upon a learned reciter of the Veda, O scorcher of foes, are born to lordship again and again with each rebirth.

**13.77.15**  Let one not lie down to sleep without praising the cattle, nor rise again without calling them to mind; let one make obeisance to the cattle at evening and at dawn, and thereby attain prosperity.

**13.77.16**  Let one never feel disgust at the urine and dung of cattle, nor eat their flesh; thus does one enjoy the abundance that flows from cattle.

**13.77.17**  Let one ever extol the cattle and never hold them in contempt; and upon beholding an ill-omened dream, let a man at once invoke the cow.

**13.77.18**  Let one ever bathe with cow-dung and rest upon dried cow-dung; and let one avoid casting phlegm, urine, and ordure where cattle are, and any act of injury to them.

**13.77.19**  Let one eat upon a fresh hide, gazing toward the western quarter, restrained in speech, with clarified butter upon the ground; thus does one enjoy the abundance that flows from cattle.

**13.77.20**  Let one offer oblation to the fire with clarified butter, pronounce the benediction with clarified butter, give clarified butter and partake of clarified butter; thus does one enjoy the abundance that flows from cattle.

**13.77.21**  He who, having consecrated with the Gomatī hymn a cow fashioned of sesame, rich in flavour and precious as a jewel, bestows it — that man shall not grieve over what he has done or left undone.

**13.77.22**  May the cattle, golden-horned and pouring forth milk, the fragrant ones and the offspring of Surabhī, attend upon me as the rivers attend upon the sea.

**13.77.23**  May the cattle ever look upon me, and I in turn look upon the cattle; the cattle are ours and we are theirs; where the cattle are, there are we.

**13.77.24**  Thus by night and by day, in smooth straits and in rough, and in great perils, the man who utters this prayer is delivered from fear.

**13.78.1**  Vasiṣṭha said: Austerity most arduous was practised for a hundred thousand years by the cattle created of old, with the thought, "May we attain to pre-eminence."

**13.78.2**  "In this world may we be the highest of all sacrificial gifts, and may we not be stained by any fault" — so they resolved, O scorcher of foes.

**13.78.3**  He whose mind harbours an injurious intent toward them is ever defiled thereby; and with their dung let gods and men perform their rites of purification.

**13.78.4**  "And so may all beings, whether unmoving or moving, and those who bestow us, attain to the worlds of cattle" — thus they wished, O bestower of honour.

**13.78.5**  To them Brahmā himself, the Lord, at the end of their austerity granted a boon: "So be it," said the mighty one, "and may you carry beings across the worlds."

**13.78.6**  They rose up, seeking perfection, the mothers of all that has been and shall be — the cattle, refuge of the worlds, at the close of their austerity, O great king.

**13.78.7**  Therefore the cattle are most blessed and are declared the supreme means of purification; and likewise the cattle stand upon the head of all beings.

**13.78.8**  Having given a tawny milch-cow with a like-coloured calf, rich in milk, gentle of nature and draped with cloth, one is honoured in the world of Brahmā.

**13.78.9**  Having given a red milch-cow with a calf of matching hue, rich in milk, gentle of nature and draped with cloth, one is honoured in the world of Sūrya.

**13.78.10**  Having given a dappled milch-cow with a like-coloured calf, rich in milk, gentle of nature and draped with cloth, one is honoured in the world of Soma.

**13.78.11**  Having given a white milch-cow with a like-coloured calf, rich in milk, gentle of nature and draped with cloth, one is honoured in the world of Indra.

**13.78.12**  Having given a black milch-cow with a like-coloured calf, rich in milk, gentle of nature and draped with cloth, one is honoured in the world of Agni.

**13.78.13**  Having given a smoke-grey milch-cow with a like-coloured calf, rich in milk, gentle of nature and draped with cloth, one is honoured in the world of Yama.

**13.78.14**  Having given a cow the colour of water's foam, with her calf, milked into a bronze vessel and draped with cloth, one attains the world of Varuṇa.

**13.78.15**  Having given a cow the colour of wind-blown dust, with her calf, milked into a bronze vessel and draped with cloth, one is honoured in the world of Vāyu.

**13.78.16**  Having given a golden-hued, tawny-eyed cow with her calf, milked into a bronze vessel and draped with cloth, one attains the world of Kubera.

**13.78.17**  Having given a cow the smoky colour of straw, with her calf, milked into a bronze vessel and draped with cloth, one is honoured in the world of the ancestors.

**13.78.18**  Having given a plump cow with her calf, white-throated and adorned, one attains the excellent and unconfined abode of the All-Gods.

**13.78.19**  Having given a fair-white milch-cow with a like-coloured calf, rich in milk, gentle of nature and draped with cloth, one attains the world of the Vasus.

**13.78.20**  Having given a cow the colour of a pale woollen blanket, with her calf, milked into a bronze vessel and draped with cloth, one attains the world of the Sādhyas.

**13.78.21**  Having given a bull with a broad, sapphire-dark back, adorned with every jewel, one attains the ageless worlds of the Maruts.

**13.78.22**  Having given a dark-bodied cow furnished with a calf and decked with every jewel, a man attains the worlds of the Gandharvas and Apsarases.

**13.78.23**  Having given a white-throated ox adorned with every jewel, one attains the worlds of Prajāpati, free from sorrow.

**13.78.24**  The man devoted to the giving of cattle, cleaving through the gathered banks of clouds, journeys in a celestial chariot of the sun's hue, shining radiant in the sky, O king.

**13.78.25**  A thousand fair women of comely raiment and lovely hips delight that man, O best of men, who is devoted to the giving of cattle.

**13.78.26**  By the strains of vīṇās and lutes, by the tinkling of anklets, and by the laughter of doe-eyed maidens, he is awakened when he sleeps.

**13.78.27**  For as many hairs as there are upon the milch-cow, for so many years is he honoured in heaven; and even when he falls from heaven, he is then born again in the world of men in a family rich in cattle.

**13.79.1**  Vasiṣṭha said: The cattle that yield clarified butter and milk, that are the womb of butter and the source of butter, that are rivers of butter and whirlpools of butter — may they ever dwell in my house.

**13.79.2**  May butter be ever in my heart, may butter be established in my navel, may butter be in all my limbs, and may butter abide in my mind.

**13.79.3**  May the cattle be ever before me, may the cattle be behind me, may the cattle be on every side of me; in the midst of cattle do I dwell.

**13.79.4**  Having sipped water, let a man recite this ever at evening and at dawn; from whatever sin he commits by day, from that he is wholly freed.

**13.79.5**  Where there are golden palaces, where flows that Stream of Wealth, where dwell the Gandharvas and Apsarases — thither go those who give a thousand cows.

**13.79.6**  Where rivers flow with mire of fresh butter, with milk for their waters, thick with curds for moss — thither go those who give a thousand cows.

**13.79.7**  He who, according to the ordinance, bestows a hundred thousand cattle, having attained the highest prosperity, is honoured in the world of cattle.

**13.79.8**  After death he upholds ten ancestors on either side, of his mother's and his father's line, in the worlds of the virtuous, and that man sanctifies his whole family.

**13.79.9**  He who gives a cow of sesame, equal in measure to a milch-cow, and likewise gives water to drink, comes to no torment whatever in the realm of Yama.

**13.79.10**  The foremost means of purification, the support of the world, the immeasurable mothers of the dwellers in heaven — let one touch them reverently, walk about them keeping them on the right, and give to a worthy recipient, having regarded the fitting time.

**13.79.11**  Having given a tawny milch-cow with her calf, with broad horns, milked into bronze and draped with an upper garment, a man passes free from fear through that hall of Yama which is otherwise so hard to traverse.

**13.79.12**  "The fair-formed, the many-formed, and the all-formed mothers — may the cattle attend upon me" — thus let one ever proclaim.

**13.79.13**  There is no gift more holy than this, no fruit more holy than this; nor can any being arise in the worlds more excellent than this.

**13.79.14**  With hide, with hair, with horns and tail, with milk and with fat, all together they sustain the sacrifice — what is there greater than they?

**13.79.15**  That milch-cow by whom all this world of moving and unmoving things is pervaded — her I revere with bowed head, the mother of what has been and what shall be.

**13.79.16**  This, O best of men, is but one portion of the gathered recital of the cattle's virtues, proclaimed by me to thee; for there is here no gift higher than cattle, nor any other refuge like to them.

**13.79.17**  Bhīṣma said: Reflecting that the seer's choice words were the highest truth, that great-souled king, his self subdued, then bestowed upon the twice-born very many herds of cattle, and won the worlds thereby.

**13.80.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: That which is the purest of pure things, and which is supreme in the world, and the highest sanctifier of all — tell me of that, O grandsire.

**13.80.2**  Bhīṣma said: Cattle are of great worth and are holy, and they carry men across; and these creatures they sustain with their milk and with the oblation.

**13.80.3**  There is nothing more holy than cattle, O best of the Bhāratas; they are pure and holy, unsurpassed throughout the three worlds.

**13.80.4**  And above even the gods the cattle have their dwelling; and by bestowing them, O lord of men, the wise go forth to heaven.

**13.80.5**  Māndhātṛ son of Yuvanāśva, and Yayāti, and Nahuṣa — these, ever giving cattle measured by hundreds of thousands, attained the supreme abode that is hard to win even for the gods.

**13.80.6**  And on this matter I shall recount to you a tale of olden days, O sinless one.

**13.80.7**  The wise Śuka, having saluted Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, foremost among the sages, and having performed the daily rites, pure and earnest of mind, questioned his father, who had beheld the higher and lower worlds.

**13.80.8**  Which sacrifice is held to be the most excellent of all sacrifices? And by doing what do the wise attain the highest heaven?

**13.80.9**  By what purifying thing, O mighty one, do the gods enjoy heaven? And wherein lies the sacrificial essence of a sacrifice, and upon what is sacrifice established?

**13.80.10**  What is the highest of gifts, and what beyond that is the supreme rite of offering? And what is the purest of pure things — tell me that, O sinless one.

**13.80.11**  Hearing these words, Vyāsa, supreme knower of dharma, told his son all of it truly, O bull of the Bhāratas.

**13.80.12**  Vyāsa said: The cows are the foundation of all beings, and the cows are their refuge; the cows are holy and pure, the very means of purification and dharma itself.

**13.80.13**  In ancient times the cows were hornless, so we have heard; and to gain horns they worshipped the imperishable Lord.

**13.80.14**  Then Brahmā, beholding the cows seated in fasting devotion, the Lord granted to each of those cows, one by one, the boon they desired.

**13.80.15**  Horns arose upon them, for each according to her heart's wish; and bearing horns of varied hues, they shone resplendent, O dear son.

**13.80.16**  Blessed by Brahmā with boons, those auspicious cows became the givers of oblations to gods and ancestors — holy, pure, fortunate, marked with divine form and feature. The cows possess a great and divine splendour, and the gift of cows is extolled.

**13.80.17**  Those righteous men, free of envy, who bestow these cows are called doers of merit and givers of every gift; and they attain the holy world of the cows, O sinless one.

**13.80.18**  There the trees bear honeyed fruit and are laden with divine blossoms and fruit, and there are fragrant celestial flowers, O best of the twice-born.

**13.80.19**  The whole ground is wrought of gems, its sand fine gold; everywhere soft to the touch, free of mire, free of dust, and lovely.

**13.80.20**  There the pools shine, set about with groves of red lotuses and with golden, jewel-stemmed stalks, gleaming like the newly-risen sun.

**13.80.21**  And with lakes thick with many lotuses, their leaves of priceless gems, their filaments gleaming like gold, mingled with blue water-lilies.

**13.80.22**  They are adorned with blossoming oleander groves girdled by a thousand eddies, with flowering saṃtānaka groves, and with fair trees.

**13.80.23**  And there the rivers cast up sand-banks heaped with spotless pearls, with gems of great worth, and with pure gold.

**13.80.24**  They are studded with wondrous peaks of every jewel, with lofty mountains, and with others of pure gold radiant as fire.

**13.80.25**  There are golden mountains, masses of rock of gems and jewels, that shine with lovely upraised peaks made of every precious stone.

**13.80.26**  There the trees, ever in flower and fruit, throng with birds, bearing blossoms and fruits of divine fragrance and savour, O bull of the Bhāratas.

**13.80.27**  There the doers of holy deeds disport themselves forever, O Yudhiṣṭhira, every desire fulfilled, free of sorrow, their wrath departed.

**13.80.28**  In gorgeous and delightful aerial cars, O Bhārata, the glorious doers of holy deeds rejoice, roaming at their pleasure.

**13.80.29**  And fair throngs of apsarases sport before them, O king. Such worlds does one attain by the gift of a cow, O Yudhiṣṭhira.

**13.80.30**  May those cows, of whom Pūṣan is lord, and the mighty, powerful Wind, and king Varuṇa over their abundance, the bearers of the yoke, protect me.

**13.80.31**  "The mothers, fair of form, of many forms, of every form, born of Prajāpati" — thus, O brāhmaṇa, let one of disciplined vows recite daily.

**13.80.32**  And to him who serves the cows and waits upon them in every way, they, well pleased, grant boons even hard to obtain.

**13.80.33**  Let one bear no malice toward cows even in thought, for they are the givers of happiness; let one ever revere them and honour them with salutations. Self-controlled and glad of heart, one thus enjoys the rich reward of the cows.

**13.80.34**  That purifier by which the gods enjoy the highest world, the purest of pure things — that clarified butter let one bear upon one's head.

**13.80.35**  With clarified butter let one offer to the fire, with clarified butter pronounce the blessing; let one taste it and bestow it — thus one enjoys the rich reward of the cows.

**13.80.36**  For three days let one drink the warm urine of cows, for three days drink their warm milk; having drunk the warm milk for three days, let one drink the warm clarified butter for three days; and having drunk the warm butter for three days, let one live for three days on air alone.

**13.80.37**  And living for a month on a handful of barley-gruel made from barley trodden out by cows, one is cleansed of every sin, even one equal to the slaying of a brāhmaṇa.

**13.80.38**  This rite of purification was performed by the gods for the undoing of the daityas; and thereby the mighty ones attained godhood and were made perfect.

**13.80.39**  The cows are pure and holy, the supreme and mighty means of purification; and by bestowing them upon the twice-born, a man attains heaven.

**13.80.40**  Made pure, in the midst of cows let one recite the Gomatī hymn in mind; having sipped purified water, he becomes pure and spotless.

**13.80.41**  In the midst of the fire, in the midst of cows, and in the assembly of brāhmaṇas — the brāhmaṇas, accomplished in knowledge, the Veda, and vows, doers of holy deeds —

**13.80.42**  should teach their pupils the Gomatī hymn, deemed equal to a sacrifice. Having fasted for three nights and heard the Gomatī, one obtains a boon.

**13.80.43**  He who longs for a son obtains a son, and wealth besides; she who longs for a husband obtains a husband; and a man obtains all his desires. The cows, when served, well pleased, bestow these things — there is no doubt.

**13.80.44**  Thus know these glorious ones, fit for sacrifice, granters of every desire, to be the Rohiṇīs; there is nothing higher than they.

**13.80.45**  Thus addressed by his great-souled father, Śuka of mighty splendour ever honoured the cows; therefore do you too honour them.

**13.81.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: I have heard that the dung of cows is graced by Śrī. This I wish to hear, for herein my doubt is great.

**13.81.2**  Bhīṣma said: On this too they recount an ancient tale, O king — a colloquy between the cows and Śrī, O best of the Bhāratas.

**13.81.3**  Śrī, having assumed a lovely form, entered into the midst of the cows; and the cows, beholding the perfection of her beauty, were amazed.

**13.81.4**  The cows said: Who are you, O goddess, and whence have you come, peerless in beauty upon the earth? We are amazed, O glorious one, at the perfection of your beauty.

**13.81.5**  We wish to know you: who are you, and whither will you go? Tell us all this truly, O you of golden lustre.

**13.81.6**  Śrī said: I am the beloved of the worlds, blessings upon you; I am renowned here by the name of Śrī. The daityas, forsaken by me, have perished for everlasting years.

**13.81.7**  Indra, Vivasvat, Soma, and Viṣṇu, the waters and Agni too, the sages and the gods — all whom I attend upon prosper.

**13.81.8**  And those whom I hate, O cows, perish utterly; bereft of dharma, wealth, and pleasure, they become beset with misery.

**13.81.9**  Know me, O cows, to be of such power, the bestower of happiness; and I desire to dwell within you all forever. I have come beseeching: be graced with Śrī, O sinless ones.

**13.81.10**  The cows said: You are unsteady and fickle, shared in common with many; we do not desire you. Blessings upon you — go where it pleases you.

**13.81.11**  We are all comely of body; what need have we of you today? Go wherever you wish; we are well content without you.

**13.81.12**  Śrī said: Is this seemly of you, O cows, that you do not welcome me here? Why do you not now receive me, hard to win as I am?

**13.81.13**  And there is a true saying current in the world, O you of good vows, which holds for certain: "What comes of itself is held in contempt."

**13.81.14**  Having wrought great and fierce austerity, men attend upon me — gods, dānavas, and gandharvas, piśācas, serpents, and rākṣasas.

**13.81.15**  It is fitting for you, O cows: receive me here. For I am not to be slighted, O gentle ones, throughout the three worlds with all that moves and is still.

**13.81.16**  The cows said: We do not slight you, O goddess, nor do we hold you in contempt; you are unsteady and fickle of mind, and for that reason we shun you.

**13.81.17**  What need of many words here? Go where you will. We are all comely of body; what need have we of you, O sinless one?

**13.81.18**  Śrī said: I shall be despised in all the worlds, O bestowers of honour, if I am refused by you. Show me your grace.

**13.81.19**  Glorious are you and worthy refuges; deliver me, who have come for shelter, who devote myself to you forever and am blameless. I desire your regard always, O auspicious ones.

**13.81.20**  I wish to dwell even in some one part of you, however lowly. Yet there is nothing lowly to be seen in your limbs, O sinless ones.

**13.81.21**  Holy, pure, and fortunate ones, grant me your bidding; in which part I am to dwell, that you should declare to me.
