**13.105.48**  there they go, dwelling in celestial form, wearing celestial garlands, blessed, rich in holy fragrance; but Dhṛtarāṣṭra surely will not go there.

**13.105.49**  Gautama said: "Where there is no fear of cold nor even the least fear of heat, no hunger or thirst, no weariness, neither pain nor likewise pleasure;"

**13.105.50**  "where there is none hateful and none dear, no kinsman and no foe, where there is neither old age nor death, neither merit nor sin—"

**13.105.51**  "—in that dustless, ample realm, established in wisdom and pure being, the holy dwelling of the Self-Existent One, shall my cause concerning the elephant be tried."

**13.105.52**  Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: "Those freed from all attachments, perfected in soul, restrained in their vows, steadfast in the discipline of the inner Self, have attained the path to heaven."

**13.105.53**  "Those endowed with goodness here attain the holy dwelling of Brahman; there your Dhṛtarāṣṭra cannot be seen, great sage."

**13.105.54**  Gautama said: "Where the Rathantara and the Bṛhat hymns are sung, where the altar is strewn with white lotuses, where the drinker of Soma comes drawn by his bay steeds—there will I haul you over this elephant."

**13.105.55**  I recognize you now as the slayer of Vṛtra, the lord of a hundred sacrifices, who ranges across all the worlds. I trust that I have never, through some seizure of the mind, spoken a single crooked word against you.

**13.105.56**  Śakra said: Since, on the pretext of this elephant, I have drawn you along the path that creatures travel to the worlds, instruct me, who bow before you; whatever you command, all of it I shall do.

**13.105.57**  Gautama said: My elephant-son, the white-tusked creature you bore away from me when he was but ten years a calf, who was a second self to me as I dwelt in the forest — that very elephant restore to me, O lord of the gods.

**13.105.58**  Śakra said: Here is your son, O foremost of the twice-born — the elephant who breathes you in as he gazes upon you, who sniffs at your feet with his trunk. Wish well for me, and may homage be yours.

**13.105.59**  Gautama said: Always do I wish you well here, O lord of the gods, and ever do I offer you worship. To me too, O Śakra, grant your blessing; the elephant given by you I gladly receive.

**13.105.60**  Śakra said: Among those wise and steadfast great-souled ones in whose secret heart the Vedas lie hidden, by you alone, great soul, have I been truly understood; and so today I am well pleased with you.

**13.105.61**  Come then, brāhmaṇa, come quickly, together with your son the elephant, and attain the auspicious worlds, both for the present and for all time to come.

**13.105.62**  Bhīṣma said: Then the wielder of the thunderbolt, setting Gautama before him along with his son the elephant, ascended with the holy ones to heaven, that realm so hard to reach.

**13.106.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: You have spoken of giving in its many forms, of peace, truth, and non-injury, of contentment with one's own wife, and of the fruit that giving bears.

**13.106.2**  What is known to grandsire that is greater than the power of austerity? If there is anything beyond austerity, you ought to explain it to me today.

**13.106.3**  Bhīṣma said: As far as men declare austerity to reach, so far do the worlds extend, Yudhiṣṭhira; but my view, son of Kuntī, is that no austerity surpasses fasting.

**13.106.4**  On this point too they recite an ancient tale: the dialogue of Bhagīratha and the great-souled Brahmā.

**13.106.5**  Having passed beyond the world of the gods, the world of the cattle, O Bhārata, and the world of the seers, Bhagīratha went onward — so runs the tradition.

**13.106.6**  Seeing him, Brahmā spoke these words to Bhagīratha, O king: How is it, Bhagīratha, that you have come to this region so hard to reach?

**13.106.7**  For neither gods nor gandharvas nor men come here, Bhagīratha, if they have not performed austerities. How then have you come to this place?

**13.106.8**  Bhagīratha said: Without misgiving I gave food to the brāhmaṇas — a hundred thousand gifts, always and unceasingly — ever holding to the sacred brahminical vow; yet know that it was not by the fruit of this that I came here.

**13.106.9**  Ten single-night rites, ten five-night rites, eleven elevenfold sacrifices, and a hundred Jyotiṣṭoma offerings I performed; yet not even by the fruit of these have I come here.

**13.106.10**  And though I dwelt ever on the bank of the Jāhnavī, practicing austerity for a hundred years, and there gave a thousand she-mules and a city full of women, not even by that have I come here.

**13.106.11**  A hundred thousand horses, and twenty times ten thousand more, I gave at Puṣkara to the twice-born, and cattle by the thousands.

**13.106.12**  Sixty thousand maidens of the finest sort, adorned with garlands and bearing golden ornaments shaped like moon and star, decked in jewelry of pure river-gold, I gave away — yet not by that did I come.

**13.106.13**  At the Gosava sacrifices I gave a hundred million cattle, ten at a time, O lord of the worlds — each with its calf and rich in milk, milked into vessels of gold and bronze — yet not by that did I come.

**13.106.14**  At each of the Aptoryāma rites I duly gave ten young red cows that gave plentiful milk — yet not even by that did I come here.

**13.106.15**  Of milch cows I gave ten million, and ten times that again, O Brahmā — yet not by that have I come here.

**13.106.16**  Of horses born in Bāhli, white steeds wearing golden chains, I gave a hundred thousand — yet not by that have I come here.

**13.106.17**  Eighty million pieces of gold, ten times over, I gave, O Brahmā — at each single sacrifice — yet not by that fruit have I come here.

**13.106.18**  Of tawny horses with dark ears, bearing golden garlands, O grandsire, I gave seventeen times ten million, O Brahmā.

**13.106.19**  Mighty-bodied elephants with tusks like chariot-poles, decked with golden garlands and accompanied by their mates — these I gave, seventeen thousand of them.

**13.106.20**  Chariots with golden frames, adorned with divine ornaments of gold, O lord of the gods, I gave away — seventeen thousand of them — and others besides, yoked to richly caparisoned horses.

**13.106.21**  Whatever portions of sacrificial fee are extolled in the Vedas, at ten Vājapeya rites I bestowed them all — yet not even by that did I come here.

**13.106.22**  As sacrificial fee I gave a thousand men equal to Śakra in their power of sacrifice and in valor, all wearing golden necklaces.

**13.106.23**  Having conquered all kings and offered sacrifices, O grandsire, even by eight Rājasūya rites I did not come here by that means.

**13.106.24**  And though the whole stream of the Gaṅgā was overspread, O lord of the world, by the sacrificial gifts that flowed from my hands, not for the sake of that did I come.

**13.106.25**  Two thousand horses adorned with a hundred ornaments of gold, and a hundred choice villages for each man, I gave threefold — an ascetic of measured food, abiding in calm and curbed in speech.

**13.106.26**  For a long age in the Himālaya I dwelt, by whose unbearable torrent of the Gaṅgā — the stream that Mahādeva once bore upon his head — yet not even by that fruit did I come here, O grandsire.

**13.106.27**  With sacrifices measured by the cast of the yoke-pin I worshiped the gods, and with ten thousand one-day rites, and thirteen- and twelve-day offerings, O god, together with the Pauṇḍarīka — yet not by the fruit of these did I come.

**13.106.28**  Eight thousand humped white bulls I gave to the brāhmaṇas, each with a single horn cased in gold, and along with them their cows wearing golden necklaces.

**13.106.29**  Mountains of jewels heaped with gold and gems I gave, and villages rich in wealth and grain, by the hundreds of thousands.

**13.106.30**  Ten thousand young cows I gave, unwearied, and offered many great sacrifices for the brāhmaṇas — yet not by that did I come here.

**13.106.31**  With eleven-day rites attended by gifts, with twice-twelve-day rites and horse-sacrifices, O god, and with sixteen Ārkāyaṇa offerings, O Brahmā — yet not by the fruit of these have I come here.

**13.106.32**  I gave away a whole forest of golden trees, a league in length and breadth — a grove of mango trees adorned with jewels, each bearing a single golden trunk — yet not by the fruit of these have I come.

**13.106.33**  The unassailable Turāyaṇa vow, free of anger, I kept for thirty years; eight hundred and one cows, day after day, I gave to the brāhmaṇas.

**13.106.34**  Milch cows, red cows, and likewise draft-oxen, O lord of the worlds, I gave continually to the brāhmaṇas, O lord of the gods — yet not by that fruit have I come here.

**13.106.35**  For thirty years, O Brahmā, I daily tended the sacred fire and worshiped with eight Sarvamedha rites and seven Naramedha rites.

**13.106.36**  And with ten Viśvajit rites, and with a hundred and eighteen others — yet not by the fruit of these, O lord of the gods, have I come here.

**13.106.37**  On the Sarayū, the Bāhudā, the Gaṅgā, and at Naimiṣa I gave a million cattle — yet not by that did I come.

**13.106.38**  That secret hidden by Indra in a cave, which Bhārgava found here through austerity — blazing here with the splendor of Uśanas — that most excellent and great rite I brought to fulfillment.

**13.106.39**  Then, when that rite was accomplished, the brāhmaṇas were pleased with me; a thousand seers were there assembled, and by them I was told: Go now to the world of Brahmā, O lord.

**13.106.40**  Thus addressed by a thousand well-pleased brāhmaṇas, O lord, I have reached this world. Let there be no doubt in you upon this point.

**13.106.41**  As the Ordainer has duly fixed, so, being asked, must I speak duly; for I hold no austerity other than fasting. Homage be to you, O best of the gods — be gracious.

**13.106.42**  Bhīṣma said: When King Bhagīratha had spoken thus, Brahmā honored him — worthy of honor as he was — with the rite ordained by sacred law.

**13.107.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: In the Vedic teaching man is said to have a span of a hundred years and the strength of a hundred. Why then, grandsire, do men die, even as children?

**13.107.2**  By what does a man become long-lived, and by what short-lived? By what does he win renown, and by what does he gain prosperity?

**13.107.3**  Is it by austerity, by chastity, by silent prayer, by oblations, or by herbs; by birth, or rather by conduct? Tell me this, grandsire.

**13.107.4**  Bhīṣma said: On this I shall instruct you in what you ask of me — by what a man becomes short-lived or long-lived.

**13.107.5**  And by what he wins renown, and by what he gains prosperity, and how, by conducting himself rightly, a man becomes joined to the good.

**13.107.6**  For it is from right conduct that a man gains long life, from conduct that he gains prosperity, and from conduct that he wins renown, both here and in the world hereafter.

**13.107.7**  For a man of evil conduct does not attain a great span of life here; creatures shrink from him, and likewise they hold him in contempt.

**13.107.8**  Therefore let one who desires his own welfare practice right conduct in this world; even in one whose body bears the marks of sin, good conduct destroys the inauspicious sign.

**13.107.9**  Dharma has conduct for its mark, and the good are known by their conduct; and whatever is the way of the virtuous, that is the very mark of good conduct.

**13.107.10**  Even a man unseen or only heard of, if he walks in dharma and performs works of welfare, him people hold dear.

**13.107.11**  Those who are deniers and idle, who transgress teacher and scripture, who know not dharma and are evil in conduct — these become short of life.

**13.107.12**  Men of bad character, who break all bounds and are forever promiscuous in their unions, become short-lived here and travelers to hell.

**13.107.13**  Even a man lacking every auspicious mark, if he is well-conducted, full of faith, and free of envy, lives a hundred years.

**13.107.14**  Free of anger, speaking the truth, harming no creature, free of envy and of guile — such a man lives a hundred years.

**13.107.15**  The man who crumbles clods, snaps off blades of grass, gnaws his nails, who is forever unclean from leavings and restless in his ways — he does not attain a great span of life here.

**13.107.16**  Let him wake in the hour sacred to Brahmā and reflect upon dharma and worldly good; rising and sipping water, let him stand with joined palms through the morning twilight devotion.

**13.107.17**  In the very same way let him attend the evening twilight devotion with curbed speech; let him never gaze upon the sun as it rises or as it sets.

**13.107.18**  The seers, through their long twilight devotions, won long life; therefore let one always stand, with curbed speech, through both the morning and the evening twilight.

**13.107.19**  Those twice-born who attend the morning twilight but not the evening — all such men a righteous king should set to the labors of a śūdra.

**13.107.20**  The wives of others must never be approached, in any of the four orders; for nothing in the world so shortens a man's life as the resorting to another's wife.

**13.107.21**  The dressing of the hair, the anointing of the eyes, the cleaning of the teeth, and the worship of the gods — these let him perform in the early part of the day.

**13.107.22**  Let him never look upon dung or urine, nor ever tread upon them; and let him never hold converse with a woman in her courses.

**13.107.23**  Let him not void his dung in a field or near a village; and let him never pass either urine or dung into water.

**13.107.24**  Let him always eat facing the east, with curbed speech, not disparaging the food; let him offer it in mind, and when he has eaten, let him touch the fire.

**13.107.25**  Facing the east, he eats what brings long life; facing the south, what brings renown; facing the west, what brings wealth; facing the north, he eats in accord with truth.

**13.107.26**  Let him never tread upon husks of grain, upon hair, ashes, or potsherds; and let him keep far away from the latrine of another.

**13.107.27**  Let him perform the oblations for peace and have the Sāvitrī rites carried out; and let him eat while seated, never in any wise while walking.

**13.107.28**  Urine should not be passed while standing, nor upon ashes, nor in a cattle-pen.

**13.107.29**  Let him eat with feet wetted, but not lie down with feet wet; eating with feet wetted, he lives a hundred years.

**13.107.30**  Let him never, while unclean from leavings, touch the three sources of splendor — the fire, the cow, and the brāhmaṇa — and thus his life will not be diminished.

**13.107.31**  One who is ritually unclean should never gaze upon the three luminaries: the sun and moon, and the stars in all their host.

**13.107.32**  When an elder draws near, the life-breaths of a young man rise up and would depart; but by standing to greet him and offering salutation, he regains them once more.

**13.107.33**  He should salute his elders and have a seat offered to them; with joined palms he should attend upon them, and when one departs he should follow behind.

**13.107.34**  He should not sit upon a broken seat, and should avoid a cracked bronze vessel; he should not eat clad in a single garment, nor bathe naked, nor sleep naked, nor lie down to rest while still ritually unclean.

**13.107.35**  While unclean he should not touch his head, for all the vital breaths have their seat there; and he should shun the seizing of the hair and any blows upon the head.

**13.107.36**  He should never scratch his head with both hands at once, nor bathe his head too frequently; thus his lifespan will not be diminished.

**13.107.37**  Having bathed his head with oil, he should touch no other limb with it, nor should he eat ground sesame; thus he attains long life.

**13.107.38**  While unclean he should never teach nor study; and in a foul-smelling wind he should not even rehearse the texts in his mind.

**13.107.39**  On this point those who know the ancient lore recite verses chanted by Yama: 'I cut short the lifespan of such a one, and likewise I take away his offspring—'

**13.107.40**  '—of the twice-born who, while unclean, recites and pursues his private study, and who through delusion practices it even in a forbidden hour.' Therefore, even when intent upon it, one should never study during a time when study is forbidden.

**13.107.41**  Those who pass water facing the sun, facing the wind, toward a cow, toward the twice-born, or upon a pathway—they become bereft of their lifespan.

**13.107.42**  He should void both urine and excrement facing north by day and facing south by night; thus his lifespan will not be diminished.

**13.107.43**  He who wishes to live long should not slight three lean creatures—the brāhmaṇa, the kṣatriya, and the serpent—for all three are venomous as fanged snakes.

**13.107.44**  The angered fanged serpent burns as far as it can see with its eyes; the kṣatriya too, when angered, burns as far as his ardor can reach.

**13.107.45**  But the brāhmaṇa can destroy a whole lineage by his meditation and his very gaze; therefore the wise should attend these three with care.

**13.107.46**  One should never persist in enmity with a teacher; an angered teacher must be appeased and won over, O Yudhiṣṭhira.

**13.107.47**  Whether a teacher acts rightly or wrongly, one must still conduct oneself dutifully toward him here; the reviling of a teacher burns away men's lifespan—of this there is no doubt.

**13.107.48**  One who seeks his own welfare should pass water far from his dwelling, wash his feet far off, and likewise discard food-leavings at a distance.

**13.107.49**  Not too early at dawn, nor too late at dusk, nor when the sun stands at noon should one set out—nor in the company of strangers, nor alone, nor in the company of the base.

**13.107.50**  The path should be yielded to a brāhmaṇa, to cattle, and to kings, to an elder, to one burdened with a load, to a pregnant woman, and to the weak.

**13.107.51**  He should make reverent circumambulation of well-known sacred trees, and keep all crossroads upon his right as he passes.

**13.107.52**  At noon, in the time of night, and at midnight—always—he should not frequent crossroads, nor at the two twilights either.

**13.107.53**  He should not wear sandals or a garment that has been worn by others; he should ever remain continent, and should not tread one foot upon the other.

**13.107.54**  On the new-moon day, the full-moon day, on every fourteenth day, and on the eighth day of both fortnights, he should always remain continent.

**13.107.55**  He should not eat meat to no sacred purpose, nor the flesh of the back; and he should shun abuse, slander, and malicious talebearing.

**13.107.56**  He should not be a wounder of others, nor a speaker of cruel words, nor should he by base means seize what belongs to another; the speech by which another would shudder—that searing, hell-winning speech he should never utter.

**13.107.57**  The arrows of speech fly forth from the mouth, struck by which a man grieves day and night; they fall upon another's tender places—the wise man should never loose them against others.

**13.107.58**  A forest pierced by arrows grows again, and one felled by the axe; but the foul wound inflicted by an ill-spoken word never heals over.

**13.107.59**  He should not mock those lacking a limb or bearing one too many, the unlettered, the aged, those bereft of beauty or wealth, or those wanting in spirit.

**13.107.60**  He should shun disbelief, the reviling of the Vedas, and the disparagement of the gods, as well as hatred, obstinacy, conceit, and harshness.

**13.107.61**  He should not raise the rod against another, nor in anger strike him down—save in the case of a son or pupil, for whom chastisement for the sake of instruction is sanctioned.

**13.107.62**  He should not speak ill of brāhmaṇas, nor point out the stars by name, nor declare the lunar day of the fortnight; thus his lifespan will not be diminished.

**13.107.63**  After voiding urine or excrement, or again after walking upon a highway, he should wash his feet—and likewise before his private study and before eating.

**13.107.64**  The gods ordained three things as purifiers for the brāhmaṇas: that which is unseen, that which is cleansed with water, and that which is commended by speech.

**13.107.65**  Wheaten cakes, rice mixed with sesame, meat, fried cakes, and milk-rice should not be prepared for one's own sake, but should be made ready for the gods' sake.

**13.107.66**  He should daily tend the sacred fire and daily give alms; restraining his speech, he should regularly use the tooth-stick; and he should not be one who sleeps past sunrise, lest he be made to perform an expiation.

**13.107.67**  On rising he should first salute his mother and father, and then his teacher as well; thus he attains long life.

**13.107.68**  He should always avoid the tooth-sticks that are forbidden, use those sanctioned by scripture, and avoid them too upon the sacred days.

**13.107.69**  Facing north and with collected mind, he should always perform his purifications.

**13.107.70**  Without first performing worship of the gods, he should never go to anyone—save to a teacher, an elder, a righteous man, or one of discernment.

**13.107.71**  Those of greater wisdom should not look into a soiled mirror, nor should one ever resort to an unknown woman or to a pregnant one.

**13.107.72**  He should not sleep with his head to the north, nor with his head to the west; the wise man should sleep with his head to the east, or else to the south.

**13.107.73**  He should not sleep upon a bed that is broken or split, nor in a hidden place, nor upon a coupled one, nor ever lying crosswise.

**13.107.74**  He should never bathe naked, nor ever bathe by night; and once bathed, the truly discerning man should not wipe down his limbs.

**13.107.75**  He should not anoint himself before bathing, nor shake out his garment after bathing; a man should always put on his garments while they are still moist; he should not pull off his garlands, nor wear them turned outward.

**13.107.76**  A red garland should not be worn; the wise should wear a white one, excepting only the lotus and the blue water-lily, O lord.

**13.107.77**  Yet upon the head a red flower may be worn, and likewise a forest blossom; and a garland of gold is never defiling. To one freshly bathed the unguent should always be applied while moist, O lord of peoples.

**13.107.78**  The wise man should not put his garment on inverted, nor wear one already worn by another, nor one whose hem is frayed.

**13.107.79**  One garment should be worn for sleeping, O best of men, another upon the highways, and yet another for the worship of the gods.

**13.107.80**  With priyaṅgu and sandal, with bilva and tagara, and with saffron the wise man should anoint himself, each used separately.

**13.107.81**  He should observe the fast, bathed, pure, and adorned; and at all the sacred seasons he should ever remain continent.

**13.107.82**  He should never eat what has been touched by something licked, nor foods whose essence has been drawn out, nor eat in the sight of onlookers without first offering a share.

**13.107.83**  The wise man should not eat while crowded close to others, nor while unclean, nor in the company of the good, nor partake of foods forbidden by the sacred laws, nor eat behind another's back.

**13.107.84**  The best of men who seeks his own welfare should not eat the fruit of the pippala or the banyan, nor the hemp-greens, nor the udumbara.

**13.107.85**  He should avoid the flesh of the goat, of the cow, and of the peacock; and he should avoid dried meat as well as what has grown stale overnight.

**13.107.86**  The learned man should not eat salt from his palm, nor curds with barley-meal by night, and he should avoid meat eaten to no sacred purpose.

**13.107.87**  He should not eat with the hair, nor at another man's funeral feast; the self-controlled man should eat at evening and at morning, but not in the interval between.

**13.107.88**  Restraining his speech, not clad in a single garment, never standing unseated, he should never eat upon the bare ground, nor seated apart, nor while making noise.

**13.107.89**  Having first given water and then food to his guests, O lord of peoples, the wise man should eat afterward, and not with his mind elsewhere.

**13.107.90**  The food set out in a single row is shared in common, O king of men; but he who eats without first offering to his well-disposed companions swallows the deadly hālāhala poison.

**13.107.91**  Water, milk-rice, clarified butter, curds, barley-meal, and honey—once the remnant of these has been set aside, it should be given to no one.

**13.107.92**  While eating, O tiger among men, one should harbor no misgivings; and he who seeks his welfare should not take curds as a draught to wash down his food.

**13.107.93**  Having sipped water and let it flow through his hand, he should then sprinkle water upon the great toe of his right foot.

**13.107.94**  Placing his hand upon his head and touching the fire with collected mind, the man skilled in proper observance attains pre-eminence among his kinsmen.

**13.107.95**  Having touched his vital organs with water and his navel with the palm of his hand, he should remain steady, and not so with a wet hand.

**13.107.96**  At the base of the thumb the sacred ford of Brahmā is declared to lie; and behind the little finger the ford of the gods is here said to be.

**13.107.97**  And with that which lies between the thumb and the forefinger, O descendant of Bharata, having touched water in due form, he should perform the rites for the ancestors.

**13.107.98**  He should never utter slander of another, nor anything unkind; the man who seeks his welfare should rouse no wrath in anyone.

**13.107.99**  He should not wish to converse with the fallen, should shun even the sight of them, and should keep no company with them; thus he attains long life.

**13.107.100**  He should not engage in intercourse by day, nor with a maiden, nor with a harlot, nor approach an unbathed woman; thus he attains long life.

**13.107.101**  Sipping water each at its proper sacred point, when the rite is duly prepared, drinking water thrice and wiping the lips twice, a man becomes purified.

**13.107.102**  Having touched his organs of sense once and sprinkled himself thrice, a man should perform the rites for the ancestors and the gods by the observances revealed in the Veda.

**13.107.103**  Hear from me too, O Kaurava, the purification that serves the brāhmaṇa's purpose, the conduct that is wholesome, declared for both the beginning and the end of a meal.

**13.107.104**  In all purifications one should touch with the sacred ford of Brahmā; and after spitting or sneezing, by touching water one becomes pure.

**13.107.105**  An aged kinsman, a friend, and one who has become poor—these should be given lodging in the house; that brings fortune and long life.

**13.107.106**  Doves in the house bring fortune, and parrots, and mynah birds; these in the home portend no evil, and likewise the small oil-drinking creatures.

**13.107.107**  But when birds of ill omen, vultures, pigeons, or bees take up their abode there, one should then perform a rite of appeasement.

**13.107.108**  These are inauspicious, as is the cursing of the great-souled; and the secrets of the great-souled should never be divulged.

**13.107.109**  He should not approach forbidden women—the wives of kings, nor their companions, nor those belonging to physicians, to children, to the aged, or to servants, O Yudhiṣṭhira—

**13.107.110**  —nor those of kinsmen, of brāhmaṇas, of one who has sought refuge, or of relatives by marriage, O lord of kings; thus he attains long life.

**13.107.111**  A dwelling that has been built by a brāhmaṇa and by a master-builder—in such a one, O lord of men, let the wise man, desiring prosperity, ever take up his abode.

**13.107.112**  At the twilight hours, O king, the discerning man should not sleep, nor pursue his studies, nor take his meal; thus he wins long life.

**13.107.113**  By night one should not perform the rites for the ancestors, nor groom oneself after eating; by him who desires prosperity, the offering of water should not be made by night.

**13.107.114**  Parched barley-meal should ever be avoided by night, O Bhārata, as should be, at a meal, white leavings and water alone.

**13.107.115**  One should not eat to repletion by night, nor should one practise it; one should not pick one's teeth, nor do so after eating.

**13.107.116**  A maiden born of a great family, commended, endowed with auspicious marks, and of fitting age—her, O greatly wise one, a man is worthy to wed.

**13.107.117**  Having begotten offspring and so established his line, a man should give his sons over to the various branches of knowledge and to the duties of the family, O Bhārata.

**13.107.118**  A daughter, when she is grown, should be given to a wise man of good family; sons should be settled in marriage, and servants should be taken from good households, O Bhārata.

**13.107.119**  Having bathed his head, a man should then perform the rites to the gods and to the ancestors; he should not perform them under the lunar mansion in which he himself was born, nor under the Proṣṭhapadās, nor under Agni's mansion (Kṛttikā), O Bhārata.

**13.107.120**  On all the harsh-natured days he should each day forbear; whatever days are named as such in the science of the stars, all of those he should avoid.

**13.107.121**  Facing the east, with collected mind, one should have the trimming of the beard performed, or else facing the north, O king of kings; thus one wins long life.

**13.107.122**  One should utter no slander, neither of others nor of oneself; slander, it is declared, conduces not to righteousness, O bull of the Bhāratas.

**13.107.123**  He should avoid a deformed woman, and likewise a deformed maiden, O best of men—and one bearing the same lineage-name (gotra), or one born of his own mother's family.

**13.107.124**  An aged woman, one who has renounced the world, one devoted to another husband, one of too dark a hue, and one of a higher class than his own—these he should avoid.

**13.107.125**  The discerning man should approach neither one unfit for wedlock nor one of an alien stock; a tawny-eyed woman or a leprous one you are not worthy to wed.

**13.107.126**  One born in a family afflicted with the falling-sickness, and one base-born, he should avoid, and one born in a family of those marked with white leprosy—these three, O lord of men.

**13.107.127**  She who is endowed with auspicious marks and is commended for those marks, who is pleasing to the mind and fair to look upon—her you are worthy to wed.

**13.107.128**  One should marry into a great family, or into one of like standing, O Yudhiṣṭhira; an inferior woman, or a fallen one, should not be taken by him who desires prosperity.

**13.107.129**  Having kindled the sacred fires with care, all those rites that are well ordained, that are declared by the brāhmaṇas in the Vedas, he should duly perform.

**13.107.130**  No jealousy should be harboured toward women, yet one's wife should be guarded in every way; jealousy shortens life, therefore one should put jealousy away.

**13.107.131**  Sleeping by day shortens life, and so does lying abed when the sun has risen; so too lying down in the early dawn and in the night, and those who sleep while still unclean from food.

**13.107.132**  Adultery shortens life, and so does eating the barber's leavings; these things one should studiously refrain from, nor make a habit of them, O Bhārata.

**13.107.133**  At twilight one should not eat, nor bathe, nor void one's bowels; one should remain pure-minded at that hour and perform no other act whatever.

**13.107.134**  Having bathed, O ruler of men, one should honour the brāhmaṇas, and, being bathed, bow down to the gods and salute one's elders.

**13.107.135**  Uninvited one should not go to a sacrifice, though one may go merely to behold it; for to go uninvited shortens life, O Bhārata.

**13.107.136**  One should not wander abroad alone, nor go forth by night; before the evening twilight has come, one should remain within the house.

**13.107.137**  The command of mother, father, and elders is simply to be carried out; whether it seem beneficial or harmful, it is not to be questioned, O bull among men.

**13.107.138**  In the science of archery and in the Veda effort should be made, O ruler of men, and on the back of the elephant, on the back of the horse, and in the handling of chariots: be diligent, O king of kings, for the diligent man thrives in happiness.

**13.107.139**  Unassailable by his foes, by his servants, and by his own kin, and devoted to the protection of his people, such a man suffers harm in no quarter.

**13.107.140**  The science of reasoning you should master, and the science of grammar, O Bhārata, and the science of music too; the arts, O ruler of men, are to be thoroughly known.

**13.107.141**  The ancient lore, the histories, and such tales as there are, and the deeds of great-souled men—these you should ever be listening to.

**13.107.142**  A wife in her courses one should not approach, nor summon; the discerning man should go to her, bathed, on the night of the fourth day.

**13.107.143**  On the fifth day a female is conceived, and on the sixth day a male; by this rule the learned man should approach his wife.

**13.107.144**  Kinsmen, connections, and friends are ever to be honoured; sacrifice should be offered to the best of one's power with rites of manifold gifts; and thereafter the forest should be resorted to, O ruler of men.

**13.107.145**  This summary account of the marks of long-life-giving conduct has been declared to you; what remains is to be learned from the elders versed in the three Vedas, O Yudhiṣṭhira.

**13.107.146**  Right conduct is the begetter of prosperity; right conduct is the increaser of renown; from right conduct life itself is prolonged, and right conduct destroys every ill-omened mark.

**13.107.147**  Of all the scriptural traditions, right conduct is declared the highest; from right conduct springs dharma, and from dharma life is increased.

**13.107.148**  This, conferring fame, conferring long life, leading to heaven, a great means of well-being, was proclaimed by Brahmā out of compassion for all the classes of men.

**13.108.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: How an elder should bear himself toward his juniors, O bull of the Bhāratas, and how juniors should bear themselves toward an elder—that tell me.

**13.108.2**  Bhīṣma said: Bear yourself as an elder, my son, for you are ever the eldest; weightier is the conduct of the teacher than that of the pupil, O Bhārata.

**13.108.3**  Toward a teacher of undeveloped wisdom a pupil cannot rightly conduct himself; for the far-sightedness that belongs to the teacher belongs not to the pupil, O Bhārata.

**13.108.4**  At the time for being blind let even the wise man be as if blind, and at the time for being dull, dull; whatever transgression there be among such matters, he should point it out only with tact.

**13.108.5**  Men whose hearts are already estranged would, before one's very eyes, deepen what division has been wrought; tormented by another's prosperity, O son of Kuntī, and likewise foes who crave disunion.

**13.108.6**  The eldest causes a family to flourish, or again brings it to ruin; the eldest may even destroy the whole family in which he is born.

**13.108.7**  But should an elder brother wrong his younger, he should forfeit his rights as eldest and his share, and he is to be restrained by kings.

**13.108.8**  For a man given to wrongdoing goes without doubt to evil worlds; like the blossom of the bamboo (vidula), his begetting is remembered as fruitless.

**13.108.9**  In whatever family a wicked man is born, the source of every calamity, he begets only ill fame and makes good repute vanish away.

**13.108.10**  And all uterine brothers who follow forbidden courses deserve no share; nor, without first giving to his juniors, should the eldest set aside a portion for himself.

**13.108.11**  A father's inheritance belongs to the younger as well; but as for the traveller, whose gain is the fruit of his own legs' toil, what he has won by his own striving he need not give away against his will.

**13.108.12**  When brothers are yet undivided, even if their exertion be in common, a father should in no wise allot to a son an unequal share.

**13.108.13**  One should not slight one's elders, be one ill-doing or well-doing; whether a woman or a younger-born, if one perceive what is better, let one act accordingly—for the better is dharma, so they say, and so the knowers of dharma understand.

**13.108.14**  A preceptor outweighs ten instructors, a father ten preceptors, and a mother ten fathers—or even the whole earth.

**13.108.15**  In claim to reverence she surpasses all; there is no elder equal to a mother. Because the mother is the weightier, therefore do people so honour her.

**13.108.16**  The eldest brother is equal to a father when the father is dead, O Bhārata; for he should be the provider of livelihood to these others, and he should protect them.

**13.108.17**  The juniors should all bow down to him, following his will, and they should look to him for their support, just as to a father.

**13.108.18**  These two, the father and the mother, bring forth the body, O Bhārata; but the birth that the teacher fashions by his instruction—that is the true one, free from age and death.

**13.108.19**  An elder sister too is the equal of a mother, O bull of the Bhāratas; and a brother's wife is likewise to be esteemed, at whose breast in childhood one may have drunk.

**13.109.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: Among all the classes, and even among the barbarian peoples, O grandsire, this inclination toward fasting exists; yet its cause we do not understand.

**13.109.2**  By the brāhmaṇa and the kṣatriya the observances are to be performed—so we have heard; yet how does fasting come to be a duty for them, O grandsire?

**13.109.3**  Declare the rule of fasts for all, O king, and what destiny he attains who is devoted to fasting.

**13.109.4**  Fasting is the supreme merit; fasting is the highest refuge. By fasting here, O best of men, what fruit does one obtain?

**13.109.5**  By what is one freed from unrighteousness, and how does one attain to righteousness? How does one win heaven and merit, O best of the Bhāratas?

**13.109.6**  And having fasted, what should be given thereafter, O ruler of men, by which, through righteousness, one might gain happiness and wealth—tell me that.

**13.109.7**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: To the son of Kuntī, knower of dharma, son of Dharma, as he spoke thus, Bhīṣma the son of Śaṃtanu, knower of the truth of dharma, said these words.

**13.109.8**  Verily, O great king, this was heard of old—what excellent virtues lie in the practice of fasting, O bull of the Bhāratas.

**13.109.9**  For I once questioned Aṅgiras, descendant of Prajāpati, O Bhārata; just as you question me, so did I question that sage rich in austerity.

**13.109.10**  Questioned by me with this very question, the blessed one, sprung from fire, set forth the meritorious rule of fasting, O bull of the Bhāratas.

**13.109.11**  Aṅgiras said: For the brāhmaṇa and the kṣatriya a fast of three nights is enjoined, O delight of the Kurus, and here also one of twice three nights is laid down, O bull among men.

**13.109.12**  But as for the vaiśya and the śūdra who out of delusion undertake a fast of three nights or of twice three nights, for those two no thriving comes of it.

**13.109.13**  The skipping of every fourth meal is ordained for the vaiśya and the śūdra; the three-night fast is not enjoined for them by the knowers of dharma, the expounders of the Veda.

**13.109.14**  By fasting on the fifth and the sixth lunar days and on the full-moon day, O Bhārata, a man is born patient, endowed with beauty, and learned.

**13.109.15**  The wise man who keeps the fifth and the sixth as fast-days and feeds the twice-born, and is given to sacrifice, becomes never childless nor ever poor.

**13.109.16**  And by fasting on the eighth and on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, O son of Kuntī, one is born free from disease and full of vigour.

**13.109.17**  He who passes the month of Mārgaśīrṣa taking but a single meal a day, and with devotion feeds the twice-born, is freed from diseases and sins.

**13.109.18**  Filled with every blessing, possessed of all healing herbs, sharing in the fruits of tillage, rich in wealth and rich in sons—so is he born.

**13.109.19**  He who passes the month of Pauṣa with but a single meal, O son of Kuntī, is born fortunate, fair to look upon, and sharing in renown.

**13.109.20**  He who, devoted to the ancestors, passes the month of Māgha with a single meal a day attains to greatness in a prosperous family, in the midst of his kinsmen.

**13.109.21**  He who passes the month presided over by Bhaga (Phālguna) with a single meal a day comes to be beloved among women, and they become devoted to him.

**13.109.22**  He who, self-controlled, passes the month of Caitra with a single meal a day is born into a great family abounding in gold, gems, and pearls.

**13.109.23**  Whoever, with senses subdued, passes through the month of Vaiśākha on a single meal a day—be it man or woman—attains pre-eminence among kinsmen.

**13.109.24**  Whoever passes the month of Jyeṣṭhāmūla taking but a single meal each day—man or woman—is reborn to sovereignty unrivalled and supreme.

**13.109.25**  He who, unwearying, keeps the month of Āṣāḍha upon a single meal each day is born rich in grain, rich in wealth, and rich in sons.

**13.109.26**  He who, self-controlled, passes the month of Śrāvaṇa upon a single meal is everywhere joined to royal consecration, and the increaser of his kinsmen.

**13.109.27**  The man who through the month of Prauṣṭhapada eats but once a day attains a lordship rich in wealth, flourishing, and unshakable.

**13.109.28**  Likewise he who passes the month of Āśvayuja upon a single meal is born blessed with offspring, rich in conveyances, and abounding in sons.

**13.109.29**  The man who, through the month of Kārttika, takes but one meal a day is born a hero, with many wives, and crowned with renown.

**13.109.30**  Thus, O tiger among men, have the months been proclaimed for those who fast through them. Now hear too, O king, the observances reckoned by the lunar days.

**13.109.31**  He who eats a meal only when each fortnight has run its course, O Bhārata, is born rich in cattle, abounding in sons, and long of life.

**13.109.32**  He who, month by month for twelve years, fasts through three nights at a stretch attains lordship over hosts, free of rivals and unsullied.

**13.109.33**  All these observances, O best of the Bhāratas, are to be performed for twelve autumns by one who keeps to the round of active life.

**13.109.34**  But he who eats at dawn and again at evening, drinking nothing between, ever devoted to non-injury and pouring oblations into Jātavedas the fire—

**13.109.35**  —that man, O king, is perfected in six years, of this there is no doubt, and gains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.

**13.109.36**  He mounts a celestial car bright as molten gold, in the dwelling of the apsarases that resounds with dance and song.

**13.109.37**  For a full thousand years he is honoured in the world of Brahmā, and when that is spent he returns here to attain greatness.

**13.109.38**  The man who through a full year takes but a single meal a day enjoys the fruit of the Atirātra sacrifice.

**13.109.39**  For ten thousand years he is honoured in heaven, and when that is spent he returns here to attain greatness.

**13.109.40**  He who through a full year eats only every fourth mealtime, ever devoted to non-injury, truthful in speech, his senses curbed—

**13.109.41**  —he indeed enjoys the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice, and for thirty thousand years he is honoured in heaven.

**13.109.42**  Should a man, O son of Kuntī, pass a whole year eating only at every sixth mealtime, he gains the fruit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice.

**13.109.43**  He travels in a celestial car yoked with cakravāka birds, and rejoices in heaven for forty thousand years.

**13.109.44**  Living through a whole year, O king, upon only every eighth meal, a man gains the fruit of the Gavāmayana sacrifice.

**13.109.45**  He travels in a celestial car yoked with swans and cranes, and rejoices in heaven for fifty thousand years.

**13.109.46**  He who for a whole year, O king, eats only when each fortnight has passed—of his half-year of abstinence the venerable Aṅgiras has spoken—dwells in heaven for sixty thousand years.

**13.109.47**  And there, O lord of peoples, as he sleeps he is roused by the sweet, well-tuned notes of vīṇās and lutes and flutes.

**13.109.48**  And he who through one year here drinks milk only once a month—that man, dear child, O king, gains the fruit of the Viśvajit sacrifice.

**13.109.49**  He travels in a celestial car yoked with lions and tigers, and rejoices in heaven for seventy thousand years.

**13.109.50**  Beyond a month, O tiger among men, no fast is ordained; but the rule of utter abstinence from food, O Pārtha, those versed in dharma declare thus.

**13.109.51**  He who, untroubled and free of disease, undertakes the fast unto death gains, at every step, the fruit of a sacrifice; of this there is no doubt.

**13.109.52**  He goes to heaven in a celestial car yoked with swans, and a hundred apsaras-maidens delight that man.

**13.109.53**  And he who, even if afflicted or diseased, undertakes the fast unto death rejoices in heaven, O lord, for a hundred thousand years, and as he sleeps is roused by the sound of girdles and anklets.

**13.109.54**  Borne in a celestial car yoked with a thousand swans, gleaming like the moon and thronged with a hundred women, he goes and there takes his delight, O bull of the Bhāratas.

**13.109.55**  For the wasted, replenishment is seen as good; for the wounded, the healing of the wound; for the diseased, a wealth of medicines; and for the angry, appeasement.

**13.109.56**  For the suffering, the bestowal of goods through wealth and honour: yet none of these please the man who longs for heaven and would prosper in happiness.

**13.109.57**  Therefore that man, his desires fulfilled and richly adorned, takes his delight in a fair celestial car bright as gold and thronged with a hundred women.

**13.109.58**  Serene, his resolve fulfilled, happy, and purged of every stain, the man who casts off his body by fasting gains this fruit.

**13.109.59**  In a celestial car gleaming like gold, radiant as the newly risen sun, inlaid with beryl and pearls, resounding with vīṇā and drum,

**13.109.60**  strewn with banners and lamps, ringing with celestial bells, attended by a thousand women—there that man thrives in bliss.

**13.109.61**  For as many thousands of years, O Pāṇḍava, as there are pores of hair upon his limbs, even so long does he rejoice in heaven.

**13.109.62**  There is no scripture higher than the Veda, no teacher like a mother; there is no gain greater than dharma, no austerity beyond fasting.

**13.109.63**  There is no purifier higher than the brāhmaṇas, in heaven or here below; and no act of austerity is known that is the equal of fasting.

**13.109.64**  By fasting in due form the gods attained the threefold heaven, and the seers won the highest perfection through fasts.

**13.109.65**  For a thousand celestial years the wise Viśvāmitra endured upon but a single meal, and thereby came to brāhmaṇahood.

**13.109.66**  Cyavana and Jamadagni, Vasiṣṭha, Gautama, and Bhṛgu—all these great seers, steadfast in endurance, attained to heaven.

**13.109.67**  This of old was made known by Aṅgiras to the great seers; he who ever makes it known meets with no sorrow.

**13.109.68**  And this rule in due order, O son of Kuntī, set forth by the great seer Aṅgiras—whoever recites it or hearkens to it without fail, no sin is found in that man.

**13.109.69**  He is freed from every defilement, nor is his mind overborne by faults; he comes to understand the cries of creatures born of other wombs, and that best of men attains enduring renown.

**13.110.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: The sacrifices have been duly declared by the great-souled grandsire, and their virtues set forth truly, in every respect, both in the next world and in this.

**13.110.2**  But those sacrifices cannot be attained by a poor man, O grandsire; sacrifices require many appurtenances and a vast array of varied materials.

**13.110.3**  They can be undertaken by kings or by princes, O grandsire, but not by those wanting in wealth, lacking in means, solitary, and unsupported.

**13.110.4**  That rule which even the poor might always be able to follow, and which would be equal to these fruits of sacrifice—tell me of it, O grandsire.

**13.110.5**  Bhīṣma said: This was declared by Aṅgiras, a rule whose essence is the fruit of fasting and which is equal to the fruits of sacrifice; learn it now, O Yudhiṣṭhira.

**13.110.6**  He who eats at dawn and again at evening, drinking nothing between, ever devoted to non-injury and pouring oblations into Jātavedas the fire—

**13.110.7**  —that man is perfected in just six years, of this there is no doubt, and he gains a celestial car of the colour of molten gold.

**13.110.8**  In the dwelling of the celestial women, resounding with dance and song, blazing like fire, he abides in the realm of Prajāpati for a padma of years.

**13.110.9**  He who for three years eats but a single meal continually, ever faithful to his wedded wife, gains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma.

**13.110.10**  And he who, eating only on every second day a single meal for all twelve months while pouring oblations into Jātavedas the fire, would thereby win the fruit of a Bahusuvarṇa sacrifice, dear to Vāsava—

**13.110.11**  —truthful in speech, given to charity, devoted to brāhmaṇas, free of malice, patient, self-restrained, his anger conquered—that man attains the highest goal.

**13.110.12**  In a celestial car bright as a pale white cloud and marked with the sign of the swan, when two padmas are complete he dwells together with the apsarases.

**13.110.13**  And he who eats only on every third day a single meal, for all twelve months pouring oblations into Jātavedas the fire—

**13.110.14**  —that man gains the unsurpassed fruit of the Atirātra sacrifice, and obtains a celestial car yoked with peacocks and swans.

**13.110.15**  In the world of the Seven Seers he dwells ever together with the apsarases, and his term there, they say, is three padmas before his return.

**13.110.16**  And he who eats only on every fourth day a single meal, for all twelve months pouring oblations into Jātavedas the fire—

**13.110.17**  —that man gains the unsurpassed fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice, and obtains a celestial car bestrode by the daughters of Indra.

**13.110.18**  At the very bounds of the ocean he dwells in the world of Vāsava, and for all time beholds the sport of the king of the gods.

**13.110.19**  And he who eats only on every fifth day a single meal, for all twelve months pouring oblations into Jātavedas the fire—

**13.110.20**  —free of greed, truthful, devoted to brāhmaṇas and harming none, without malice and standing clear of sin, he gains the fruit of the Dvādaśāha rite.

**13.110.21**  He mounts a divine celestial car wrought of pure gold, marked with the sign of the swan and gleaming like a wreath of suns—a pale and shining mansion.

**13.110.22**  There he dwells in bliss for four returns and twelve padmas, a span measured by the count of the arrows and the fires.

**13.110.23**  And the sage who eats his meal only on every sixth day, for all twelve months pouring oblations into Jātavedas the fire—

**13.110.24**  —ever bathing at the three appointed times, chaste, and free of malice, he gains the unsurpassed fruit of the Gavāmayana sacrifice.

**13.110.25**  He wins a supreme vehicle, fashioned of gold and yoked, bright as the flame of fire and attended by swans and peacocks.

**13.110.26**  And asleep there in the lap of the apsarases, he is awakened by the chime of anklets and the jingling of girdles.

**13.110.27**  A thousand koṭis of years, and three hundred koṭis besides, eighteen padmas, and likewise two patākas—

**13.110.28**  —and fifty myriads more: by a span equal to the number of hairs on a hundred bear-skins, he is honoured in the world of Brahmā.

**13.110.29**  And he who eats only on every seventh day a single meal, for all twelve months pouring oblations into Jātavedas the fire—

**13.110.30**  —guarding his speech, practising chastity, and shunning flowers, fragrant unguents, honey, and meat—

**13.110.31**  —such a man goes to the world of the Maruts and to the world of Indra, and there, his aim achieved, he is borne aloft by the daughters of the gods.

**13.110.32**  That man gains the fruit of the Bahusuvarṇa sacrifice, and rejoices in those worlds for a span beyond all reckoning.

**13.110.33**  And the man who, patient through a whole year, eats only on every eighth day, ever intent upon the service of the gods and pouring oblations into Jātavedas the fire—

**13.110.34**  —gains the unsurpassed fruit of the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice, and mounts a celestial car of the hue of the lotus.

**13.110.35**  Women dark of hue, and others golden-fair, and yet others of dusky complexion — graced with youth, beauty, and charm — he wins: of this there is no doubt.

**13.110.36**  But he who, for a full year, eats only on every ninth day, ever for twelve months pouring oblations into Jātavedas, the fire,

**13.110.37**  that man gains the fruit of the horse-sacrifice, and obtains a celestial chariot bright as the white lotus.

**13.110.38**  With the splendor of blazing sun and fire, adorned with heavenly garlands, he is borne aloft by the maidens of Rudra to the eternal firmament.

**13.110.39**  For eighteen thousand years, indeed for an entire aeon, and for a hundred thousand crores of years, he rejoices in those worlds.

**13.110.40**  But he who, for a full year, eats only when each tenth day has passed, ever for twelve months pouring oblations into Jātavedas, the fire,

**13.110.41**  in the dwelling of the maidens of Brahmā, enchanting to all beings, attains the unsurpassed fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices.

**13.110.42**  And lovely maidens ever delight that man, some hued like the blue lotus, others like the red lotus.

**13.110.43**  He wins a supreme celestial chariot, circling in spirals, wreathed in deep whorls, resembling the billows of the ocean.

**13.110.44**  Resounding with strings of wondrous gems, with conches and lotuses, with pillars of crystal and adamantine essence, its terraces finely wrought — he mounts that great chariot drawn by swans and cranes.

**13.110.45**  But he who eats his portion only when the eleventh day has come, ever for twelve months pouring oblations into Jātavedas, the fire,

**13.110.46**  who covets not another's wife in word or even in thought, and speaks no falsehood, not even for the sake of mother or father,

**13.110.47**  he draws near to Mahādeva the mighty, seated upon his celestial chariot, and beholds the Self-Existent One, his own chariot waiting before him.

**13.110.48**  Maidens of golden radiance and lovely form bear him to that enchanting heavenly abode of the Rudras in the sky.

**13.110.49**  For years beyond measure he dwells there, even to the ending of an age — a hundred thousand crores of years, and ten hundred crores besides.

**13.110.50**  Ever he bows to Rudra, honored by gods and dānavas alike, and day after day he is granted the sight of him.

**13.110.51**  But he who eats his portion when the twelfth day has come, ever for twelve months, gains the fruit of the all-sacrifice.

**13.110.52**  For him a celestial chariot is fashioned by the twelve Ādityas, made splendid with precious gems, pearls, and corals.

**13.110.53**  Encircled by rows of swans, thronged along the elephants' avenue, made beautiful with peacocks and ruddy geese that cry aloud,

**13.110.54**  furnished with lofty turrets, established in the world of Brahmā — there forever he dwells, O king, surrounded by men and women. Thus did the illustrious sage Aṅgiras, knower of dharma, declare.

**13.110.55**  But he who eats his portion when the thirteenth day has come, ever for twelve months, gains the fruit of the gods' sacrificial session.

**13.110.56**  That man wins a celestial chariot named 'Rising of the Red Lotus,' wrought of gold and adorned with heaped-up jewels,

**13.110.57**  thronged with celestial maidens decked in heavenly ornaments, breathing forth holy fragrances, divine, made fair by gentle breezes.

**13.110.58**  There, where banners fly upon their staffs, he dwells until the ending of an age, indeed an aeon, a myriad of myriads, a padma of years, even an ocean of them.

**13.110.59**  Amid songs and the strains of gandharvas, the sound of kettledrums and tabors, ever rejoicing, he is praised by those celestial maidens.

**13.110.60**  But he who eats his portion when the fourteenth day is full, ever for twelve months, gains the fruit of the great sacrifice.

**13.110.61**  Celestial maidens of indescribable youth and beauty, finely adorned, wearing armlets of burnished gold, follow him in their chariots.

**13.110.62**  By the calls of wild geese, the tinkling of anklets, and the swing and chime of girdle-belts, he is roused now here, now there.

**13.110.63**  And in that dwelling of the celestial maidens, strewn with the sands of the Jāhnavī, that man abides for a full year of such reckoning.

**13.110.64**  But he who, when a fortnight has passed, takes a single meal, his senses subdued, ever for twelve months pouring oblations into Jātavedas, the fire, attains the unsurpassed fruit of a thousand royal consecrations.

**13.110.65**  He mounts forever a chariot attended by swans and peacocks, dazzling with circlets of gems, sheathed all in gold,

**13.110.66**  graced by lovely women radiant in heavenly ornaments — single-pillared, four-gated, seven-storied, most auspicious, made splendid by a thousand banners and the sound of song.

**13.110.67**  He ascends that celestial chariot endowed with divine qualities, adorned with gems, pearls, and corals, gleaming like lightning, and there he dwells a thousand ages, borne by rhinoceros and elephant.

**13.110.68**  But he who eats his portion when the sixteenth day has come, ever for twelve months, gains the fruit of the Soma sacrifice.

**13.110.69**  He dwells forever in the abodes of the daughters of Soma, anointed with gentle fragrances, and moves wherever his will may take him.

**13.110.70**  Seated upon his chariot, he is honored by women fair to look upon and sweet of speech, and is waited upon with every delight of desire.

**13.110.71**  His fruit, reckoned as a hundred padmas, lasts a great aeon and ten more; four cycles of the ocean's turning does that man endure.

**13.110.72**  He who eats his portion when the seventeenth day has come, ever for twelve months pouring oblations into Jātavedas, the fire,

**13.110.73**  attains the realms of Varuṇa, of Indra, and of Rudra, and reaches the worlds of the Maruts and of Uśanas, and the world of Brahmā.

**13.110.74**  There he is attended with a seat of honor by the maidens of the gods, and beholds earth and mid-air and the divine sage of universal form.

**13.110.75**  There the maidens of the God of gods delight him — two-and-thirty in number, of varied forms, sweet of voice and finely adorned.

**13.110.76**  As long as moon and sun, O lord, journey through the sky, so long does that hero roam, feeding on the nectar-sweet draught of immortality.

**13.110.77**  But he who eats a single meal on the eighteenth day, ever for twelve months, beholds the seven worlds.

**13.110.78**  He is followed from behind by chariots ringing with joyous sound, gleaming and finely decked, bearing the maidens of the gods.

**13.110.79**  Yoked with tigers and lions, resounding like a thundercloud, that supreme celestial chariot he mounts in perfect ease.

**13.110.80**  There for a thousand aeons he rejoices in the company of his beloveds, and feeds on the nectar-draught, supreme and like the elixir of immortality.

**13.110.81**  He who takes a single meal on the nineteenth day, ever for twelve months, beholds the seven worlds.

**13.110.82**  He gains a supreme abode, attended by hosts of apsarases, and a chariot bright as the sun, hymned by the gandharvas.

**13.110.83**  There, freed from all fever of grief, he rejoices with the fairest women of the immortals, clad in heavenly raiment and full of splendor, for a hundred myriads of years.

**13.110.84**  And he who takes a single meal when the twentieth day is full, ever for twelve months, speaking truth and steadfast in his vow,

**13.110.85**  eating no flesh, observing chastity, devoted to the welfare of all beings, attains the vast and heavenly worlds of the Ādityas.

**13.110.86**  By gandharvas and apsarases, with heavenly garlands and unguents, in celestial chariots of gold, he is followed from behind.

**13.110.87**  He who takes a single meal on the twenty-first day, ever for twelve months pouring oblations into Jātavedas, the fire,

**13.110.88**  reaches the heavenly world of Uśanas and the world of Śakra, ever delighting in the joys of the Aśvins and the Maruts.

**13.110.89**  A stranger to all sorrows, seated upon his choice chariot, served by lovely women, he sports like a lord among the immortals.

**13.110.90**  He who takes a single meal when the twenty-second day has come, ever for twelve months pouring oblations into Jātavedas, the fire,

**13.110.91**  steadfast, devoted to non-injury, truthful and free from envy, attains the worlds of the Vasus, radiant as the day-making sun.

**13.110.92**  Moving where he wills, feeding on nectar, seated upon his choice chariot, he revels with celestial maidens decked in heavenly ornaments.

**13.110.93**  But he who eats a single meal on the twenty-third day, ever for twelve months, moderate in food and master of his senses,

**13.110.94**  reaches the worlds of Vāyu, of Uśanas, and of Rudra — moving where he wills, going as he desires, honored by hosts of apsarases.

**13.110.95**  Seated upon his choice chariot, endowed with manifold excellences, he revels with celestial maidens decked in heavenly ornaments.

**13.110.96**  He who eats a single meal on the twenty-fourth day, ever for twelve months pouring oblations into Jātavedas, the fire,

**13.110.97**  dwells long, rejoicing, in the abode of the Ādityas, wearing heavenly garlands and raiment, anointed with celestial fragrances.

**13.110.98**  In a golden, heavenly chariot, swan-yoked and lovely, he revels with thousands and myriads of celestial maidens.

**13.110.99**  But he who eats a single meal on the twenty-fifth day, ever for twelve months, ascends an ample chariot.

**13.110.100**  By chariots yoked with lions and tigers, resounding like thunderclouds and ringing with joyous sound, he is followed from behind.

**13.110.101**  Mounting a supreme, heavenly, most enchanting chariot, escorted by spotless, shining silver ones bearing the maidens of the gods,

**13.110.102**  there for a thousand aeons he dwells, encircled by a hundred women, living upon the nectar-draught, supreme and like the elixir of immortality.

**13.110.103**  But he who eats a single meal on the twenty-sixth day, ever for twelve months, self-restrained and measured in his eating,

**13.110.104**  his senses subdued and his passions stilled, pouring oblations into Jātavedas, the fire — that illustrious man attains his reward, honored by hosts of apsarases.

**13.110.105**  He gains the worlds of the seven Maruts and of the Vasus, upon a heavenly chariot of crystal, adorned with every jewel.

**13.110.106**  Honored by gandharvas and apsarases, he rejoices for two thousand divine ages, radiant with celestial splendor.

**13.110.107**  He who eats a single meal on the twenty-seventh day, ever for twelve months pouring oblations into Jātavedas, the fire,

**13.110.108**  attains an abundant reward and is honored in the world of the gods; dwelling there and feeding on nectar, fully content, he rejoices.

**13.110.109**  That realm trodden by the divine sages, O king, and ruled over by royal sages, the heavenly-souled one inhabits, seated upon his choice chariot.

**13.110.110**  Revelling with women that ravish the mind, flushed with delight, he dwells in bliss for three thousand age-aeons.

**13.110.111**  And he who eats a single meal on the twenty-eighth day, ever for twelve months, his self conquered and his senses wholly mastered,

**13.110.112**  attains the abundant reward of the realm trodden by the divine sages; abounding in delights, he shines with splendor, spotless as the thousand-rayed sun.

**13.110.113**  And tender, radiant women, full-breasted, with rounded thighs and hips, decked in heavenly ornaments, take their delight with him,

**13.110.114**  those beloved ones delight his mind upon a chariot bright as the sun, heavenly and going wherever desire may lead, for a hundred myriad aeons of years.

**13.110.115**  He who on the twenty-ninth day takes but a single meal, doing so steadily for twelve months, devoted to the vow of truth—

**13.110.116**  his are auspicious, celestial worlds honored by the king of the gods and by royal seers, and he attains a divine chariot radiant with the brightness of the moon.

**13.110.117**  Wrought of gold, well fashioned, adorned with every jewel, thronged with hosts of apsarases and resounding with the music of gandharvas.

**13.110.118**  There lovely women decked in divine ornaments, ravishing the mind, sweet and flushed with ardor, give him their delight.

**13.110.119**  Rich in enjoyment, endowed with splendor, bright as the all-consuming fire, he is divine, shining in a divine form like an immortal.

**13.110.120**  He attains the worlds of the Vasus and the Maruts, of the Sādhyas and the two Aśvins, of the Rudras as well, and reaches the world of Brahmā.

**13.110.121**  But he who, when a month has passed, eats a single meal, his nature given to tranquility, doing so for twelve months, shall win the world of Brahmā.

**13.110.122**  Taking nectar's essence for his food, glorious and altogether enchanting, he shines with splendor, with beauty, and with majesty, like the radiant sun.

**13.110.123**  Wearing celestial garlands and raiment, anointed with celestial fragrances, the yogin delights in pleasures and knows nothing of sorrows.

**13.110.124**  Seated in his chariot he is exalted by women luminous of themselves, and is forever worshipped by the daughters of the Rudras and the divine seers.

**13.110.125**  By women fair in manifold forms, of manifold passions, of manifold sweet speech, and of manifold delights.

**13.110.126**  In a chariot vast as a city, blazing like the sun and resembling the sun, behind glowing like the moon, and on its northern side like a cloud.

**13.110.127**  Red-hued on its southern side, with a dark orb below and a many-colored brilliance above—there he dwells, honored and never alone.

**13.110.128**  For as many years as the rain pours down upon Jambūdvīpa through a thousand years, so long, they say, is his sojourn in the world of the wise Brahmā.

**13.110.129**  And for as many raindrops as fall from the vault of heaven in the season when it rains, so long does that one, splendid as an immortal, abide there.

**13.110.130**  He who fasts for a month at a time, after ten years attains the highest heaven, and gaining the rank of a great seer, passes thither in his very body.

**13.110.131**  A sage, self-controlled, having conquered anger, having mastered the appetites of sex and belly, ever offering oblations to the fires, restrained, and faithful to worship at the twilight hours.

**13.110.132**  The man who thus, through many observances, takes his food but once a month and lives content under the open sky—of him such a dwelling is declared.

**13.110.133**  Having gone to heaven in his own body, O king, like an immortal, he enjoys the holy heaven at will, according to the ordinance.

**13.110.134**  This, O best of the Bhāratas, is the supreme ordinance of sacrifices, expounded to you in due order, which yields the fruit of fasting.

**13.110.135**  Thus, O Pārtha, the fruit of sacrifice may be won even by men of no means; by performing this fast one shall attain the supreme goal, O best of the Bhāratas, if he delights in the worship of gods and of the twice-born.

**13.110.136**  This ordinance of fasting has been proclaimed at length, ordained for the restrained, the vigilant, the pure, the great of soul,

**13.110.137**  for those who have turned from deceit and malice, whose minds are made up, O Bhārata, who are steadfast and unshaken—let no doubt of yours linger here.

**13.111.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: Which is the best of all sacred bathing-places, O grandsire—tell me that; where the highest purity lies, that you ought to expound to me.

**13.111.2**  Bhīṣma said: All sacred fords, indeed, hold virtue for the wise; but what is the true ford and what is purity, hear from me with attentive mind.

**13.111.3**  In the fathomless, stainless, pure ford of the mind, whose waters are truth and whose pool is steadfastness, one must bathe, taking hold of the eternal goodness.

**13.111.4**  The purity of the ford is freedom from greed, gentleness, truth, uprightness, harmlessness toward all beings, mercy, self-restraint, and tranquility.

**13.111.5**  They who are free from the sense of mine, free from egoism, beyond the pairs of opposites, free from possessions, and who live upon alms—those are pure and are themselves as sacred fords.

**13.111.6**  He who knows the truth and is free from the notion of "I" is called the supreme ford; this is the mark of purity for you, to be watched for in all things everywhere.

**13.111.7**  They from whose self passion, darkness, and even goodness have been washed clean—such men, intent on their own true task, are not bound by the pure and the impure.

**13.111.8**  Delighting in every renunciation, all-knowing, all-seeing, having achieved purity of conduct through purity itself—those are sacred fords, and those are the pure.

**13.111.9**  Not he whose limbs are merely wet with water is called bathed; he is the truly bathed who has bathed in self-restraint and is pure both without and within.

**13.111.10**  They who care nothing for what is past and claim no ownership in the goods that have come to them—theirs is the highest purity, in whom no craving arises.

**13.111.11**  Wisdom is purity here, especially of the body; so too are utter possessionlessness and serenity of mind.

**13.111.12**  Purity of conduct, purity of mind, the purity of the ford—a supreme blessing; but the purity born of knowledge, that is held to be the highest purity of all.

**13.111.13**  They who have bathed in the ford of the mind, by the lamp of the mind and the strength of the knowledge of Brahman—those knowers behold the Knower of the field.

**13.111.14**  But the man in whom purity is established, ever endowed with right disposition, perfect in virtue alone, is forever pure indeed.

**13.111.15**  These sacred fords that dwell within the body have been declared, O Bhārata; now hear also of the holy fords that are upon the earth.

**13.111.16**  As certain regions of the body are fashioned pure, so too are there holy tracts of the earth and holy waters.

**13.111.17**  By yearning for the sacred ford, by bathing there, and by the offering of water to the ancestors, men shake off their sin at the fords and, purified, go in bliss to heaven.

**13.111.18**  Through the resort of holy men, through the power of the earth, and through the power of the water, those tracts become exceedingly holy.

**13.111.19**  There are holy fords of the mind and of the earth alike; and he who has bathed in both shall swiftly attain perfection.

**13.111.20**  As strength without action, or action without strength, accomplishes nothing here, but joined together they succeed—

**13.111.21**  so the man endowed with purity of body and with purity of the ford thereby attains perfection; the twofold purity is supreme.

**13.112.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: O grandsire, mighty-armed, learned in all the scriptures, I wish to hear the supreme law of the round of births and deaths for mortals.

**13.112.2**  By what conduct, O lord of kings, do men who live in the world attain the highest heaven, and how, O king, do they come to hell?

**13.112.3**  Casting off the dead body, like a log or a clod of earth, people pass from here to that other world; who, then, follows after them?

**13.112.4**  Bhīṣma said: Yonder comes the lord Bṛhaspati, of noble understanding; ask him, that most blessed one, of this eternal mystery.

**13.112.5**  For this cannot be told by any other man today; nowhere is there found another expounder equal to Bṛhaspati.

**13.112.6**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: As the son of Pṛthā and the son of Gaṅgā were thus conversing, the lord Bṛhaspati of utterly pure soul came near.

**13.112.7**  Then the king, with Dhṛtarāṣṭra at their head, rose up, and all those seated in the assembly paid him honor beyond compare.

**13.112.8**  Then the king, the son of Dharma, true to his vows, drew near to the lord Bṛhaspati and, in due form, put his question.

**13.112.9**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: O lord, knower of all duties, learned in all the scriptures, who is the mortal's true companion—father, mother, son, or teacher?

**13.112.10**  Casting off the dead body, like a log or a clod of earth, people go to that world beyond; who, then, follows him?

**13.112.11**  Bṛhaspati said: Alone the creature is born, O lord of kings, and alone it perishes; alone it crosses the hard passages, and alone it goes to its evil plight.

**13.112.12**  No helpmate then is father or mother, brother, son, or teacher, nor the throng of kinsmen and connections, nor the company of friends.

**13.112.13**  When the body lies dead, like a log or a clod of earth, people stand by it for a moment, then turn their faces away and depart; once that body is forsaken by them, righteousness alone follows after.

**13.112.14**  Therefore men must ever cultivate righteousness for the sake of a companion; the living being joined with righteousness goes to the supreme path of heaven, and joined with unrighteousness he comes to hell.

**13.112.15**  Therefore let the wise man practice righteousness with wealth honestly gotten; righteousness alone is the companion of men in the world beyond.

**13.112.16**  Out of greed, delusion, misplaced pity, or fear, the man of little learning, bewildered by greed, does deeds that ought not to be done for another's sake.

**13.112.17**  Duty, wealth, and pleasure—this triad is the fruit of life; this triad is to be attained while shunning all unrighteousness.

**13.112.18**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: I have heard the lord's words, righteous and supremely beneficial; now there arises in me the wish to understand the analysis of the body.

**13.112.19**  When the dead one is bereft of the body, has grown subtle, passed into the unmanifest, and become no object for the eye, how does righteousness follow after it?

**13.112.20**  Bṛhaspati said: Earth, air, ether, water, and light as the fifth, together with the intellect and the self, behold righteousness without ceasing.

**13.112.21**  For all living beings here these are unceasing witnesses, and through these does righteousness itself follow after that living soul.

**13.112.22**  Skin, bone, flesh, semen, and blood, O greatly wise one—these forsake the body once it is bereft of life.

**13.112.23**  Then that living soul, joined with righteousness, thrives in happiness both in this world and in the next. What more shall I tell you?

**13.112.24**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: The lord has shown how righteousness follows after; but this I wish to learn—how does the seed come forth?

**13.112.25**  Bṛhaspati said: The deities that dwell within the body and consume the food, O ruler of men, are earth, air, ether, water, light, and likewise the mind.

**13.112.26**  Then, O lord of kings, when those five elements with the mind for a sixth are satisfied, O pure-souled one, the abundant seed is formed.

**13.112.27**  Thereupon, at the union of woman and man, O Pārtha, the embryo comes into being. All this has been told to you; what more do you wish to hear?

**13.112.28**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: You have told how the embryo comes to be; now let it be said how, once born, a man fares onward.

**13.112.29**  Bṛhaspati said: No sooner has it drawn near than it is constantly overpowered by those elements; and when released from those elements it passes again to another state—yet still it is joined with the elements that the living soul attains.

**13.112.30**  Then the deities seated in the five elements watch over its deeds, whether fair or foul. What more do you wish to hear?

**13.112.31**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: Casting off skin, bone, and flesh, and forsaken by those elements, where, O lord, does that living soul abide while it tastes of pleasure and pain?

**13.112.32**  Bṛhaspati said: The living soul, joined with righteousness, swiftly comes into the state of seed and, reaching the flowering of women, is brought to birth in time, O Bhārata.

**13.112.33**  Torment at the hands of Yama's servants, slaughter at the hands of Yama's servants, sorrow, the wheel of transmigration, and affliction—these the man finds.

**13.112.34**  And in this world that living being, from birth onward, O king, reaps the deeds it has itself wrought, resting upon the fruit of righteousness.

**13.112.35**  If from birth onward he practices righteousness to the best of his power, then, becoming a man, he ever after enjoys happiness.

**13.112.36**  But if in the midst of righteousness he turns to practice unrighteousness, then that living soul attains, hard upon its happiness, to sorrow.

**13.112.37**  Bound to unrighteousness, he passes into the realm of Yama; and having undergone immense suffering there, he is reborn into the womb of a beast.

**13.112.38**  By which particular deed, and in which womb, the deluded living being is reborn here—hear that now from me as I declare it.

**13.112.39**  What is taught in the scriptures, together with the legends and the sacred meters: the mortal world enters the dreadful realm of Yama.

**13.112.40**  A twice-born who has studied the four Vedas, yet who, possessed by delusion, accepts a gift from a fallen man, is reborn thereafter into the womb of an ass.

**13.112.41**  As an ass he lives fifteen years, O Bhārata; and the ass, once dead, lives on as an ox for seven years.

**13.112.42**  And the ox, when it too has died, is born as a brahma-rākṣasa; as a brahma-rākṣasa for three months, and after that he is born a brāhmaṇa.

**13.112.43**  But one who has performed sacrifices for a fallen man is reborn into the womb of a worm; there he lives fifteen years, O Bhārata.
