**13.112.44**  Released from the condition of a worm, he is then born a donkey; as a donkey for five years, as a boar for five years, and he becomes a dog for one year—after that he is born a man.

**13.112.45**  A foolish pupil who does evil to his teacher—that soul, beyond all doubt, attains here three rounds of transmigration.

**13.112.46**  First he becomes a dog, O lord of kings, then a flesh-eating beast, then an ass; then a tormented hungry ghost, and afterwards he is born a brāhmaṇa.

**13.112.47**  A sinful pupil who approaches his teacher's wife even in his mind—he, through that unrighteous intent, passes here into the basest rounds of rebirth.

**13.112.48**  Born in the womb of a dog, he lives three years; and meeting his death there too, he is reborn into the womb of a worm.

**13.112.49**  Having attained the state of a worm, he lives one year; and meeting his death thereafter, he is reborn into the womb of a brāhmaṇa.

**13.112.50**  If a teacher, without cause and at his own willful whim, should slay a pupil who is like a son to him, he too is reborn as a goose.

**13.112.51**  And a son who despises his father or his mother—that creature too, O king, when dead, is first born a donkey.

**13.112.52**  As an ass he lives ten months, as a dog fourteen, and as a cat seven months; after that he is born a man.

**13.112.53**  Having reviled mother and father, one is born a mynah bird; and having struck those very two, he is born a tortoise, O king.

**13.112.54**  As a tortoise ten years, as a porcupine three years; and having been a serpent for six months, after that he is born a man.

**13.112.55**  He who, while eating his master's bread, serves the king's enemies—that man too, sunk in delusion, when dead is born a monkey.

**13.112.56**  As a monkey ten years, as a rat three years; and having been a dog for six months, after that he is born a man.

**13.112.57**  But a man who steals a deposit entrusted to him passes into the realm of Yama; having gone through a hundred rounds of rebirth, he is reborn into the womb of a worm.

**13.112.58**  There he lives fifteen years, O Bhārata; and once his evil deed is exhausted, after that he is born a man.

**13.112.59**  A spiteful, envious man, when dead, is born a śārṅgaka bird; and the betrayer of trust, that evil-minded man, is born a fish.

**13.112.60**  Having been a fish for eight years, he is born a deer, O Bhārata; and as a deer for four months, after that he is born a goat.

**13.112.61**  And the goat, meeting its death at the close of a full year, is then born as an insect; that creature thereafter is born a man.

**13.112.62**  Grains, barley, sesame, black gram, horse-gram, mustard, chickpeas, peas, green gram, wheat, and linseed too—

**13.112.63**  the thieving creature who, witless through delusion, steals these or any other crop—he is born, O great king, as a shameless rat.

**13.112.64**  Then, having died, O great king, he is born again as a boar; and the boar, just newly born, dies of disease, O king.

**13.112.65**  By that deed the deluded soul is then born a dog, O lord of the earth; and having been a dog for five years, after that he is born a man.

**13.112.66**  Having laid hands upon another's wife, one is indeed born a wolf; then a dog, a jackal, a vulture, a serpent, a heron, and likewise a crane.

**13.112.67**  The evil-minded man who, deluded, violates his brother's wife attains the state of a male cuckoo, and that for a full year, O king.

**13.112.68**  He who out of lust violates a friend's wife, his teacher's wife, or likewise the king's wife, when dead is born a boar.

**13.112.69**  As a boar five years, as a porcupine five years, as an ant six months, and as an insect but a single month; having passed through these rebirths, he is reborn into the womb of a worm.

**13.112.70**  There in the worm's womb he lives thirteen months; and having then worked off his unrighteousness, he is born a man once more.

**13.112.71**  When a wedding, a gift-giving, or a sacrifice is at hand, O lord, he who out of delusion raises an obstruction to it is born, when dead, a worm.

**13.112.72**  As a worm he lives fifteen years, O Bhārata; and having worked off his unrighteousness, after that he is born a man.

**13.112.73**  He who, having first given his daughter in marriage, then bestows her upon a second suitor—that creature too, O king, when dead, is reborn into the womb of a worm.

**13.112.74**  There he lives thirteen years, O Yudhiṣṭhira; and when his unrighteousness is fully spent, after that he is born a man.

**13.112.75**  He who, having begun the rite for the gods and likewise the rite for the ancestors, eats his meal without first making the offerings—after that he is born a crow.

**13.112.76**  As a crow ten years, then he is born a cock; he is born too a quail for a month, and from that he becomes a man.

**13.112.77**  He who despises an elder brother, who is the equal of a father—that one too, having met his death, is reborn into the womb of a curlew.

**13.112.78**  As a curlew he lives ten months, two, seven, and five; and meeting his death thereafter, he attains the state of a man.

**13.112.79**  A low-born man who consorts with a brāhmaṇa woman is reborn into the womb of a worm; and having there begotten offspring, he is afterwards born a rat.

**13.112.80**  But the ingrate, O king, when dead, passes into the realm of Yama; and in Yama's realm he suffers a fearful slaughter at the hands of the wrathful.

**13.112.81**  The spiked club, the mallet, the spear, the dreadful cauldron of fire, the terrible Sword-Leaf Forest, the burning sands, and the thorny Śālmali tree—

**13.112.82**  these and many other fierce torments he undergoes, having passed into Yama's realm; and there he is put to death, O Bhārata.

**13.112.83**  Entering the wheel of transmigration, he is reborn into the womb of a worm; as a worm he lives fifteen years, O Bhārata; then, entering a womb, the infant dies there itself.

**13.112.84**  Thereafter the creature is born through many hundreds of wombs; and having passed through many rounds of rebirth, it is then born as a beast.

**13.112.85**  Having met his death and undergone suffering here through many sequences of years, deprived of release from rebirth, he is then born a tortoise.

**13.112.86**  The basest of men who, bearing weapons, slays an unarmed man—whether out of greed for wealth or out of enmity—when dead is born an ass.

**13.112.87**  As an ass he lives two years and is then slain by a weapon; and he, once dead, is born into the womb of a deer, forever trembling in fear.

**13.112.88**  As a deer he is killed by a weapon when a year has passed; the slain deer then becomes a fish, and that too is caught in a net.

**13.112.89**  When the fourth month has come, he is born a beast of prey; as a beast of prey ten years, and as a leopard five years.

**13.112.90**  Then, meeting his death, driven on by the turning of time, and having worked off his unrighteousness, after that he is born a man.

**13.112.91**  The evil-minded man who slays a woman passes into the realm of Yama; having undergone many afflictions and twenty rounds of rebirth—

**13.112.92**  thereafter, O great king, he is reborn into the womb of a worm; and having been a worm for twenty years, he is born a man.

**13.112.93**  Having stolen food, a man is born a fly; subject to a swarm of flies, he remains so for many months; then, having worked off his sin, he attains the state of a man.

**13.112.94**  Having stolen a musical instrument, a man is born a mosquito; and the man who steals food mixed with oil-cake is born a dreadful rat, tawny like a mongoose.

**13.112.95**  Having stolen salt, one is born a cricket; having stolen curds, a heron; and a waterfowl, by stealing fish not dressed for cooking.

**13.112.96**  And having stolen milk, one is born a crane; he who steals oil is born an oil-drinking insect; and the evil-minded man who steals honey is born a stinging fly.

**13.112.97**  Having stolen iron, the evil-minded man is born a crow; and having stolen rice-milk pudding, he attains the state of a partridge.

**13.112.98**  Having stolen a cake of flour, one is born a horned owl; and having stolen fruit, a root, or a cake, an ant.

**13.112.99**  Having stolen a bronze vessel, the evil-minded man is born a green pigeon; and having stolen a silver vessel, he is born a dove.

**13.112.100**  Having stolen a vessel of gold, one is reborn into the womb of a worm; having stolen cotton goods, one becomes a curlew, and when dead is born a man.

**13.112.101**  Having stolen silk cloth, or woolen cloth, O Bhārata, or having taken a garment of fine linen, the creature is born a hare.

**13.112.102**  Having stolen dyes, a man, when dead, is born a peacock; and having stolen red garments, he is born a jīvajīvaka pheasant.

**13.112.103**  And the man given over to greed who steals pigments, perfumes, and the like attains the state of a musk-shrew, O king.

**13.112.104**  The man who denies a deposit placed with him in trust—such a man, when his breath has departed, is reborn into the womb of a fish.

**13.112.105**  Having attained the womb of a fish, when dead he is born a man; and having attained the human state, he is one whose lifespan is short.

**13.112.106**  Having committed sins, a man is born a beast, O Bhārata; and such creatures have no measure of themselves, nor do they know anything of dharma.

**13.112.107**  Those men who, having committed sins, ever cast them off by vows—they become mingled with both pleasure and pain, and afflicted with disease.

**13.112.108**  Men of sinful conduct, possessed by greed and delusion, are born outcasts beyond fellowship, and barbarians too—of this there is no doubt.

**13.112.109**  But those men who shun sins from their very birth become free of disease, fair of form, and wealthy as well.

**13.112.110**  Women too, by this same order, attain the fruit of the sin they commit; they come to be the mates of these very same creatures.

**13.112.111**  The faults arising from seizing another's property have all been proclaimed; this I have told you, O sinless one, in but the briefest measure; on another occasion of discourse you shall hear of it again, O Bhārata.

**13.112.112**  This, O great king, I once heard from Brahmā as he spoke in the midst of the divine sages, when he was questioned, exactly as it is.

**13.112.113**  And by me it has been recounted to you in full, just as it is; having heard this, O great king, set your mind ever upon dharma.

**13.113.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: The course of unrighteousness, O holy one, you have recounted to me, O sinless one; but I wish to hear the course of righteousness, O best of speakers. After committing sinful deeds, how do men attain an auspicious destiny?

**13.113.2**  Bṛhaspati said: Having committed sinful deeds, fallen under the sway of unrighteousness, with a mind gone astray, a man passes into hell.

**13.113.3**  But he who, having committed unrighteousness through delusion, afterwards feels remorse, and is endowed with composure of mind, will not pursue evil deeds again.

**13.113.4**  In the measure that a man, with a mind well composed, rightly acknowledges his own unrighteousness, in that same measure he is released from it, as a serpent slips free from the old, worn-out slough it once inhabited.

**13.113.5**  Even without having bestowed gifts of various kinds, a man who is composed and joined to a steady concentration of mind attains a happy course hereafter.

**13.113.6**  But I shall tell of those gifts, O Yudhiṣṭhira, by bestowing which a man, though he has done deeds that ought not to be done, is even then made one with righteousness.

**13.113.7**  Of all gifts whatever, food is declared the most excellent; food first of all should be given by the upright man who desires righteousness.

**13.113.8**  Food indeed is the very life-breath of men, and from it the living creature is born; the worlds are established upon food, and therefore food shines forth supreme.

**13.113.9**  The gods, the sages, the ancestral fathers, and men all extol food alike; for by the gift of food a son of the Kuśika line attains heaven.

**13.113.10**  Food obtained by lawful means should be given, the finest food, to the twice-born who are devoted to the recitation of the Veda, and given with an inmost self made glad.

**13.113.11**  He upon whose food ten hundred brāhmaṇas feed, food given with a gladdened mind, shall never sink into the course of the beasts.

**13.113.12**  Feeding ten thousand brāhmaṇas, O bull among men, a man, though ever given to sins, would be set free from unrighteousness.

**13.113.13**  Having gathered food by begging, a brāhmaṇa who keeps the Veda foremost, and given it here to a brāhmaṇa intent upon his Vedic recitation, thrives in happiness.

**13.113.14**  The kṣatriya who, never harming a brāhmaṇa and protecting his people by lawful rule, bestows food won by his own strength —

**13.113.15**  — giving it to the twice-born grown ripe in the Veda, restrained and well composed, by that, O son of Pāṇḍu, the righteous soul wipes away his evil deeds.

**13.113.16**  And the vaiśya who gives to the twice-born the portion earned from his tillage, purified by the sixth part rendered to the king, is released from his sins.

**13.113.17**  Having amassed by harsh toil, at the very hazard of his life, the food he has earned, the śūdra who gives it to the twice-born is set free from sin.

**13.113.18**  He who, doing harm to none, earns food by the strength of his own breast and bestows it upon the brāhmaṇas, never resorts to the realms of hardship.

**13.113.19**  But the man free from greed who, having won food by lawful means, gives it to the twice-born grown ripe in the Veda, is released from sin.

**13.113.20**  Food is the giver of vigor in the world; giving it, a man becomes full of vigor, and treading the path of the good, he is freed from every sin.

**13.113.21**  A road has been laid down by those who make their gifts, along which the wise go their way; they are the givers of life itself, and from them flows the eternal righteousness.

**13.113.22**  Food earned by lawful means should always, in every condition, be set by a man into a worthy vessel; for food is the supreme goal.

**13.113.23**  For by the giving of food a man does not resort to the realm of hardship; therefore food should be given, food untainted by unlawful gain.

**13.113.24**  Let the householder ever strive to eat his food only after the brāhmaṇa has eaten first; thus by the gift of food let a man make no day of his barren.

**13.113.25**  Feeding a thousand men who know the Veda, O king, who are versed in the law and in righteousness and likewise learned in the ancient lore —

**13.113.26**  — he does not go to the dreadful hell, nor does he resort to the rounds of rebirth; endowed with all desires fulfilled, he enjoys his reward even after death.

**13.113.27**  Thus joined to happiness he takes his delight, his fever gone; and he is born again comely of form, renowned, and rich in wealth.

**13.113.28**  All this great fruit of the gift of food has been declared to you; for this, O descendant of Bharata, is the root of all observances of dharma and of giving.

**13.114.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: Non-harming, the rites enjoined by the Veda, meditation, the restraint of the senses, austerity, and service to one's elders — which of these is best for a man?

**13.114.2**  Bṛhaspati said: All these, every one, are separate gateways of dharma; hear them, O bull of the Bhāratas, all six as I proclaim them in full.

**13.114.3**  Come, I shall declare the unsurpassed and highest good of every creature: the dharma that rests upon non-harming, which a man should indeed bring to fulfillment.

**13.114.4**  Laying aside ever the three faults toward all beings, and curbing both desire and wrath, a man thereby attains perfection.

**13.114.5**  He who, seeking his own happiness, strikes down with the rod creatures that do no harm, shall not be happy in the world to come.

**13.114.6**  But the man who holds all beings as like unto himself, who has laid down the rod and conquered his wrath, thrives in happiness in the world to come.

**13.114.7**  Of him who has become the self of all beings, who beholds all beings as himself, even the gods lose the trail, as they seek the footprints of one who leaves no footprint.

**13.114.8**  Let no man do to another what is hateful to himself; this, in brief, is dharma — all else proceeds from desire.

**13.114.9**  In refusal and in giving, in pleasure and pain, in what is dear and what is hateful, by measuring others against himself a man attains to inner harmony.

**13.114.10**  As one man behaves toward others, so will another behave toward him; let this be your measure in the world of the living, even as dharma has been skillfully taught to you.

**13.114.11**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus to Yudhiṣṭhira, the king of righteousness, the wise preceptor of the gods ascended to heaven, even as we looked on.

**13.115.1**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then King Yudhiṣṭhira of great splendor once more questioned his grandsire, best of all who speak, where he lay upon his bed of arrows.

**13.115.2**  O greatly wise one, the sages, the brāhmaṇas, and the gods extol the dharma marked by non-harming, since they see the authority of the Veda for it.

**13.115.3**  O best of kings, a man who works harm by deed, by word, and by thought — how is he set free from sorrow?

**13.115.4**  Bhīṣma said: This non-harming has been laid down as fourfold by those who expound the sacred word; O slayer of foes, if it falls away even on one side, it ceases to be.

**13.115.5**  As any four-footed beast cannot stand upon three feet, so too, O lord of the earth, this is said to fail when held by only three of its grounds.

**13.115.6**  As in the elephant's footprint all other footprints of creatures that go on foot, every kind of footprint, are wholly contained, so in the worlds is non-harming declared the highest by the measure of dharma.

**13.115.7**  A creature is stained by deed, by word, and by thought alone.

**13.115.8**  But first renouncing harm in thought, then in word, then in deed — this threefold ground is laid down and is heard so taught by the expounders of the sacred word.

**13.115.9**  In the mind, in speech, and likewise in the relish of taste — in these the faults are seated; and therefore the wise who are given to austerity do not eat flesh.

**13.115.10**  But hear from me, O king, the faults in the eating of flesh here below: it is a man bereft of sense who eats it, knowing it to be like the flesh of his own son.

**13.115.11**  As sonship is born from the union of mother and father, and as awareness of taste is born to the tongue, so too, it is settled in the scriptures, craving arises from the savoring.

**13.115.12**  Unseasoned and seasoned, salted and saltless — according as such flavors are discerned, so is the mind bound fast to them.

**13.115.13**  How shall dull men who feed on flesh deserve to enjoy the abundant sounds of the kettledrum, the conch, the tabor, and the strings?

**13.115.14**  Overcome by greed for its taste, those who seek a reward praise flesh — a thing unthought-of, unprescribed, and unintended; yet the very praise of flesh is bound up with the fruit of sinful deeds.

**13.115.15**  For many good men, casting aside their very lives, have gone to heaven by shielding the flesh of others with their own flesh.

**13.115.16**  Thus, O great king, this non-harming, encompassed by its four grounds, has been laid down for you, containing within it the whole aim and meaning of dharma.

**13.116.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: Non-harming is the highest dharma — so you have said many times; and yet at the rites for the dead you have said that the ancestral fathers long for flesh.

**13.116.2**  Long ago you set forth the rule of the funeral rite with flesh of many kinds; yet without slaying, whence comes flesh? In this way these teachings stand at odds.

**13.116.3**  A doubt has arisen in us concerning the dharma of abstaining from flesh: what fault would there be in one who eats it, and what merit in one who does not?

**13.116.4**  Whether a man slays and then eats, or eats what another has brought, or slays for another's sake, or buys and eats —

**13.116.5**  — this I wish to have told to me in its very truth by you, O sinless one; with sure resolve I desire to follow out this eternal dharma.

**13.116.6**  How does a man attain long life? How does he become full of vigor? How does he come to be free of any defect, and how is he born marked with auspicious signs?

**13.116.7**  Bhīṣma said: O king, O bull of the Kurus, hear from me, even as it truly is, the unrighteousness that lies in the eating of flesh, and what is the highest rule concerning it.

**13.116.8**  Men of perfected souls, desiring to win beauty, soundness of body, long life, understanding, vigor, strength, and memory, have indeed renounced all harming.

**13.116.9**  On this matter there has been much discourse among the sages, O bull of the Kurus; hear, O Yudhiṣṭhira, what their settled opinion is.

**13.116.10**  He who, holding firm to his vows, should offer the horse-sacrifice month after month, and he who renounces wine and flesh — these two, O Yudhiṣṭhira, are reckoned equal.

**13.116.11**  The Seven Sages, the Vālakhilyas, and likewise the Marīcipas, the wise ones, all extol the eating of no flesh, O king.

**13.116.12**  He who eats no flesh, who neither slays nor causes to be slain — him Manu, son of the Self-Existent, declared the friend of all beings.

**13.116.13**  By abstaining from flesh a man becomes unassailable by all beings, trusted among all living creatures, and ever esteemed by the good.

**13.116.14**  He who would make his own flesh grow by the flesh of another — the righteous-souled Nārada has declared that such a man assuredly comes to ruin.

**13.116.15**  By turning away from wine and flesh a man both gives and sacrifices and becomes one given to austerity — thus did Bṛhaspati declare it.

**13.116.16**  He who should offer the horse-sacrifice month after month for a hundred years, and he who eats no flesh — these two I hold to be equal.

**13.116.17**  By abstaining from wine and flesh a man ever offers the long sacrificial session, ever bestows gifts, and is ever one given to austerity.

**13.116.18**  Not all the Vedas, O descendant of Bharata, nor all the sacrifices, could achieve what he achieves who, having eaten flesh, thereafter turns away from it.

**13.116.19**  Hard indeed it is for one who has known its taste to abstain from flesh; yet to keep this most excellent vow is to grant freedom from fear to every living thing.

**13.116.20**  The wise man who bestows upon all beings the gift of fearlessness becomes in the world a giver of life itself — herein is no doubt.

**13.116.21**  Thus indeed do the wise extol this highest dharma: as life is dear to oneself, so too is it dear to all beings.

**13.116.22**  By measuring others against oneself should the wise and great-souled proceed, knowing that there is fear of death even for the learned who long for prosperity.

**13.116.23**  How much more, then, the terror of creatures violently slain — creatures that long to live, free of disease and free of sin — by the sinful who make their living on flesh!

**13.116.24**  Therefore know, O great king, that abstaining from flesh is the most excellent abode of dharma, and of heaven, and of happiness.

**13.116.25**  Non-harming is the highest dharma; non-harming, likewise, is the highest austerity; non-harming is the highest truth, and from it dharma proceeds.

**13.116.26**  For flesh is not born of grass, nor of wood, nor of stone; flesh comes only from the slaying of a creature, and therein lies the fault of eating it.

**13.116.27**  The gods, who feed on the offerings of svāhā and svadhā and on the nectar of immortality, love truth and uprightness; but know the flesh-eating rākṣasas to be devoted to crookedness and falsehood.

**13.116.28**  In dreadful wildernesses, in fastnesses and dense thickets, by night and by day, at the twilights, at the crossroads and in the assembly halls — O king, for one who eats no flesh no fear comes at the last.

**13.116.29**  If there were no eater, there would be no slayer; it is for the eater's sake that a man has the creature killed.

**13.116.30**  When one resolves, 'this is not to be eaten,' the killing ceases; it is for the eater's sake that the slaughter of deer and the rest goes forward.

**13.116.31**  Since it devours the very lifespan of those who do violence, O greatly radiant one, let him who desires his own welfare abstain from flesh.

**13.116.32**  The cruel ones who do violence to living beings find no protector; they are dreaded by all creatures, just as beasts of prey are.

**13.116.33**  Out of greed, or delusion of mind, or for the sake of strength and vigor, or through the company of the wicked, men come to take delight in unrighteousness.

**13.116.34**  He who wishes to fatten his own flesh with the flesh of another dwells in a state of perpetual dread, born again wherever such a fate awaits him.

**13.116.35**  The disciplined supreme sages declare the abstention from flesh to be auspicious, bringing renown, long life, heaven, and great well-being.

**13.116.36**  Now this, O son of Kuntī, I once heard long ago from the lips of Mārkaṇḍeya as he spoke of the faults that lie in the eating of flesh.

**13.116.37**  He who eats the flesh of living creatures that long for life, whether slain or already dead, is just as guilty as the slayer himself.

**13.116.38**  The buyer kills with his wealth, the eater by his enjoyment, the slayer by killing and binding: thus the killing is threefold.

**13.116.39**  Even the man who does not eat but approves is stained by the fault of his intent; he who consents that a creature should be slain is likewise tainted by the sin.

**13.116.40**  The man who eats no flesh and is compassionate toward living beings becomes here unassailable by all creatures, long-lived, free of disease, and happy.

**13.116.41**  The sacred teaching holds that the merit in abstaining from flesh surpasses in every way the gift of gold, of cattle, and of land.

**13.116.42**  Let none eat flesh unconsecrated, taken in vain and outside the ordinance; the man who eats it goes to hell—of this there is no doubt.

**13.116.43**  Flesh consecrated and sprinkled, or eaten at a brāhmaṇa's wish, is to be known as of slight fault here; but in the contrary case one is defiled.

**13.116.44**  The basest of men who slays a creature for the eater's sake works a great sin there; in such a case it is the eater, not the slayer alone, who bears the guilt.

**13.116.45**  The witless man, greedy for flesh, who slays a creature under the pretext of sacrifice, ritual, and scripture, is verily one doomed to hell.

**13.116.46**  Even he who has eaten flesh but afterward turns away from it gains great merit, for he turns back from sin.

**13.116.47**  The fetcher, the consenter, the butcher, the buyer and seller, the cook, and the consumer—all of these are slayers.

**13.116.48**  But now I shall tell you another authority, established by ordinance, ancient, honored by the sages, and determined in the Vedas.

**13.116.49**  This is taught, O tiger among kings, within the dharma marked by ritual action, sought by those who desire its fruits; but it is not for those who long for liberation.

**13.116.50**  The oblation hallowed by sacred verses, consecrated and sprinkled and pure, by the authority declared in the Veda and used in the rites for the ancestors—anything otherwise is flesh taken in vain and not to be eaten, so Manu has declared.

**13.116.51**  Such eating bars heaven and renown and is fit for demons, O bull of the Bhāratas; for in former times men ate flesh, O king, only according to the ordinance.

**13.116.52**  The man who would have himself wholly free from harm should in every way shun the flesh of living beings here.

**13.116.53**  For we hear that in the ancient age men used a sacrificial victim made of rice, with which the sacrificers, devoted to holy worlds, performed their offerings.

**13.116.54**  Long ago, when the sages put to Vasu, lord of the Cedis, the doubt whether flesh was not to be eaten, he declared, O lord, that it was to be eaten.

**13.116.55**  Fallen from the sky to the earth, that lord of the world, having again spoken these very words, sank into the surface of the ground.

**13.116.56**  But the great-souled Agastya, desiring the good of all creatures, by his austerity consecrated the wild deer of the forest as sacred to all the gods.

**13.116.57**  Thus the rites that pertain to the ancestors and the gods are not abandoned, and the fathers too are pleased when satisfied with flesh in the proper manner.

**13.116.58**  But hear this, O lord of kings, as I proclaim it, O sinless one: in the abstention from flesh lies every happiness, O ruler of men.

**13.116.59**  He who should practice the most severe austerity for a full hundred years, and he who should renounce flesh but once—these two I hold to be equal.

**13.116.60**  And especially in the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, O ruler of men, let one abstain from all flesh, for therein merit is ordained.

**13.116.61**  He who shuns flesh through the four months of the rainy season obtains the four blessings: renown, long life, fame, and strength.

**13.116.62**  Or even for a single month abstaining from all flesh, having passed beyond every sorrow, he lives happy and free of disease.

**13.116.63**  For those who shun flesh by months, or even by fortnights, who have desisted from violence, the world of Brahmā is ordained.

**13.116.64**  Flesh was shunned during the Kārttika fortnight, O Pārtha, by those kings who looked on all beings as their own self and who knew things high and low.

**13.116.65**  By Nābhāga, by Ambarīṣa, and by the great-souled Gaya, by Āyus and Anaraṇya, by Dilīpa, Raghu, and Pūru,

**13.116.66**  by Kārtavīrya and Aniruddha, by Nahuṣa and Yayāti, by Nṛga and Viṣvagaśva, and likewise by Śaśabindu, by Yuvanāśva too, and by Śibi the son of Uśīnara,

**13.116.67**  by Śyenacitra, O lord of kings, by Somaka and Vṛka, by Raivata, by Rantideva, by Vasu and Sṛñjaya,

**13.116.68**  by Duḥṣanta, by Karūṣa, by Rāma, Alarka, and Nala, by Virūpāśva, by Nimi, and by the wise Janaka,

**13.116.69**  by Sila and by Pṛthu, and by Vīrasena too, by Ikṣvāku and Śambhu, by Śveta and Sagara—

**13.116.70**  by these and others, O lord of kings, no flesh was eaten of old during the autumnal month of Kārttika, and thereby they attained heaven.

**13.116.71**  And they abide in the world of Brahmā, blazing and endowed with splendor, attended by gandharvas and surrounded by thousands of women.

**13.116.72**  The great-souled ones who practice this supreme and auspicious dharma, marked by non-violence, dwell upon the vault of heaven.

**13.116.73**  The righteous who from birth forever shun honey, flesh, and liquor are all reckoned as sages, and they attain eminence among their kinsmen—of this there is no doubt.

**13.116.74**  One in distress is freed from his distress, the bound is loosed from his bonds, the sick is delivered from disease, and the suffering from his suffering.

**13.116.75**  Such a man does not pass to the wombs of beasts, but becomes comely and wise, O best of the Kurus, and attains great renown.

**13.116.76**  This, O king, has been told to you—the ordinance fashioned by the sages concerning the shunning of flesh, both in its practice and in its renunciation.

**13.117.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: These men in the world are exceedingly greedy for flesh; forsaking the many other foods, they crave it as the hosts of rākṣasas do.

**13.117.2**  They do not desire cakes of various shapes, nor the many kinds of vegetables, nor the six-flavored relishes and savory dishes, as they desire meat.

**13.117.3**  Herein my mind is bewildered upon this very point of renouncing it; for I do not think there is anything in flavor superior to flesh.

**13.117.4**  Therefore I wish to hear the virtues that lie in the abstention from flesh, and also the faults there are in eating it, O bull among men.

**13.117.5**  Tell me all of this truly and in accordance with dharma, O knower of dharma: what is to be eaten and what is not to be eaten—declare it all to me.

**13.117.6**  Bhīṣma said: It is even so, O mighty-armed Bhārata, as you say; there is nothing else on earth that surpasses flesh in flavor.

**13.117.7**  For those wounded, wasted, and feverish, for those given to the householder's life, and for those worn down by travel, there is nothing better than flesh.

**13.117.8**  It at once strengthens the vital breath and gives the highest nourishment; there is no food whatever superior to flesh, O scorcher of foes.

**13.117.9**  Yet many are the virtues that come to men from abstaining from it, O joy of the Kurus; hear these from me as I tell them.

**13.117.10**  There is no man meaner, none more cruel, than he who wishes to fatten his own flesh with the flesh of others.

**13.117.11**  For in this world nothing is dearer than one's own life; therefore let a man show compassion to others as he would to himself.

**13.117.12**  Flesh, my son, arises here from the seed of life—of this there is no doubt; and in eating it there is great fault, joined with killing.

**13.117.13**  Those who know the Veda understand that dharma is marked by non-violence; whatever deed is free of harm, that let the self-possessed man perform.

**13.117.14**  In the sacrifices to the ancestors and the gods, the consecrated oblation is so named according to the ordinance seen in the Veda; having eaten that, one is not defiled.

**13.117.15**  The sacred teaching is also heard that 'animals were created for sacrifice'; for those who act otherwise than this, the rite is called demonic.

**13.117.16**  But hear from me also the rule prescribed for the kṣatriyas, how one eating flesh won by valor is not defiled.

**13.117.17**  The wild deer of the forest were of old consecrated as sacred to all the gods by Agastya, O king, by whom the hunt is thus sanctioned.

**13.117.18**  There is no hunting without staking one's own self; meeting the beast on equal terms, he may slay it or be slain, O king.

**13.117.19**  Hence all the royal sages go to the hunt, O Bhārata; they are not stained by fault, nor do they reckon this a sin.

**13.117.20**  For there is nothing higher than this, here or hereafter, in all the worlds—nothing higher than compassion, O joy of the Kurus.

**13.117.21**  No fear ever befalls a compassionate man here; these worlds belong to the compassionate, and the higher worlds belong to ascetics.

**13.117.22**  He who, given to compassion, grants freedom from fear to all creatures—to him the creatures in turn grant freedom from fear: so have we heard.

**13.117.23**  All beings protect him—wounded, stumbling, fallen, afflicted, or struck down—both on even ground and on rough.

**13.117.24**  Beasts of prey do not slay him, nor piśācas, nor rākṣasas; in times of peril those are set free who set others free.

**13.117.25**  No gift greater than the gift of life has ever been or shall ever be, for it is certain that nothing is dearer to anyone than one's own self.

**13.117.26**  Death, O Bhārata, is unwelcome to all beings; for at the hour of death a trembling arises at once in living things.

**13.117.27**  In the ocean of transmigration, with its ceaseless sorrow of birth, caste, and old age, creatures revolve and shrink in dread from death.

**13.117.28**  In their dwellings in the womb they are cooked by the briny, sour, and pungent humors, and by the exceedingly grievous touch of urine, phlegm, and excrement.

**13.117.29**  And even when born, those greedy for flesh are seen there helpless, torn apart again and again, and cut to pieces, powerless.

**13.117.30**  They are boiled in the Kumbhīpāka hell, and entering one womb after another, set upon and slain, they are made to wander again and again.

**13.117.31**  Considering well, there is on earth none dearer to a being than its own self; therefore let the self-possessed man be compassionate toward all living creatures.

**13.117.32**  He who, O king, eats no flesh at all so long as he lives shall obtain a vast abode in heaven—of this there is no doubt.

**13.117.33**  Those who eat the flesh of creatures that long to live shall themselves be eaten by those very creatures—of this I have no doubt.

**13.117.34**  "Since he devours me, I too shall devour him"—this is the very flesh-nature of flesh; understand it thus, O Bhārata.

**13.117.35**  The slayer is ever slain in turn, and the binder is bound; the reviler, O king, is reviled, and the hater becomes an object of hatred.

**13.117.36**  With whatever body a man performs whatever deed, with that very body he reaps its fruit.

**13.117.37**  Non-harming is the highest dharma; non-harming is the highest self-restraint; non-harming is the highest gift; non-harming is the highest austerity.

**13.117.38**  Non-harming is the highest sacrifice; non-harming is the highest strength; non-harming is the highest friend; non-harming is the highest happiness; non-harming is the highest truth; non-harming is the highest sacred lore.

**13.117.39**  Gifts at all sacrifices, bathing at all sacred fords, the fruit of every act of giving—none of these is equal to non-harming.

**13.117.40**  The austerity of the harmless one is imperishable; the harmless one sacrifices unceasingly; the harmless one is to all creatures as a mother, as a father.

**13.117.41**  Such is the fruit of non-harming, and more besides, O bull of the Kurus; its virtues could not be told here even in a hundred years.

**13.118.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: Those slain in this great battle, whether unwilling or willing—into what wombs have they passed? Tell me that, grandfather.

**13.118.2**  The surrender of life by men in great combat is a grievous thing; I know the truth of it, O knower of dharma—giving up one's breath is most hard.

**13.118.3**  Whether in prosperity or in ruin, in fortune or in misfortune, tell me the reason for it; for in my judgment you are all-knowing.

**13.118.4**  Bhīṣma said: Whether in prosperity or ruin, in fortune or misfortune, living beings are born together into this round of existence, O lord of the earth.

**13.118.5**  By what disposition they are bound—hear from me the reason for it; and this further question you have asked is well put, O Yudhiṣṭhira.

**13.118.6**  On this I shall relate to you an ancient happening, O king—the dialogue of Dvaipāyana and a worm, O Yudhiṣṭhira.

**13.118.7**  Of old, the brāhmaṇa Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, who had become one with Brahman, while wandering, saw a worm running swiftly along a cart-track.

**13.118.8**  He who knew the ways of all beings and the cries of all embodied creatures, the all-knowing one, seeing the worm before him, spoke these words.

**13.118.9**  O worm, you seem terrified and you appear to be in haste; where are you running? Tell me that—whence has fear come upon you?

**13.118.10**  The worm said: Hearing the loud rumble of this great cart, fear has come upon me, O greatly wise one; for this din that is heard is terrible. "Let it not crush me"—therefore I flee away.

**13.118.11**  And thus I hear close by the panting of the goaded oxen as they haul the mighty load, O lord; and the many sounds of the men driving them are heard.

**13.118.12**  This cannot be endured by one of my kind, born in a worm's womb; therefore I am fleeing away from this most terrible peril.

**13.118.13**  Death is grievous for living beings, and life is very hard to win; therefore, in fear, I flee, that I may not pass from comfort into misery.

**13.118.14**  Bhīṣma said: Thus addressed, the sage replied to it: How can there be any comfort for you, O worm? I deem death to be your comfort, for you dwell in the womb of a beast.

**13.118.15**  Sound, touch, taste, smell, and the many pleasures high and low—of these, O worm, you have no knowledge; death itself is better for you.

**13.118.16**  The worm said: A living creature finds delight in every state, and so even here I have my happiness; I am aware of it, O greatly wise one, and therefore I wish to live.

**13.118.17**  Even here every realm of sense-objects is set in motion according to the body one has; men and beasts have their separate enjoyments, each in its own kind.

**13.118.18**  I was once a man, a śūdra of great wealth, hostile to brāhmaṇas, cruel, miserly, and living by usury.

**13.118.19**  Sharp of tongue, cunning of mind, a thief of everything from everyone, a breaker of trusts who hid away his deposits, bent on seizing others' goods.

**13.118.20**  And the servants and guests in my house I let go hungry through the night, out of grudging spite, craving the dainties for myself, cruel and greedy to keep all for my own.

**13.118.21**  Food prepared with faith for the gods and for the sacrifice to the ancestors I, greedy for gain, did not give away—yet food that ought to be given purifies indeed.

**13.118.22**  Those who, seeking safety in their fears, took refuge under my protection I abandoned without cause in their terror, nor did I shelter them who sought refuge.

**13.118.23**  Seeing men's wealth, their grain, their dear wives, their carriages and splendid dwellings and prosperity, I begrudged it all to no purpose.

**13.118.24**  Envious at the sight of others' happiness, an aggressor unwilling to let others thrive, a destroyer of the threefold aim of life in others, following only my own desires.

**13.118.25**  The deeds I did of old were full to overflowing with cruelty; remembering them, I grieve, as one who has lost a beloved son.

**13.118.26**  Yet I know too the fruit of good deeds I performed: my aged mother I honored, and a brāhmaṇa I revered.

**13.118.27**  Once, a guest endowed with high birth and virtue came by chance to my house, and I honored him, O brāhmaṇa; for that reason, memory has not forsaken me.

**13.118.28**  By that deed I look for a hope of happiness even here; I wish to hear from you what is best, O you whose wealth is austerity.

**13.119.1**  Vyāsa said: That through a good deed you are not bewildered even in the womb of a beast—that, O worm, is my own working, by which you are not led astray.

**13.119.2**  For by my very sight I deliver you, through the power of austerity; for than the power of austerity there is no other power more mighty.

**13.119.3**  I know that by your own sins you have come, O worm, to the state of a worm; yet you shall attain the highest dharma, if, abiding in dharma, you so resolve.

**13.119.4**  The deeds wrought upon earth the gods enjoy, and so do the beasts; even more than dharma, among men, do pleasure and gain accrue according to one's qualities.

**13.119.5**  What is lacking to a man endowed with speech, intellect, hands, and feet, and with discernment—what is lacking even to a dull man, so long as he lives?

**13.119.6**  While he lives, the foremost of brāhmaṇas offers worship to the moon and the sun, even by reciting a holy tale; to that estate, O worm, you shall come.

**13.119.7**  There you shall enjoy creatures of fine quality; there I shall guide you to brāhmaṇa-hood, which you desire.

**13.119.8**  Saying "So be it" in assent, the worm stood still upon the track, and in all the other births it underwent it came to behold that seer.

**13.119.9**  In the wombs of the porcupine, the iguana, and the boar, and likewise of deer and birds, of the dog-cooker, the vaiśya, the śūdra, and the kṣatriya.

**13.119.10**  Addressed as "worm" by the truth-speaking seer, it remembered its past, and with folded hands and bowed head it grasped his feet.

**13.119.11**  The worm said: This is that incomparable station, longed for with its tenfold excellences, in that I, who had reached worm-hood, have attained the rank of a king's son.

**13.119.12**  Mighty elephants garlanded with gold bear me, and in my chariots are yoked excellent steeds of the Kāmboja breed.

**13.119.13**  Carriages yoked with camels and mules bear me, and with my kinsmen and counselors I dine on rice and meat.

**13.119.14**  In well-appointed houses and on comfortable couches of the costliest sort, O blessed one, I sleep here, held in high honor.

**13.119.15**  In every last watch of the night the bards, the panegyrists, and the minstrels, sweet-spoken, sing my praises as though I were the god great Indra.

**13.119.16**  By the grace of you, true to your word and of measureless splendor, I, who had fallen into worm-hood, have attained the rank of a king's son.

**13.119.17**  Homage be to you, O greatly wise one; what shall I do? Command me. For this estate has been attained by me as decreed by the power of your austerity.

**13.119.18**  Vyāsa said: I am honored by you, O king, with these unsought words today; today, having passed through worm-hood, an unrevolted memory has arisen in you.

**13.119.19**  Yet there is no destruction of the evil that you heaped up of old, when you were a śūdra who set wealth above all, cruel and an aggressor.

**13.119.20**  My sight was gained by you, and that too was a good deed of old; though born in a beast's womb, you yet did me honor.

**13.119.21**  From this estate of a king's son you shall attain to brāhmaṇa-hood, by offering up your own life in battle for the sake of cows and brāhmaṇas.

**13.119.22**  Having gained the happiness of a king's son and performed the seasonal rites with their full priestly fees, you shall then rejoice in heaven, become one with Brahman, imperishable and happy.

**13.119.23**  From the beast's womb one comes to śūdra-hood; the śūdra to vaiśya-hood, and the vaiśya to kṣatriya-hood; the kṣatriya praised for his conduct attains brāhmaṇa-hood, and the brāhmaṇa of righteous conduct attains holy heaven.

**13.120.1**  Bhīṣma said: Having attained the duty of a kṣatriya, that valiant one, still remembering his past and having cast off worm-hood, O king, practiced abundant austerity.

**13.120.2**  Seeing that abundant austerity of his, who knew dharma and gain, the best of the twice-born, Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, then came to him.

**13.120.3**  Vyāsa said: The vow of the kṣatriya, O worm, is the guarding of living beings; meditating on that vow of the kṣatriya, you shall thence come to brāhmaṇa-hood.

**13.120.4**  Protect all your subjects rightly, knowing good from evil, self-possessed, dispensing wholesome pleasures and purifying the evildoers.

**13.120.5**  Be self-possessed, well content, delighting in the practice of your own dharma; casting off the kṣatriya body, you shall thence come to brāhmaṇa-hood.

**13.120.6**  Bhīṣma said: Then, O Yudhiṣṭhira, having heard the great seer's word, and having protected his subjects with dharma, he set his mind once more upon the forest.

**13.120.7**  In no long time, O best of kings, the worm, by the duty of protecting his subjects, departed this life and came to brāhmaṇa-hood.

**13.120.8**  Then, seeing him become a brāhmaṇa, the greatly renowned and greatly wise Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana came to him once again.

**13.120.9**  Vyāsa said: Ho there, O illustrious bull among brāhmaṇas, be not troubled in any way! The doer of good is born into good wombs, the doer of evil into evil wombs, O knower of dharma, each according to his dharma and as the scriptures declare.

**13.120.10**  Therefore, O worm, be not troubled in any way by the fear of death; let your fear be of the lapse from dharma—therefore practice the highest dharma.

**13.120.11**  The worm said: I have attained, O blessed one, a happiness happier than happiness, through your doing; having gained prosperity rooted in dharma, my sin is this day destroyed in me.

**13.120.12**  Bhīṣma said: At the word of the blessed sage, the worm, having attained the hard-won state of a brāhmaṇa, made the earth marked with a hundred sacrificial posts, O king; thereafter, that best of knowers of Brahman went to share the world of Brahman.

**13.120.13**  And the worm attained, O Pārtha, the supreme eternal Brahman, brought about by the fruit of his own deeds and by the word of Vyāsa.

**13.120.14**  Since those bulls among kṣatriyas too were slain in accordance with their very nature, they have attained a holy destiny; therefore do not grieve, my son.

**13.121.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: Sacred learning, austerity, and giving—which of these is the most excellent? I ask you, O best of the good; tell me that, grandfather.

**13.121.2**  Bhīṣma said: On this too they recount an ancient tale—the dialogue of Maitreya and Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana.

**13.121.3**  Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, O king, while wandering in disguise unrecognized, came to attend upon Maitreya at Vārāṇasī, in the dwelling of a wanton woman.

**13.121.4**  Knowing that best of sages had come and was seated before him, Maitreya honored him and fed him excellent food.

**13.121.5**  Having eaten that excellent food, of fine quality and satisfying every desire, the great-souled Kṛṣṇa, well pleased, smiled as he made ready to depart.

**13.121.6**  Beholding him smiling, Maitreya said to Kṛṣṇa: Tell me the reason, O righteous one, why you smiled; and whence has this joy come upon you, an ascetic firm of resolve?

**13.121.7**  This I ask of you, O learned one, after saluting and bowing low: the blessing of your austerity, and your great good fortune as well.

**13.121.8**  Though we two practice apart, dear one, and each lives within his own self, I reckon the difference between us small—or, it may be, that you surpass me.

**13.121.9**  Vyāsa said: This smile of mine arose at excessive cutting-down and excessive speech. False is the word of the Veda?—why should the Veda utter an untruth?

**13.121.10**  Three steps alone, they say, make up a man's highest vow: he should do no injury, he should give, and he should speak supreme truth. This is our duty now, and it is remembered as the highest hereafter as well.

**13.121.11**  Even a small gift of such a kind becomes great in its fruit—that which is given to one who craves it, from a heart that bears no grudging.

**13.121.12**  Yourself hungering, you gave this food of mine to one who hungered, and thereby you have won, O mighty one, vast worlds, as though by great sacrifices. Therefore I am pleased—by the sanctity of your gift, and by your austerity too.

**13.121.13**  For your very fragrance is that of merit, and the very sight of you is meritorious; meritorious is the scent that breathes from you—and that, I think, comes from the ordering of your deeds.

**13.121.14**  More than any scrubbing clean, dear one, and more than any anointing—auspicious beyond all purifiers—giving alone becomes the supreme.

**13.121.15**  Of all those highest things declared in the Veda which you here extol, giving is the most excellent—of this I have no doubt.

**13.121.16**  The path is made by the givers of gifts, by which the wise go their way; for they are the givers of life itself, and in them dharma stands firm.

**13.121.17**  As the Vedas well studied, as the restraint of the senses, as total renunciation here—even so is giving unsurpassed.

**13.121.18**  For you, dear one, will pass from happiness to lovely happiness; from happiness to the gaining of a greater happiness does the wise man attain.

**13.121.19**  This is plain to our very sight, grasped beyond doubt: riches attain the man of fortune, and so do giving, and sacrifice, and ease.

**13.121.20**  From happiness comes a further sorrow, and from sorrow another, higher happiness; for so it is seen, O greatly wise one, fixed by its very nature.

**13.121.21**  Threefold, the wise declare, are the courses of a man's conduct here: one is meritorious, another sinful, and one neither meritorious nor sinful.

**13.121.22**  He approves not the conduct of one man, and deems another's sinful; so too, that which arises from one's own appointed work is neither meritorious nor sinful.

**13.121.23**  Delight, prosper, rejoice, and give, and sacrifice too: neither the learned in lore nor the practisers of austerity shall overmaster you.

**13.122.1**  Bhīṣma said: Thus addressed, Maitreya, who honored action—born in a most illustrious family, wise and deeply learned—made reply.

**13.122.2**  Beyond doubt, O greatly wise one, it is just as you have said; yet with your leave, mighty one, I would say a word.

**13.122.3**  Vyāsa said: Whatever you wish, Maitreya, however much and in whatever way—speak it, O greatly wise one; I would gladly hear your words.

**13.122.4**  Maitreya said: Faultless and unblemished is your speech, charged with the praise of giving; for by learning and austerity your self is purified—of this there is no doubt.

**13.122.5**  Because your self is so purified, this gift of mine becomes very great; the more I consider it with my mind, the more it seems like the fruit of richly accomplished austerity.

**13.122.6**  From the mere sight of you, indeed, great prosperity comes to me; I deem this your grace—for such is action by its very nature.

**13.122.7**  Austerity, sacred learning, and high birth—these are the grounds of brahmanhood; endowed with these three qualities, a man then becomes a twice-born indeed.

**13.122.8**  When such a one is satisfied, the ancestors and the gods are satisfied too; for among those rich in learning there is nothing higher than a brāhmaṇa.

**13.122.9**  For just as a man reaps fruit from a well-tilled field, so the giver, having given to one rich in learning, enjoys his fruit.

**13.122.10**  Were there no brāhmaṇa endowed with learning and good conduct to be the receiver of a gift, the wealth of the wealthy would be in vain.

**13.122.11**  For an ignorant man, eating, destroys the food, and the food being eaten destroys him; and he destroys the one whose food it was—thus destroying, the fool is himself destroyed.

**13.122.12**  But the learned man, the master, eating food, the capable one, brings it forth again; and he himself is born of food—hence the transition between them is a subtle one.

**13.122.13**  The very merit of the giver is the merit of the receiver; for a single wheel cannot roll—thus the seers have understood.

**13.122.14**  Where there are brāhmaṇas endowed with learning and good conduct, there the giver enjoys the meritorious fruit of his gift, both here and in the world beyond.

**13.122.15**  Those who are pure in birth, ever ardently devoted to austerity, accomplished in giving and in study—they indeed are most worthy of worship always.

**13.122.16**  For the path made by those good men—he who is mindful of it does not go astray; for they are the guides to heaven, the eternal bearers of sacrifice.

**13.123.1**  Bhīṣma said: Thus addressed, the venerable one answered Maitreya in turn: Happily do you understand things thus; happily is your understanding such! For this world, for the most part, praises only the virtues.

**13.123.2**  Pride of beauty, pride of age, and pride of fortune—undoubtedly, happily, these do not overmaster you; this is heaven's grace upon you. Now hear what I shall set forth as even higher than giving.

**13.123.3**  Whatever scriptures of tradition there are here, and whatever undertakings of any kind, these have all proceeded, each in its order, with the Veda set before them.

**13.123.4**  I extol giving, and you extol austerity and sacred learning; austerity is the sanctifier of the Veda, austerity is the means to heaven.

**13.123.5**  By austerity one attains greatness, and by knowledge—so we have heard; and by austerity alone one may wipe away whatever other evil has been done.

**13.123.6**  For whatever a man, fixing his aim, performs austerity for, all this the brāhmaṇa who has crossed to the far shore of the Veda attains.

**13.123.7**  What is hard to follow, hard to assail, hard to win, hard to overcome—all of it one reaches through austerity; for austerity is the mightier power.

**13.123.8**  The drinker of liquor, the taker of what was not granted, the slayer of an embryo, the defiler of his teacher's bed—through austerity he crosses over all, and is released from his sin.

**13.123.9**  The man of all knowledge, the man of clear sight, of whatever rank he be—both these they call ascetics, and to both reverence should ever be made.

**13.123.10**  All who are rich in sacred learning are worthy of worship, and so too the ascetics; the givers of gifts attain happiness after death, and fortune here below.

**13.123.11**  This world, and the world of Brahmā, and the mightier world beyond—by gifts of food the well-doing folk of this world attain them all.

**13.123.12**  Being honored, men honor these in return; being esteemed, they give esteem; but the non-giver, wherever he goes, is on every side thrust away.

**13.123.13**  The doer and the non-doer alike obtain each what his deeds deserve; whether you go upward or downward to your world hereafter—

**13.123.14**  —you will obtain such food and drink as you may give. You are wise, nobly born, learned, and free from cruelty.

**13.123.15**  Holding the vow of taking a wife in your youth, O Maitreya, be devoted to it; embrace this first, the course commended for householders.

**13.123.16**  Where the husband is content with his wife and the wife content with her husband—in that household where it is so, all that is good prevails.

**13.123.17**  As dirt is washed from the limbs by water, as darkness is dispelled by the light of fire, so by giving and by austerity all sin is driven away.

**13.123.18**  Fare you well, Maitreya; I now take my leave and go to my dwelling. Keep this in mind, and so your welfare shall come to be.

**13.123.19**  Then Maitreya bowed to him and walked round him keeping him to the right, and with hands joined in reverence said, "May the venerable one fare well."

**13.124.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: The course of conduct of virtuous women, O best of all upholders of dharma, I wish to hear from you; tell it to me, grandfather.

**13.124.2**  Bhīṣma said: In the world of the gods, a Kaikeyī princess named Sumanā questioned Śāṇḍilī—the all-knowing, the knower of every dharma, the high-minded woman.

**13.124.3**  By what conduct, O fair one, or by what course of life, having shaken off all sins, have you come to the world of the gods?

**13.124.4**  Blazing with your own splendor like the tongue of the fire-god, you have come to heaven by your radiance, as though you were the daughter of the moon, the lord of stars.

**13.124.5**  Wearing spotless garments, free of all weariness, seated in your celestial car, you shine, O lovely one, with a thousandfold strength of light.

**13.124.6**  Not by any small austerity, nor giving, nor self-restraint have you attained this world; therefore tell me the truth of it.

**13.124.7**  Thus questioned by Sumanā, Śāṇḍilī of the sweet and lovely smile spoke this measured word to Sumanā:

**13.124.8**  Not by becoming a wearer of ochre robes, nor of bark garments, nor shaven-headed, nor matted-haired did I attain to godhood.

**13.124.9**  Words unkind, and all words that were harsh—heedful, I never at any time spoke them to my husband.

**13.124.10**  In the worship of the gods, the ancestors, and the brāhmaṇas I was ever heedful and intent, devoted to my mother-in-law and father-in-law.

**13.124.11**  I never engaged in slander, nor did such a thing enter my mind; I did not loiter where there was no doorway, nor talk for long.

**13.124.12**  Any unseemly laughter, or anything hurtful in deed, secret or open—in this I never engaged at all.

**13.124.13**  And my husband, gone out on some errand and returned home, I would settle on a seat and honor with collected mind.

**13.124.14**  And whatever he did not recognize, whatever food he did not relish, whether to be chewed or to be licked—all that I would set aside.

**13.124.15**  Whatever task there was, brought together for the household's sake, rising at dawn I would have all of it done, and did it myself.

**13.124.16**  If my husband went abroad on some business, I would devote myself, ever restrained, to many auspicious observances.

**13.124.17**  Eye-salve and yellow pigment, bathing, garlands and unguents, and adornment—when my husband had gone out, in none of these did I take delight.

**13.124.18**  I never roused my husband when he was sleeping at ease, even in pressing tasks; and by that my mind found contentment.

**13.124.19**  I never wearied my husband over household matters at any time; ever I kept secrets well-guarded, and my dwelling well-swept and clean.

**13.124.20**  A woman who guards this path of dharma with a collected mind is exalted in heaven among women, like Arundhatī.

**13.124.21**  Bhīṣma said: Having declared to Sumanā this dharma of devotion to one's husband, that goddess, the ascetic and greatly blessed lady, then passed from sight.

**13.124.22**  And whoever reads this tale told to the Pāṇḍava, at each parva-juncture, will reach the world of the gods and dwell in supreme bliss in the Nandana grove.

**13.125.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: By conciliation or by giving—which do you hold the better? Declare to me, O best of the Bhāratas, which of the two prevails here.

**13.125.2**  Bhīṣma said: One man is won over by conciliation, and another by a gift; having understood a man's nature, one should resort to one of these two.

**13.125.3**  But hear from me, O king, the virtues of gentle speech, O bull of the Bhāratas—how even fierce creatures may be propitiated by gentleness.

**13.125.4**  On this they cite an ancient tale: how a twice-born man, seized by a rākṣasa in the forest, was set free.

**13.125.5**  A certain brāhmaṇa, endowed with intelligence, in a lonely wood was seized and brought to a sore strait by a rākṣasa about to devour him.

**13.125.6**  He, endowed with intelligence and learning, beholding that exceedingly terrible being, employed gentle speech upon him; he neither lost his wits nor trembled.

**13.125.7**  But the demon, honoring him with courteous speech, put a question to the brāhmaṇa: "You shall go free—answer me my question: by what cause am I so green and gaunt?"

**13.125.8**  Then the brāhmaṇa, having reflected for a moment, calmly answered that demon's question with these verses.

**13.125.9**  "Living abroad, dwelling apart, surely cut off from your friends, you enjoy peerless pleasures all alone—that is why you are green and gaunt.

**13.125.10**  Surely your friends, O demon, though well treated by you, are estranged through your own fault—that is why you are green and gaunt.

**13.125.11**  Surely men richer in wealth and power, arrogant, yet in worth far beneath you, look down upon you—that is why you are green and gaunt.

**13.125.12**  Being yourself a man of merit, you surely see others without merit being honored; wise and disciplined, you see the unwise so treated—that is why you are green and gaunt.

**13.125.13**  Though afflicted by lack of livelihood, you scorn the means of getting one, and out of high-mindedness you suffer—that is why you are green and gaunt.

**13.125.14**  Out of nobility you pressed yourself hard to oblige someone, and he, good sir, thinks he has bested you—that is why you are green and gaunt.

**13.125.15**  I think you brood over people who, their hearts shrouded in lust and anger, torment themselves on wrong paths—that is why you are green and gaunt.

**13.125.16**  Honored by the wise but not befriended by fools, you—modest yet impatient under the ill-conducted—that is why you are green and gaunt.

**13.125.17**  Surely some enemy with a friend's face, behaving as a noble man would, has deceived you and gone his way—that is why you are green and gaunt.

**13.125.18**  Open in your dealings, yet skilled in counsel and accomplished, you are surely not honored by those who should know your worth—that is why you are green and gaunt.

**13.125.19**  When you speak your settled conviction among the wicked who are bent on their own way, your virtues do not shine—that is why you are green and gaunt.

**13.125.20**  Lacking wealth, cleverness, and learning, possessed only of inner fire, you surely strive after some great thing—that is why you are green and gaunt.

**13.125.21**  I think your kinsfolk will not accept you, for your heart is fixed on austerity and you long for the forest—that is why you are green and gaunt.

**13.125.22**  Surely among men of wealth your speech, though faultless and uttered in good season, finds no luster—that is why you are green and gaunt.

**13.125.23**  A fool dear to your heart, fixed in his old beliefs and now angered, you are unable to win back—that is why you are green and gaunt.

**13.125.24**  Surely, having entangled you in some task he desired, someone now presses you exceedingly hard—that is why you are green and gaunt.

**13.125.25**  A friend whom you honor for his own qualities surely takes it for granted, "This man's purpose is served through me"—that is why you are green and gaunt.

**13.125.26**  Surely, out of shame, you do not wish to disclose the intention hidden within you, slack as you are in pursuing gain—that is why you are green and gaunt.

**13.125.27**  Surely you wish to win over by your own virtues all the men of the world, with their differing minds and tastes—that is why you are green and gaunt.

**13.125.28**  Unlearned, timid, and poor, you yet long for the fame born of learning, valor, and giving—that is why you are green and gaunt.

**13.125.29**  Some fruit long desired you have not won at all; what you wrought, others have carried off—that is why you are green and gaunt.

**13.125.30**  Surely, seeing no fault of your own making within yourself, you have been blamed without cause—that is why you are green and gaunt.

**13.125.31**  You feel, untainted by gain or means, the grief, born of irreparable loss, of vigilant friends—that is why you are green and gaunt.

**13.125.32**  Seeing virtuous householders and unvirtuous forest-dwellers, the freed still bound to their dwelling—that is why you are green and gaunt.

**13.125.33**  A righteous and profitable word, spoken by you in the right time and place, surely takes no hold—that is why you are green and gaunt.

**13.125.34**  Wise yet wishing to live, you surely subsist on wealth given by the inept—that is why you are green and gaunt.

**13.125.35**  Seeing the wicked flourish and the good sink down, you surely search for what is fitting—that is why you are green and gaunt.

**13.125.36**  Surely you wish to do good to friends who are at odds with one another, yet without setting them against each other—that is why you are green and gaunt.

**13.125.37**  I think you brood over people—learned men engaged in wrongful acts, and wise men who have not conquered their senses—that is why you are green and gaunt."

**13.125.38**  The demon, thus honored, honored that brāhmaṇa in return; he made him his friend, and, having endowed him with wealth, set him free.

**13.126.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: O grandfather, greatly wise, versed in all the scriptures, abounding in many traditions, you are renowned in our line.

**13.126.2**  From you, O tamer of foes, I wish to hear what is joined with dharma and artha, bringing happiness in time to come, and a wonder to the world.

**13.126.3**  This time has come upon us when kinsmen and friends are hard to keep, and there is no teacher for us but you, O bull of the Bhāratas.

**13.126.4**  If I, together with my brothers, am worthy of your grace, O sinless one, then deign, O king, to answer us the question that I ask you.

**13.126.5**  This glorious Nārāyaṇa, honored by all kings, waits upon you with great regard and with reverence.

**13.126.6**  In his presence, and before all the kings and my brothers, you should, out of affection, speak for my pleasure.

**13.126.7**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard that speech of his, Bhīṣma, son of Bhāgīrathī, moved with affection and eager joy, spoke these words.

**13.126.8**  "Come now, I shall tell you a most delightful tale; long ago, O king, I heard of this power of Viṣṇu.

**13.126.9**  Hear from me too the power of the god marked with the bull, and hear from me the doubt of Rudrāṇī, the doubt that arose between that divine pair.

**13.126.10**  The righteous Kṛṣṇa undertook a vow of twelve years, and the two seers Nārada and Parvata came to behold him at his consecration.

**13.126.11**  And Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana too, and Dhaumya, best of those who murmur prayers, and Devala, and Kāśyapa, and Hastikāśyapa as well,

**13.126.12**  and other holy sages, endowed with consecration and self-restraint, all followed by their pupils, ascetics rich in penance, godlike.

**13.126.13**  For them the son of Devakī, well pleased, prepared a godlike welcome, the worshipful honoring of guests befitting his line.

**13.126.14**  Upon fresh green seats of gold strewn with kuśa grass the great seers, well pleased, took their places.

**13.126.15**  Then those ascetics who dwell apart, rich in penance, made sweet discourses bound up with dharma, concerning royal sages and the gods.

**13.126.16**  Then the divine energy of Nārāyaṇa, kindled as fuel by the practice of his vow, issued forth as fire from the mouth of Kṛṣṇa of wondrous deeds.

**13.126.17**  That fire burned up the mountain with its trees, its creepers and shrubs, with its throngs of birds and beasts, with its predators and creeping things,

**13.126.18**  and with deer of many shapes; the peak of that mountain, churned and blazing to behold, was rendered senseless, filled with cries of woe.

**13.126.19**  But that great-flamed fire, having burned everything utterly, came near to Viṣṇu and touched his feet like a pupil.

**13.126.20**  Then Viṣṇu, scourge of foes, seeing the forest burned away, by gentle castings of his gaze restored it to its natural state.

**13.126.21**  And so that mountain once more had its creepers and trees in full flower, resounding with flocks of birds, with predators and creeping things.

**13.126.22**  Seeing that wonder, beyond thought, the company of sages then became amazed, their hair bristling and their eyes wet with tears.

**13.126.23**  Then Nārāyaṇa, best of speakers, seeing those seers filled with amazement, asked them modestly, sweetly, and tenderly:

**13.126.24**  "Why has amazement come upon this throng of seers, who have forever renounced attachment, who are free of 'mine' and versed in sacred lore?

**13.126.25**  This whole doubt of mine the blameless seers, rich in penance, ought to resolve for me truly and with certainty."

**13.126.26**  The seers said: "You send forth the worlds, and you withdraw them again; you are the cold, you are the heat, and it is you yourself who send down the rain.

**13.126.27**  Of all beings upon the earth, the unmoving and the moving, you are the father and the mother, the lord, and the very source.

**13.126.28**  Explain to us this thing that fills us with wonder, O slayer of Madhu; you alone, O blessed one, are fit to tell of the issuing-forth of that fire.

**13.126.29**  Then we too, our terror gone, O scourge of foes, O Hari, shall tell you what we have heard and what we have seen."

**13.126.30**  Vāsudeva said: "This is that Vaiṣṇava energy that issued from my mouth—the dark-tracked fire, bright as the world's end, by which this mountain was churned.

**13.126.31**  And you seers, who have conquered anger and subdued your senses, godlike, rich in penance, fell into distress and were shaken.

**13.126.32**  From me, wholly absorbed in the practice of my vow through the keeping of ascetic observances, this fire arose; you should not be troubled at all.

**13.126.33**  I have come to this fair mountain to perform my vow, and I have come to bring forth by penance a son equal to myself in valor.

**13.126.34**  Then my own self that dwells in this body, becoming fire, issued forth and went to behold the boon-giving grandfather of all the worlds.

**13.126.35**  And by him, O best of sages, I was instructed regarding sonship: the bull-bannered god said, 'A son shall be yours from half of this energy.'

**13.126.36**  That fire, drawing near to me, to the soles of my feet, attended me like a pupil and then, grown calm, returned to its natural state.

**13.126.37**  This secret of the wise lotus-naveled one I have told you out of love; let no fear be felt, O you rich in penance.

**13.126.38**  Yours is an untroubled passage everywhere, O far-seeing ones, blazing with ascetic vows, resplendent with knowledge and discernment.

**13.126.39**  Whatever you have heard or seen, in heaven or upon earth, that is some surpassing wonder—that, I pray, you tell to me.

**13.126.40**  I have a longing for that honeyed speech, like nectar, spoken here by you who dwell in the penance-grove."

**13.126.41**  "Even though I, O you of stainless vision, may see something divine and wondrous to behold, unseen before, whether in heaven or on earth,

**13.126.42**  that supreme nature of mine is nowhere thwarted, and the sovereign power that abides within myself appears no wonder to me.

**13.126.43**  For a matter that is credible, once told and reaching the ears of the good, abides long upon the earth, like a writing graven on rock.

**13.126.44**  Therefore, in that gathering, I shall day after day repeat what has come from the mouths of the good, which kindles the understanding of men."

**13.126.45**  Then all the throngs of sages, reverent in the presence of Kṛṣṇa, gazed upon Janārdana with eyes like lotus petals.

**13.126.46**  Some, in like manner, exalted him; others honored him; and they praised the slayer of Madhu with words whose meanings were adorned with verses of the Ṛg.

**13.126.47**  Then all the throngs of sages appointed to the discourse Nārada, who beholds the gods and is skilled in speech.

**13.126.48**  "That wonder, beyond thought, O lord, which was experienced upon the Himālaya mountain by the throngs of sages intent on pilgrimage to the holy fords—

**13.126.49**  Therefore, urged by all, you should relate everything for the welfare of the assembly of sages, just as you witnessed it concerning Hṛṣīkeśa.

**13.126.50**  Thus addressed by the sages, the blessed seer Nārada, the divine sage, narrated an auspicious tale of what had happened of old.

**13.127.1**  Bhīṣma said: Then the blessed seer Nārada, friend of Nārāyaṇa, recounted the dialogue of Śaṃkara with Umā.

**13.127.2**  The righteous lord of the gods, marked with the bull, practised austerities upon the holy mountain Himavat, frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas.

**13.127.3**  Upon that lovely mountain, rich with manifold healing herbs, thronged with flowers of every kind, crowded with troops of Apsarases, and attended by hosts of spirits.

**13.127.4**  There the god, filled with delight, was surrounded by hundreds of bands of spirits, of various forms and misshapen, divine and wondrous to behold.

**13.127.5**  Some resembling lions, tigers, and elephants, drawn from every species, some with the faces of jackals and leopards, others with the heads of bears and bulls.

**13.127.6**  With terrible owl-faced ones, and others with the faces of hawks and vultures, resembling beasts of every hue and gathered from all kinds, together with Kiṃnaras, divine Gandharvas, and hosts of Yakṣas and spirits.

**13.127.7**  That assembly-hall of the bull-bannered god was strewn with divine flowers, adorned with divine garlands, anointed with divine sandal, fumed with divine incense, and resounding with divine music.

**13.127.8**  It rang with the beat of drums and tabors and the blare of conches and kettledrums, with troops of spirits and peacocks dancing on every side.

**13.127.9**  There the Apsarases danced; the divine place was attended by throngs of celestial women, lovely to the eye, indescribable, divine, and wondrous to behold.

**13.127.10**  By the austerity of that lord of beings, the mountain shone resplendent.

**13.127.11**  Resounding with the Vedic chants of brahmins devoted to recitation, and with the humming of bees, the mountain was matchless as the springtime.

**13.127.12**  Beholding that place, resembling a great festival yet bearing a terrible aspect, the host of sages was filled with supreme delight, O Janārdana.

**13.127.13**  The illustrious sages, and the Siddhas of unbroken chastity, the Maruts, the Vasus, the Sādhyas, and the eternal Viśvedevas;

**13.127.14**  The Yakṣas, Nāgas, and Piśācas, the guardians of the worlds, the fires, and all the elemental beings, humbled, were gathered there together.

**13.127.15**  The seasons scattered all their flowers, marvellous beyond measure, and the herbs, blazing with light, illumined that forest.

**13.127.16**  And the birds, filled with joy, danced and sang, calling out upon the lovely mountain slopes, beloved of all.

**13.127.17**  There upon the mountain-slope, adorned with divine minerals, the high-souled god sat, shining as upon a couch.

**13.127.18**  Clad in a tiger's skin, with a lion's hide for an upper garment, wearing a serpent for his sacred thread, and adorned with red armlets.

**13.127.19**  Tawny-bearded, matted-haired, terrible, a striker of fear into the foes of the gods, yet the giver of safety to all beings and to his devotees—he, the bull-bannered one.

**13.127.20**  Beholding him, all the seers touched the earth with their heads, and were released from every sin, made patient and freed from impurity.

**13.127.21**  The abode of that lord of beings shone, bearing a terrible aspect, utterly unassailable, and teeming with great serpents.

**13.127.22**  In a single moment, O slayer of Madhu, all became wondrous; that assembly of the bull-bannered god shone, bearing its terrible form.

**13.127.23**  To him approached the daughter of the mountain, surrounded by troops of spirit-women, clad in raiment like Hara's own, observing the selfsame vow.

**13.127.24**  Bearing a golden pitcher brimming with the waters of all sacred fords, the fair goddess came, followed on every side by the holy mountain-streams.

**13.127.25**  Raining down showers of flowers and manifold fragrances, frequenting the slopes of Himavat, she drew near to Hara's side.

**13.127.26**  Then, smiling, the fair-faced goddess, in sport, suddenly covered Hara's beautiful eyes with her two hands.

**13.127.27**  But with his eyes thus covered, that whole assembly was at once plunged into darkness, senseless, void of oblation and of the cry of vaṣaṭ.

**13.127.28**  And all the people grew disheartened, seized with terror and dread; with the lord of beings' eyes shut, the world became as though the sun had perished.

**13.127.29**  Then in an instant the world grew free of darkness, for a great blazing flame issued forth from his forehead.

**13.127.30**  And there arose upon him a third eye, like unto the sun, blazing as at the end of an age, by which that mountain was scorched.

**13.127.31**  Then the mountain's daughter, beholding Hara whose eye was like blazing fire, bowed to him with her head and gazed with her wide eyes.

**13.127.32**  As that forest burned, with its sāla and pine trees, its lovely groves of sandal, lit up with divine herbs;

**13.127.33**  That assembly grew crowded with herds of deer, fleeing in terror, drawing close to Hara's side, finding no refuge anywhere.

**13.127.34**  Then with flames touching the sky, brilliant with quivering lightning-rays, like the twelve suns, like a second fire of the age's end—
