**13.135.42**  He is Subhuja, the fair-armed; Durdhara, hard to hold or bear; Vāgmī, the eloquent; Mahendra, the great lord; Vasuda, the giver of wealth; Vasu, wealth itself; Naikarūpa, of manifold forms; Bṛhadrūpa, of vast form; Śipiviṣṭa, who dwells within the rays; and Prakāśana, the illuminator.

**13.135.43**  He is Ojastejodyutidhara, who holds vital force, splendor, and brilliance; Prakāśātmā, of luminous self; Pratāpana, who blazes forth heat; Ṛddha, the abounding; Spaṣṭākṣara, made manifest in the syllable Oṃ; Mantra, the sacred utterance; Candrāṃśu, ray of the moon; and Bhāskaradyuti, with the radiance of the sun.

**13.135.44**  He is Amṛtāṃśūdbhava, from whom the nectar-rayed moon arose; Bhānu, the shining; Śaśabindu, the hare-marked moon; Sureśvara, lord of the gods; Auṣadha, the healing herb; Jagataḥsetu, the bridge across the world; and Satyadharmaparākrama, whose valor is truth and righteousness.

**13.135.45**  He is Bhūtabhavyabhavannātha, lord of past, future, and present; Pavana, the wind; Pāvana, the purifier; Anila, the breath that needs no support; Kāmahā, destroyer of desire; Kāmakṛt, fulfiller of desire; Kānta, the beautiful and beloved; Kāma, desire itself; Kāmaprada, the granter of wishes; and Prabhu, the lord.

**13.135.46**  He is Yugādikṛt, the maker of the ages' beginning; Yugāvarta, who turns the cycle of yugas; Naikamāya, of manifold illusion; Mahāśana, the great devourer; Adṛśya, the invisible; Vyaktarūpa, of manifest form; Sahasrajit, conqueror of thousands; and Anantajit, the ever-victorious.

**13.135.47**  He is Iṣṭa, the beloved; Viśiṣṭa, the most excellent; Śiṣṭeṣṭa, dear to the righteous; Śikhaṇḍī, the crested one; Nahuṣa, who binds all beings; Vṛṣa, the embodiment of dharma; Krodhahā, slayer of wrath; Krodhakṛt, who rouses wrath against the wicked; Kartā, the doer; Viśvabāhu, of universal arms; and Mahīdhara, the upholder of the earth.

**13.135.48**  He is Acyuta, the unfallen; Prathita, the renowned; Prāṇa, the breath of life; Prāṇada, giver of life; Vāsavānuja, the younger brother of Indra; Apāṃ nidhi, the treasure-house of the waters; Adhiṣṭhāna, the foundation of all; Apramatta, the ever-vigilant; and Pratiṣṭhita, the self-established.

**13.135.49**  He is Skanda, who flows forth as nectar; Skandadhara, upholder of the path of dharma; Dhurya, who bears the yoke of creation; Varada, the granter of boons; Vāyuvāhana, who drives the winds; Vāsudeva, the indwelling and all-pervading; Bṛhadbhānu, of vast radiance; Ādideva, the primeval god; and Puraṃdara, the breaker of strongholds.

**13.135.50**  He is Aśoka, the sorrowless; Tāraṇa, who ferries beings across; Tāra, the deliverer; Śūra, the hero; Śauri, born in the line of Śūra; Janeśvara, lord of men; Anukūla, the ever-favorable; Śatāvarta, of a hundred manifestations; Padmī, the lotus-holder; and Padmanibhekṣaṇa, whose eyes resemble lotuses.

**13.135.51**  He is Padmanābha, the lotus-naveled; Aravindākṣa, the lotus-eyed; Padmagarbha, who is contemplated in the lotus of the heart; Śarīrabhṛt, the sustainer of bodies; Maharddhi, of great prosperity; Ṛddha, the abounding; Vṛddhātmā, the ancient soul; Mahākṣa, the great-eyed; and Garuḍadhvaja, who bears Garuḍa on his banner.

**13.135.52**  He is Atula, the incomparable; Śarabha, who dwells within the body; Bhīma, the terrible; Samayajña, knower of the proper occasions; Havis, the oblation; Hari, the tawny and the remover of sin; Sarvalakṣaṇalakṣaṇya, known by every auspicious mark; Lakṣmīvān, the consort of Lakṣmī; and Samitiṃjaya, the victor in battle.

**13.135.53**  He is Vikṣara, the imperishable; Rohita, the assumer of forms like the fish; Mārga, the path; Hetu, the cause; Dāmodara, bound at the waist with a cord; Saha, the all-enduring; Mahīdhara, upholder of the earth; Mahābhāga, of great fortune; Vegavān, the swift; and Amitāśana, of boundless appetite.

**13.135.54**  He is Udbhava, the source of all; Kṣobhaṇa, who stirred creation into being; Deva, the resplendent; Śrīgarbha, in whose womb all glory abides; Parameśvara, the supreme lord; Karaṇa, the instrument; Kāraṇa, the cause; Kartā, the doer; Vikartā, the maker of manifold worlds; Gahana, the unfathomable; and Guha, the hidden one.

**13.135.55**  He is Vyavasāya, resolute knowledge; Vyavasthāna, the ordainer of order; Saṃsthāna, the final dissolution; Sthānada, the giver of abodes; Dhruva, the immovable; Pararddhi, of supreme prosperity; Parama, the highest; Spaṣṭa, the manifest; Tuṣṭa, the contented; Puṣṭa, the full; and Śubhekṣaṇa, of auspicious gaze.

**13.135.56**  He is Rāma, the delightful; Virāma, the end and cessation; Virāṭa, the desireless; Mārga, the path; Neya, who is to be guided to by wisdom; Naya, the guide; Anaya, who needs no guide; Vīra, the hero; Śaktimatāṃ śreṣṭha, foremost of the powerful; Dharma, righteousness; Dharmavid uttama, the highest knower of dharma.

**13.135.57**  He is Vaikuṇṭha, who unites the scattered worlds; Puruṣa, the cosmic Person; Prāṇa, the breath of life; Prāṇada, the giver of life; Praṇava, the sacred Oṃ; Pṛthu, the vast and expanded; Hiraṇyagarbha, the golden womb; Śatrughna, slayer of foes; Vyāpta, the all-pervading; Vāyu, the wind; and Adhokṣaja, who never declines from his own nature.

**13.135.58**  He is Ṛtu, the season; Sudarśana, of fair vision; Kāla, time itself; Parameṣṭhī, established on high; Parigraha, the receiver and embracer of all; Ugra, the formidable; Saṃvatsara, the year; Dakṣa, the able and swift; Viśrāma, the place of rest; and Viśvadakṣiṇa, skillful in all things and most liberal.

**13.135.59**  He is Vistāra, the expanse in which all worlds abide; Sthāvarasthāṇu, the firm and unmoving ground; Pramāṇa, the measure and proof of all; Bīja avyaya, the imperishable seed; Artha, the goal of all desire; Anartha, who has no want of his own; Mahākośa, the great treasury; Mahābhoga, of great enjoyment; and Mahādhana, of great wealth.

**13.135.60**  He is Anirviṇṇa, the never-despondent; Sthaviṣṭha, the most massive; Bhū, the abode of being; Dharmayūpa, the sacrificial post of righteousness; Mahāmakha, the great sacrifice; Nakṣatranemi, the hub of the stars; Nakṣatrī, the lord of constellations; Kṣama, the all-capable; Kṣāma, who abides when all is dissolved; and Samīhana, who wills the good of all.

**13.135.61**  He is Yajña, the sacrifice; Ijya, the one to be worshipped; Mahejya, supremely worshipped; Kratu, the rite; Satra, the prolonged offering; Satāṃ gati, the refuge of the good; Sarvadarśī, the all-seeing; Vimuktātmā, the ever-liberated soul; Sarvajña, the omniscient; and Jñānam uttamam, the highest knowledge.

**13.135.62**  He is Suvrata, of holy vows; Sumukha, of fair countenance; Sūkṣma, the subtle; Sughoṣa, of auspicious sound; Sukhada, the giver of joy; Suhṛt, the true friend; Manohara, the captivator of the mind; Jitakrodha, conqueror of wrath; Vīrabāhu, of heroic arms; and Vidāraṇa, the render of the wicked.

**13.135.63**  He is Svāpana, who casts beings into the sleep of ignorance; Svavaśa, subject to none but himself; Vyāpī, the all-pervading; Naikātmā, of manifold selves; Naikakarmakṛt, the doer of countless deeds; Vatsara, the abode of all; Vatsala, the affectionate; Vatsī, the loving father; Ratnagarbha, in whose womb lie all jewels; and Dhaneśvara, lord of wealth.

**13.135.64**  He is Dharmagub, the protector of dharma; Dharmakṛt, the doer of righteousness; Dharmī, the upholder of dharma; Sat, the existent; Asat, the non-existent; Kṣara, the perishable; Akṣara, the imperishable; Avijñātā, who is beyond all knowing; Sahasrāṃśu, the thousand-rayed; Vidhātā, the ordainer; and Kṛtalakṣaṇa, who has fixed the marks of all.

**13.135.65**  He is Gabhastinemi, the hub at the center of the rays; Sattvastha, abiding in the heart of all beings; Siṃha, the lion; Bhūtamaheśvara, the great lord of beings; Ādideva, the primeval god; Mahādeva, the great god; Deveśa, lord of the gods; Devabhṛt, the upholder of the gods; and Guru, the teacher.

**13.135.66**  He is Uttara, who lifts beings out of the ocean of being; Gopati, lord of the earth and of cows; Goptā, the protector; Jñānagamya, to be reached by wisdom; Purātana, the ancient; Śarīrabhūtabhṛt, who upholds the elements of the body; Bhoktā, the enjoyer; Kapīndra, lord of monkeys as Rāma; and Bhūridakṣiṇa, of abundant sacrificial gifts.

**13.135.67**  He is Somapa, the drinker of soma; Amṛtapa, the drinker of nectar; Soma, the moon that nourishes the herbs; Purujit, conqueror of many; Purusattama, supreme among beings; Vinaya, who humbles the proud; Jaya, victory; Satyasaṃdha, true to his word; Dāśārha, worthy of all offerings; and Sātvatāṃ pati, lord of the Sātvatas.

**13.135.68**  He is Jīva, the living soul; Vinayitā, the bestower of discipline; Sākṣī, the witness; Mukunda, the giver of liberation; Amitavikrama, of measureless valor; Ambhonidhi, the treasure-house of waters; Anantātmā, of infinite being; Mahodadhiśaya, who reposes upon the great ocean; and Antaka, the maker of the end.

**13.135.69**  He is Aja, the unborn; Mahārha, supremely worthy of worship; Svābhāvya, established in his own nature; Jitāmitra, conqueror of foes; Pramodana, the giver of joy; Ānanda, bliss itself; Nandana, the delighter; Nanda, the abounding in joy; Satyadharmā, whose dharma is truth; and Trivikrama, who strode across the three worlds.

**13.135.70**  He is Maharṣi Kapilācārya, the great seer who taught as Kapila; Kṛtajña, knower of all that is wrought; Medinīpati, lord of the earth; Tripada, the three-stepped; Tridaśādhyakṣa, overseer of the thirty gods; Mahāśṛṅga, the great-horned who saved the Vedas; and Kṛtāntakṛt, the maker of all ends.

**13.135.71**  He is Mahāvarāha, the great boar; Govinda, the finder of the earth; Suṣeṇa, of goodly hosts; Kanakāṅgadī, adorned with golden armlets; Guhya, the secret one; Gabhīra, the profound; Gahana, the unfathomable; Gupta, the hidden; and Cakragadādhara, the bearer of discus and mace.

**13.135.72**  He is Vedhā, the creator; Svāṅga, who is his own instrument; Ajita, the unconquered; Kṛṣṇa, the dark and all-attracting; Dṛḍha, the firm; Saṃkarṣaṇa, who draws all beings into himself; Acyuta, the unfallen; Varuṇa, who gathers his rays at evening; Vāruṇa, son of Varuṇa as Vasiṣṭha; Vṛkṣa, the tree that stands unshaken; Puṣkarākṣa, the lotus-eyed; and Mahāmanas, of vast mind.

**13.135.73**  He is Bhagavān, the blessed lord of the six excellences; Bhagahā, who withdraws those powers at dissolution; Nandī, ever joyful; Vanamālī, wearer of the forest garland; Halāyudha, who wields the plow as Balarāma; Āditya, the son of Aditi; Jyotirāditya, the radiance within the orb of the sun; Sahiṣṇu, the all-enduring; and Gatisattama, the supreme refuge.

**13.135.74**  He is Sudhanvā, of the goodly bow; Khaṇḍaparaśu, who bore the battle-axe as Rāma Jāmadagnya; Dāruṇa, the merciless to the wicked; Draviṇaprada, the giver of riches; Divaḥspṛk, who touches the heavens; Sarvadṛk, the all-seeing; Vyāsa, the arranger of the Vedas; Vācaspati, lord of speech; and Ayonija, who is born of no womb.

**13.135.75**  He is Trisāmā, hymned by the three Sāmans; Sāmaga, the singer of the Sāman; Sāma, the chant itself; Nirvāṇa, supreme extinction in bliss; Bheṣaja, the medicine; Bhiṣak, the physician; Saṃnyāsakṛt, who ordained renunciation; Śama, tranquility; Śānta, the peaceful; Niṣṭhā, the final ground; Śānti, peace itself; and Parāyaṇa, the supreme goal.

**13.135.76**  He is Śubhāṅga, of beautiful form; Śāntida, the giver of peace; Sraṣṭā, the creator; Kumuda, who delights in the earth; Kuvaleśaya, who reposes upon the waters; Gohita, the well-doer of the earth and cattle; Gopati, lord of the earth; Goptā, the protector; Vṛṣabhākṣa, whose eyes rain down all desires; and Vṛṣapriya, the lover of righteousness.

**13.135.77**  He is Anivartī, who never turns back from righteousness; Nivṛttātmā, the soul withdrawn from the world; Saṃkṣeptā, who draws the vast worlds together; Kṣemakṛt, the bestower of welfare; Śiva, the auspicious; Śrīvatsavakṣas, who bears the Śrīvatsa mark upon his breast; Śrīvāsa, the dwelling-place of Śrī; Śrīpati, lord of Śrī; and Śrīmatāṃ vara, foremost of the glorious.

**13.135.78**  He is Śrīda, the giver of fortune; Śrīśa, lord of Śrī; Śrīnivāsa, the abode of Śrī; Śrīnidhi, the treasury of glory; Śrīvibhāvana, the dispenser of fortune to all; Śrīdhara, who bears Śrī upon his breast; Śrīkara, the maker of prosperity; Śreyas, the highest good; Śrīmān, the glorious; and Lokatrayāśraya, the refuge of the three worlds.

**13.135.79**  He is Svakṣa, of beautiful eyes; Svaṅga, of fair limbs; Śatānanda, of a hundred joys; Nandi, supreme bliss; Jyotirgaṇeśvara, lord of the host of luminaries; Vijitātmā, who has conquered the self; Vidheyātmā, ever at his own command; Satkīrti, of true renown; and Chinnasaṃśaya, in whom all doubt is severed.

**13.135.80**  He is Udīrṇa, who transcends all beings; Sarvataścakṣus, whose eyes are turned in every direction; Anīśa, over whom there is no lord; Śāśvata, the everlasting; Sthira, the steadfast; Bhūśaya, who reposes upon the earth and the waters; Bhūṣaṇa, the ornament of the worlds; Bhūti, pure existence and prosperity; Viśoka, the sorrowless; and Śokanāśana, the destroyer of grief.

**13.135.81**  He is Arciṣmān, the effulgent; Arcita, the worshipped; Kumbha, the vessel in which all abides; Viśuddhātmā, of utterly pure self; Viśodhana, the purifier; Aniruddha, the unobstructed; Apratiratha, who has no equal foe; Pradyumna, of surpassing wealth; and Amitavikrama, of measureless valor.

**13.135.82**  He is Kālaneminihā, slayer of the demon Kālanemi; Vīra, the hero; Śūra, the valiant; Śauri, born in the line of Śūra; Janeśvara, lord of men; Trilokātmā, the soul of the three worlds; Trilokeśa, lord of the three worlds; Keśava, of beautiful locks and lord of Brahmā and Śiva; Keśihā, slayer of the demon Keśin; and Hari, the remover of sin.

**13.135.83**  He is Kāmadeva, the god of love and the object of all desire; Kāmapāla, the guardian of desires fulfilled; Kāmī, in whom all wishes are complete; Kānta, the beautiful; Kṛtāgama, the author of the sacred scriptures; Anirdeśyavapus, of indefinable form; Viṣṇu, the all-pervading; Vīra, the hero; Ananta, the infinite; and Dhanaṃjaya, the winner of wealth.

**13.135.84**  He is Brahmaṇya, the well-wisher of Brahman and the brāhmaṇas; Brahmakṛt, the maker of sacred austerity; Brahmā, the creator; Brahmā, the absolute itself; Brahmavivardhana, who increases all that is holy; Brahmavid, the knower of Brahman; Brāhmaṇa, the proclaimer of the Veda; Brahmī, who possesses all sacred power; Brahmajña, the knower of Brahman; and Brāhmaṇapriya, dear to the brāhmaṇas.

**13.135.85**  He is Mahākrama, of mighty stride; Mahākarmā, of great deeds; Mahātejas, of great splendor; Mahoraga, the great serpent; Mahākratu, the great sacrifice; Mahāyajvā, the great performer of rites; Mahāyajña, the great offering; and Mahāhavis, the great oblation.

**13.135.86**  He is Stavya, the one to be praised; Stavapriya, who loves the hymns of praise; Stotra, the hymn itself; Stuti, the praise; Stotā, the praiser; Raṇapriya, who delights in battle; Pūrṇa, the all-complete; Pūrayitā, the fulfiller; Puṇya, the holy; Puṇyakīrti, of sacred renown; and Anāmaya, free from all affliction.

**13.135.87**  He is Manojava, swift as thought; Tīrthakara, the maker of sacred fords of knowledge; Vasuretas, whose essence is golden; Vasuprada, the giver of wealth; again Vasuprada, the bestower of riches; Vāsudeva, the indwelling and all-pervading; Vasu, the abode of all; Vasumanas, of generous mind; and Havis, the oblation.

**13.135.88**  He is Sadgati, the refuge of the good; Satkṛti, of righteous deeds; Sattā, pure existence; Sadbhūti, the abundance of being; Satparāyaṇa, the supreme goal of the virtuous; Śūrasena, of valiant armies; Yaduśreṣṭha, foremost of the Yadus; Sannivāsa, the abode of the good; and Suyāmuna, attended by the dwellers along the Yamunā.

**13.135.89**  He is Bhūtāvāsa, the dwelling-place of all beings; Vāsudeva, who veils the worlds with his māyā; Sarvāsunilaya, the resting-place of all life-breaths; Anala, the fire and the never-sufficient; Darpahā, destroyer of the pride of the wicked; Darpada, who grants just pride to the righteous; Dṛpta, the ever-content; Durdhara, the hard to hold; and Aparājita, the unvanquished.

**13.135.90**  He is Viśvamūrti, whose form is the universe; Mahāmūrti, of vast form; Dīptamūrti, of blazing form; Amūrtimān, the formless; Anekamūrti, of countless forms; Avyakta, the unmanifest; Śatamūrti, of a hundred forms; and Śatānana, the hundred-faced.

**13.135.91**  He is Eka, the one; Naika, the manifold; Sava, the sacrifice of soma; Ka, who is bliss; Kim, the one worthy to be inquired after; Yat, the self-existent; Tat, the That of which all is; Padam anuttamam, the supreme abode beyond which there is none; Lokabandhu, the kinsman of all the worlds; Lokanātha, lord of the worlds; Mādhava, lord of fortune; and Bhaktavatsala, tender toward his devotees.

**13.135.92**  He is Suvarṇavarṇa, of golden hue; Hemāṅga, of golden body; Varāṅga, of beautiful limbs; Candanāṅgadī, adorned with sandal-scented armlets; Vīrahā, slayer of heroes among the foe; Viṣama, who has no equal; Śūnya, the void devoid of all attributes; Ghṛtāśīs, whose blessings never fail; Acala, the immovable; and Cala, the ever-moving.

**13.135.93**  He is Amānī, free from all conceit; Mānada, who bestows honor and humbles the proud; Mānya, the venerable; Lokasvāmī, lord of the worlds; Trilokadhṛk, upholder of the three worlds; Sumedhā, of fine intelligence; Medhaja, born of sacrifice; Dhanya, the blessed; Satyamedhā, of unfailing wisdom; and Dharādhara, the bearer of the earth.

**13.135.94**  He is Tejovṛṣa, who showers down splendor; Dyutidhara, the bearer of brilliance; Sarvaśastrabhṛtāṃ vara, foremost of all who bear arms; Pragraha, the receiver of his devotees' offerings; Nigraha, who holds all in his grasp; Avyagra, the undistracted; Naikaśṛṅga, of manifold horns; and Gadāgraja, the elder brother of Gada, made manifest by the sacred syllable.

**13.135.95**  He is Caturmūrti, of fourfold form; Caturbāhu, the four-armed; Caturvyūha, of fourfold manifestation; Caturgati, the fourfold goal of beings; Caturātmā, of fourfold self; Caturbhāva, the source of the four orders of life; Caturvedavid, knower of the four Vedas; and Ekapāt, the single-footed who stands above all with the rest of his being.

**13.135.96**  He is Samāvarta, the skilled turner of the wheel of being; Nivṛttātmā, the soul withdrawn from the world; Durjaya, hard to conquer; Duratikrama, hard to transgress; Durlabha, hard to attain; Durgama, hard to approach; Durgā, the impassable; Durāvāsa, hard for the yogins to enshrine within; and Durārihā, slayer of dangerous foes.

**13.135.97**  He is Śubhāṅga, of auspicious form; Lokasāraṅga, who draws forth the essence of the worlds; Sutantu, of beautiful weave who spread out the universe; Tantuvardhana, who extends or withdraws that weave; Indrakarmā, whose deeds are like Indra's; Mahākarmā, of mighty deeds; Kṛtakarmā, whose work is accomplished; and Kṛtāgama, the author of the sacred lore.

**13.135.98**  He is Udbhava, the supreme source; Sundara, the beautiful; Sunda, of tender compassion; Ratnanābha, of jewel-like navel; Sulocana, of lovely eyes; Arka, the worshipful sun; Vājasana, the giver of food and sustenance; Śṛṅgī, the horned one who became the fish; Jayanta, the all-victorious; Sarvavid, the all-knowing; and Jayī, the ever-conquering.

**13.135.99**  He is Suvarṇabindu, of golden-hued limbs; Akṣobhya, the unshakable; Sarvavāgīśvareśvara, lord of all lords of speech; Mahāhrada, the great deep wherein the yogins find delight; Mahāgarta, the great chasm and ground of all; Mahābhūta, the great being beyond all elements; and Mahānidhi, the great treasure in which the worlds repose.

**13.135.100**  He is Kumuda, who gladdens the earth; Kuṃdara, who cleaves the earth as the boar; Kunda, fair as the jasmine; Parjanya, the rain-cloud that quenches all thirst; Pavana, the purifying wind; Anila, the breath that needs no prompting; Amṛtāṃśa, whose portion is nectar; Amṛtavapus, of immortal body; Sarvajña, the omniscient; and Sarvatomukha, whose faces are turned in every direction.

**13.135.101**  He is easily attained, of noble vows, the Perfected One, vanquisher of foes, scorcher of foes; the banyan, the fig, the holy aśvattha tree, the slayer of Cāṇūra of the Andhras.

**13.135.102**  Of a thousand rays, seven-tongued, seven-fuelled, borne by seven steeds; formless, sinless, inconceivable, maker of fear and destroyer of fear.

**13.135.103**  The atom and the vast, the slender and the gross, bearer of the qualities yet beyond all qualities, the great; unsupported yet self-supported, fair of face, ancient of lineage, increaser of lineage.

**13.135.104**  Bearer of the burden, the proclaimed one, the yogin, lord of yogins, granter of every desire; the resting-place, the toiler, the patient, the fair-winged, borne upon the wind.

**13.135.105**  Bearer of the bow, the science of archery, the rod of chastisement, the subduer, restraint itself; unconquered, all-enduring, the controller, discipline, the curber.

**13.135.106**  Endowed with goodness, of the nature of sattva, the True, devoted to truth and righteousness; the goal of intention, worthy of love, the worshipful, doer of what is dear, increaser of delight.

**13.135.107**  He whose path is the sky, the Light, of fair radiance, the eater of oblations, the all-pervading; the sun, the shining one, Sūrya, the impeller, whose eye is the sun.

**13.135.108**  The endless, eater of oblations, the enjoyer, giver of bliss, the manifold giver, the first-born; never wearied, ever forbearing, the wondrous foundation of the worlds.

**13.135.109**  The eternal, most ancient of the ancient, Kapila, the tawny one, the imperishable; giver of weal, maker of weal, weal itself, enjoyer of weal, bestower of weal as his largesse.

**13.135.110**  Free of fury, wearer of earrings, bearer of the discus, the valiant, of mighty command; beyond the reach of words, enduring all sound, the cool one, maker of the night.

**13.135.111**  The gentle, the graceful, the able, the dexterous, best among the forbearing; most learned, free of fear, the hearing and proclaiming of whom is holy.

**13.135.112**  The deliverer, destroyer of evil deeds, the holy, dispeller of evil dreams; slayer of heroes, the protector, the existent, the life, the all-abiding.

**13.135.113**  Of endless forms, of endless splendour, conqueror of wrath, remover of fear; foursquare, of profound nature, the intermediate quarters, the commander, the directions themselves.

**13.135.114**  The beginningless, the earth, the splendour of the firmament, the valiant, wearer of gleaming armlets; the begetter, origin of the birth of creatures, the terrible, of terrible prowess.

**13.135.115**  The abode of all support, the ordainer, whose laughter is the bursting of blossoms, the ever-wakeful; the upward-mover, treader of the path of the good, giver of breath, the sacred Oṃ, the pledge.

**13.135.116**  The measure, the resting-place of life-breath, maker of breath, the life of the breath; the Reality, knower of Reality, the one Self, who transcends birth, death, and old age.

**13.135.117**  Earth, mid-air, and heaven, the tree, the deliverer, the impeller, the great-grandsire; the sacrifice, lord of the sacrifice, the sacrificer, the limb of sacrifice, the vehicle of sacrifice.

**13.135.118**  Upholder of sacrifice, performer of sacrifice, the sacrificer, enjoyer of sacrifice, the means of sacrifice; bringer of sacrifice to its end, the mystery of sacrifice, the food, and the eater of food as well.

**13.135.119**  Self-originated, self-born, the digger-forth, the singer of the Sāman chants; the joy of Devakī, the creator, lord of the earth, destroyer of sin.

**13.135.120**  Bearer of the conch, wielder of the Nandaka sword, holder of the discus, armed with the Śārṅga bow, bearer of the mace; whose hand holds the chariot-wheel, the unshakable, armed with every weapon of war.

**13.135.121**  Thus has this thousand of the divine names of the praiseworthy and great-souled Keśava been wholly proclaimed.

**13.135.122**  The man who listens to this daily, and who also recites it, shall meet with nothing inauspicious, neither here nor in the world beyond.

**13.135.123**  A brāhmaṇa shall reach the end of the Veda, a kṣatriya shall become victorious, a vaiśya shall grow rich in wealth, and a śūdra shall attain happiness.

**13.135.124**  He who seeks righteousness shall gain righteousness, he who seeks wealth shall obtain wealth, he who desires shall win his desires, and he who longs for offspring shall obtain offspring.

**13.135.125**  The devoted man who, ever rising at dawn, purified and with his mind fixed upon Him, recites this thousand of the names of Vāsudeva—

**13.135.126**  —attains abundant fame and preeminence among his kinsmen; he gains unshaken fortune and the highest, unsurpassed welfare.

**13.135.127**  He meets with fear nowhere, and gains valour and lustre; he becomes free of disease, radiant, endowed with strength, beauty, and virtue.

**13.135.128**  One afflicted by disease is freed from disease, one bound is freed from bondage, the frightened is freed from fear, and one in distress is freed from his distress.

**13.135.129**  A man swiftly crosses over all hardships who, with this thousand of names, praises the Supreme Person daily and full of devotion.

**13.135.130**  The mortal who takes refuge in Vāsudeva, who is wholly devoted to Vāsudeva, his soul cleansed of every sin, attains to the eternal Brahman.

**13.135.131**  For the devotees of Vāsudeva there exists nothing inauspicious anywhere; nor does there arise in them any fear of birth, death, old age, or disease.

**13.135.132**  He who recites this hymn, endowed with faith and devotion, shall be joined with inner happiness, patience, fortune, steadfastness, memory, and renown.

**13.135.133**  Neither anger, nor envy, nor greed, nor any base intent arises in those of accumulated merit who are devoted to the Supreme Person.

**13.135.134**  The heaven with its moon, sun, and stars, the sky, the quarters, the earth, and the great ocean—all are upheld by the might of the great-souled Vāsudeva.

**13.135.135**  This whole world, with its gods, asuras, and gandharvas, with its yakṣas, serpents, and rākṣasas, with all that moves and moves not, abides under the sway of Kṛṣṇa.

**13.135.136**  The senses, the mind, the intellect, goodness, lustre, strength, and steadfastness—these they declare to have Vāsudeva for their essence, as too the field and the knower of the field.

**13.135.137**  Right conduct is reckoned the foremost of all the scriptures; righteousness springs from conduct, and the lord of righteousness is Acyuta, the Imperishable.

**13.135.138**  The seers, the ancestors, the gods, the great elements, the bodily constituents, and this whole world of the moving and the unmoving—all spring from Nārāyaṇa.

**13.135.139**  Yoga, knowledge, and Sāṃkhya, the sciences, the crafts, and ritual action, the Vedas, the treatises, and discernment—all this comes forth from Janārdana.

**13.135.140**  Viṣṇu is the one great Being, yet the beings are manifold and severally apart; pervading the three worlds, the Soul of all beings, the imperishable enjoyer of the universe, He enjoys them all.

**13.135.141**  This hymn of the Lord Viṣṇu, proclaimed by Vyāsa, let that man recite who wishes to attain welfare and happiness.

**13.135.142**  Those who worship the lotus-eyed Lord of the universe, the unborn god, the origin and dissolution of the world, never come to defeat.

**13.136.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: Who are to be honoured, who are to be saluted, how should one conduct oneself, and toward whom? What conduct, and toward what sort of men, O grandsire, brings no harm?

**13.136.2**  Bhīṣma said: Contempt of the brāhmaṇas would lay low even the gods; he who salutes the brāhmaṇas, O Yudhiṣṭhira, comes to no harm.

**13.136.3**  They are to be honoured, they are to be saluted; conduct yourself toward them as a son, for those wise ones uphold all these worlds.

**13.136.4**  The brāhmaṇas are the great ones of all the worlds, the bridges of righteousness, delighting in the renunciation of wealth and devoted to restraint of speech.

**13.136.5**  Delightful to all beings and their treasure-house, firm in their vows, the guides of the worlds, and the renowned masters of the scriptures.

**13.136.6**  Those whose wealth is ever their austerity and whose speech is their abundant strength, who are the source of all duties, knowers of righteousness, and seers of the subtle.

**13.136.7**  Lovers of righteousness, established in righteousness, bridges of righteousness by their good deeds, upon whom all creatures of the four kinds depend for their living.

**13.136.8**  They are the paths, the leaders of all, the eternal bearers of sacrifice, who ever carry the heavy yoke handed down from fathers and forefathers.

**13.136.9**  Who, like good oxen, do not sink beneath the yoke on rough ground, who set the ancestors, the gods, and guests foremost, and eat only after the offerings to gods and ancestors.

**13.136.10**  Who by that very eating save the worlds from great peril; they are the lamps of all the world, the very eye even of those who have eyes.

**13.136.11**  Treasuries of all crafts and lore, skilled, seers of the subtle, knowers of the courses of all beings, ponderers of the path of the inner Self.

**13.136.12**  Knowers of the beginning, the middle, and the end, their doubts cut away, discerners of the distinction between the high and the low, travellers to the supreme goal.

**13.136.13**  Liberated, their sins shaken off, beyond the pairs of opposites, free of possessions, worthy of honour and ever honoured by the great-souled knowers of wisdom.

**13.136.14**  The same toward sandal-paste and toward foul mire, the same in eating and in fasting; to whom fine silk and coarse hemp, linen, and skins are all alike.

**13.136.15**  They can abide without eating even for many days, and with senses controlled they wear down their bodies by the study of the sacred texts.

**13.136.16**  They could make a god of what is no god and a no-god of a god; when angered they could create other worlds and other world-guardians.

**13.136.17**  By whose curse, great-souled as they are, the ocean became undrinkable, and whose fire of wrath even to this day is not quenched in the Daṇḍaka forest.

**13.136.18**  They who are gods even of the gods, the cause of the cause, and the authority of authority itself—what wise man could overpower them?

**13.136.19**  Among whom both the old and the young, every one of them, deserves honour; yet according to the distinction in austerity and learning they honour one another.

**13.136.20**  Even an unlearned brāhmaṇa is a god, a worthy and greatly purifying vessel; but the learned brāhmaṇa is a god yet greater, like the brimming ocean.

**13.136.21**  Whether unlearned or learned, the brāhmaṇa is a great deity, just as fire, whether consecrated or unconsecrated, is a great deity.

**13.136.22**  For even in the cremation-ground the blazing fire is not defiled; and bearing the oblation in sacrifices it shines forth still more.

**13.136.23**  So too, even if a brāhmaṇa engages in all manner of unworthy deeds, he is in every way to be honoured; know him to be the highest deity.

**13.137.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: What reward, O lord of men, did you behold in the honouring of brāhmaṇas, and what outcome of deeds did you reckon, that you, O greatly wise one, worship them?

**13.137.2**  Bhīṣma said: On this point too they recount this ancient tale, the dialogue of the Wind-god and of Arjuna, O Bhārata.

**13.137.3**  There was a glorious lord, Kārtavīrya, bearer of a thousand arms, sovereign over all this world, the mighty one who ruled from Māhiṣmatī.

**13.137.4**  That Haihaya of true valour ruled the entire earth, rich with the ocean's gems, with its islands, girdled by the sea.

**13.137.5**  For a purpose he gave his own wealth to Dattātreya, setting foremost the duty of a kṣatriya, with humility and sacred learning.

**13.137.6**  And the son of Kṛtavīrya propitiated that sage, and the well-pleased twice-born one offered him three boons.

**13.137.7**  Pressed by him to choose boons, the king spoke these words: "May I become thousand-armed in the midst of an army, yet otherwise but two-armed at home."

**13.137.8**  "Let the soldiers behold my thousand arms in battle; by my prowess may I conquer the whole earth, O man of great vows, and having won it by righteousness, may I guard it untiringly."

**13.137.9**  "A fourth boon I ask of you, O best of the twice-born; deign to grant it for my favour, O blameless one: let the good men reproach me, should I, who lean upon them, act falsely."

**13.137.10**  Thus addressed, the twice-born one said to the king, "So be it," and thus came to pass for that king of blazing splendour those boons.

**13.137.11**  Then, mounting his chariot, radiant as fire and the sun, in the bewilderment of his strength he said: "Who indeed is equal to me in valour, in steadfastness, in fame and purity, in prowess, or in might?"

**13.137.12**  At the end of his speech, a bodiless voice spoke from the sky: "O fool, you do not understand that the brāhmaṇa is greater than the kṣatriya; only joined with the brāhmaṇa does the kṣatriya protect the people here."

**13.137.13**  Arjuna said: When pleased, I can bring beings into being; when angered, I likewise lead them to destruction. In deed, in thought, and in word there is no twice-born one greater than I.

**13.137.14**  The first claim sets the brāhmaṇa above, the second sets the kṣatriya above; both grounds have been stated by you, yet a distinction is seen here.

**13.137.15**  The brāhmaṇas lean upon the kṣatriya power; the kṣatriya power does not lean upon the brāhmaṇas. The brāhmaṇas, under the pretext of sacred lore, devour the kṣatriyas of the earth who give them shelter.

**13.137.16**  In the Kṣatriyas resides dharma — the protection of the people; and from the Kṣatriya comes the livelihood of the Brāhmaṇas. By what reckoning, then, is the Brāhmaṇa the greater?

**13.137.17**  Those Brāhmaṇas who deem themselves the foremost of all beings, yet live by begging and are puffed up with their own conceit — them I ever hold in subjection to my will.

**13.137.18**  For the truth has been spoken in heaven by this maiden, the Gāyatrī: I shall conquer all the unruly Brāhmaṇas, those clad in hides.

**13.137.19**  In the three worlds no one could cast me out from my realm — neither god nor man. Therefore am I superior to the twice-born.

**13.137.20**  This day I shall make the world, which holds the Brāhmaṇa supreme, a world in which the Kṣatriya is supreme; for no one in battle has the power to withstand my might.

**13.137.21**  Hearing Arjuna's words, the night-ranging spirit was struck with terror. Then Vāyu, abiding in the sky, addressed him.

**13.137.22**  Cast off this defiled disposition and bow before the Brāhmaṇas; for if you do them wrong, ruin will come upon your kingdom.

**13.137.23**  Else, O lord of the earth, the twice-born, mighty in power, will subdue you, or will drive you from your realm, your spirit broken.

**13.137.24**  The king said to him, 'Who are you?' Then the Wind-god replied to him: 'I am Vāyu, the messenger of the gods; I speak to you for your good.'

**13.137.25**  Arjuna said: Ah, what devoted attachment to the Brāhmaṇas you have shown this day! Tell me, then — to what created thing is the Brāhmaṇa like? Is he as the earth?

**13.137.26**  Or tell me, is the best of Brāhmaṇas in any way like the wind? Tell me — is he like the waters, or like the sun, or like the sky?

**13.138.1**  Vāyu said: Hear, O fool, some of the virtues of the high-souled Brāhmaṇas. By those very things you have named, O king, the Brāhmaṇa is shown to be the greater.

**13.138.2**  When the Earth, through rivalry with king Aṅga, forsook her own earthhood and went to ruin, the Brāhmaṇa Kaśyapa upheld her once again.

**13.138.3**  Imperishable are the Brāhmaṇas, O king, in heaven and on earth forever. Of old, Aṅgiras himself drank up the waters by his own fiery power.

**13.138.4**  Drinking them as though they were milk, the great ascetic was not sated; and then with a mighty flood he filled the whole earth again, O son of Pṛthā.

**13.138.5**  When he was wroth, I too forsook the world and departed, and for a long while took refuge in the agnihotra fire, in fear of Aṅgiras.

**13.138.6**  Even the lord Purandara was cursed by Gautama when he lusted after Ahalyā; yet for the sake of dharma he was not slain.

**13.138.7**  So too the ocean, O king, once full of sweet water, was cursed by the Brāhmaṇas and made into a sea of salt, O mighty one.

**13.138.8**  Fire — gold-hued, smokeless, its flame leaping upward in a single mass, the wise one — was cursed by the wrathful Aṅgiras and stripped of these very qualities.

**13.138.9**  Behold the Maruts ground to dust, who once laughed at the great ocean — cursed forever by the gold-bearing twice-born one.

**13.138.10**  You are not the equal of the twice-born; know them to be supreme, O ruler of men. The Lord himself, they say, duly does reverence to Brāhmaṇas while they are yet in the womb.

**13.138.11**  The great kingdom of the Daṇḍakas was destroyed by a Brāhmaṇa; the great Kṣatriya host of the Tālajaṅghas was destroyed by Aurva alone.

**13.138.12**  And by you a vast kingdom, strength, dharma, and learning — gifts most hard to win — were obtained through the grace of Dattātreya.

**13.138.13**  You ever worship Fire, O Arjuna — and what is Fire but a Brāhmaṇa? For he is the bearer of oblations for all the world. Do you not know him?

**13.138.14**  Or, knowing him to be the foremost of Brāhmaṇas, the protector of beings, the maker of the world of the living — why are you, knowing this, so bewildered?

**13.138.15**  So too is Brahmā, the Lord of creatures, the Unmanifest, the source and the dissolution of all, by whom this entire universe, moving and unmoving, was brought forth.

**13.138.16**  Some, the unlearned, hold that Brahmā was born from an egg, and that from the egg, when it split, came the mountains, the quarters, the waters, the earth, and the sky.

**13.138.17**  But it is not to be regarded thus — for how could he, the very greatest, be so born? Space itself is remembered as the egg, and from it the Grandsire came forth.

**13.138.18**  Tell me — on what could it have rested? At that time nothing whatever existed. He is named Ego (ahaṃkāra), the Lord in whom all radiance dwells.

**13.138.19**  There is no egg; there is only Brahmā, O king, the maker of the worlds. Thus addressed, the king then fell silent, and Vāyu spoke to him again.

**13.139.1**  Vāyu said: Long ago a king named Aṅga wished to give this earth as a sacrificial gift to the Brāhmaṇas; and at that, O king, the Earth fell into anxious thought.

**13.139.2**  'Having obtained me, the bearer of all beings — how does this best of kings desire to give me, the daughter of Brahmā, away to the twice-born?'

**13.139.3**  'Forsaking my earthhood, I shall go to the abode of Brahmā — let not this king keep his realm.' And so she departed.

**13.139.4**  Then Kaśyapa, seeing the Earth thus departing, at once entered into her, releasing his own self, his mind composed.

**13.139.5**  Held fast on every side, she came forth again endowed with grass and herbs; and the Earth, O king, became rich in dharma and free from fear.

**13.139.6**  Thus for thirty thousand divine years, O king, Kaśyapa of vast vows was the Earth, untiring.

**13.139.7**  Then, O great king, the Earth came and made obeisance to Kaśyapa, and so became Kāśyapī, the daughter of that high-souled one.

**13.139.8**  Such, O king, was that Brāhmaṇa Kaśyapa. Now name me, if you can, any Kṣatriya greater than Kaśyapa.

**13.139.9**  The king fell silent, and the Wind-god spoke again: Hear now, O king, of Utathya, born in the line of Aṅgiras.

**13.139.10**  Bhadrā, the daughter of Soma, was deemed peerless in beauty; and Soma saw in Utathya a husband worthy of her.

**13.139.11**  And that illustrious, glorious lady practised fierce austerities, and for that end she chose the great-souled Utathya.

**13.139.12**  Then Soma summoned Utathya and gave the glorious maiden to him to wife; and he, the giver of bounteous gifts, received her duly.

**13.139.13**  But the glorious Varuṇa had desired her even before; and coming to the forest-dwelling, he carried her off at the Yamunā.

**13.139.14**  The lord of waters, having seized her, bore her away toward his own city — a city of utmost wonder, with six hundred thousand lakes.

**13.139.15**  There was no lovelier place than that finest of cities, adorned with palaces, with apsarases, and with divine delights; and there the god, the lord of waters, took his pleasure with her, O king.

**13.139.16**  Then the violation of his wife was made known to Utathya.

**13.139.17**  Hearing all this from Nārada, Utathya said to Nārada: 'Go and speak harsh words to Varuṇa — by my command, release my wife! Why have you carried her off?'

**13.139.18**  'You are a guardian of the worlds, not a despoiler of the world. My wife was given me by Soma, and this day you have stolen her away.'

**13.139.19**  Thus addressed by Nārada in Utathya's words — 'Release Utathya's wife!' — Varuṇa replied: 'She is my own dear wife; I cannot bring myself to give her up.'

**13.139.20**  So answered by Varuṇa, Nārada came back to the sage Utathya and spoke to him, his heart none too glad.

**13.139.21**  'Seizing me by the throat, Varuṇa has flung me out, O great sage. He will not give you your wife — do what you must.'

**13.139.22**  Hearing Nārada's words, the descendant of Aṅgiras blazed up in wrath; and that mighty ascetic, holding them fast, drank up the waters by his fiery power.

**13.139.23**  And as all the waters were being drunk up, the lord of the waters, though pressed by his friends, would still not release her then.

**13.139.24**  Then Utathya, best of Brāhmaṇas, wrathfully commanded the Earth: 'Show me dry ground, O gentle one, where now there are six hundred thousand lakes!'

**13.139.25**  Then that place became a barren waste, and the sea drew back; and from that region the best of the twice-born addressed the river as well.

**13.139.26**  'Vanish from sight, O timid Sarasvatī, and flow toward the desert; let this region, forsaken by you, O fair one, become unholy.'

**13.139.27**  When that region was thus laid waste, the lord of waters, taking up Bhadrā, came seeking refuge and gave the wife back to the son of Aṅgiras.

**13.139.28**  Receiving his wife again, Utathya was glad at heart, and he freed the world — and Varuṇa with it — from its distress, O Haihaya.

**13.139.29**  Then, having recovered his wife, Utathya — knower of dharma, of mighty splendor — spoke to Varuṇa; hear what he said, O ruler of men.

**13.139.30**  'By my austerity I have won her back, O lord of waters, while you cried out in vain.' So saying, he took her up and went to his own dwelling.

**13.139.31**  Such, O king, was that Utathya, that bull among Brāhmaṇas. So I declare — now name me, if you can, any Kṣatriya greater than Utathya.

**13.140.1**  Bhīṣma said: Thus addressed, the king fell silent, and Vāyu then spoke: Hear, O king, the greatness of the Brāhmaṇa Agastya.

**13.140.2**  The gods, vanquished by the Asuras, were robbed of their spirit; all their sacrifices were carried off, and likewise the svadhā offering to the ancestors.

**13.140.3**  And the rites and sacrifices of men were seized by the Dānavas, O bull of the Haihayas. Then the gods, fallen from their sovereignty, wandered the earth — so says the sacred tradition.

**13.140.4**  Then once, O king, they beheld Agastya of vast vows, blazing with the splendor of the sun, endowed with fiery glory.

**13.140.5**  And the gods, having saluted him and seen him girt with glory, spoke this word to the high-souled one at the fitting time, O ruler of men.

**13.140.6**  'We have been broken in battle by the Dānavas and cast down from our sovereignty. Deliver us, therefore, from this dire fear, O foremost of sages!'

**13.140.7**  Thus addressed by the gods, Agastya then grew wroth, and the resplendent one blazed up like the fire of Time at the world's dissolution.

**13.140.8**  By that web of blazing rays the Dānavas were then consumed, and from the sky, O great king, they fell in their thousands.

**13.140.9**  Burning in the fiery power of Agastya, those Daityas forsook both worlds and fled to the southern quarter.

**13.140.10**  But Bali, having gone into the earth, was performing the horse-sacrifice; and the other great Asuras who were at ease and dwelt within the earth were not consumed.

**13.140.11**  Then the worlds were regained by the gods, and that turmoil was stilled. Thereupon the gods said to him: 'Slay also the Asuras who dwell within the earth.'

**13.140.12**  So addressed, he answered the gods: 'I cannot burn those who have gone into the earth, for were I to burn them, my austerity would be spent,' O son of Pṛthā.

**13.140.13**  Thus, O king, were the Dānavas burnt by the lord Agastya through his own fiery power, by him whose soul was perfected through austerity.

**13.140.14**  Such, O sinless one, was Agastya, of whom I have told you. So I declare — now name me, if you can, any Kṣatriya greater than Agastya.

**13.140.15**  Thus addressed, the king fell silent, and Vāyu then spoke: Hear, O king, of the chief deed of the glorious Vasiṣṭha.

**13.140.16**  The Ādityas were holding a sacrificial session near the Mānasa lake, having approached Vasiṣṭha in their minds and learned that the place lay within his domain.

**13.140.17**  But seeing them sacrificing, intent and worn thin by their consecration, certain Dānavas called the Khalins, huge as mountains, desired to slay them.

**13.140.18**  Not far from there was a lake granted as a boon by Brahmā; and those Dānavas, slain again and again, would yet live, plunging into it and rising up.

**13.140.19**  Seizing dreadful mountains, iron clubs, and trees, churning up the waters, they rose to a height of a hundred yojanas.

**13.140.20**  Ten thousand of them rushed upon the gods; and the gods, sorely afflicted by them, went for refuge to Vāsava.

**13.140.21**  And Śakra too, harried by them, went for refuge to Vasiṣṭha; then the blessed sage Vasiṣṭha granted them safety.

**13.140.22**  Perceiving them thus in distress, the sage, devoted to compassion, effortlessly burned up all the Khalins with his own radiant power.

**13.140.23**  And that great ascetic led the river Gaṅgā, which had set out toward Kailāsa, to that celestial lake, and by her the lake was cleft open.

**13.140.24**  The lake cleft by that river became the Sarayū; and the region where the Khalins were slain came to be known as Khalina.

**13.140.25**  Thus were the dwellers of heaven, with Indra, protected by Vasiṣṭha; and the great-souled one slew the Daityas who had been granted a boon by Brahmā.

**13.140.26**  This deed of Vasiṣṭha I have recounted to you, O sinless one. I say to you—or do you name to me a Kṣatriya superior to Vasiṣṭha.

**13.141.1**  Bhīṣma said: Thus addressed, Arjuna fell silent, and the Wind said to him: Hear from me, O best of the Haihayas, the deed of the exceedingly great-souled Atri.

**13.141.2**  In dread darkness the gods and the Dānavas fought together; there Svarbhānu pierced both Soma and the Sun with his shafts.

**13.141.3**  Then, seized by darkness, the gods were being slain by the Dānavas, O tiger among kings, together with the mighty ones at that time.

**13.141.4**  Slaughtered by the Asuras, their vital force ebbing away, the dwellers of heaven beheld the brahmin Atri practising austerities in the great forest.

**13.141.5**  Then the gods said to him, whose anger was stilled and whose senses were mastered: These two, the Moon and the Sun, have been pierced by the arrows of the Asuras.

**13.141.6**  And we too are being slain by our foes in the enveloping darkness, and we find no peace; deliver us from our fear, O lord.

**13.141.7**  "How shall I protect you?" he asked. They said: "Become the Moon, and be for us the Sun that dispels darkness and the slayer of our robber-foes."

**13.141.8**  Thus addressed, Atri then became the Moon that drives away darkness, and he beheld the gentle aspect and the reappearing of the Sun's light.

**13.141.9**  Seeing the Moon dim in lustre and likewise the Sun, O king, Atri by his own austerity made light in the battle.

**13.141.10**  He made the world free of darkness and ablaze with light, and by his own radiant power he vanquished the hosts of the gods' enemies.

**13.141.11**  Seeing those great Asuras burning under Atri's power, the gods too, protected by Atri, slew them in turn by their valour.

**13.141.12**  The Sun was made to shine forth, the gods were rescued, and the Asuras slain; and the office of the Moon was assumed by Atri of supreme radiance.

**13.141.13**  By the peerless sage, murmuring his prayers, clad in deerskin, living on fruit—behold, O royal sage, the deed done by Atri.

**13.141.14**  The deed of that exceedingly great-souled Atri too has been told you in full. I say to you—or do you name a Kṣatriya superior to Atri.

**13.141.15**  Thus addressed, Arjuna fell silent, and the Wind said to him: Hear, O king, the great deed of the great-souled Cyavana.

**13.141.16**  Having made a promise to the Aśvins, Cyavana said to the Chastiser of Pāka, in company with the gods: "Make the two Aśvins drinkers of Soma."

**13.141.17**  Indra said: These two, excluded by us, how should they become drinkers of Soma? They are not reckoned the equals of the gods; therefore speak not thus to us.

**13.141.18**  We do not wish to drink Soma together with the Aśvins, O great in vows. Let others drink at will; I cannot bring myself to drink here with them.

**13.141.19**  Cyavana said: If you will not do as I have bidden, O slayer of Bala, then, overpowered by me, you shall this very moment drink Soma at the sacrifice.

**13.141.20**  Then the rite was begun at once for the benefit of the Aśvins; and thereupon the gods were overpowered by Cyavana through his sacred spells.

**13.141.21**  But when Indra saw that rite begun, faint with wrath, lifting up a vast mountain, the lord rushed upon Cyavana, his eyes troubled with fury, the thunderbolt also in hand.

**13.141.22**  Seeing him swooping down, Cyavana, endowed with the power of austerity, sprinkled him with water and paralysed him, thunderbolt, mountain, and all.

**13.141.23**  Then the great sage created for Indra a most terrible foe, Mada, born of spells and oblations, his maw gaping wide.

**13.141.24**  His thousand teeth were a hundred yojanas long, his fangs, most fearsome, two hundred yojanas; one jaw of his rested upon the earth and one touched the heavens.

**13.141.25**  All the gods, with Vāsava, stood at the root of his tongue, fallen into his mouth as fish into the maw of a great whale in the vast ocean.

**13.141.26**  Then the gods, gone into the mouth of Mada, took counsel together and said to Śakra: "Bow down to this twice-born one, and freed of our distress let us drink Soma together with the Aśvins."

**13.141.27**  Then Śakra, bowing low, did as Cyavana wished, and Cyavana made the two Aśvins drinkers of Soma.

**13.141.28**  Then the mighty sage withdrew his rite and distributed Mada among dice, hunting, drink, and women.

**13.141.29**  By these vices a man comes to ruin, O king—of this there is no doubt; therefore a man should ever keep them far from himself.

**13.141.30**  This deed of Cyavana too has been proclaimed to you, O king. I say to you—or do you name a Kṣatriya superior to Cyavana.

**13.142.1**  Bhīṣma said: Arjuna remained silent, and the Wind spoke again: Hear from me, O lord of men, a foremost deed among the brahmins.

**13.142.2**  When the dwellers of heaven, with Indra, had fallen into the mouth of Mada, then their earth was here seized away by Cyavana.

**13.142.3**  Deeming both worlds taken from them, the gods grew sorrowful, and afflicted with grief they went for refuge to the great-souled Brahmā.

**13.142.4**  The gods said: O you whom the worlds revere, from us who were cast into the mouth of Mada the earth has been seized by Cyavana, and heaven too by the Kapas, O lord.

**13.142.5**  Brahmā said: Go quickly for refuge to the brahmins, O dwellers of heaven with Indra; by winning their grace you shall regain both worlds as before.

**13.142.6**  They went for refuge to the brahmins, who asked: "Whom shall we conquer?" Thus addressed, they said to the twice-born: "Conquer here the Kapas"—for, O son of Pṛthā, the brahmins said, "We shall be the conquerors of those who dwell upon the earth."

**13.142.7**  Then a rite for the destruction of the Kapas was begun by the brahmins; hearing of it, the Kapas sent Dhanin as their envoy to the brahmins.

**13.142.8**  And Dhanin said to those brahmins, as the Kapas had bidden: "All the Kapas are the equals of yourselves; what then is afoot here?

**13.142.9**  All are knowers of the Veda and wise; all are performers of sacrifices; all are vowed to truth; all are the equals of the great sages.

**13.142.10**  Prosperity delights in them and they uphold prosperity; they do not approach wives in vain, nor do they eat flesh in vain.

**13.142.11**  They make oblation to the blazing fire and abide by the word of their elders; all are self-controlled and share their portion with children.

**13.142.12**  They travel by approaching with carts, they do not consort with a woman in her courses, they do not eat while others remain unfed, and by day they do not sleep.

**13.142.13**  How then will you conquer the Kapas, endowed with these and many other virtues? Turn back; for those who desist, all shall be well."

**13.142.14**  The brahmins said: We shall conquer the Kapas; they who are the gods, those are reckoned to be we ourselves. Therefore the Kapas are to be slain by us; go, Dhanin, the way you came.

**13.142.15**  Dhanin went and told the Kapas: "The brahmins mean you no kindness." Then, taking up their weapons, all the Kapas charged upon the brahmins.

**13.142.16**  Seeing the Kapas with their banners raised high, all the twice-born loosed blazing fires that destroyed the lives of the Kapas.

**13.142.17**  The eternal fire-gods, created by Brahmā, eaters of oblations, having devoured the Kapas, shone like clouds in the sky, O lord of men, and praised the twice-born and the illustrious Brahmā.

**13.142.18**  Then the radiance and might of those gods waxed great, and they attained immortality, honoured throughout the three worlds.

**13.142.19**  To the Wind who had spoken thus Arjuna replied, having paid him honour; hear, O mighty-armed lord of men, what he said.

**13.142.20**  I live always and in every way for the sake of the brahmins, O lord; to Brahman and to the brahmins I bow down perpetually.

**13.142.21**  And by the grace of Dattātreya this glory was won by me, and supreme renown in the world, and great dharma practised.

**13.142.22**  Ah, O Wind, the deeds of the brahmins, just as they truly are, told by you in full, have been heard by me with diligent care.

**13.142.23**  The Wind said: Protect the brahmins by the law of the Kṣatriya, and protect your senses; a dread peril to you shall come from the Bhṛgus, but that shall arise in due time.

**13.143.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: You ever honour the brahmins of firm vows, O king; but seeing what fruit of their deeds do you honour them, O lord of men?

**13.143.2**  Or what reward in the worship of brahmins have you seen, O great in vows, that you honour them, O mighty-armed one? Tell me all this.

**13.143.3**  Bhīṣma said: This Keśava of great wisdom will declare it all to you—the reward in the worship of brahmins, he of great vows who has himself seen its fruit.

**13.143.4**  My strength, my hearing, my speech, my mind, my eyes, and my knowledge are no longer clear in me this day; the laying down of my body is, I think, not far off, and yet the Sun does not pass too swiftly today.

**13.143.5**  The great duties that are told in ancient lore, of brahmins, of Kṣatriyas, and of Vaiśyas, and the ancient rule of governance which men observe—the rest learn from Kṛṣṇa, O son of Pṛthā.

**13.143.6**  For I know this Kṛṣṇa in truth—who he is and what his ancient might is; Keśava of immeasurable spirit, O lord of the Kurus, he it is who will declare dharma where doubts arise.

**13.143.7**  Kṛṣṇa created the earth, the sky, and the heavens; this is the ancient Boar of dreadful strength. From him came the lower region, the firmament, and heaven, the four quarters and the four intermediate quarters; this creation too was brought forth from him—he it was who fashioned this ancient universe.

**13.143.8**  From his navel sprang the lotus, wherein arose, of himself, the one of boundless power, by whom that dread darkness was cleft, O son of Pṛthā, the darkness that abides menacing over the ocean.

**13.143.9**  In the Kṛta age dharma was entire; in the Tretā age knowledge took its course; strength prevailed in the Dvāpara, O son of Pṛthā—Kṛṣṇa; and in the Kali age unrighteousness came upon the earth.

**13.143.10**  He, the primeval god, slew the Daityas; he, the primeval god, became sovereign; he is the nourisher of beings, who has been and shall be; and he is the protector of all this universe.

**13.143.11**  When the dharma of the gods grows faint, then Kṛṣṇa is born among men; and he, of disciplined spirit, abiding in dharma, passes to the higher worlds and the lower.

**13.143.12**  Forsaking what is to be forsaken, for the slaying of the Asuras, he is the cause of what should and should not be done, O son of Pṛthā; the god is what has been done, what shall be done, and what is being done; know him too to be again and again Soma and Śakra.

**13.143.13**  He is the maker of all, and he is the all-formed; he is the upholder of all, the creator of all, and the conqueror of all; he is the bearer of the trident, the bearer of blood, the terrible one; him, known by his deeds, they praise.

**13.143.14**  Him the Gandharvas and the Apsarases attend continually, and hundreds of the wise gods; the Rākṣasas too bear him about; he alone is the increase of wealth and the seeker of conquest.

**13.143.15**  Him the reciters praise at the sacrifice, and the singers of the Sāman praise him in the Rathantara; the brahmins praise him with the spells of Brahman, and for him the Adhvaryus prepare the oblation.

**13.143.16**  Having entered the ancient cave of Brahman, he beheld at the dawn of the Bhārata age the great sacrificial session of the earth; and he, of foremost deeds, lifted up the earth, having confounded the Daityas, the serpents, and the Dānavas.

**13.143.17**  They declare his many foods; him alone they declare to be the conveyance in battle; the firmament, the earth, and heaven—all stands in the power of the eternal one.

**13.143.18**  He, whose seed was held in the pot, created in ancient time that wherein, they say, was born the sage Vasiṣṭha; he is Mātariśvan, the all-pervading, swift as a steed; he is the radiant Sun, the primeval god.

**13.143.19**  By him all the Asuras were vanquished; by his strides the three worlds here were won; the worlds of the gods, of men, and of the fathers—him alone the knowers of sacrifice call the spreading of the sacrificial fires.

**13.143.20**  He it is who rises, apportioning time; his are the two courses, the northern and the southern; his are the rays that move upward, sideways, and downward, scorching the earth.

**13.143.21**  The Brāhmaṇas learned in the Veda delight in him, and the sun, drawing its radiance from him, shines forth. Month after month he, the performer of sacrifice, ordains the rite, and those versed in the Veda chant of him at the sacrifice.

**13.143.22**  Yoked to a single steed, he drives this wheel of three naves, drawn by seven horses, he of the three abodes. Of mighty splendor, all-pervading, conqueror of all, Kṛṣṇa alone upholds the worlds. Eating and yet not eating, steadfast as ever—know Kṛṣṇa, O Pārtha, to be forever the Maker; come to him.

**13.143.23**  Once that great-souled, all-pervading lord, entering the thicket of the Khāṇḍava as smoke-bannered fire, was sated; vanquishing the Rākṣasas and serpents, he who goes everywhere offered all things into the flame.

**13.143.24**  He himself, as the white horse, bestowed the steed; he himself fashioned all the horses. His chariot has three frames and three wheels, its top is threefold, and its body four-square.

**13.143.25**  He fashioned the sky with its five hubs; he formed the earth, the heaven, and the firmament; thus he created the lovely mountains—Hṛṣīkeśa, blazing with the boundless splendor of fire.

**13.143.26**  Leaping over the rivers and seeking to slay, he flung back the very thunderbolt that struck at him. He, as great Indra, is praised at the mighty sacrifice; the Brāhmaṇas alone extol him with thousands of ancient hymns.

**13.143.27**  By none other than him, O king, could the mighty Durvāsas be lodged in one's house; and him alone they call the one ancient sage. The maker of all, he ordains the modes of his own being.

**13.143.28**  He, the supreme deity, who reveals the Vedas and who upholds the ancient ordinances—whatever fruit there is in desire, in the Veda, and in worldly life, know all this to reside in Viṣvaksena.

**13.143.29**  The shining lights throughout all the world, the three worlds and the three world-guardians, the three sacred fires and the three sacred utterances—all the gods are none other than the son of Devakī.

**13.143.30**  He is the year, the season, the fortnight; he is day and night, the kalā and the kāṣṭhā; the moments, the muhūrtas, the instants and the seconds—know all this to reside in Viṣvaksena.

**13.143.31**  Moon and sun, the planets, lunar mansions, and stars, all the new-moon and full-moon days, the conjunctions of the constellations and the seasons, O Pārtha—all this is sprung forth from Viṣvaksena.

**13.143.32**  The Rudras, the Ādityas, the Vasus, and the two Aśvins, the Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, and the six hosts of the Maruts, Prajāpati and Aditi the mother of the gods—all these, and the seven seers too, are from Kṛṣṇa.

**13.143.33**  Becoming the wind, he sweeps through the universe; becoming fire, he of every form consumes it; becoming the waters, he submerges all; becoming Brahmā, he creates the assembled hosts of the world.

**13.143.34**  What is to be known and the Vedas that he reveals, the ordinance and the things that it ordains—in dharma, in the Veda, and in might, all that moves and is unmoving—know it all to be Keśava.

**13.143.35**  That supreme one, become very light, was there before all, illumining with his radiance, he of universal form. Self-born, the source of himself, having created the waters, he of old made this entire universe.

**13.143.36**  The seasons, the portents, the manifold marvels, the clouds, the lightning, and all the rainbow—every moving and unmoving thing—are from Kṛṣṇa; know this Viṣṇu, called the All.

**13.143.37**  They call him Vāsudeva, the abode of all, devoid of qualities; Saṃkarṣaṇa, who has become the living soul; then Pradyumna, and fourth Aniruddha—and the great-souled, self-born one commands them all.

**13.143.38**  Impelling fivefold this universe peopled with the five kinds of beings, desiring to create, he then made earth and wind, ether, light, and the waters too, O Pārtha.

**13.143.39**  Having thus fashioned this world of four kinds, both the unmoving and the moving, he then established the earth with its five seeds, that heaven might pour abundant waters upon her. By him, O king, this universe was made, and he, the source of himself, gives it life by himself alone.

**13.143.40**  Then the lord of beings, ever desiring to create the gods, the Asuras, and men, the worlds, the seers, the ancestors, and the creatures—in short, the manifold worlds of living things, all of them.

**13.143.41**  The good and the evil, the unmoving and the moving—know all this to be from Viṣvaksena; what exists now and what shall come to be here—know all this to be Keśava.

**13.143.42**  And death itself for living beings at their final hour is the eternal Kṛṣṇa made manifest, the bearer of dharma; and whatever being here we do not know at all—know all this to be from Viṣvaksena.

**13.143.43**  Whatever is esteemed in the worlds, and whatever is meritorious, whatever is good and evil—all that is the inconceivable Keśava, and whatever stands opposed to this proceeds from him as well.

**13.143.44**  Such is this Keśava, the self-existent, Nārāyaṇa, supreme and imperishable; he is the middle of this world both moving and still, and the origin and the dissolution of all beings.

**13.144.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: Tell me the fruit of honoring the Brāhmaṇas, O Madhusūdana; you are the knower of this matter, for the grandsire knows you well.

**13.144.2**  Vāsudeva said: Listen attentively, O king, bull of the Bhāratas, as I tell truly of the virtues of the twice-born, O best of the Kurus.

**13.144.3**  Pradyumna, vexed by certain Brāhmaṇas, once asked me: What fruit is there, O Madhusūdana, in honoring the Brāhmaṇas, for one who is himself a lord, both here and in the world beyond?

**13.144.4**  By ever honoring the twice-born, what is the fruit therein, O giver of honor? Tell me all this, father, for great is my doubt in this matter.

**13.144.5**  Thus addressed by Pradyumna with these words, I then made answer, O great king; hear now, with mind composed, what I said.

**13.144.6**  Learn from me, O son of Rukmiṇī, the fruit of honoring the Brāhmaṇas; for these are kings among the soma-drinkers, lords over joy and sorrow.

**13.144.7**  In this world, O son of Rukmiṇī, and likewise in the world beyond, my child, all happiness has the Brāhmaṇa at its head—of this I have no doubt.

**13.144.8**  Valor has the Brāhmaṇa at its head, and so do long life, renown, glory, and strength; the worlds and the lords of the worlds—all have the Brāhmaṇa first among them.

**13.144.9**  How then should I fail to honor them, saying, 'I am a lord,' my child? Let no anger arise in you, O mighty-armed one, against the twice-born.

**13.144.10**  For the Brāhmaṇa is a mighty being in this world and the next; in their wrath, those who see directly could reduce this whole world to ashes.

**13.144.11**  They could create other worlds as well, and lords of the worlds besides; how then, knowing this well, should I not conduct myself rightly toward those of mighty splendor?

**13.144.12**  There dwelt in my house, my son, a Brāhmaṇa tawny as a lion, clad in bark, bearing a bilva staff, with long beard and nails and the rest, taller in stature on earth than even the tallest of men.

**13.144.13**  He would roam through the worlds, both the divine and the human, singing these verses in the courtyards and in the assemblies.

**13.144.14**  'Who would lodge Durvāsas, the honored Brāhmaṇa, in his house? And who, hearing my reproaches, would yet grant me shelter? Whoever should lodge me—let him not provoke me to anger here.'

**13.144.15**  No one would receive him; so it was I who gave him lodging.

**13.144.16**  At one time he would eat food enough for many thousands; at another he would eat but a little, and would not return again to the house.

**13.144.17**  Without cause he would laugh aloud, and without cause he would weep; nor was there then upon the earth any equal to him in years.

**13.144.18**  Going into our dwelling, he burned the couches and the coverings and the bedecked maidens, and then departed of his own accord.

**13.144.19**  Then again that sage of stern vows said to me in haste: 'Kṛṣṇa, I wish to eat milk-rice porridge.'

**13.144.20**  But I, ever reading his mind, had already directed the household: 'Let all manner of food and drink and viands, high and low, be kept ready and well prepared.'

**13.144.21**  Then I presented to him the porridge while it was still steaming hot; and having eaten it, he straightway spoke these words: 'Quickly, smear your limbs with this porridge.'

**13.144.22**  And without a moment's hesitation I did just so, smearing my limbs and my head with the leavings of his meal.

**13.144.23**  Then he saw nearby your mother of lovely face, and smiling, he smeared her too with the porridge.

**13.144.24**  Her limbs now anointed with the porridge, the sage swiftly yoked her to a chariot, and mounting that car he drove forth from my house.

**13.144.25**  Fire-colored and blazing, that wise Brāhmaṇa, as though she were a draft-beast yoked to the car, goaded the young Rukmiṇī with his whip before my very eyes.

**13.144.26**  Yet not the slightest grief born of jealousy arose in me then; and so he passed out along the great royal highway.

**13.144.27**  Seeing this great marvel, the Dāśārhas were filled with wrath, and some spoke among themselves, conferring with one another there.

**13.144.28**  'Brāhmaṇas alone should be born, and no other caste at all; for what other man here could mount this chariot and yet live?'

**13.144.29**  'Sharp is the venom of the fanged serpent, but sharper still is this venom; for one burned by the serpent-venom of a Brāhmaṇa there is no physician whatsoever.'

**13.144.30**  As that unassailable one went on his way, Rukmiṇī stumbled on the path; the glorious sage brooked it not, and at once urged her sharply on.

**13.144.31**  Then, exceedingly enraged, that Brāhmaṇa leapt down from the chariot and ran off on foot by an untrodden path, facing southward.

**13.144.32**  I ran after that best of the twice-born as he sped along the trackless way, still smeared with the porridge, crying, 'Be gracious, O blessed one!'

**13.144.33**  Then the resplendent Brāhmaṇa, looking upon me, said: 'You have conquered anger, Kṛṣṇa, by your very nature, O mighty-armed one.'

**13.144.34**  'In no respect have I seen a fault in you, O man of good vows; I am pleased with you, Govinda—choose the boons you desire. And see, my son, the due reward of my being well pleased.'

**13.144.35**  'As long as men shall feel love toward food, so long shall their love toward you be even as toward food.'

**13.144.36**  'And as long as holy renown of you shall endure in the worlds, so long shall you hold pre-eminence in the three worlds; you shall be dearly beloved of all the world, O Janārdana.'

**13.144.37**  'Whatever of yours was broken and burned and in any way destroyed, all that you shall behold restored even as before, or finer still, O Janārdana.'

**13.144.38**  'As long as this is smeared upon your limbs, O Madhusūdana, there is no fear of death for you, O Acyuta, for as long as you wish.'

**13.144.39**  'But the soles of your feet you did not anoint—why not, my child, today?' For this did not please me, he said to me, well pleased; and being thus addressed, I beheld my own body endowed with splendor.

**13.144.40**  And well pleased he said to Rukmiṇī: 'You shall attain the foremost glory among all women, and renown unsurpassed in the world, O lovely one.'

**13.144.41**  'Neither age nor disease nor pallor shall touch you, O fair-faced one; fragrant with holiness, you shall do honor to Kṛṣṇa.'

**13.144.42**  'Of the sixteen thousand wives of Keśava you shall be the highest, and you shall share the same world with Keśava.'

**13.144.43**  Having spoken thus to your mother, Durvāsas of mighty splendor, blazing like fire, then setting forth, said to me once more:

**13.144.44**  'Let just this be your disposition toward the Brāhmaṇas, O Keśava.' And so saying, my son, he then and there vanished from sight.

**13.144.45**  When he had vanished, I laid upon myself a silent vow: that whatever a Brāhmaṇa might bid me, all of it I would do, O lord.

**13.144.46**  Having undertaken this vow together with your mother, my child, then, with heart exceedingly glad, I entered the house once more.

**13.144.47**  And the moment I entered the house, I saw it all made new—whatever had been broken and whatever had been burned by that Brāhmaṇa, my child.

**13.144.48**  Then I was filled with wonder, seeing it all renewed and whole, and in my mind, O son of Rukmiṇī, I rendered homage to that Brāhmaṇa.

**13.144.49**  Thus, O bull of the Bhāratas, when the son of Rukmiṇī inquired, I then recounted in full the greatness of that foremost of the twice-born.

**13.144.50**  So you too, O son of Kuntī, O lord, ever honor the highly blessed Brāhmaṇas always, with words and with gifts.

**13.144.51**  Thus did I obtain the reward born of the grace of the Brāhmaṇas; and what this Bhīṣma has told you is the truth, O bull of the Bhāratas.

**13.145.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: That knowledge which you then gained, O Madhusūdana, by the grace of Durvāsas—this you ought to expound to me.

**13.145.2**  And the great glory of that exalted one, and the names of the great-souled god—all this I wish to know truly, O best of the wise.

**13.145.3**  Vāsudeva said: Come then, I shall tell you—having first made obeisance to the matted-haired god—what good I gained and what renown I won, O great king.

**13.145.4**  Purified, rising at dawn, with hands joined in reverence, I recite the Śatarudrīya, O lord of peoples; hear it now as I declare it.

**13.145.5**  Prajāpati of great austerity created it at the end of his penance; but it was Śaṃkara, my son, who created the creatures, the unmoving and the moving.

**13.145.6**  There is no being higher than Mahādeva, O lord of peoples; for here in all three worlds he is the source from which all beings arise.

**13.145.7**  No one dares to stand before that great-souled one, for no being equal to him is found in the three worlds.

**13.145.8**  In battle, by his very scent when he is enraged, his enemies lose their senses, are all but slain, tremble, and fall.

**13.145.9**  Hearing his terrible roar, like the thundercloud's thunder, in battle the very heart of the gods would burst asunder.

**13.145.10**  Those whom the wielder of the Pināka, enraged, looks upon with his terrible form—neither gods nor demons in this world, neither gandharvas nor serpents thrive in ease when he is wrathful, even if they have fled into a cave.

**13.145.11**  When the Prajāpati Dakṣa was performing his far-extended sacrifice, Bhava, enraged and fearless, pierced the sacrifice through; releasing an arrow from his bow, he roared aloud with a great cry.

**13.145.12**  The gods found no refuge—how then peace?—but only despair, when the sacrifice was suddenly scattered and Maheśvara was enraged.

**13.145.13**  By that twang of the bowstring against the wristguard all the worlds were thrown into turmoil and grew helpless, O Pārtha, and gods and demons alike sank in despair.

**13.145.14**  The waters were churned up, the earth quaked, the mountains ran loose, and the heavens split apart on every side.

**13.145.15**  Shrouded in blinding darkness, the worlds shone no longer, and the radiance of the luminaries, along with the sun, was lost, O Bhārata.

**13.145.16**  Then, sorely afraid, the sages, seeking the welfare of all beings and of themselves, performed rites of appeasement and benediction.

**13.145.17**  Then he, of terrible prowess, in his fury rushed upon the gods, and in his wrath struck out Bhaga's eyes with a single blow.

**13.145.18**  Endowed with a transcendent form, he charged upon Pūṣan, and as he was eating the sacrificial cake he knocked out his teeth.

**13.145.19**  Then those gods, trembling, bowed down to Śaṃkara; yet Rudra fitted again to his bow a blazing, keen-edged arrow.

**13.145.20**  Beholding Rudra's might, the gods together with the sages grew afraid; then those foremost of the wise sought to propitiate Śarva.

**13.145.21**  With folded hands the gods then murmured the Śatarudrīya, and, praised by the thirty, Maheśvara was appeased.

**13.145.22**  They assigned to Rudra a special share in the sacrifice, and in their fear, O king, the thirty took refuge in him.

**13.145.23**  Through that very excess of his wrath the sacrifice was made whole again, and whatever had been destroyed there was restored just as it had been.

**13.145.24**  The mighty asuras had three cities in the sky: one of iron, one of silver, and yet another of gold.

**13.145.25**  Maghavan could not breach them even with all his weapons; then all the immortals, sore beset, went to Rudra for refuge.

**13.145.26**  Then all the great-souled gods, assembled together, spoke: 'Rudra, in every rite the sacrificial victims shall be yours; slay the daityas together with their cities and save the worlds, O giver of honor!'

**13.145.27**  Thus addressed, he answered 'So be it,' and making Viṣṇu his choicest shaft, Agni its barb, and Yama son of Vivasvat its feathered tip, making all the Vedas his bow and the supreme Sāvitrī its string,

**13.145.28**  and making the gods his excellent chariot, and yoking them all together, with that three-jointed, three-barbed arrow he pierced those cities through.

**13.145.29**  By that arrow, sun-colored and blazing like the fire of doom, those asuras together with their cities were burned up there by Rudra, O Bhārata.

**13.145.30**  And when she saw him seated on her lap as a child with five locks of hair, Umā, wishing to know, then asked, 'Who is this?'

**13.145.31**  And when Śakra, resentful, made ready to strike with his thunderbolt, he froze fast that arm, club-like, together with its thunderbolt.

**13.145.32**  The gods did not recognize him, that lord of the worlds; all of them, together with the Prajāpatis, were bewildered before that Lord.

**13.145.33**  Then the lord Brahmā, meditating, knew that one of boundless energy: realizing 'This is the supreme one,' he bowed down to that consort of Umā.

**13.145.34**  Then those gods propitiated Umā and Rudra, and the arm of the slayer of Bala became then as it was before.

**13.145.35**  And that same one, becoming a brāhmaṇa, the mighty Durvāsas by name, dwelt for a long while in my house at Dvāravatī.

**13.145.36**  He inflicted many vexations within my dwelling, and out of magnanimity I bore patiently with him things hard to bear and beyond his deserving.

**13.145.37**  He is Indra lord of gods, and Vāyu; he is the two Aśvins, and he is the lightnings; he is the moon, he is Īśāna, he is the sun and Varuṇa.

**13.145.38**  He is Time, he is the Ender, Death; he is darkness, the nights and the days, the months and the half-months, the seasons, the twilights, and the year.

**13.145.39**  He is Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, he is Viśvakarman the all-knowing; the constellations, the quarters and intermediate quarters, and likewise the planets—he, whose form is the universe, whose self is immeasurable, the lord of boundless splendor.

**13.145.40**  He is onefold, and twofold, and manifold; he becomes a hundredfold, and a thousandfold, and likewise a hundred-thousandfold.

**13.145.41**  Such is that Mahādeva, and the lord is yet more than this; for his virtues cannot be told even in a hundred years.

**13.146.1**  Vāsudeva said: O mighty-armed Yudhiṣṭhira, learn from me the great glory of the great-souled one, of Rudra of many forms and many names.

**13.146.2**  They call him Agni, Mahādeva, and Sthāṇu, Maheśvara, the One-Eyed, the Three-Eyed, and the All-Formed, and Śiva.
