**13.146.3**  The brāhmaṇas learned in the Veda know that god to have two bodies—the one terrible, the other benign; and these two bodies are again of many kinds.

**13.146.4**  His fierce and terrible body is Agni, the lightning, the sun; while his benign and gentle one is Dharma, the waters, and the moon.

**13.146.5**  Half of his self is said to be Agni, O bull of the Bhāratas; and that benign body of his practices chastity.

**13.146.6**  His most terrible form, by which he dissolves the world—because of his lordship and his greatness he is therefore remembered as Maheśvara, the Great Lord.

**13.146.7**  Because he burns wholly, because he is fierce, because he is dreadful, because he is full of fiery power, and because he devours flesh, blood, and marrow—therefore he is called Rudra.

**13.146.8**  Because he is the greatest of the gods, because his domain is great, and because he guards the whole great universe, he is therefore remembered as Mahādeva, the Great God.

**13.146.9**  Because he ever prospers all aims through all rites, desiring the welfare of men, he is therefore remembered as Śiva, the Auspicious.

**13.146.10**  Because, standing erect, he burns, because he is the origin and continuance of life, and because his emblem stands ever firm, he is therefore remembered as Sthāṇu, the Steadfast.

**13.146.11**  Because his form is manifold—the past, the future, and the present, the unmoving and the moving alike—he is therefore remembered as Bahurūpa, the One of Many Forms.

**13.146.12**  Because his form is smoke-gray, he is therefore called Dhūrjaṭi, the Smoke-Matted; and because the All-Gods are within him, he is therefore remembered as Viśvarūpa, the All-Formed.

**13.146.13**  Thousand-eyed, or ten-thousand-eyed, or made of eyes on every side—he is the source of sight, the radiance of vision, and there is no end to his eyes.

**13.146.14**  Because in every way he protects the creatures, and again because he sports with them, and because he is their overlord, he is therefore remembered as Paśupati, Lord of Creatures.

**13.146.15**  Because his emblem stands firm through perpetual chastity, and because the worlds magnify him, he is therefore remembered as Maheśvara, the Great Lord.

**13.146.16**  Whoever worships the image of that great-souled one, or his emblem—he who ever worships the emblem attains to great prosperity.

**13.146.17**  And the sages too, and the gods, and the gandharvas and apsarases, worship that very emblem which stands erect on high.

**13.146.18**  When it is being worshipped, Maheśvara rejoices, and with gladdened heart he grants happiness to his devotees, he who cherishes those who love him.

**13.146.19**  This same god dwells perpetually in the cremation grounds, and there men worship him, the haunter of heroes' places.

**13.146.20**  Lodged in the body's disorders, he is the death of living creatures here; and he is the breath within bodies, the prāṇa and apāna of the embodied.

**13.146.21**  His many forms, terrible and blazing, which are worshipped in the world—the wise brāhmaṇas know them.

**13.146.22**  His many names in the Vedas are derived according to their meaning—from his greatness, his all-pervading power, and his deeds.

**13.146.23**  And in the Veda the brāhmaṇas know his supreme Śatarudrīya, and the worship of that great-souled one that follows immediately upon the dispersion.

**13.146.24**  He is the bestower upon all the worlds, and he is called the great universe; the brāhmaṇas and other sages declare him to be the eldest-born of beings.

**13.146.25**  For he is the first of the gods; Agni was born from his mouth; and though life-breaths are held fast by manifold seizures, he sets them free.

**13.146.26**  That holy-souled one, the giver of refuge, delivers those who come to him for refuge, granting them long life, health, lordship, wealth, and abundant desires.

**13.146.27**  These he gives to men, and these again he takes away; and his lordship is declared to abide in Śakra and the other gods.

**13.146.28**  He alone is ever supreme in the weal and woe of the three worlds; and because he is sovereign over all desires, he is again called Īśvara, the Lord.

**13.146.29**  He is Maheśvara, the great lord of the worlds, and the lord of the mighty ones; by his many and various forms this whole universe is pervaded; and the mouth of that god is the mare's-mouth fire within the ocean.

**13.147.1**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When Kṛṣṇa, the son of Devakī, had spoken this discourse, Yudhiṣṭhira once more questioned Bhīṣma, the son of Śaṃtanu.

**13.147.2**  O greatly wise one, foremost of all upholders of dharma, in reaching a certain conclusion, which of the two—direct perception or scriptural tradition—should be the authority?

**13.147.3**  Bhīṣma said: My judgment holds that there is no doubt at all in this matter. Listen, O wise one; I shall tell you, for you ask rightly.

**13.147.4**  Doubt is easy to reach, O king, but certainty here is hard to attain; for where doubt appears, the seen and the heard are without end.

**13.147.5**  The reasoners, who fancy themselves wise, hold direct perception to be the seen authority and conclude 'it does not exist,' thus turning truth itself into mere doubt; childish men who deem themselves learned conclude what is unfitting.

**13.147.6**  But if you ask which one might be the true authority, that can be reached, O Bhārata, only over a long time, by one who is disciplined and untiring and who has provided for the sustenance of many lives.

**13.147.7**  This authority can be grasped only by one wholly devoted to it and by no other; reaching the limit of all causes, he attains vast and supreme knowledge, the boundless light of all the world.

**13.147.8**  Arriving at the truth, O king, and so reaching the end of causes, one must shun all speech that is ungraspable and unfounded.

**13.147.9**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: Direct perception is established from the world, and the worlds rest upon scriptural tradition; the conduct of the cultivated is of many kinds—explain this to me, O grandsire.

**13.147.10**  Bhīṣma said: When dharma is being carried off by the powerful and the wicked, even the order established by great efforts is broken down by time.

**13.147.11**  Unrighteous deeds, wearing the guise of dharma, are like wells hidden over with grass; by these, right conduct is broken—hear this, O Yudhiṣṭhira.

**13.147.12**  Those who, by their misconduct, break down right conduct—who are bent on abandoning the sacred lore, who hate dharma, and who are dull-witted—about such men doubt has been declared to arise.

**13.147.13**  But those whose minds rest upon scripture, who are never sated of the company of the good, and who are content saying 'This is supreme'—wait upon such men and question them.

**13.147.14**  Those who, casting behind them desire and gain—which follow upon greed and delusion—are awakened to dharma alone: wait upon such men and question them.

**13.147.15**  Their conduct is never broken by the rites of sacrifice and Vedic study; and these three again—right practice, scriptural authority, and dharma—stand firm.

**13.147.16**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: Once again my mind is bewildered here, sunk in doubt, like one searching across a shoreless flood who can see no farther bank.

**13.147.17**  The Vedas, direct perception, and established custom—these three are authoritative. If a difference is found among them, yet dharma is one, how can it be threefold?

**13.147.18**  Bhīṣma said: O king, when dharma is being carried off by the powerful and evil-minded, if you think thus, then the inquiry into dharma proceeds along three paths.

**13.147.19**  Know it to be but one; its display is threefold. And my judgment too holds the same about the distinctness of these three.

**13.147.20**  The path of the three has been declared; act accordingly. No quibbling inquiry should be made by over-reasoning about dharma.

**13.147.21**  Always, O best of the Bhāratas, let there be no doubt in you here. Trusting like a blind, dull man, do what I tell you.

**13.147.22**  Non-violence, truth, freedom from anger, and giving—cultivate this fourfold practice, O Ajātaśatru; this is the eternal dharma.

**13.147.23**  And the conduct toward Brāhmaṇas that befits your fathers and forefathers—follow that, O mighty-armed one; for these are the guides to heaven.

**13.147.24**  The foolish man who would make the authoritative unauthoritative does not deserve to be deemed authoritative himself, for he is a breeder of dispute.

**13.147.25**  Serve the Brāhmaṇas alone, honoring and esteeming them greatly; know that in them rest all these worlds entire.

**13.148.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: Those who revile dharma and those who wait upon it—let your reverence tell me this: where do such men go?

**13.148.2**  Bhīṣma said: Men whose minds are wholly overspread by passion and darkness, who hate dharma, fall into hell.

**13.148.3**  But those, O great king, who ever attend upon dharma, devoted to truth and uprightness—those good men are the enjoyers of heaven.

**13.148.4**  Their delight is in dharma itself, arising from service to the teacher; those who wait upon dharma attain the world of the gods.

**13.148.5**  Whether men or gods, the righteous who have mortified the body and are freed from greed and hatred flourish in happiness.

**13.148.6**  The wise call Dharma the firstborn son of Brahmā; the righteous attend upon it as the storehouse cherishes ripened fruit.

**13.148.7**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: What is the character of the wicked, and what do the good do? Let your honor tell me this: of what sort are the good and the bad?

**13.148.8**  Bhīṣma said: The wicked are ill-behaved, unapproachable, and foul-mouthed; the good are endowed with virtue—such is the mark of cultivated conduct.

**13.148.9**  On the highway, amid cattle, and within the cow-pen the righteous do not, O lord of kings, indulge in the discharge of urine and excrement.

**13.148.10**  Having given food to the five, the good eat what remains; while eating they do not chatter, nor do they sleep with hands still wet.

**13.148.11**  The fire, the ox, a deity, the cow-pen, a crossroads, a righteous Brāhmaṇa, and a sacred shrine—these they circumambulate to the right.

**13.148.12**  To the aged, to the burdened, to women, to the child and the sick, to Brāhmaṇas, to cattle, and to kings they yield the path.

**13.148.13**  Of all guests, of servants, and of one's own kin, and of those who seek refuge, one should be a protector and a bestower of welcome.

**13.148.14**  Evening and morning is the meal of men ordained by the gods; no eating between is prescribed—that indeed is the rule of fasting.

**13.148.15**  As fire at the time of oblation awaits only its due time, so a wife awaits only her season; and he who goes to no other woman—that is remembered as celibacy.

**13.148.16**  The nectar of immortality, Brāhmaṇas, and cows—these three are as one; therefore one should always honor cow and Brāhmaṇa according to the rule.

**13.148.17**  One does not sin by eating flesh consecrated with the sacrificial formula; but flesh from the back, flesh taken in vain, and the flesh of one's son are all alike.

**13.148.18**  Whether in one's own land or in a foreign land, one should not let a guest go fasting; having performed an act fruitfully, one should dedicate it to the elders.

**13.148.19**  A seat should be offered to elders, with salutation and honor; by worshiping elders men increase in life, in fame, and in fortune.

**13.148.20**  One should never speak harshly to elders, nor send them on errands, nor remain seated while they stand—thus his life is not diminished.

**13.148.21**  The wise man does not gaze upon a naked woman, nor even upon naked men; he should keep both union and eating ever private.

**13.148.22**  Among sacred fords, the elders are the holy ford; among the pure, the heart is the purifier; among insights, knowledge is supreme; contentment is the highest happiness.

**13.148.23**  Evening and morning one should listen to the abundant words of elders; for a man attains learning by constant service to elders.

**13.148.24**  In recitation and in eating one should raise the right hand; one should ever restrain speech and mind and the wandering of the senses.

**13.148.25**  Consecrated milk-rice, gruel, sesame-and-rice, and oblation, the Aṣṭaka rites belonging to the ancestral deities, and the honoring of elders—these are duties.

**13.148.26**  There is auspicious blessing at the trimming of the beard, a greeting for those who sneeze, and for all the sick a wish of long life in return.

**13.148.27**  One should never say 'thou' to a greater man, even when in distress; among the learned, the familiar 'thou' is reckoned no better than a blow. Such address one may use toward inferiors, equals, and pupils.

**13.148.28**  The heart of evildoers ever betrays their sin; knowingly they perish, though they conceal it before the multitude.

**13.148.29**  The wicked conceal a deed done knowingly, thinking 'men do not see me, the gods do not see me'; but the sinner, struck down by his sin, is reborn only as sin.

**13.148.30**  As a usurer awaits his increase until the breaking of the body, so sin concealed beneath dharma only makes dharma itself grow.

**13.148.31**  As salt drenched in water dissolves away, so sin, struck down by expiation, at once perishes.

**13.148.32**  Therefore one should not hide a sin, for when hidden it increases; having committed it, one should confess it among the good, and they indeed allay it.

**13.148.33**  The wealth heaped up in hope that is not enjoyed in its time—others come to possess it at the embodied one's parting.

**13.148.34**  The wise call dharma the inner disposition of all beings; therefore all beings rest in dharma alone.

**13.148.35**  Alone one should practice dharma, and not become a parader of dharma; for they are traffickers in dharma who make a living off it.

**13.148.36**  One should worship the gods without ostentation and serve elders without deceit; one should lay up a treasure for the world beyond—called charity—for the sake of the onward journey.

**13.149.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: A man without his portion of fate gains no wealth, however strong he be; but one blessed with his destined share, though feeble and a child, comes by riches.

**13.149.2**  In a time of non-gain one gains nothing even when effort is made; in a time of gain, without effort, one obtains abundant wealth. And by the hundreds men are seen whose efforts bear no fruit.

**13.149.3**  If effort were decisive, a mortal would gain every fruit, and nothing unattainable would remain unattained for men, O best of the Bhāratas.

**13.149.4**  For one man is seen fruitless though he has made effort, seeking wealth by a hundred prudent ways; while another, taking no proper course at all, is happy.

**13.149.5**  Some men are seen poor though they have done forbidden deeds again and again; while others, set in unrighteousness, are seen possessed of wealth.

**13.149.6**  One who has studied statecraft is not seen acting by its precepts, while the ignorant has been raised to a minister's post—by what cause? And the learned is destitute, while the unlearned is rich.

**13.149.7**  If a man could win happiness by leaning on knowledge, then the learned would not, for a livelihood, attach himself to one devoid of learning.

**13.149.8**  As a man conquers thirst when he has found water, so a man whose aim is fulfilled by knowledge should cast off ignorance.

**13.149.9**  He whose time has not come does not die, though pierced by a hundred arrows; but he whose time has come, though touched by only the tip of a blade of grass, does not live.

**13.149.10**  Bhīṣma said: If, striving through his undertakings, a man does not win wealth, let him mount to fierce austerity; for what is unsown does not sprout.

**13.149.11**  By giving one becomes an enjoyer, by service to elders wise, and by non-violence long-lived—so the sages have declared.

**13.149.12**  Therefore one should give and not beg, and should honor the righteous, being fair-spoken, doing what is dear, pure, and harming no living creature.

**13.149.13**  Since the measure and the inborn nature in pleasure and pain are common even to gnats, worms, and ants, be steadfast, Yudhiṣṭhira.

**13.150.1**  Bhīṣma said: What is caused to be done and what is done may be good or bad in the doing; therefore, having done good, let one feel assured, but having done evil, let one not feel secure.

**13.150.2**  It is Time alone here that, granting through time both punishment and grace, enters the minds of beings and sets them moving toward dharma and gain.

**13.150.3**  But when a man's mind becomes righteous and revealing of true gain, then let the righteous-souled one feel assured; one of unsteady mind should not feel secure.

**13.150.4**  This much alone is the mark of wisdom in beings: even when bound by time, one who knows both should yet carry out the remaining aim.

**13.150.5**  For just as men whose lordship has arrived honor other men, so here the righteous honor their own self by their own self.

**13.150.6**  For Time can in no way render dharma into unrighteousness; therefore one should know the self of a practicer of dharma to be wholly pure.

**13.150.7**  Unrighteousness is unable so much as to touch dharma—ever guarded by Time—as one cannot touch a blazing fire.

**13.150.8**  Both these are to be wrought by Time; for dharma is the bringer of victory, and it becomes the light-maker of all the three worlds.

**13.150.9**  Therein some wise man may lead another, taking him by the very hand; himself borne along by dharma, in dharma full of many fears and deceits.

**13.151.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: What is best for a man here? By doing what does he flourish in happiness? By what does he become free of evil, and what is the destroyer of sin?

**13.151.2**  Bhīṣma said: This lineage of the gods, joined with the lineage of seers, recited at the two twilights, my son, is the supreme remover of sin.

**13.151.3**  The god who is teacher of gods and Asuras, revered by all beings, unthinkable and indefinable, the life of all, born of no womb—

**13.151.4**  the Grandsire, Lord of the world; Sāvitrī, the true consort of Brahmā; the womb of the Vedas, and the Maker; and Viṣṇu, Lord Nārāyaṇa—

**13.151.5**  Umā's lord, the odd-eyed one; Skanda the army-commander likewise; Viśākha, the fire that consumes oblations, Vāyu, and the moon and sun, makers of light—

**13.151.6**  Śakra the god, lord of Śacī; Yama together with Dhūmorṇā; Varuṇa, and with Gaurī, and with Ṛddhi the lord of wealth—

**13.151.7**  the gentle cow, the goddess Surabhī; and Viśravas the great seer; the six seasons, the ocean, the Gaṅgā, the rivers, and then the host of the Maruts—

**13.151.8**  the Vālakhilyas, perfected in austerity; Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana likewise; Nārada, and Parvata too; Viśvāvasu, Hāhā and Hūhū—

**13.151.9**  Tumbaru and Citrasena, and the renowned messenger of the gods; the blessed daughters of the gods, and the divine hosts of Apsarases—

**13.151.10**  Urvaśī, Menakā, Rambhā, Miśrakeśī, Alambuṣā, and Viśvācī, and Ghṛtācī, Pañcacūḍā, Tilottamā—

**13.151.11**  the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, with the Aśvins, and the ancestors too; Dharma, Truth, Austerity, Consecration, Resolve, the Grandsire—

**13.151.12**  the nights and the days; Mārīca and Kaśyapa likewise; Śukra, Bṛhaspati, Mars, Mercury, Rāhu, and Saturn—

**13.151.13**  The lunar mansions, the seasons, the months, the twilights, and the years; the sons of Vinatā, the oceans, and the serpents born of Kadrū—

**13.151.14**  the Śatadru and the Vipāśā, the Candrabhāgā and the Sarasvatī, the Sindhu and the Devikā, and the holy ford of Puṣkara—

**13.151.15**  the Gaṅgā, the great river, the Kapilā and the Narmadā, the Kampunā and the Viśalyā, and the water-bearing Karatoyā—

**13.151.16**  the Sarayū and the Gaṇḍakī, and the Lohitya, that mighty stream, the Tāmrāruṇā, the Vetravatī, the Parṇāśā, and the Gautamī—

**13.151.17**  the Godāvarī and the Veṇṇā, the Kṛṣṇaveṇā and the mountain-born streams, the Dṛṣadvatī and the Kāverī, the Vaṃkṣu and the Mandākinī—

**13.151.18**  Prayāga and Prabhāsa, and the holy Naimiṣa forest, and that abode of Viśveśvara where lies that spotless lake—

**13.151.19**  and Kurukṣetra, renowned and dense with holy fords, the supreme Sindhu, the ground of austerity and almsgiving, and the Jambūmārga as well—

**13.151.20**  the Hiraṇvatī and the Vitastā, and likewise the river Ikṣumatī, the Vedasmṛti, the Vaidasinī, and the river Malavāsā too—

**13.151.21**  the holy tracts of earth, and the Gate of the Gaṅgā as well, the streams of the sages, the sacred rivers, and the Citrapathā—

**13.151.22**  the Kauśikī, the Yamunā, the Sītā, and the river Carmaṇvatī, the river Bhīmarathī and the Bāhudā, that great stream, the Mahendravāṇī, the Tridivā, the Nīlikā, and the Sarasvatī—

**13.151.23**  the Nandā and the Aparanandā, and that ford, the Great Lake, then Gayā and the ford of the Phalgu, and the Dharmāraṇya frequented by the gods—

**13.151.24**  and the holy river of the gods, and the lake fashioned by Brahmā, sacred, famed throughout the three worlds, auspicious, the remover of every sin—

**13.151.25**  the Himavān, that mountain endowed with divine herbs, the Vindhya whose flanks are bright with minerals, rich in fords and abounding in healing plants—

**13.151.26**  the Meru, the Mahendra, the Malaya, and the Śveta heaped with silver, the Śṛṅgavān, the Mandara, the Nīla, the Niṣadha, and the Dardura—

**13.151.27**  the Citrakūṭa and the collyrium-hued mountain, the Gandhamādana, the holy Somagiri, and all the other upholders of the earth, the quarters and the intermediate quarters, the soil, and all that grows from it—

**13.151.28**  the All-Gods, the firmament, the lunar mansions, and the planets—may these deities, named and unnamed by me, ever protect you all.

**13.151.29**  The man who recites these names is freed from all his sins; praising and rejoicing in them, the one who delights in the praise of the deities is delivered from every fear and from all the sins of confusion.

**13.151.30**  After the deities, I shall now proclaim the renowned brāhmaṇas, perfected through austerity and abounding in penance, who release one from every sin.

**13.151.31**  Yavakrīta and Raibhya, Kakṣīvān the son of Uśij, Bhṛgu and Aṅgiras, then Kaṇva, the mighty Medhātithi, and Barhin endowed with every virtue—these have taken their stand in the eastern quarter.

**13.151.32**  In the auspicious southern quarter dwell the greatly blessed Ulmuca and Pramuca, the high-souled Mumuca, and the valiant Svastyātreya.

**13.151.33**  And the majestic Agastya, son of Mitra and Varuṇa, and Dṛḍhāyu and Ūrdhvabāhu, those two most eminent and renowned sages.

**13.151.34**  Learn now of those who flourish, resting in the western quarter: Uṣadgu together with his brothers, and the valiant Parivyādha—

**13.151.35**  the sage Dīrghatamas, Gautama, and Kaśyapa, the great seers Ekata, Dvita, and Trita, the righteous son of Atri, and the mighty Sārasvata.

**13.151.36**  Learn now of those who flourish, resting in the northern quarter: Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Śakti, and the valiant son of Parāśara—

**13.151.37**  Viśvāmitra, Bharadvāja, and Jamadagni likewise, Rāma the grandson of Ṛcīka, and the sage son of Uddālaka—

**13.151.38**  Śvetaketu and Kohala, Vipula and Devala, Devaśarman and Dhaumya, and Hastikāśyapa too—

**13.151.39**  Lomaśa and Nāciketa, and Lomaharṣaṇa as well, the sage Ugraśravas, and Cyavana of the line of Bhṛgu.

**13.151.40**  This, O king, is the foremost gathering, made up of sages and gods, which I have proclaimed to you—the deliverer from every sin.

**13.151.41**  Nṛga, Yayāti, Nahuṣa, Yadu, and the valiant Pūru, Dhundhumāra and Dilīpa, and the majestic Sagara—

**13.151.42**  Kṛśāśva and Yauvanāśva, Citrāśva and the truthful one, Duḥṣanta and Bharata, that emperor of mighty fame—

**13.151.43**  Yavana and Janaka, and the king Dṛḍharatha, Raghu, that best of men, and the king Daśaratha—

**13.151.44**  Rāma the hero, slayer of the rākṣasas, Śaśabindu, Bhagīratha, Hariścandra and Marutta, and Jahnu attended by the daughter of Jāhnavī—

**13.151.45**  Mahodaya and Alarka, and the king Aila, Karaṃdhama, best of men, and the king Kadhmora—

**13.151.46**  Dakṣa, Ambarīṣa, Kukura, and Ravata of great renown, the royal sage Mucukunda, and Mitrabhānu the kindly—

**13.151.47**  and king Trasadasyu, Śveta the most eminent royal sage, the renowned Mahābhiṣa, king Nimi, and Aṣṭaka—

**13.151.48**  Āyu, the royal sage Kṣupa, and the king Kakṣeyu, Śibi the son of Uśīnara, and king Gaya—

**13.151.49**  Pratardana, Divodāsa, Saudāsa lord of Kosala, Aila, the royal sage Nala, and Manu the Lord of Creatures—

**13.151.50**  Havidhra and Pṛṣadhra, Pratīpa and Śaṃtanu, the royal sage Kakṣasena, and others who have not been named one by one—

**13.151.51**  may there be for me no obstacle, no sin, and no adversaries; may victory be ever steadfast for me, and in the world beyond, the supreme goal.

**13.152.1**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When Bhīṣma had fallen silent, like a figure painted upon a canvas, Vyāsa the son of Satyavatī, having pondered for a moment, then spoke these words to the recumbent king, the son of Gaṅgā:

**13.152.2**  "O king, Yudhiṣṭhira, the lord of the Kurus, has regained his composure, together with all his brothers and the princes who follow him.

**13.152.3**  He waits upon you, O tiger among men, together with the wise Kṛṣṇa; it is fitting that you grant him leave to return to the city."

**13.152.4**  Thus addressed by the venerable Vyāsa, the lord of the earth, the son of the river, gave Yudhiṣṭhira leave together with his counselors.

**13.152.5**  And the king, the son of Śaṃtanu, then spoke to him sweetly: "Enter the city, O king; let the fever of your mind depart.

**13.152.6**  Offer sacrifice with rites of many kinds, abounding in food and rich in well-earned gifts to the priests, O lord of kings, like Yayāti, with faith and self-restraint going before you.

**13.152.7**  Devoted to the dharma of the warrior, O Pārtha, gratify the ancestors and the gods; you shall be joined with good fortune—let the fever of your mind depart.

**13.152.8**  Bring delight to all your subjects, console the people of your realm, and honor your well-wishers with fitting rewards, each according to his due.

**13.152.9**  May your friends and well-wishers live in your shelter, my son, even as the twice-born find shelter beneath a fruit-laden tree standing in a sacred place.

**13.152.10**  And you must come to me at the appointed time, O prince, when the maker of day has turned back and the northern course of the sun has begun."

**13.152.11**  Saying "So be it," the son of Kuntī saluted the grandsire and set out with his retinue for the city named after the elephant.

**13.152.12**  Placing Dhṛtarāṣṭra at the head, with Gāndhārī faithful to her lord, together with all those sages, with his brothers and with Keśava—

**13.152.13**  and with the townsfolk and country-folk and the aged counselors, the prince, O best of the Kurus, entered the city named after the elephant.

**13.153.1**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then the king, the son of Kuntī, having honored the people of the town and the countryside as was right, dismissed them to their homes.

**13.153.2**  And the king, the son of Pāṇḍu, consoled the women whose heroes were slain, whose lords were slain, with abundant gifts of wealth.

**13.153.3**  Consecrated and having gained the kingdom, the deeply wise Yudhiṣṭhira, that best of men, then set all his subjects firmly in their places.

**13.153.4**  Receiving the foremost blessings from the brāhmaṇas, the chief warriors, and the townsmen on every side, that best of the upholders of dharma—

**13.153.5**  the illustrious bull among men, having passed fifty nights in that finest of cities, called to mind the appointed time of the foremost of the Kurus.

**13.153.6**  Seeing that the sun had turned and the northern course had begun, he set forth from the City of the Elephant, surrounded by his officiating priests.

**13.153.7**  Clarified butter, garlands and perfumes, garments of fine linen, choice sandalwood and aloe, and black aloe-wood besides—

**13.153.8**  the son of Kuntī sent on ahead for the honoring of Bhīṣma, together with precious garlands and jewels of many kinds.

**13.153.9**  Placing at his head Dhṛtarāṣṭra and the renowned Gāndhārī, and his mother Pṛthā, the wise bull among men, with his brothers—

**13.153.10**  followed by Janārdana and the wise Vidura, by Yuyutsu and by Yuyudhāna, O lord, the Kaurava—

**13.153.11**  surrounded by a great train of kingly splendor and praised, O great king, set out, leading after him the fires for Bhīṣma's rite.

**13.153.12**  He went forth from that city even as the lord of the gods would go, and then on Kurukṣetra he came upon the king, the son of Śaṃtanu—

**13.153.13**  attended by the wise Vyāsa the son of Parāśara, and by Nārada, O royal sage, and by Devala and Asita—

**13.153.14**  and by the other kings who had survived the slaughter, gathered from many lands, and that great soul guarded all around by his protectors.

**13.153.15**  Then the king beheld him lying upon his bed of a hero, and the King of Dharma alighted from his chariot together with his brothers.

**13.153.16**  The son of Kuntī then saluted the grandsire, that subduer of foes, and the brāhmaṇas led by Dvaipāyana, and he was greeted in return by them.

**13.153.17**  With the officiating priests, who were like Brahmā himself, and with his brothers and with the imperishable Kṛṣṇa, he approached the one who lay upon the bed of arrows, encircled by sages—

**13.153.18**  and the King of Dharma, Yudhiṣṭhira, together with his brothers, O Kaurava, spoke to that best of the Bhāratas, the recumbent son of the river:

**13.153.19**  "I am Yudhiṣṭhira, O king; homage to you, son of Jāhnavī. If you can hear me, O mighty-armed one, tell me—what may I do for you?

**13.153.20**  I have come at the appointed time, O king, bringing your fires, O lord; the teachers and the brāhmaṇas, the officiating priests, and my brothers are here—

**13.153.21**  and your son, the mighty-splendored Dhṛtarāṣṭra, lord of men, stands present with his counselors, and the valiant Vāsudeva as well.

**13.153.22**  And the kings who survived the slaughter, and all the people of the Kuru lands—behold them, O tiger of the Kurus; open wide your eyes."

**13.153.23**  "Whatever was to be done here, all of it has been accomplished by me; just as you bade me at the time, all of it indeed has been done."

**13.153.24**  Thus addressed by the wise son of Kuntī, the son of Gaṅgā beheld all the Bhāratas standing gathered around him.

**13.153.25**  Then Bhīṣma, the wrinkles of his brow trembling, raising his mighty arm, the eloquent one with a voice like the roar of flooding storm-clouds, spoke these timely words:

**13.153.26**  "By good fortune you have come, O son of Kuntī, with your counselors, Yudhiṣṭhira; for the blessed maker of day, the thousand-rayed one, has indeed turned upon his course.

**13.153.27**  Fifty-eight nights have now passed for me as I have lain upon the keen-pointed arrows, and they have seemed to me as long as a hundred years.

**13.153.28**  This holy month of Māgha has now arrived, O Yudhiṣṭhira; a third part of it remains, and this fortnight ought now to be the bright one."

**13.153.29**  Having spoken thus to Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, the son of Gaṅgā then addressed Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and at that fitting hour he spoke these words.

**13.153.30**  O king, you are versed in dharma, and you have well resolved every doubt of meaning; for many deeply learned brāhmaṇas have you served and attended upon.

**13.153.31**  All the Vedas and the śāstras and the laws of dharma, O lord of men, and the four Vedas with their ancillary limbs, you comprehend entirely.

**13.153.32**  You must not grieve, O scion of the Kurus, for what was destined had to come to pass; the secret of the gods you have heard even from Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana himself.

**13.153.33**  As the sons of Pāṇḍu are, O king, even so are they yours in dharma; cherish them, abiding in dharma, for they delight in serving their elders.

**13.153.34**  For the king of dharma, pure of soul, will abide by your command; I know him to be devoted above all to gentleness and tender toward his elders.

**13.153.35**  Your own sons were evil of soul, given over to wrath and greed, overcome by envy and wicked in conduct; for them you ought not to grieve.

**13.153.36**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken these words to the wise Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the Kaurava then addressed the mighty-armed Vāsudeva.

**13.153.37**  O blessed Lord, god of gods and ruler of gods, honored by gods and demons alike, O Trivikrama, homage be to you, wielder of conch, discus, and mace.

**13.153.38**  Grant me leave to depart, O Kṛṣṇa, dweller in Vaikuṇṭha, supreme among men; the sons of Pāṇḍu are to be guarded by you, for you are their final refuge.

**13.153.39**  Of old I told the foolish, dull-witted Duryodhana: where Kṛṣṇa is, there is dharma; and where dharma is, there is victory.

**13.153.40**  Again and again I said: through Vāsudeva as your means of approach, my son, make peace with the Pāṇḍavas; this is the supreme hour for your reconciliation.

**13.153.41**  But that deluded one, exceedingly dull of mind, did not act upon my word; having brought slaughter upon the earth, he thereafter went to his destruction.

**13.153.42**  And I know you, O hero, to be the ancient god, the highest of seers, who together with Nara dwelt long ages at Badarī.

**13.153.43**  So Nārada told me, and Vyāsa of great austerities as well: these two, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, have been born among men.

**13.153.44**  Vāsudeva said: I grant you leave, Bhīṣma; attain the Vasus, O king. No taint of sin in you have I ever beheld, O greatly resplendent one.

**13.153.45**  You are devoted to your father, O royal seer, like a second Mārkaṇḍeya; and for that reason death stands subject to your will, bowed low like a servant.

**13.153.46**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed, the son of Gaṅgā spoke this to the Pāṇḍavas and to all those led by Dhṛtarāṣṭra, together with their friends.

**13.153.47**  I wish now to release my life-breaths; grant me leave for this. You must strive after truth, for truth is the supreme strength.

**13.153.48**  You must ever be devoted to gentleness, self-controlled, reverent toward the brāhmaṇas, righteous in conduct, and guided by austerity and wise policy, O Bhārata.

**13.153.49**  Having spoken thus and embraced all his loved ones, the wise one once more addressed to Yudhiṣṭhira these words.

**13.153.50**  The brāhmaṇas, and the wise especially, the teachers and the officiating priests, are ever to be honored by you, O lord of men.

**13.154.1**  Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus to all the Kurus, Bhīṣma the son of Śaṃtanu, that scion of the Kurus, then fell silent for a moment, O subduer of foes.

**13.154.2**  He held his self steady in the fixations of yoga, each in due order; and the life-breaths of that great soul, drawn together and held in check, rose upward.

**13.154.3**  And this wonder occurred in the midst of those great souls: whatever part of his limbs the son of Śaṃtanu then released, that very part, as he was joined in yoga, became free of its arrows.

**13.154.4**  In an instant, before their watching eyes, he became wholly free of arrows; and seeing this, all were amazed, led by Vāsudeva, together with all those sages headed by Vyāsa, O king.

**13.154.5**  His self, held fast by him in all its seats, then broke through the crown of his head and sprang up into heaven.

**13.154.6**  Like a great meteor, O lord of men, it issued forth from the region of Bhīṣma's head, entered the sky, and in a moment vanished from sight.

**13.154.7**  Thus, O tiger among kings, the king, the son of Śaṃtanu, upholder of the line of the Bhāratas, was then united with his own worlds.

**13.154.8**  Then, taking timber and many varied fragrances, the great-souled Pāṇḍavas, and Vidura, and Yuyutsu the Kaurava, built the funeral pyre; the others stood by as onlookers.

**13.154.9**  Yudhiṣṭhira and the deeply wise Vidura, both of them, covered the Kaurava son of Gaṅgā with fine linen and garlands.

**13.154.10**  Then Yuyutsu held over him a splendid royal parasol; Bhīmasena and Arjuna, the two of them, plied the bright yak-tail fans; and the two sons of Mādrī took up the place at the headdress.

**13.154.11**  The women of the lord of the Kauravas, taking up palm-leaf fans, fanned Bhīṣma, born of the Kuru line, on every side.

**13.154.12**  Then they performed for that great soul the funeral rites according to ordinance; the officiating priests poured oblations into the fire, and the singers of the Sāman chanted the Sāman hymns.

**13.154.13**  Then with billets of sandalwood, and with kāleyaka aloeswood, and with black aloe and other fragrances, high and low alike,

**13.154.14**  having covered over the son of Gaṅgā and kindled the fire, the kings led by Dhṛtarāṣṭra made the rightward circumambulation around him.

**13.154.15**  And having performed the rites for the best of the Kurus, the son of Gaṅgā, those foremost of the Kurus, upholders of the Kuru line, went to the bank of the Bhāgīrathī, frequented by sages.

**13.154.16**  Followed by Vyāsa, by Nārada and Asita, by Kṛṣṇa, by the women of the Bhāratas, and by such townsfolk as had gathered there,

**13.154.17**  those best of kṣatriyas, and all that assembled folk, then offered the water-libation for the great-souled son of Gaṅgā, according to ordinance.

**13.154.18**  Then the goddess Bhāgīrathī, when the water-rite for her son had been performed, rose up out of those waters, weeping, lost in grief.

**13.154.19**  Lamenting there, she addressed the Kauravas: Hear, O sinless ones, what truly came to pass, as I now tell it.

**13.154.20**  Endowed with royal conduct, with wisdom and noble birth, an honorer of the Kuru elders, devoted to his father, firm in his vows—

**13.154.21**  he whom of old Rāma, son of Jamadagni, could not vanquish even with his celestial weapons—that one of mighty valor has today been slain by Śikhaṇḍin.

**13.154.22**  Surely, O kings, this heart of mine is wrought of iron-hard stone, that even now it does not burst within me, beholding no more my beloved son.

**13.154.23**  He who, single-charioted, in battle defeated the whole assembled royal warrior-host at the bride-choosing in the city of Kāśi, and carried off those maidens—

**13.154.24**  he who in strength had not one equal anywhere on earth—hearing that he has been slain by Śikhaṇḍin, how is it that my mind does not break apart?

**13.154.25**  He, that great soul, by whom the son of Jamadagni was hard-pressed in battle on Kurukṣetra—he has been slain, and with no great effort, by Śikhaṇḍin.

**13.154.26**  As the great river thus lamented at length in such wise, the mighty Dāmodara then consoled her with gentle words.

**13.154.27**  Take comfort, gentle lady; do not grieve, O fair to behold. Your son has attained the supreme perfection—of this there is no doubt.

**13.154.28**  This one of great splendor was a Vasu, O lovely one, who through the blemish of a curse had come to dwell in the state of a man; for him you ought not to grieve.

**13.154.29**  This very one, fighting by the dharma of the kṣatriya on the field of battle, was slain by Dhanaṃjaya; it was not he who was struck down by Śikhaṇḍin.

**13.154.30**  For Bhīṣma, that tiger among the Kurus, with weapon raised in the great battle, not even Śatakratu himself could have slain in combat face to face.

**13.154.31**  By his own free will your son has gone to heaven, O fair of face; for not all the gods together could have slain him in battle.

**13.154.32**  Therefore, O best of rivers, do not grieve for the delight of the Kurus; to the Vasus has this son of yours gone, O goddess—be free of your fever of sorrow.

**13.154.33**  Thus addressed by Kṛṣṇa and by Vyāsa, that best of rivers, O great king, cast off her grief and descended back into her own waters.

**13.154.34**  Having honored that river, the kings led by Kṛṣṇa, all those lords of men, took their leave of her and then turned back homeward.
